Renderers Vulkan: chunkGPU.fine sets pc.b.x = 1 ; voxel.vert , water.vert , shadow.vert and shadowcut.vert scale positions (and UVs) by 1/16 for such chunks. The .spv files are rebuilt with make shaders . Soft ( -shaders off , the reference): a kShape cell is ray-traced against the quads of its variant with the same UVs and cut-out rule ( render/soft/shapes.go ). Limitation: shaped cells do not cast shadows in the soft renderer. Physics and interaction voxel.MoveAABB , Overlaps and Raycast become shape-aware automatically when the reader knows a registry with shapes ( ChunkMap.SetShapeRegistry , set by sim ; View and the editor reader implement voxel.ShapeSource ). Multiple boxes per cell, fences are 1.5 high, plants/torches/carpets/plates/buttons have no collision. Hit.Point is the exact entry point; the normal is the face of the sub-box. The controller ( app ) steps up one block ( Config.StepHeight , default 1.05), so stairs are ramps and never need a jump; the physics character steps by StepHeight too. Placement ( blockset.Place , used by the editor place tool and the game controller): stairs face the camera, slab/trapdoor half from the face and the hit point, doors are two blocks (refused without headroom), wall torches/buttons/ladders/vines from the clicked face (a torch cannot hang from a ceiling), snow layers stack. Nothing is stored beyond the ids: the undo step of a door is both halves. Interaction: blockset.Toggle / Editor.Interact / MCP editor_interact {pos} open or close doors (both halves), trapdoors and gates as one undoable journaled edit (plain SetBlock s). Water ( fluid/ , untouched): cross plants, torches, ladders, carpets, snow layers, plates, buttons and vines are Fragile (flow destroys them); slabs, stairs, fences, doors, panes block like walls. Where things are shape/ (models), blockset/shapes.json + shapes.go + place.go , scripts/genshapes , mesh/shapes.go , voxel/shapes.go , render/soft/shapes.go , assets/blocktex/mcshapes.go (images), assets/blockicon/shape.go (isometric icons), character/held.go (held shapes), engine/gallery_shapes.go . Visual check docs/img/blocks-shapes-gallery.png ( go run ./examples/voxel_sandbox -gallery-shapes -textures pixelperfection -look natural -freeze -nohud -radius 4 -frames 3 -w 1800 -h 1000 -cam 14,52,17,0,-40 , second half -cam 43,52,17,0,-40 ) and docs/img/worldgen-meadow-shapes.png (before: cubes; after: cross plants; -gen v2 -seed 1 -cam 34,66,-22,0,-30 , -shapes for the right half). Honest defects: see the end of this page. Limits and known defects Wall torches are straight boxes (no 22.5 degree tilt shear beyond a lean); trapdoor, fence and door textures are the block-space window of the planks image (no vanilla crop). Corner stairs: neighbours that are themselves corner variants are seen as straight ones by the culling bitmap (conservative: never a hole, sometimes a hidden face drawn). Ladders do not climb (no physics), vines have one stored face per state (no multi-face vines), no double slabs (use the cube), no waterlogging, no banners, beds, signs, candles, lanterns, chains, rails, crops. Animated textures (lantern, kelp, seagrass) show frame 0. The soft renderer has no shadows from shaped blocks and no AO on them.

h: Project registry: the blocks stay in the project
Radial symmetry, model stamps and micro events
x: Blocks (extended set) The engine ships a small neutral block set (the 47 classic blocks plus about twenty building blocks and a few shaped ones: cobblestone, stone bricks, planks, glass, metal and wool blocks, torch, slabs, stairs, fences, doors, ladder, glass pane). The full Minecraft catalog (338 full cubes and about 230 shaped items) is an optional content pack, minecraft , that a project enables explicitly; it pairs with the Pixel Perfection CE textures (see texture-packs.md ). The default textures are the engine's own neutral pack, generated in code: nothing from the Mojang game or a third-party texture pack is used unless a project asks for it. Behaviour is data Core code never looks at block names. Light, heat, fluids and wind read explicit voxel.Block properties, set by the block definition ( blockset/*.json and runtime.custom_blocks ): emit , emit_color (light), heat (haze), light_loss (per channel), translucency ( foliage : leaves, absorb 1 per channel and sway; tinted : stained glass keeps its colour), fluid ( water flows with the water rules, level liquid , a source by default; lava ), fragile . A custom block named dice is not ice, one named leaves does not sway, one with "fluid": "water" flows. Lava cooling results are fluid.Config.CoolSource/CoolFlow/CoolWater (default obsidian, cobblestone, stone). Project registry: the blocks stay in the project A project can keep its own copy of the block registry so that no engine release changes its blocks: burrow blocks export # writes blocks/blocks.json + blocks/shapes.json, sets runtime.block_registry burrow blocks export --pack minecraft # the same, with the full Minecraft catalog included burrow blocks packs # the optional packs this engine carries burrow new does this for every new project. With runtime.block_registry set, the project's files ARE the registry: the engine's own blocks and the packs are not used, file order is id order, and each entry has the format of blockset/blocks.json (properties, palette data, family). runtime.custom_blocks are still appended after it. The folder ships with burrow build . Without it, runtime.block_packs (for example ["minecraft"] ) chooses the packs on top of the neutral set. burrow migrate adds ["minecraft"] to projects made before 0.7, when that catalog was built in. Edit the copy freely (a block renamed or reordered there is your decision); burrow blocks export refuses to overwrite it without --force . Maps are matched to the registry by block name. A .voxworld lists the blocks it was written with, in the order of its own registry; opening it renumbers its chunks to the project's ids, so a map made with another engine version, other packs or another generator still opens. Only a block the registry does not have at all is an error, and the message names it. Opt in, ids The neutral set is data: blockset/blocks.json and blockset/shapes.json ; the Minecraft pack is blockset/packs/minecraft/{blocks,shapes}.json (all committed, described by package blockset ). A program enables packs with engine.VoxelWorldPlugin{BlockPacks: []string{"minecraft"}} (or blockset.SetPacks ); their blocks are appended after the neutral set, in order. Since runtime.blocks: "shapes" is the only supported value, every project gets it (new projects from burrow new are created with "blocks": "shapes" and "texture_pack": "pixelperfection" ; "classic" and "extended" are deprecated , still accepted and resolved to "shapes" ). A program passes engine.VoxelWorldPlugin{ExtendedBlocks: true} or calls blockset.Register(registry) last. Old projects without the field or with classic / extended now get the shaped registry: ids of the extended set are unchanged, but worlds, journals and hashes of classic projects change. Registration order = ids and is frozen: defaults (7: stone dirt grass sand water wood leaves) , generator v2 blocks (33), water levels water_1..7 (ids 1..47, "core"), then the extended blocks in the order of blocks.json (ids 48..385 in a v2 world with water). The set is registered by a late setup hook ( App.OnSimSetupLate ) so nothing registered by other plugins moves. blockset/testdata/ids.golden freezes every id; the test fails if one moves, new blocks may only be appended ( go test ./blockset -update after appending). Shapes (level shapes , stage B2) "runtime": {"blocks": "shapes"} is the extended set plus the non-cubic shapes: the default and the only supported level. Engine: engine.VoxelWorldPlugin{ShapedBlocks: true} or blockset.RegisterShapes(reg) . burrow new and the editor scratch session use shapes . Every stored state is its own registry block, appended after the extended set: about 1109 new ids for about 254 items (slabs, stairs, walls, fences, fence gates, doors, trapdoors, pressure plates, buttons, carpets, snow layers, glass panes and iron bars, torches, ladders, vines, cross plants (flowers, grasses, saplings, mushrooms, corals), tall plants, cactus, lily pad). The default state carries the bare item name ( oak_stairs ), the others the state in brackets ( oak_stairs[facing=east,half=top] ). Neighbour-derived state (stair corners, fence, pane and wall connections) is computed at meshing and collision time and never stored. Models live in package shape (boxes in sixteenths, quads); blockset/shapes.json is generated by go run ./scripts/genshapes . voxel.Block.Shape links a block to its model. voxel.MoveAABB , Overlaps and Raycast become shape-aware when the registry has shaped blocks ( ChunkMap.SetShapeRegistry ); voxel.Hit.Point is the exact hit point. The mesher gives chunks that contain shaped blocks mesh.Mesh.Fine meshes (positions and UVs in sixteenths; the shader push constant pc.b.x=1 scales by 1/16); other chunks are unchanged. The soft renderer ray-traces the shape quads. Under this level generator v2 flowers, mushrooms, tall grass and dead bush become cross plants, and cactus a real cactus (ids unchanged). Editor: placement orients shaped blocks from the face, point or camera ( blockset.Place ); Editor.Interact toggles doors, trapdoors and fence gates ( blockset.Toggle ). A right click (without sneaking) toggles a door (both halves), trapdoor or fence gate. Breaking a door removes both halves, and breaking a block removes the plants, doors, torches, buttons, ladders and vines that rested on it. Gallery: go run ./examples/voxel_sandbox -gallery-shapes -textures pixelperfection ... writes docs/img/blocks-shapes-gallery.png . Details: block-shapes.md . Metadata (palette, search, MCP) blockset.Info(name) returns for each block: Display (readable name), Category , Aliases (English and French search keywords), Hardness (-1 unbreakable), Material (sound family), Tint , Placeholder , plus the registry attributes. Also All , Extended , ByCategory , Search(q) . Categories: Naturel, Pierre, Bois, Laine/Couleurs, Verre, Minerais, Nether/End, Décoration, Lumière, Liquide, Technique. The editor MCP tool editor_blocks lists category, display name, aliases, hardness and material of every registered block. The palette UI (T1) can read the same API; this stage does not touch it. category extended blocks examples Laine/Couleurs 81 16 wools, concretes, concrete powders, terracottas, glazed terracottas, terracotta Bois 46 logs, stripped logs, wood, stripped wood, planks of 11 species, crimson/warped stems Pierre 41 granite, diorite, andesite, polished, bricks, mossy, cracked, chiseled, deepslate family, tuff, calcite, sandstones, prismarine, obsidian Minerais 34 ores (stone, deepslate, nether), iron/gold/diamond/emerald/lapis/coal/netherite blocks, copper and oxidised variants, raw blocks, ancient debris Nether/End 31 netherrack, soul sand, nylium, wart blocks, nether bricks, blackstone family, basalt, quartz, end stone, purpur, magma, crying obsidian Technique 28 crafting table, furnaces, dispenser/dropper/observer, command blocks, TNT, spawner, slime, honey, note block, jukebox, target Naturel 27 dirt, coarse dirt, podzol, mycelium, grass block, mud, clay, gravel, sands, snow, ices, 14 leaves, moss, mushroom blocks, sculk Décoration 25 bookshelf, barrel, hay, melon, pumpkin, sponge, coral blocks, bee nest, beehive, bone block, honeycomb Verre 17 glass and 16 stained glasses Lumière 8 glowstone, sea lantern, shroomlight, jack o'lantern, redstone lamp, 3 froglights (Emit 15) Liquide 8 (core) water , water_1..7 : W1's model, untouched. Lava is not in the set: fluid.Config{Lava: true} registers lava and lava_1..3 (docs/water-physics.md) Counts above are the extended blocks (core blocks carry metadata too). Names are the canonical game names (lower snake case, no namespace); the colour of a block is the average texel of its Pixel Perfection texture (plains tint applied to foliage). Conventions One block = one entry; texture overrides which mcnames.json block draws it ( redstone_lamp uses the lit image because a registry block has no state and redstone_lamp emits by name). Faces: cube_all , cube_column (logs: side + end on top and bottom), top_side_bottom and orientable (furnace, dispenser, command blocks, ...). Limit : the mesher has no per-block orientation, so an orientable block always shows its front on +z; the other three sides use the side texture. Opacity: leaves, glass, ice, frosted ice, spawner and mangrove roots are solid and not opaque (cut-out or blended pass); everything else is solid and opaque. No extended block is fragile or a liquid. Light: Emit 15 for glowstone, sea lantern, shroomlight, jack o'lantern, redstone lamp and froglights, 10 for crying obsidian; magma block uses its by-name default (4). Excluded on purpose: cactus, chorus, farmland, dirt path, dragon egg, end portal frame, beacon, powder snow (not full cubes, B2), structure block and jigsaw (not useful), infested blocks. Lava is registered by the fluid plugin ( Config.Lava ), not by the block set, like water. Placeholders 75 extended blocks are 1.17+ blocks with no image in Pixel Perfection 1.16: they render as a flat colour (suggested average colour from mcnames.json ) and carry placeholder: true : amethyst_block, azalea_leaves, bamboo_block, bamboo_mosaic, bamboo_planks, budding_amethyst, calcite, cherry_leaves/log/planks, chiseled_bookshelf, chiseled_copper, chiseled_deepslate, chiseled_tuff, cobbled_deepslate, the copper family (copper_block, copper_bulb, copper_grate, cut_copper, exposed/weathered/oxidized and their cut variants, raw_copper/gold/iron_block), crafter, creaking_heart, deepslate bricks/tiles and their cracked variants, polished_deepslate, reinforced_deepslate, all deepslate_*_ore , dripstone_block, flowering_azalea_leaves, the three froglights, mangrove leaves/log/planks/roots and muddy_mangrove_roots, moss_block, pale_moss_block, pale_oak leaves/log/planks, mud_bricks, packed_mud, polished_tuff, resin_block, resin_bricks, rooted_dirt, sculk, sculk_catalyst, sculk_shrieker, smooth_basalt, stripped_bamboo_block, suspicious_gravel/sand, tuff, tuff_bricks, vault, stripped bamboo. A later pack can fill them without changing ids. (Core blocks deepslate and mud of generator v2 have no image either and stay flat.) Visual check docs/img/blocks-gallery.png : wall of every solid block at a one-block pitch, natural look, rendered with go run ./examples/voxel_sandbox -gallery-wall -textures pixelperfection -look natural -freeze -nohud -radius 3 -frames 3 -w 2400 -h 1500 -cam 11,49,20,0,0 -shot out.png (categories in order, left to right, top to bottom: nature, stone, wood, colours, glass, ores, Nether/End, decoration, light, technical). Contact sheets per category come from go run ./scripts/blocksheet -out .build/sheets (CPU icons of assets/blockicon , orange label = placeholder): docs/img/blocks-sheet-naturel.png , -couleurs.png , -technique.png . Honest defects: the placeholders are flat squares and look unfinished next to the textured ones; stained glass shows a dark frame with a faint pane (Pixel Perfection's art, 46/255 pane); the sun and bloom wash out the light-emitting blocks and the lit blocks cast a coloured glow on the floor; animated textures (command blocks, lanterns, magma, froglights, sea lantern, prismarine) show frame 0 only, the strips are cropped to the first 16x16 frame, never shown whole; leaves are cut-out and look flat on a wall seen straight on; no texture is gray unintentionally after the tint recalibration, but terrain far away still gets the biome tint of the column. Add a block If the pack has its image, make sure assets/blocktex/mcnames.json knows it ( scripts/gen-mcnames.py ); otherwise add it under missing with a colour (it becomes a placeholder). Adjust the rules or the excluded / texOverride tables in scripts/genblocks/main.go when the default category, hardness, opacity or light is wrong. go run ./scripts/genblocks (keeps the order of the existing file and appends the new blocks alphabetically), then go test ./blockset -update for the id golden, then go test ./blockset ./scripts/genblocks . Never reorder or delete an entry: ids are saved in worlds. Run go run ./scripts/blocksheet and read the sheet of the category. Project blocks A project adds its own blocks, the building material of a machine mod, with one JSON file named by runtime.custom_blocks in vox.project (project relative, under an asset directory so burrow build packs it; the build adds the file itself and the textures/ folder). { "blocks" : [ { "name" : "mymod:gear" , "display" : "Gear" , "color" : [ 200 , 160 , 40 ], "material" : "metal" , "hardness" : 2 , "texture" : "gear" }, { "name" : "mymod:chest" , "color" : [ 120 , 80 , 30 ], "top" : "chest_top" , "side" : "chest_side" , "interact" : true }, { "name" : "mymod:lamp" , "color" : [ 255 , 230 , 150 ], "emit" : 15 } ] } field meaning name registry name, [a-z][a-z0-9_]* with an optional namespace: (at most 20 + 28 characters). It must not exist yet: a project block never shadows a built-in one display , category , aliases palette text ( category is one of the palette categories, default Technique ) solid , opaque default true ; opaque follows solid color colour of a face without a texture. Unset: the average colour of the block's textures (mid grey for a block without textures), in the editor preview and in the game alike; with textures off (flat colours) the registry colour, the colour field or mid grey, is drawn emit , emit_color block light 0..15 and its colour (default: the block colour) heat heat haze 0..15 light_loss , translucency light levels each channel absorbs entering a non-opaque block; or foliage / tinted / clear for the standard filters fluid , liquid water (non-solid; liquid 1..7 flowing, 8 or unset a source) or lava ; flows by the water rules, no name needed fragile non-solid block destroyed by flowing liquid hardness , material mining time factor (-1 = unbreakable, default 1.5) and sound family (default stone ) texture , top , bottom , side texture names: texture draws every face, the others override a face group. Images are the project files textures/block/<name>.png (any size, resampled to 16x16); a missing file draws the flat colour model , facing boxes instead of the cube (see below) random_tick the block receives random ticks ( OnBlockRandomTick : crops, grass spread, leaf decay); needs runtime.plugins.blocks interact a right click without sneaking sends a block.use event instead of placing a block (needs runtime.plugins.blocks ) Ids. The blocks are appended after every built-in block, in file order, so ids stay stable as long as the file is only appended to (reordering or removing a block, or changing facing , changes the ids of the saved worlds that use it). The editor applies appended blocks and property changes without a restart (see Block editor, Live blocks). Models. "model": [[x0,y0,z0,x1,y1,z1], ...] replaces the cube by up to 32 boxes in sixteenths of a block ( 0 <= min < max <= 16 on each axis). The boxes are the collision, the selection and the look: the player walks on them, rays hit them, neighbours show the faces they do not cover. The faces are textured like the cube ( texture , top , bottom , side ), each box face showing the part of the texture that lies under it. A model block is solid (it can be targeted) and not opaque. "facing": true makes four stored states, the model authored facing north (its front looks toward -Z) and turned a quarter turn clockwise for each other state: name , name[facing=east] , name[facing=south] , name[facing=west] , consecutive ids in that order. The placed state faces the player. Scripts get the state in the event names ( BlockProp(name, "facing") ) and the base name in the topics ( block.set/mymod:belt covers all four), and interact and OnBlockUse("mymod:belt") work for every state. Models are shared by the process: do not run two projects with different models in one process. { "name" : "mymod:belt" , "model" : [[ 0 , 0 , 0 , 16 , 4 , 16 ],[ 0 , 4 , 0 , 2 , 6 , 16 ],[ 14 , 4 , 0 , 16 , 6 , 16 ]], "facing" : true , "texture" : "belt" } Hotbar. runtime.hotbar lists up to nine names put in the first slots at start ( "hotbar": ["mymod:gear", "mymod:chest"] ); the other slots keep the default fill and the middle click picks any block as before. Determinism. The registry is part of the world identity: the file must be the same for every peer and every replay of a session. A project without the key keeps its hashes. Scripts see the blocks like any other by name ( BlockByName("mymod:gear") , BlockInfo ); the editor palette lists them and editor_blocks returns them. Items. A machine mod declares what its blocks and machines carry with runtime.items (names, stable ids, stack limits); the engine provides the registry and the 6-byte stack, not an inventory. See items . Block editor The editor makes a project block from textures alone, with no JSON to write. Right-click a PNG in the Content panel and choose Create block , or use Content > New block... (the Block editor also lists the project's blocks, and a click on one edits it). It opens full screen, like the other asset editors: the block turns in the middle, the Block settings panel on the right holds the form. Block : the name (validated as above), the display name and the palette category. A saved block can be renamed (it keeps its place, so its id, and its textures) unless the open world places it or a project world file lists it: a world file names every registered block and only loads when that list is a prefix of the registry. A block that was saved but never registered in a running editor renames freely; a registered one is renamed in the file and the registry follows after a restart. Textures : one texture for every face, or one for the top, the bottom and the four sides. Each is a PNG of the project (a textures/block/ file, or any PNG, which is copied to textures/block/<name>.png on save; the face files of a block are <name>_top , <name>_bottom , <name>_side ). A texture must be square with an edge that is a power of two from 8 to 256 (16 is the block size; larger images are resampled); anything else is refused with the reason. Properties : colour (off = the average of the textures), solid, opaque, light 0..15, hardness, sound family and interact. A face without a texture wears the colour field, else the average of the block's textures, else grey: the preview and the game use the same colour. Switching to another block, New block or Create block on a PNG while the form has unsaved changes opens an Unsaved block prompt (Save, Discard, Cancel); the header shows unsaved . The form is also part of the editor's shared unsaved-asset guard: Quit , closing the window, Back to world and Restart editor ask Save / Discard / Cancel for it like the model, texture, particle and game UI editors do. Closing the full-screen editor with the X keeps the form. References. Before a block is renamed or deleted, the project is searched for its name and the hits are listed in a dialog (file:line, or the file and the kind): scenes and prefabs ( voxel.group palettes, world.edits boxes, particle_emitter textures, any other component string), data/*.json (items, recipes: values and keys), Go sources under scripts/ (string literals equal to the name or name[...] ), .level palettes, .ui.json and .particles.json files, and the block's textures. A state name[prop=value] follows its block everywhere (the suffix is kept). A rename offers Rename references too , per category: scene/prefab palettes and world edits (on), data JSON values (on), UI and effects ( .ui.json , .particles.json , block:<name> sprites; on), the block's own textures ( textures/block/<name>[_top|_bottom|_side].png become <new>... and the block's texture fields follow; on; a texture another block uses stays), plain string literals in scripts ( "name" , "name[...]" ; off) and level palettes (off). Keys and other components are only listed. A level is decoded, renamed and re-encoded, so its content hash changes: a journal that pinned the old hash keeps the old bytes (that replay stays valid) and the level library cache is dropped; a level whose palette already holds the new name has the two entries merged (the stored chunks are remapped to the first one). The files are rewritten as one action after a backup of the originals in .burrow-cache/block-rename-<time>/ (with a manifest of the file hashes); the open scene is edited in memory as one undo step (Ctrl+Z). World files that place or list the block still refuse the rename and the delete. Restore backup (block editor header, shown while a backup exists) lists the last five rename backups and puts one back as one action: the rewritten files, the moved textures and the block file, so the block gets its old name again. It refuses when a file changed since the rename (the dialog marks it) unless confirmed with Restore anyway ; if the block file itself was edited since, only the renamed block's entry is put back (merged into the current file, every other edit stays); a restored backup is consumed and older ones are pruned. The open scene is not part of it (Ctrl+Z). Save writes the block to the file named by runtime.custom_blocks ( data/blocks.json is created and set when the project has none): a new block is appended, an existing one is replaced in place, so ids stay stable. Delete removes it from the file. The file is checked like a project load before it is written. Live blocks. A saved block is applied to the running editor at once, with no restart: new blocks are appended to the block registry (next free ids), the shape table, the texture layers (the renderer re-uploads its atlas next frame) and the palette, and the meshes are rebuilt. The colour, solid, opaque, emission, heat, model, textures, hardness, sound, category and interact of an existing block are redefined in place (same name, same id), and a changed texture file also changes the derived colour of a block without colour (the registry keeps the file's colour only: it is part of snapshots, so it never depends on texture files; the average is applied by the texture layers). Only edit mode applies them: blocks saved while playing wait for Stop (the status line says so), because Stop restores the play snapshot, which carries the registry it was taken with. Determinism: ids are append-only and never renumbered, and the registry is not part of the state hash. It is part of the journal stamp ( Registry.Fingerprint : name, solid, opaque, fragile, liquid, shape) and of every snapshot, so after a live change the editor starts a new journal from a checkpoint snapshot ( editor_verify_replay keeps working); a replay engine registers the live block list, not the startup one. A game running a project registers its blocks at startup from the file as before. What still needs a restart (the block editor shows a Restart editor button, which asks about unsaved scenes and assets, closes the window and relaunches the editor on the same project): removing a block, renaming a registered block, moving a block, and switching facing (the number of states changes). Delete never renumbers a block under saved data: it is refused while the open world places the block (or a later one, whose id would move) and while a project world file lists it; a block that was only saved, never registered, is removed freely. Editing is only possible in edit mode. Block logic Blocks alone are inert. Block logic is off by default ( runtime.plugins.blocks: true enables it; it is hashed simulation state, package blocklogic ) and gives scripts what a machine mod needs. Block data (what other engines call a block entity). A string of at most 16 KiB (JSON by convention) attached to a cell that holds a block: 131,072 cells and 16 MiB in all. The SDK reads and writes it with BlockData , SetBlockData , BlockDataJSON , SetBlockDataJSON , DeleteBlockData ; BlockDataIn(min, max, limit) lists the cells of a box, BlockDataMany reads up to 4,096 cells with one host call and BlockDataApply updates up to 4,096 with one. It is saved, hashed, rolled back and replayed with the game. The data is bound to the block the cell held when it was written: when the cell later holds another block (broken, replaced by a piston, a script, a fluid) the data is deleted, and the change event carries it ( BlockEvent.Data , up to 512 bytes) so a script can drop the contents of a machine. Writes are buffered with the other effects of the call and applied at commit, in order, together with its voxel writes: writing the data right after SetVoxel of the same call works. Block events. Every change of a voxel (a player, a script, a command, a tool; not flowing water) is queued (at most 65,536 per tick, then dropped and counted: blocklogic.State.Dropped ) and handed to the scripts that subscribed, in the script run of the same tick (edits made before it) or of the next one (edits made by scripts): handler (topic) when OnBlockChange ( block.change ) any change of a voxel OnBlockSet(name) ( block.set/<name> ) the voxel now holds block <name> OnBlockBreak(name) ( block.break/<name> ) the voxel held <name> and does not any more (broken or replaced) OnBlockUse(name) ( block.use , block.use/<name> ) a player right clicked an interact block OnBlockTick(name) ( block.tick , block.tick/<name> ) scheduled cells that are due OnBlockRandomTick(name) ( block.random , block.random/<name> ) randomly drawn cells of a random_tick block A script gets its events as batches ( KindBlockBatch , up to 16 KiB of JSON each), so a burst of thousands of changes costs a few inbox slots and one unit of the per-tick event budget per batch. The SDK handlers hand you one BlockEvent per event ( Topic , X, Y, Z , Old , New , Block , ID , the clicked face NX, NY, NZ , Data , Truncated , and on a brick Micro , MicroN , MicroBlock ). A script holds at most 32 subscriptions: one manager script per mod (not one per machine) is the design that scales. Random ticks. A block declared "random_tick": true in runtime.custom_blocks receives Minecraft-style random ticks: every tick, each loaded chunk (the voxel map's chunks: edited, placed or streamed in) draws runtime.random_tick_rate random cells (default 24 per 32^3 chunk, the equivalent of Minecraft's 3 per 16^3 section; 1..4096), and the drawn cells that hold an opted-in block reach OnBlockRandomTick(name, fn) in the same binary batches as OnBlockTick (a cell drawn twice appears twice; at most 16,384 cells per tick). The draw is a pure function of the sim seed, the tick and the chunk coordinate, so it does not depend on the order chunks were loaded in, needs no stored RNG state, replays identically and leaves the StateHash untouched until a script subscribes and acts. Grow a crop by reading its state with BlockData and writing the next block with SetVoxel . Scheduled machines. BlockSchedule(x, y, z, delay, every) makes a cell a ticking machine: it comes back in OnBlockTick delay ticks after the next tick, then every every ticks (0 = once). Only the machines that are due cost anything: the host keeps the schedule in the simulation state and hands the script the due cells of a tick as binary batches of about 1,000 cells ( KindBlockTick ), at most 65,536 cells per tick (the rest stays due for the next tick, in order). The schedule is bound to the block like the data (another block in the cell cancels it) and survives snapshots, rollbacks and replays; BlockUnschedule or DeleteBlockData cancels it, SetBlockData keeps it. Hosts and tests use the journaled block_schedule and block_unschedule commands. Networks. BlockFlood(x, y, z, through, ends, max) walks a cable, pipe or belt network natively: the blocks named in through are listed and expanded, the ones in ends (machines, tanks) are listed but not expanded, breadth first in a fixed order, up to 60,000 cells, with one host call. A script balances the network it got with BlockDataMany and BlockDataApply . Block use. The first person controller sends the journaled block_use command for an interact block (multiplayer clients may send it too, 10 per second, the whitelist checks it). Sneaking places a block as usual, so a machine can still be built against. Journaled commands for hosts and tests: block_data_set , block_data_delete , block_use , block_schedule , block_unschedule . Water Pumps, tanks, drains and fountains move water through FluidAmount(x, y, z) , FluidPour(x, y, z, units) and FluidDrain(x, y, z, units) (needs the fluid automaton, runtime.plugins.fluid: true ): a full cell is FluidFull = 64 units, a source block counts 64, a coarse flowing level is 8. A pour or a drain acts at once (the amount returned is exact, a later fault of the call does not give the water back); the water then flows by the rules of the automaton, and in the fine water every pour is entered in the ledger ( Created , Displaced ). A pump is FluidDrain on its intake cell, a credit on the tank's block data, and a FluidPour on the output: water is conserved because the script credits what the drain returned. Only water exists: other fluids and gases are numbers in block data (tanks, pipes: BlockFlood finds the network, the script moves the amounts). Scaling The costs a mod meets and what the engine gives for each: problem answer polling thousands of machines every tick BlockSchedule + OnBlockTick : the work follows the machines that are due. Measured on an M2 Max ( go test ./script -bench MachineTick ): 1,000 machines due every 10 ticks 0.2 ms per tick, 10,000 machines 1.2 ms, 50,000 machines (5,000 due per tick) 6.1 ms of the 50 ms tick JSON in a guest costs tens of thousands of instructions per cell the hot calls ( OnBlockTick , BlockDataMany , BlockDataApply , BlockFlood ) are binary: a few instructions per cell. Keep machine state as a short string you parse by hand, not JSON, when thousands of machines tick 1,000 host calls and 4,096 voxel edits per script transaction batch with BlockDataMany and BlockDataApply (each operation counts as one edit); raise the budgets in runtime.script_limits (below) a burst of block events batches, plus the 65,536 queue; a burst beyond it is dropped and counted cable networks BlockFlood walks 60,000 cells with one call per-tick event budget (4,096) batches count once each; raise per_tick.events when needed runtime.script_limits raises the limits of the scripting host for the project (the game and the editor's Play mode build the same host from it): gas per call (default 50,000,000, at most 2,000,000,000), memory_pages , max_faults , and the host call budgets per_script and per_tick ( calls , bytes , spawns , voxel_edits , events ). A zero field keeps its default. The limits are part of the simulation identity: the same project file must be used to record and to replay. { "runtime" : { "plugins" : { "blocks" : true }, "custom_blocks" : "data/blocks.json" , "script_limits" : { "gas" : 200000000 , "per_script" : { "voxel_edits" : 32768 , "calls" : 8000 }, "per_tick" : { "events" : 100000 } } } } Building a machine A furnace is a block, a record of data, and a schedule. This script sets a new furnace up when it is placed, adds fuel on a right click, and burns the fuel of the furnaces that are due, one batch of reads and one batch of writes per call, however many furnaces the world holds: package main import ( "strconv" "burrow-engine/sdk/burrowsdk" ) // the state of a furnace is "fuel,progress" func parse(s string ) (fuel, progress int ) { for i := 0 ; i < len(s); i++ { if s[i] == ',' { fuel, _ = strconv.Atoi(s[:i]) progress, _ = strconv.Atoi(s[i+ 1 :]) return } } return } func init() { burrowsdk.OnBlockSet( "mymod:furnace" , func (self burrowsdk.Entity, ev burrowsdk.BlockEvent) { _ = burrowsdk.SetBlockData(ev.X, ev.Y, ev.Z, "0,0" ) _ = burrowsdk.BlockSchedule(ev.X, ev.Y, ev.Z, 0 , 10 ) // ticks every 10 ticks (0.5 s) }) burrowsdk.OnBlockUse( "mymod:furnace" , func (self burrowsdk.Entity, ev burrowsdk.BlockEvent) { d, ok, _ := burrowsdk.BlockData(ev.X, ev.Y, ev.Z) if !ok { return } fuel, progress := parse(d) _ = burrowsdk.SetBlockData(ev.X, ev.Y, ev.Z, strconv.Itoa(fuel+ 100 )+ "," +strconv.Itoa(progress)) }) burrowsdk.OnBlockTick( "mymod:furnace" , func (self burrowsdk.Entity, cells [][ 3 ] int ) { data, ok, err := burrowsdk.BlockDataMany(cells) if err != nil { return } var ops []burrowsdk.BlockDataOp for i, c := range cells { if !ok[i] { continue } if fuel, progress := parse(data[i]); fuel > 0 { ops = append(ops, burrowsdk.BlockDataOp{X: c[ 0 ], Y: c[ 1 ], Z: c[ 2 ], Data: strconv.Itoa(fuel- 1 ) + "," + strconv.Itoa(progress+ 1 )}) } } _ = burrowsdk.BlockDataApply(ops) }) } func main() {} Conveyors, cables and pipes follow the same pattern: the network is data in the cells (a belt keeps the item it carries, a cable its stored energy), a block event re-links the neighbours when one is placed or broken ( BlockFlood finds the network), and the loop moves the contents a step per tick. The engine provides item identity, stable ids and the 6-byte stack format ( items ); what it does not provide, and a mod writes itself: the items and recipes (the engine ships no item list), dropped items and an inventory API (keep counts in block data or the save store, show them with the game UI), fluids other than water, and per-block animation or particles beyond the models and the effects a script can already spawn. Micro-voxels A single world cell can be subdivided into a brick of micro-voxels (a "chisel"), next to normal blocks, on top of the per-world voxel size. A brick is N x N x N voxels, N = 2, 4, 8 or 16 (default 16: it matches the 1/16 units of shapes and custom block boxes; every N divides 16, so a micro edge is a whole number of sixteenths). Storage. The cell holds the reserved block id voxel.MicroID (65535, not a registry block: Registry.Get returns the zero block) and the chunk keeps the brick in a sparse map cell -> *voxel.Brick (palette of block ids, at most 255, plus one byte per voxel, x + N*(y + N*z) ). Bricks are immutable once installed (copy on write), so undo pre-images, snapshots and the mesher share them. A brick whose voxels are all one block collapses back to that plain block ( Chunk.SetMicro , ChunkMap.SetMicro ); a plain SetBlock over a brick drops it, and SetBlock(p, MicroID) is ignored. Limits: voxel.MaxBricksPerChunk (1024) and voxel.MaxMicroBytes (512 MiB over the world, checked by sim.MicroEdits ). Memory: a 16^3 brick is about 4.2 KB, 8^3 about 0.6 KB, 4^3 about 0.2 KB (a chunk of 1024 16^3 bricks is 4.2 MB); a world without bricks pays nothing. State and files. Bricks are part of the chunk overlay: Chunk.Hash and StateHash mix them in only when bricks exist, so every existing hash is unchanged. Chunk.MarshalBinary writes format version 1 for a chunk without bricks (byte for byte what it was) and version 2 (the runs, then a brick section: count, then cell, length and Brick.MarshalBinary per brick in cell order) when it has some; .voxworld files and engine snapshots carry the chunk blobs, so they gain bricks with no other change. Replica tracking and undo recordings use the same chunk copies. Commands. One journaled command, micro_edit ( sim.MicroEdits{Edits} ), with these edits ( op ): set (voxels [x,y,z,block] into the brick of p ; a plain cell is first subdivided at resolution n , filled with its block), fill (micro box [min,max) with block b , 0 carves), clear (the cell becomes Air), to_brick (subdivide a plain cell at n , optionally carving min / max ; a brick equal to a plain block stays a plain block), to_block (collapse to block b , 0 = the majority block) and put (install a Brick.MarshalBinary blob in data , or the plain block b ; what undo uses). Example: {"edits":[{"op":"fill","p":{"X":3,"Y":40,"Z":3},"n":8,"min":[0,4,0],"max":[8,8,8]}]} . Validation: world limit, registry ids, n , voxel ranges, brick limits; a failing command changes nothing. The editor wraps them in Editor.SetMicro , FillMicro , ConvertToMicro , ConvertFromMicro , ClearMicro , ApplyMicro (several edits, one undo step) and MicroAt ; undo restores the exact previous cell. VoxelOp keeps the bricks it replaces, so any voxel tool can erase one and undo it. Queries. Raycast / RaycastReg , MoveAABB , Overlaps and SelectionBoxes see a brick as its solid micro voxels (registry Solid ), merged greedily into boxes (x, then y, then z, like model.BlockBoxes ; cached per brick and registry revision), so a ray hits the exact micro face ( Hit.MicroVoxel(n) gives the voxel) and the player stands on a half-slab brick. They need a reader that implements voxel.MicroReader ( ChunkMap , ReadView , engine.View ) and take the box path only once the map ever held a brick, so worlds without bricks keep the cube code. Breaking: the default break ( SetBlock Air) removes the whole cell; tools use micro_edit to remove one micro voxel. Navigation reads a brick's solid micro voxels (walk on a micro slab, through a carved doorway; see navigation-ai.md). Fluids treat a brick as a solid cell: water neither enters nor displaces it (unknown ids are walls in the automaton). Light. The light field is per cell, so partial opacity is one rule: a brick is opaque (blocks block light and skylight in every direction) only when every micro voxel is an opaque block; otherwise light and sky pass undimmed through the cell. Micro voxels do not emit light. Meshing. A chunk with bricks is meshed like one with shaped blocks ( Mesh.Fine : positions and UVs in sixteenths). The cube pass skips brick cells; a cube next to a brick keeps its face unless the brick fully covers that face with opaque voxels. The brick pass merges visible micro faces greedily per direction and layer (equal block, AO and light), draws opaque blocks in the opaque mesh and glass-like blocks in the transparent one, culls faces between equal transparent blocks and against opaque neighbours (also across bricks of different resolution), and computes AO at micro resolution. A micro face maps to the 1/N sub-rectangle of the block texture it covers (a brick of stone looks like stone; with MetreTex it follows the metre tiling like shapes); Opts.MicroTile gives each micro voxel the whole texture instead. Light is the light of the cell (the open side's cell on the brick boundary). Distance LOD meshes draw a brick as its majority block. The vertex format is unchanged, so no renderer change is needed ( BURROW_GPU=1 BURROW_GPU_ONLY=micro go test ./render/vulkan -run GPUChecks checks that a pillar and a plate brick render their shape). Chisel tools (editor). Three tools sculpt micro voxels ( editor/core/chisel.go , editor/ui/chisel_ui.go ): Chisel ( C : add, cut or paint with a micro brush, radius 0..16 micro voxels, cube or sphere; Shift swaps add and cut; Ctrl picks the block under the pointer; the wheel sets the radius, Alt+wheel the resolution), Micro box ( V : drag a box of micro voxels, Shift carves) and Micro smooth ( J : majority smoothing, Shift erodes the skin). Options: resolution 4 / 8 / 16 (Shift+C cycles; default 16, 2 stays available through the API), Mirror X / Y / Z around the symmetry origin, block. The hover preview shows the exact micro voxels (green adds, red cuts, yellow repaints) with the count and the size in micro voxels and metres (a micro voxel is 1/(voxels per metre * resolution) m). A stroke is one undo step. Where a cell already holds a finer brick the tool writes at the brick's resolution; a coarser brick is resampled up first (lossless). The Voxels menu has Merge bricks of the region into blocks (each brick becomes a block under the merge rule below) and Resample bricks ... to the chisel resolution . The world default resolution is GenParams.MicroN ( Editor.SetWorldMicroN , the World button of the chisel options): stored in the world settings and in the .voxworld header ( gen.micro_n ), absent for 16, so existing files do not change. Copy, paste and prefabs. Region copy / cut / paste / move / rotate / mirror carry bricks ( ClipCell.Brick ; rotating or mirroring the clipboard turns each brick with its cell). A voxel.group node keeps the bricks of its cells in the optional bricks field (base64 of (cell index, length, Brick blob) records in the group's local frame; the cells name the palette entry #micro ): placing, moving, rotating, undoing and duplicating the node carries them, the prefab editor preview meshes them at micro resolution, and a group without bricks encodes exactly as before. What a group covers is recorded cell by cell, plain blocks and bricks alike ( under palette; the covered bricks are in the optional under_bricks field, same encoding as bricks but in the world frame, the palette entry #micro ), so deleting, moving or undoing a group puts back the exact previous content; a group saved without under_bricks loads as before. Scripts. voxel_micro_get , voxel_micro_set , voxel_micro_fill and voxel_micro_res (SDK: Micro , SetMicro , FillMicro , MicroResolution ) read and write micro voxels; writes are buffered like voxel_set , charged as voxel edits and applied at commit by the rules of micro_edit . Network. micro_edit is in the default client whitelist (20 per second, at most 16 edits, 128 listed voxels, ops set , fill , clear , to_brick , to_block , never put ) and is replicated like set_block . Agents. editor_micro (get, set, fill, convert, clear, brush) edits bricks, each call one undo step. Merge rules. Editor.ConvertFromMicro(p, 0, opts...) , MergeBricks(cells, opts) and ChiselConvert(0, opts...) take a MergeOptions{Rule, MinSolid, Tolerance} (zero value = default). majority_solid (default): the most common non-air block when at least MinSolid (default 0.5) of the voxels are filled, else the cell becomes air (ties: lowest id). majority : Brick.Majority , air as soon as more than half the voxels are air. keep_shape : when the brick matches, within Tolerance (default 4 % of the 16^3 grid) and better than a plain cube, the first variant of a shaped block of its material (a slab, stairs, wall, ... named <material>_<family> , oak_planks also matches oak_* ; a brick made of a shaped block keeps its own item, so chisel then merge gives the same block back), it becomes that block with the matching orientation; otherwise it falls back to majority_solid . MergeBlock(brick, opts) previews the result. Shaped blocks. Chiselling a shaped block (stairs, slab, fence, wall, plant, door, trapdoor, project block with a model ) first converts it into the brick that reproduces its boxes ( Editor.ShapedBrick : selection boxes, else collision boxes, in sixteenths with the state and neighbour-derived variant it has in the world; exact at N = 16, nearest voxel at 2, 4 and 8; the voxels hold the shaped block itself, so texture and softness are kept), and the chisel then carves that brick; the conversion is part of the same undo step. Placing from the hotbar. player.build.micro stores only ids the micro mesher draws as cubes ( microBlock in app/microplace.go ): a shaped block of a family with a material cube (slab, stairs, wall, fence, fence gate, trapdoor, pane, carpet) is placed as that full cube ( oak_stairs becomes oak_planks ; the stem is the item name without _<family> , tried with the suffixes `` / _planks / _block / s / _bricks / _wool ), and a state id never enters a brick. A shaped block without such a cube (plants, torches, doors, buttons, ladders, vines) and any liquid are refused: nothing is placed and Controller.OnNotice gets the reason. Other blocks go in as they are, event-driven logic included (micro events name the voxel); the hotbar attaches no block data. Not covered: micro voxels have no per voxel block data or fluids (events and interact work per micro voxel, see below), and to_brick of an uncarved plain cell is a no-op by design (a brick equal to a plain block is a plain block). Radial symmetry, model stamps and micro events Radial symmetry (chisel). The chisel tools have a Radial option (Off, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8; Tool.Radial , any count up to MaxRadial through the API) next to Mirror: every dab is repeated N times around the vertical axis through the middle of the symmetry-origin voxel (a pure rotation of 360/N degrees; quarter turns are exact, other angles round each micro voxel centre) and combines with Mirror X / Y / Z (mirror first, then rotate: mirror images x N copies). Unless Pin is on, the centre is the voxel under the pointer when the stroke starts (the ghost follows the pointer until then; it moves Tool.SymOrigin ); with Pin on the centre stays at SymOrigin (set it with the Origin button of the tool panel). The ghost shows every copy and the whole stroke is one undo step; the cap MaxChiselVoxels counts the copies. editor_tool takes radial for the chisel brush too. Stamp a model as micro-voxels. A .bmodel or .vox becomes bricks of the world instead of a free render.voxmodel node: Editor.StampModelMicro(rel, hit, MicroStampOpts) (or LoadMicroStamp + PlaceMicroStamp(stamp, originCell, label) ), one undo step. The model is read at its own voxels_per_block ( .vox : 16; override with VoxelsPerBlock ): 16 per block gives N = 16 bricks exactly (a 16^3 model fills one cell voxel for voxel), any other ratio is resampled to the brick resolution N (default 16, 2/4/8/16): nearest voxel when scaling up, the majority block of the covered voxels when scaling down (solid when at least half are). Colours map to the nearest solid registry block ( Block forces one block, Palette maps "#rrggbb" to blocks first). Yaw turns it in quarter turns; the stamp sits on the hovered face like the old stamp ( MicroStampOrigin , the model's bounding box in whole cells, cropped for .vox , the whole grid for .bmodel ) and keeps existing content where the model is empty. Limits: 4096 blocks ( MaxMicroStampCells ) and 2^23 micro voxels ( MaxMicroStampVolume ); beyond them the error says "model too large to stamp" with the size. UI: Content context menu Stamp as micro-voxels at focus , and when dragging a model into the viewport M (toggle) or Alt at the drop stamps bricks (R still rotates; the preview outlines the cells and shows the size); the default drop stays the free node. Agents: editor_micro op: stamp_model ( asset , cell = minimum corner cell, n , voxels_per_block , yaw 0..3, block , palette , dry_run ). Micro block events. Block events on a brick name the micro voxel. block_use ( blocklogic.Use ) takes micro_n (the brick resolution) and micro ( [x,y,z] ): the event reports the micro voxel's block ( block.use/<micro block> , Event.New ) and block_use is only sent when that block is interact , so an interactive block chiselled into a brick works per micro voxel. A new journaled command block_micro_event ( blocklogic.MicroChange{Pos, MicroN, Micro, Old, New} , validated: New must be what the brick holds now, a brick the edit collapsed counts) queues a change event for one micro voxel ( block.change , block.set/<New> , block.break/<Old> ); micro events are saved in snapshots (kind byte flag 0x80 , absent for whole-cell events, so existing states keep their bytes). The SDK BlockEvent gets Micro [3]int , MicroN (0 = whole cell) and MicroBlock (the micro voxel's block name, air when broken). The first person controller sends them: a right click on a brick uses the aimed micro voxel ( block_use with micro_n / micro ), and player.build.micro: true makes left click break and right click place a single micro voxel with the hotbar block (a brick at its own resolution, a plain cell subdivided at Config.MicroN , default 16; break on a plain cell carves one voxel out of it): each is a micro_edit plus block_micro_event , one controller undo step (Z / Y). Without the option the break stays the whole cell. The runtime does not read the world's GenParams.MicroN yet: the host sets app.Config.MicroN . Memory and layers Textures are a GPU 2D array (layer = unique 16x16 image, deduplicated; blocktex.MaxLayers 2048 = the engine cap in render/vulkan , MoltenVK/Metal report 2048). All 385 blocks need 399-435 layers (albedo + normal + spec arrays with 5 mips: 1.56 MiB measured by the renderer, about 0.5 MiB of albedo). If a pack ever needs more, blocktex.NewTable keeps the longest prefix of blocks that fits and draws the others flat ( Table.Truncated counts them); a device with fewer than 2048 layers (the Vulkan minimum is 256) is rejected by the renderer with an explicit message.

Branding and theme Burrow's identity is a cyan mascot peeking out of a voxel burrow of grass and dirt blocks, on deep navy, with a bold rounded white wordmark. Every colour below was measured from the artwork in assets/brand/ (the most frequent exact value of each colour family), not guessed. Palette role hex use Navy #0c182a logo background, dark panel surface Cyan #00a6d6 brand colour, primary accent, focus ring, selection Grass #9bc649 success / confirm, progress bars in games Dirt #955c3a warm neutrals: tooltips and their border, secondary surfaces Off-white #fdfdfd wordmark, text on dark The editor and Hub themes derive the rest (all in ui/theme.go , one definition used everywhere): token dark light surface0 (window) #070c15 #e4e9f0 surface1 (panel) #0c1420 #f4f6f9 surface2 (fields, raised) #131d2c #ffffff surface3 (hover) #1b283b #e2e8f0 divider / border #24324a / #04070d #d2dae5 / #b4c0d0 border_strong #6e819c #66788f warm / warm_border #261d19 / #4a362a #eee5db / #cfbaa4 text / text_dim / text_faint #ecf1f8 / #a7b4c6 / #7d8ca2 #0c182a / #445468 / #56657a accent / accent_fill / accent_text #1fb6e3 / #00a6d6 / #07111f #006a8f / #006a8f / #ffffff success / warning / error #9bc649 / #f5c242 / #ff7a7a #336a0f / #835200 / #b51f29 play #f08a3c #9e4806 ui/contrast_test.go computes the WCAG contrast of every pair the chrome draws: body text 4.5:1 on all surfaces, state colours 4.5:1 as text, accent and strong borders 3:1 as UI components, text on the cyan fill and on selected rows 4.5:1. State is never carried by hue alone: toasts and badges pair the colour with an icon (info, check, triangle, circle) or a label. Shape language, as in the app icon: rounded corners everywhere (radius steps 3, 5, 7, 10 px, tabs rounded on top), soft borders, cyan focus rings and selection, accent underline on the active tab. Typography is Inter (Regular, Medium, SemiBold): 11/12 px small labels, 13 px body, 14 px panel titles, 16-20 px headings. Logo file use assets/brand/burrow-app-icon.png the source of every icon (rounded cyan square, 296 px) assets/brand/burrow-lockup-dark.png mascot + wordmark for dark backgrounds assets/brand/burrow-lockup-light.png the same for light backgrounds assets/brand/icons/{game,editor,hub}/ per tool icons, 16 to 1024 px Clear space : keep at least the height of the mascot's tunnel opening (about a quarter of the logo height) free on all sides. Minimum sizes : lockup 120 px wide, mascot alone 16 px (the icons are tuned for 16, 24 and 32 px; tool badges stay readable at 16 px). Use the dark lockup on navy or photos darker than #40485a , the light one on white or pale surfaces. The icon sits on any background. Do : keep the proportions, the colours and the transparent surround. Don't : recolour, stretch, rotate, add shadows or outlines, put the wordmark on a busy or mid-grey background, or redraw the mascot. The tool variants (plain game, pencil badge for the editor, grid badge for the Hub) exist so the taskbar tells the windows apart. The source art is 296 px, so the 512 and 1024 px icons are an enlargement (Catmull-Rom plus a mild unsharp mask) with a rebuilt, analytically anti-aliased rounded edge: the silhouette is crisp but the interior detail is as soft as an upscale of a 296 px image can be. For a sharp store listing, redraw or re-export the mascot at high resolution and replace burrow-app-icon.png . Regenerating the assets make brand # or: go run ./scripts/genbrand [icons|banners] Reads assets/brand/burrow-app-icon.png and burrow-lockup-dark.png , writes (deterministically) the icon PNGs, .ico and .icns per tool, the Linux hicolor tree, the banners ( docs/img/banner-readme-1280x320.png , assets/brand/social-preview-1280x640.png , download-cover-630x500.png , hub-header-1600x320.png , hub-header-slim-1600x96.png ), the splash ( splash-960x540.png ) and hub/ui/header.png . The banners are drawn by a small 2D rasteriser in the tool (layered voxel hills, a burrow with the mascot peeking out, the lockup composited on a navy to cyan sky), not by the engine renderer. The Windows build embeds burrow-editor.ico and burrow-hub.ico in BurrowEditor.exe and BurrowHub.exe ( scripts/lib-dist-windows.sh ). Linux packagers install assets/brand/hicolor/*/apps/*.png ; macOS bundles can use the .icns files. Game icon burrow new writes an icon.png and vox.project carries "icon": "icon.png" : a PNG inside the project (square, 256 x 256 or larger is best). The sandbox/game window uses it at runtime (all sizes are scaled from it), and burrow build --app turns it into the macOS bundle icon (a missing, non-PNG or non-square icon falls back to the Burrow icon with a warning). burrow icon from art.png --set makes the square 1024 PNG from any image, writes it as icon.png in the project ( -C dir ; -out must stay inside it) and sets "icon" in vox.project in one go. On a Windows host, burrow build also gives the exe your icon: it generates a COFF resource object in pure Go ( assets/winres : PNG-compressed 16/32/48/256 px icon entries, the shared manifest, a VERSIONINFO with the game title), drops it as a .syso in cmd/burrowplay of the Burrow checkout for the duration of one go build , and removes it afterwards. The prebuilt player is not patched (its PE tail carries the archive), so this needs the checkout ( BURROW_ROOT ) and a Go toolchain; without them, with --burrowplay , or with an invalid icon, the exe keeps the Burrow icon and a warning says why. Other hosts build the native target only, so there is no Windows exe to brand. Customising the theme Put a theme.json in the user config folder ( ~/Library/Application Support/burrow-editor/ , %AppData%\burrow-editor\ , ~/.config/burrow-editor/ ) for every project, and/or next to vox.project for one project (applied on top). It is validated (16 KiB cap, unknown keys rejected, colours as #rrggbb ), hot reloaded in the editor, and also read by the Hub. Contrast problems are reported in the console but the colours are applied. { "version" : 1 , "colors" : { "accent" : "#ff8a3d" , "accent_fill" : "#ff8a3d" , "accent_text" : "#0c182a" }, "dark" : { "surface1" : "#101820" }, "light" : { "surface1" : "#fbfaf7" } } colors applies to every variant, dark / light only to that one ( high-contrast counts as dark). Tokens: surface0 surface1 surface2 surface3 border divider border_strong warm warm_border text text_dim text_faint accent accent_hover accent_fill accent_press accent_text success warning error play selection tooltip tooltip_text . selection also accepts #rrggbbaa ; every other token must be opaque. The 3D viewport is not affected: this is chrome only. In-game UIs keep their own theme ( gameui , base dark / light / hud , see game-ui.md ); the defaults follow the same palette.

Building guide for agents Models that build with fill_box tend to produce the same thing: a plain box in three or four unrelated blocks with a flat roof. This page explains the tools that fix that. They give an agent the rules of the public Minecraft building guides, palettes of block names that exist in the world it is building in, generators for the geometry that is easy to get wrong (pitched roofs with correctly oriented stairs, towers, domes, arches) and a review that reads the finished structure back and says what looks poor. burrowedit (the editor, full block set) burrowd (sessions, a handful of blocks) rules, styles, palettes editor_build_guide vox_build_guide roofs, round shapes, arches editor_build_plan vox_build_plan structure review editor_build_review vox_build_review The data behind them (16 styles with their palettes, about 50 rules, roof recipes, proportions, furniture, the limits of the block set) is listed on the building guide data page. It comes from package buildguide ; every block it names is checked against the engine's block set by a test, so a palette never contains an invented block. The workflow the guide teaches Decide the style, the site, the footprint and the storeys. Use odd widths where something must be centred (a single door, a ridge). Palette. editor_build_guide with topic: "style" and a style name returns one block per role, resolved against the world: foundation , wall , wall_alt , frame , roof , roof_stairs , trim , window , light , floor , path , door , fence , plus shaped variants ( roof_slab , wall_stairs , shutter , ...). Keep to three to five blocks plus accents: a base of about half of the surface, a secondary of about a third, an accent of about a fifth, darker below and lighter above, a frame of another tone than the infill. Masses. editor_build_plan with kind: "house" builds a whole house from a style in one call (below); or fill the foundation, walls (hollow boxes) and floors with editor_tool_apply ( box , hollow ) or vox_act ( fill_box ). Break the rectangle: an L, T or U footprint, two or three volumes of different heights, a porch or a tower. Roof. editor_build_plan with kind: "gable_roof" , "hip_roof" or "shed_roof" . Round towers: cylinder for the shaft, cone for the roof, dome for a dome. Relief. No facade is a single plane: pillars every 3 to 5 blocks, windows recessed one block and framed with trapdoors, a plinth, a cornice of upside-down stairs, a chimney. Openings and interior. A framed door with a step, windows 1 to 2 blocks above the floor in varied sizes, floor patterns, furniture from stairs, slabs, fences, trapdoors and plates ( topic: "interior" ), light every 6 to 8 blocks hidden in the structure. Surroundings. A path of two or three mixed blocks, a garden, a hedge, a fence, trees; dig into slopes instead of leaving a flat lawn square. Review. editor_build_review on the box around the building; fix the warnings, look at a screenshot, repeat. topic: "overview" returns this workflow with the ten most important rules and the style list; topic: "checklist" is the final check; topic: "mistakes" lists the usual failures and their fixes. Palettes that exist A style lists candidates per role, most preferred first, and the first one the world has is chosen. That matters because worlds differ: the editor's block set has no gravel or sandstone unless world generation v2 created them, and a burrowd session may have only stone , dirt , grass , sand , water , wood and leaves . When no candidate exists, a block of a suitable kind is chosen (a solid, opaque, non-loose block for walls, the brightest emitter for light) and a warning says so; a role with nothing suitable is listed in missing (leave an opening, or reuse a neighbouring role). The block set has limits an agent must know ( topic: "engine" ): no lanterns, chains, candles, beds, signs or chests (light comes from glowstone, sea lanterns, redstone lamps, shroomlights, torches); stairs exist for about 38 materials only (none for deepslate, tuff, mud brick, concrete, wool, cherry, bamboo or mangrove); there is no double slab (use the cube); stair corners and fence, wall and pane connections are derived from the neighbours. Stairs: facing is the direction a stair climbs toward (its tall back is on that side), half=top turns it upside down for cornices and eaves, and the default state (facing north, bottom) is the bare item name: wanted block name stair climbing north oak_stairs stair climbing east oak_stairs[facing=east,half=bottom] upside-down stair climbing south oak_stairs[facing=south,half=top] top slab oak_slab[type=top] editor_blocks takes query , category , material , family , limit , names_only and states : family: "stairs" with names_only: true and states: false lists the stair materials in one short answer, instead of the roughly 1500 entries of the full list. Generators editor_build_plan and vox_build_plan return a plan: a list of inclusive fill boxes, later boxes overwriting earlier ones, with the bounds and the cell count. Nothing is written unless apply: true , which writes one undoable step in the editor ( vox_build_plan returns ready fill_box commands for vox_act and also accepts apply ). Pass style to take the blocks you leave out (stairs, ridge block, slab, gable fill, shape block) from the style's palette. kind parameters result house style , origin , size , storeys , door , roof , no_porch , no_chimney a whole house in the style's palette: foundation and plinth, framed walls whose intermediate pillars stand one block out of the wall, a belt beam per storey, windows with sills in every bay, a door framed by two pillars with a step and a porch, floors and a stair for upper storeys, lamps, the roof ( roof : gable , hip or flat with a parapet; the default comes from the style: flat for modern and desert, hip for japanese) and a chimney gable_roof origin , size , ridge_axis , overhang , gable_overhang , stairs , block , fill stairs on both slopes facing the ridge, a ridge row, closed gable ends; an odd span gets a block ridge, an even span two stairs back to back hip_roof same, plus slab rings of inward-facing stairs shrinking one block per layer, a slab or block cap; corner shapes come from the engine's own stair rule shed_roof facing , origin , size , ... one slope climbing toward facing disc , cylinder , sphere , dome , cone origin , diameter , height , block , hollow , thickness , step round shapes by the pixel-circle rule; an odd diameter is centred on a block arch origin , axis , width , height , depth , shape an opening to carve out of a wall: piers up to the spring line, then a semicircle or a gothic point For roofs origin is the minimum corner of the footprint (the outer wall faces) with y on the row right above the top row of the walls, and size is the footprint in x and z. With an eaves overhang of one the lowest stairs sit one block outside the walls and one block lower, which is how the slope continues past the wall. A world without stairs (a burrowd session) gets a stepped roof of full blocks with a second block under every step, so it stays watertight. { "kind" : "house" , "style" : "nordic" , "origin" : [ 10 , 9 , 10 ], "size" : [ 11 , 9 ], "storeys" : 2 , "door" : "south" , "apply" : true } { "kind" : "gable_roof" , "style" : "nordic" , "origin" : [ 10 , 14 , 10 ], "size" : [ 9 , 7 ], "overhang" : 1 } A house stays within five material families (a floor, trim or gable fill that would be a sixth is folded into a neighbour), and the generated houses of all 16 styles pass the review without warnings in the tests. Treat the result as a base: vary the plan (add a wing with a second house or a roof), furnish it, add a path and a garden. Review editor_build_review takes the box that bounds one building (terrain, water and plants are ignored, but terrain blocks inside the box count) and reports the materials with their shares, findings and a score from 0 to 100. Each finding has a severity ( error , warn , info ), a code, a message and a fix: code what it means too-many-materials , single-material , no-secondary more than five material families above 3 percent; one material only; one material above 85 percent noisy-weathering cracked or mossy variants make up more than a quarter of a family: random noise instead of age flat-facade 90 percent of a side lies in one plane flat-roof , low-roof-relief 70 percent of the footprint ends at the same height without a parapet (with one it is only the note flat-roof-parapet ); almost no height variation no-windows , no-door , no-light , sparse-light too little glass for the walls; no door; no light source; fewer than one source per 60 footprint cells loose-blocks , illogical-floor , fire-hazard dirt, sand or gravel in the walls; glass, wool, leaves or ice as floor; wood or wool touching lava, fire or a campfire perfect-symmetry , small , low mirror symmetry to the block; footprint under 5; under 4 blocks tall It is a heuristic, not a judge: a modern house is allowed a flat roof, a ruin is meant to look weathered. Read the findings against the style you chose. Where the knowledge comes from The rules are distilled from the public Minecraft Wiki building tutorials (adding beauty, colour palette, materials, floors, furniture, architectural terms, roof types and construction guidelines, walls and buttresses, creating shapes, water features, settlements, villages and the metropolis themes) and from several community building-tip guides. Facts and rules of thumb are restated in our own words; the wiki is licensed CC BY-NC-SA 3.0. The list of sources is topic: "sources" and the end of the data page . To add or change a style, edit buildguide/styles.go : list the candidate blocks of every role, most preferred first. go test ./buildguide fails if a block does not exist in the engine, if a style cannot resolve every role in the editor's block set, or if a roof cannot get stairs and a slab.

h: Overriding a builtin for the whole game
x: Builtin assets Every asset the engine ships is a visible, read-only builtin asset addressed as builtin:<name> . A project uses it as is, or copies it into the project as an editable variant that overrides it (Unity/Unreal style). Kind Names Project file form particles builtin:smoke sparks dust splash fire soul_fire debris .particles.json texture (sprites) builtin:soft puff spark flame square ring .png mesh builtin:cube sphere plane (also the bare cube , sphere , plane of render.mesh ) .obj prefab, ui, sound registered by their own packages ( builtinprefabs , ...) .prefab , .ui.json , ... Registry Package builtinassets imports nothing heavy. Get(kind, name) , List(kinds...) and Entry.Bytes() return the file content in the same format a project asset has. Another package adds its kind from init (no import cycle: it imports builtinassets , never the reverse): func init() { builtinassets.Register(builtinassets.Entry{Name: "builtin:player.prefab" , Kind: builtinassets.Prefab, Ext: ".prefab" , Data: func () [] byte { return playerPrefab }}) } The embedded files live in builtinassets/data/{particles,textures,meshes} . They are generated from Go: go test ./particles -run TestBuiltinUpdate -update-builtin rewrites the effects and sprites from the reference definitions in particles/presets_legacy_test.go , and go test ./render/rworld -run TestBuiltinMeshUpdate -update-builtin the meshes. Golden tests ( TestBuiltinMatchesGo , TestBuiltinSpritesMatchGo , TestBuiltinMeshOBJ ) keep the files and the Go definitions equal. Engine folder and variants The Content panel has a virtual Engine folder (read-only, thumbnails for sprites). Its context menu offers: Copy to project : writes assets/particles/fire.particles.json , assets/meshes/cube.obj , assets/textures/flame.png , ... ( _2 , _3 when the name is taken). Copy to project and replace references in the open scene : also switches every builtin:x (or cube ) in the open scene's components to the copy, as one undo step. Create variant : kinds that register editorui.EngineVariantHooks[kind] run their own variant flow; otherwise it is Copy to project. A prefab becomes a project .prefab that links the built-in with no overrides (see prefabs ) and opens in the prefab editor; a game UI is copied into the project and opens in the designer. The Inspector offers the built-in and project assets in one picker: game.mode.player_prefab (prefabs holding a player component), game.ui slots (game UI files, with (none) ), material_ref / material ( .material.json ), particle_emitter.asset (effects), audio_source.asset (sounds). The picker's icon buttons open the asset or make a variant. Overriding a builtin for the whole game partplug.Plugin.Overrides / particles.Library.SetOverrides map a builtin name to a project file; everything naming the builtin (emitters, sub-emitters, BlockDebris , BlockBreak ) then uses it, and a broken file falls back to the builtin. Block break debris is the effect builtin:debris : &partplug.Plugin{Component: true , Overrides: map [ string ] string { "builtin:debris" : "assets/particles/debris.particles.json" }} rworld.RegisterBuiltinMeshes(assets) registers the meshes under both names; MemAssets.Mesh("builtin:cube") resolves to cube , so a project mesh registered as cube overrides it.

h: What the plugin does each frame
Fixed rig in a menu scene
x: Cameras Burrow's camera system is frame domain : a rig reads simulation state (the player or a node) and produces the view, so it can never change a StateHash . Packages: camera (rigs, behaviours, shake, blends; no engine dependency), camera/camplug (the engine plugin) and, for drawing, the orthographic projection in scene.Camera , render/soft and render/vulkan . Quick start Enable it in vox.project and declare rigs (rigs can also be camera_rig scene components, which enables the plugin by itself): { "runtime" : { "plugins" : { "camera" : true }, "camera" : { "start" : "fps" , "seed" : 7 , "rigs" : [ { "name" : "fps" , "kind" : "first_person" }, { "name" : "third" , "kind" : "third_person" , "distance" : 6 , "collide" : true , "smooth" : 0.06 }, { "name" : "iso" , "kind" : "isometric" , "ortho_size" : 9 , "smooth" : 0.15 , "look_ahead" : 2 }, { "name" : "side" , "kind" : "side_scroller" , "axis" : "z" , "plane" : 0 , "dead_zone" : [ 2 , 1 ] } ] } } } In code ( examples/camera_ui_demo is the full program, go run ./examples/camera_ui_demo , keys C / I / P / K / L): a.AddPlugin(&camplug.Plugin{Rigs: rigs, Start: "third" , Seed: 7 }) // frame code cm := camplug.Res(c) cm.Ctl.Switch( "iso" , 0.6 ) // blend over 0.6 s (a switch between perspective and orthographic cuts) cm.Ctl.AddTrauma( 0.7 ) // shake Registering the camera_rig component changes StateHash (the registry is hashed). The plugin is off by default ( runtime.plugins.camera: true enables it; false together with a scene that uses the component is a build error). Without a rig configured the plugin stays passive and does not drive the camera at all. Rig kinds kind view notes first_person at the target's eye ( offset , default y 1.6), looks where the target looks third_person orbits the focus at distance along the target's look angles collide : five rays (centre + 0.25 block in the screen plane) are marched through the voxels, the camera is pulled in to the nearest hit ( min_distance , default 0.4) at once and eases out in about 0.15 s; an eye inside a block does not collapse the camera top_down pitch -89 (default) above the focus, distance 24, yaw free perspective, or orthographic with ortho_size isometric yaw 45, pitch -35.264, orthographic ( ortho_size default 10), distance 64 the camera stands back along the view axis side_scroller 2.5D: axis z (camera on +Z looks -Z) or x, the focus sits on the constant plane of that axis distance 20; perspective or ortho_size free detached fly camera: Input.Move (right, up, forward) at speed blocks/s, Input.LookYaw/LookPitch the plugin keeps the movement keys and the mouse away from the player controller while it is active fixed static at pos ; aim : empty ( yaw / pitch ), point ( look_at ) or target cinematic shots A zero number means the default of the kind; every number is clamped by Rig.Sanitized , and Rig.Validate rejects unknown kinds, NaN and huge values. At most 32 rigs, names up to 64 bytes. Behaviours Follow with smoothing ( smooth , seconds): exponential, frame-rate independent ( 1 - exp(-dt/smooth) ). Near plane ( near , blocks, 0 = 0.1, at most 16): raise it so a third person camera that grazes a wall does not show its inside; in the Cameras tool it is the Near row of Lens. Dead zone ( dead_zone [right, up], blocks): the target moves freely inside a window in the screen plane; the focus only follows the excess. Look-ahead ( look_ahead , blocks): the focus leads along the horizontal velocity, eased over about 0.35 s. Bounds ( use_bounds , bounds min xyz / max xyz): the final camera position is clamped. Shake ( AddTrauma , request shake ): trauma 0..1 decays at shake_decay per second; the amplitude is trauma squared times shake_angle degrees and shake_offset blocks, from smooth value noise at shake_freq Hz seeded with Controller.Seed (the same seed and inputs shake identically). Blends ( Switch(name, seconds) ): position, yaw (shortest way), pitch and FOV are interpolated with a smoothstep from the pose the previous rig had; the new rig's smoothing state starts fresh. Perspective and orthographic poses cannot be interpolated, so such a switch is a cut. Cuts : a zero-second switch, a projection change, a target that jumps more than 32 blocks in a frame (teleport) and Controller.Cut() set Output.Cut ; the plugin copies it to app.FrameState.CameraCut and the render plugin calls Renderer.ResetHistory() , so TAA, FSR 2 and the ray tracing denoiser start a clean history. The renderer also detects large jumps and projection changes on its own. What the plugin does each frame camera.input (Update, before the controller) keeps movement away from the player while a free rig is active; camera.update (PostUpdate) reads the target (the rig's target node, else the app.Controller player; the velocity is smoothed from position differences), applies queued requests, updates the rig and writes the pose into app.FrameState (position, yaw, pitch, FOV, Ortho , CameraCut ). For the fixed-angle rigs (top-down, isometric, side scroller) the player's look yaw is aligned with the rig so WASD means screen directions. The voxel world, the scene meshes (hybrid frame) and the world-space UI labels all follow FrameState . Cost per frame is O(1) plus at most five voxel rays of 3 * distance cell steps. Orthographic projection scene.Camera.Ortho > 0 (half the visible height in blocks) and app.FrameState.Ortho select an orthographic camera everywhere: render/soft : parallel rays from points of the image plane ( Camera.Origin64 ); Camera.Project and ViewProj are orthographic too. render/vulkan : Camera.ViewProj builds the orthographic matrix (the voxel world, the scene meshes and shadows follow it); the hybrid scene camera carries the ortho projection. The sky is a flat gradient behind an orthographic view (every sky ray is the view direction). Limits: depth-based screen-space effects of the HDR levels (AO, FSR 2 depth clip, the ray tracing G-buffer) assume a perspective matrix, so use the classic pipeline ( -shaders off ) or accept slightly off AO/RT on isometric views; fog is computed from the distance to the camera position. Scripts and SDK Scripts (module vox , ABI additive, see script/ABI.md ) queue frame-domain requests with camera_cmd , delivered with engine.SendFixed after the tick (ignored without the plugin, dropped during a replay verify): burrowsdk.CameraSwitch( "iso" , 0.5 ) // rig name from camera_rig / runtime.camera burrowsdk.CameraShake( 0.6 ) burrowsdk.CameraCut() From a fixed system use camplug.Emit(fixedCtx, camera.Request{Op: camera.OpSwitch, Rig: "top", Blend: 0.4}) . Editor and agents The inspector shows the camera_rig fields (every field has a tip and a range). Tools > Cameras is a full-screen tool: the rigs of the scene as cards (the active one badged, + New rig adds a node with a camera_rig ), the world seen through the selected rig (drawn by the GPU at the panel's resolution, a CPU image only in headless runs, following the editor camera focus, with rule-of-thirds guides and the dead zone drawn) or from outside with the rig and its view pyramid drawn in the world, Switch to rig (with the blend slider) and Test shake. Camera settings holds the rig (kind, target, distance, height), the lens (field of view, dead zone, smoothing) and the shake (amplitude, frequency, decay). Every edit is one undo step on the rig's component.
