MCP tool editor_camera : without action it moves the editor camera as before; rigs (rigs, active, pose, trauma), validate {rig} , switch {name, blend} , shake {amount} , cut , preview {rig | name, target, look, width, height} (a CPU render from the rig's pose as an image). Fixed rig in a menu scene A title-screen background uses a fixed camera rig plus scene.settings with "controller": false : the first-person controller, hotbar and break/place are off for that scene only (the project keeps runtime.plugins.controller ), so the rig drives the camera and the real game scene is unaffected. See lighting.md . Voxel size Rig lengths ( offset , distance , min_distance , near , ortho_size , dead_zone , look_ahead , bounds , pos , look_at , plane , speed , shake_offset , the defaults such as the 1.62 m eye and the 4.5 m third-person distance, and the collision margins) are metres. camplug tells the controller the world's voxels per metre ( Controller.SetSubdiv ) and the rig works in voxels, so it frames the player the same way at every voxel size. Controller.Rigs() and the camera_rig component keep the authored metres. At one metre voxels nothing changes. Budgets and robustness Rigs are clamped, never trusted: at most 32 rigs, names 64 bytes, distances 256, ortho size 1024, coordinates 1e7; NaN and infinities become defaults or are rejected; dt is clamped to 0.25 s; requests per frame 64 (the rest are dropped and counted in editor_camera rigs ). Limits One active rig; during a blend only the new rig is updated (the old pose is a snapshot). The side scroller locks the camera, not the player: movement along the locked axis is a game rule (constrain it with physics or a script). No camera roll, no spline paths, no multiple viewports; third-person collision samples voxels only (no scene colliders).

x: Changelog history The detailed, stage-by-stage history of the engine up to version 0.1.0, kept for reference. The short release notes are in the changelog . Details of some stages (the development texture pack, scratch measurements) describe private development builds only: released builds ship Pixel Perfection CE as their texture pack. Development history up to 0.1.0 Fine water: tall falls and opposing flows (docs/water-fine.md) Tall falls ( fluid.FineRules = 3 ): a stream covers 256 cells (was 64) and falls with a terminal speed of 30 blocks/s, so a 150-block fall is one stream that lands after 5.5 s instead of three streams restarting from rest in bricks hanging in mid-air (a splash ring and a thin filet in the sky every 64 blocks). The curtain grows with the front of the water ( voxel.FineStream.FrontGap / TailGap ) instead of appearing whole at the first tick, has no splash before the water arrives, keeps its streaks moving down the whole fall (the fall attribute saturated 64 blocks down), and is meshed in the chunk layers above the terrain that hold no edited block (the curtain had a gap in each). -demo tower -demo-n H in the sandbox. Opposing flows: the water push on bodies ( voxel.LiquidTable.Flow ) grows with the head difference up to full strength at one level (coarse water is unchanged): a fine film no longer pushes at full speed, and where two flows meet the push no longer flips between full speed one way and the other. Tests for channels fed from both ends, springs facing each other, crossings, loops, a spring against a coarse lake or lava (settling, no oscillation, symmetry, conservation). -demo opposing in the sandbox. Fine water under overload (water-fine.md, "Overload") Many water sources no longer freeze the fine water. At FineMaxBricks a refused spill kept its brick dirty, which kept its whole sheet from folding: the pool never emptied, the water stopped half spread with straight cut edges and dry ground between sources, and the world was never idle (100 sources on a plane: 2048 bricks, 1248 of them dirty, forever). The demands were also served from the lowest cell every step: of 300 sources, some never got any water. Rules version 2 ( fluid.FineRules = 2 ; journals recorded under version 1 fail their first hash check, older snapshots restore): demands are served from a hashed spawn cursor in rotation; on a step where the cap refuses water, the calm water behind the waiting fronts folds into coarse cells (overload fold), and when nothing can fold that way, whole components of calm water and waiting fronts fold with the lateral tests waived (forced fold, every 20 steps, at most 1/8 of the cap). Exact conservation at every tick; the scenes settle to the same coarse water as with an unlimited pool. A fold no longer ranks a full brick as a residue (its share did not fit, the cached volume drifted from the fills and a later rollback lost the difference; TestFineFoldResidueFits ). FineMaxBricks defaults to 4096 (was 2048). Overload signal: Stats.FineOverload , FineCapRefused , FineCapSources , FineCapSteps , FineOverFolds , FineOverFolded , State.Overloaded / OverloadNote ; fluid.Plugin logs entering and leaving an overload ( Log , Quiet ) and shows the note in the HUD with OverloadHUD (on in the sandbox). Water meshing of large sheets is 4.6x faster (dense brick index, dense memo of the surface candidates and corner normals, same output): an overloaded chunk took up to 140 ms per build, so the drawn water lagged the simulation by seconds; the lateral pass caches the cell under each brick. examples/voxel_sandbox -demo sources -demo-n N -demo-layout plane|terrace|bowl|cliff|cave : the stress scene. Tests: fluid/fine_overload_test.go (settling, fairness, determinism and snapshots, bounded cost with 500 sources, mesh/simulation agreement), BenchmarkFineWaterSheet . Website, Hub wiring and release pipeline (releasing.md) cmd/burrowsite + internal/site ( make site ): a dependency-free, reproducible static site generator for GitHub Pages. Landing page, download page (reads the signed manifest.json , "coming soon" without), the allow-listed docs with sidebar and full-text search, templates and screenshot gallery, changelog and Atom feed, licences and credits, about and brand downloads, 404.html , robots.txt , sitemap.xml , .nojekyll , optional CNAME ; English at / , French at /fr/ (docs in English only). Inter bundled, dark and light themes, strict CSP, no external request; screenshots resized and recompressed (38 MiB to about 6 MiB). The build fails on a leak (local paths, private URLs, secrets), a broken link or anchor, an external resource, an unclassified docs page or a size overrun. Hub: DefaultSiteURL ( -X burrow-engine/hub.DefaultSiteURL , HUB_SITE_URL in the dist scripts) derives the manifest, docs, news and download addresses; the Home buttons open the website through a same-origin-only opener; the website is editable in developer mode only. Signed, plain-text, size-capped news in the manifest ( burrowrelease manifest -news-file , -tag-prefix v ); the consent screen names the fetched file and host. release/burrow-release.pub is the committed release public key (the dist scripts default to it); scripts/publish-release.sh ( make publish-release ) prints the plan by default, builds and signs with --build-only , and publishes to the public releases repository only with --execute and a typed confirmation. Vulkan bindings merged into the engine module third_party_vulkan is now a package of the burrow-engine module (import path burrow-engine/third_party_vulkan , package name vulkan ) instead of a separate module github.com/goki/vulkan wired by replace . third_party_vulkan/go.mod , the replace / require in the root go.mod , and the replace github.com/goki/vulkan lines written by burrow new , burrow script new , burrowscript new and the project templates are gone (a project needs only replace burrow-engine => <checkout> ). Cgo-dependent hand-written files carry //go:build cgo , so CGO_ENABLED=0 go build ./... still passes (the package keeps only doc.go and version.go ). make lint excludes the package from go vet (generated code; one unsafe.Pointer finding in util.go ) and gofmt . THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES, third_party_vulkan/README.md and REGEN_NOTES.md describe the new layout and the modifications. Visual identity (branding.md) go run ./scripts/genbrand ( make brand ) regenerates everything from assets/brand/ (replaces scripts/genico ): icon PNGs 16..1024, .ico , .icns , Linux hicolor PNGs for the game, editor (pencil badge) and hub (grid badge) variants, the README / social / download / Hub banners and the splash image. Crash safe Hub self-update (journal, .new / .old , ResolveHubExe ), state bound to the executable, single-instance lock, wall-clock confirm; OS file locks for installs and downloads, .part named by sha256, previous engine kept until the replace succeeded. Burrow Hub (hub.md) New native launcher cmd/burrowhub (+ hub/ui , drawn with the engine UI over Vulkan): project list (recent, pin, search, import, duplicate, remove, delete with double confirmation), templates gallery, side-by-side engine versions, per-project engine pin, upgrade with release notes, backup zip, burrow migrate hook and revert, first-run wizard, Home with Learn links. Package hub (no UI, no cgo): Ed25519-signed manifest with channels and per-OS assets, HTTPS-only client (proxy env, redirect limits, Range resume, size caps, sha256 before unpack), zip-slip / symlink / decompression-bomb safe unzip, atomic engine install with rollback, Hub self-update with swap and automatic rollback, opt-in update check, no telemetry. No update source or key is compiled in: the Hub reports "no update source configured" and works offline. cmd/burrowrelease ( keygen , manifest , verify ) builds and signs manifest.json from dist/ zips; the private key is only read from a file you pass (never inside a checkout). vox.project engine accepts pre-release versions ( 0.4.0-beta.1 ). The creator kit gains BurrowHub.exe and engine.json ; make hub-test , make hub-run , make dist-hub-windows . Stabilisation pass third_party_vulkan : the C copies made for slice arguments ( vkCreateGraphicsPipelines , barriers, submits, ...) were freed by a finalizer attached to a dead result variable, i.e. at the next GC, possibly during the call. The finalizer now sits on the allocation map and every wrapper keeps it alive until it returns ( tools/fixalloc.pl , run by make regen ). Closes the MoltenVK start-up SIGSEGV race. Sound: Pack.Warm decodes the step, block break and other block events first (first variant of every event before the other variants, 96 files); an alphabetical 64 file cap used to leave every step.* event cold, so the first footsteps were dropped. Windows log files are named Burrow.log and BurrowEditor.log ; the Windows README describes sounds, diagnostics variables and the F1 help; the FSR and SMAA licences ship in licences\ . burrowd exposes 20 tools (test updated). Windows creator kit (scripts/dist-engine-windows.sh) make dist-engine-windows writes Burrow-Engine-windows-x64.zip (BurrowEditor, burrow, burrowplay, burrowscript, burrowasset, burrowctl, burrowd, docs, templates, script SDK module sdk/ , licences, bilingual GETTING-STARTED); make dist-windows now writes Burrow-Sandbox-windows-x64.zip ; make dist-all builds both. Atmosphere: sun shafts (high+), light DoF + camera motion blur (ultra); no TAA (justified in docs/rendering.md). render.ShaderQuality gains Refraction , SSRSteps , WaveOctaves , Caustics , Precip , Wet , Sway , GodRaySamples , DoF , MotionBlur . Fine water, stage W3: adaptive sub-cell bricks (opt-in fluid.Config.Fine ) Water that moves lives in N x N x N sub-cell bricks (N = 2, 4 or 8, default 4; 32 units per sub-cell) and folds back into water_1..7 / new water_full blocks when calm; water stays an infinite source with a constant head. Integer rules: falls, lateral equalisation with a film threshold, communicating vessels through full cells (pressure), seams with coarse cells with a one-level tolerance, lava, fragile blocks, void. Exact volume ledger ( State.Ledger ). Deterministic by construction: the dirty bits of the bricks and the pending chunk scans are hashed, wake-ups are synchronous for bricks, stale coarse wake-ups cost no budget; snapshot/restore, rollback, chunk-mode undo (burrowd) and replay after a world load are exact. Caps: FineMaxBricks (2048), FineSpawn (128 per step), FinePressure , and the wake-up queue overflows to chunk scans at 8192 writes. Off by default: existing projects, worlds, journals and hashes are unchanged. On for burrow new (sandbox template, runtime.plugins.fine_water ), the editor without a project ( burrowedit -no-fine-water to opt out) and burrowd sessions with fine_water: true . Commands fluid_pour , fluid_cell , fluid_refine ; editor tools editor_water (fine fields), editor_water_pour , editor_water_wake (refine is one undo step). .voxworld stores the bricks. Water physics, stage W1: flow, buoyancy, swimming New package fluid : a deterministic cellular automaton for water on the voxel grid. Levels are blocks ( water = source, water_1 .. water_7 flowing, registered after the terrain blocks, so ids and old .voxworld files stay valid), so flowing water lives in the sparse overlay, in StateHash , snapshots, undo and the editor document without new storage. Bounded and canonical: a work list sorted by (y, z, x) behind a voxel.Observer change feed (every write, undo and world load wakes the cells around it), MaxUpdates / MaxActive / ChunkScans caps per step (all candidates are evaluated, so stale wake-ups never consume a budget), a queue overflow becomes the sorted set of the chunks written, then a sweep; write order never matters. The work list is derived data: in snapshots (restore mid-flow resumes exactly) but not in StateHash , so "place then undo" and the hashes of worlds without moving water are unchanged. Water and foliage look (natural and vivid looks only; classic is unchanged) Water ( shaders/water.glsl ): the flat registry blue is leaned to a blue-green and made translucent with a light-turquoise shallow band that deepens with the liquid column (absorption: red first, then green), richer colour, stronger Fresnel sky reflection, a 1.8x ripple normal with light variation on wave slopes (faded with distance), and thin drifting foam streaks on one-block-deep water instead of the dot lattice. The alpha is capped at 0.88 so deep water is never an opaque flat blue. Foliage ( shaders/voxel_body.glsl , soft twin in render/soft/tex.go ): leaves are found from the top mip alpha of the tinted layer (< 1 = cut-out texture). They get lifted dark texels (no near-black speckle), a deterministic per-block hue variation (yellow-green to blue-green, render only), softer AO, an ambient floor, light leaking through the canopy (softer sun shadow, wrap term) and no specular/env reflection (leaves were picking up bright sky reflections). Alpha test coverage is kept across mips (alpha scaled by the mip level) so distant leaves do not thin out. Found while debugging: a second hash3 call inside the leaf block made MoltenVK write garbage and blue speckles on the -shaders off natural look; the per-block variation reuses the existing tone hash instead. Characters The player avatar and animated characters: package character (rig, skins, animation, .vox import, held items), character/charplay (the engine plugin: views, camera, scene nodes), the Character editor panel and the character scene component. Everything is frame domain (visual): it never writes simulation state, never changes StateHash or the journal, and the animation clock is the frame dt you give it, never the wall clock. physics / controller state --(read only)--> character.Motion --> Animator --> Pose --> part matrices | skin (64x64 PNG) or .vox --> Rig (named parts, pivots, meshes) ------------------------+--> rworld.MeshItem (render.extract input hook; soft AND Vulkan) The rig A character.Rig is a hierarchy of named parts in world units: +Y up, the character faces -Z (camera yaw 0), its right hand is +X , the origin is the centre of the feet. Each Part has a role, a parent, a pivot (the joint position at rest) and a mesh whose vertices are relative to the pivot. Animated roles: torso , head , arm_r , arm_l , leg_r , leg_l . Any other part is a static child of its parent (a tail, a backpack). Parents precede children. A Pose holds a root yaw/pitch/offset and a rotation (degrees: pitch X, yaw Y, roll Z) and an offset per role. Positive pitch swings a hanging limb forward and makes the head look up . Rig.Solve(root, pose) returns one object-to-world matrix per part. Two model sources feed the same rig: model id source look humanoid boxes + a 64x64 skin, 4 px arms 1.8 blocks tall (one skin pixel = 1.8/32 block) humanoid_slim same, 3 px arms voxel_hero the bundled voxel humanoid, 16 voxels tall assets/x.vox any .vox split into named parts (below) scaled to 1.8 blocks, times scale Skins (64x64) The format is the usual 64x64 RGBA layout: head 8x8x8, body 8x12x4, limbs 4x12x4 (3 px wide arms in the slim variant), an inner layer and an outer overlay layer (hat, jacket, sleeves, pants) drawn as a box 0.5 px larger and alpha masked (transparent texels show nothing). Each box is unfolded as U+D U+D+W V +--- top ---+-- bottom --+ V+D +---+---front---+---left-----+---back---+ |right| W x H | D x H | W x H | right is the character's right side (+X), left is -X, front is -Z. The layout table is character.BoxUV / FaceRect ; the tests paint every face of every box with its own colour and check that the mesh samples it. character.SampleNearest is the reference nearest-texel sampler. Because both renderers filter bilinearly and choose mips from the pixel footprint, the texture handed to them is the skin enlarged 4x with nearest neighbour ( SkinTexture ), which keeps the blocky look. Default skin. character.DefaultSkin draws an original skin ("Wanderer": cap, green tunic, red scarf) pixel by pixel from code; a golden PNG ( character/testdata/default_skin.png ) pins it. It is not derived from any third-party skin. Importing a skin. Skins are plain PNG files: import one in the Character panel ( Import PNG... , it must be exactly 64x64) or reference any project PNG in the component's skin field. New... writes a copy of the default skin into the project and opens it in the texture editor window, and Edit opens the current skin there (pixel grid, mirror drawing, layers); the preview picks the saved file up. No network download, no pack loader. A wrong size falls back to the default skin with a console warning. Skins of the old 64x32 layout are not supported. Voxel characters ( .vox ) character.ImportVox splits a MagicaVoxel file into parts. In MagicaVoxel axes (Z up) the character faces -Y , so its right hand is at -X . Name each body piece (the object name in the scene panel, stored as the transform node's _name ; groups are fine, the nearest named transform wins): name meaning head , torso (or body ), arm_r , arm_l , leg_r , leg_l the animated parts ( arm_r = the character's right) head.hat , arm_r.glove more voxels merged into that part ( <role>.<anything> ) tail@torso a static extra part attached to torso ( <name>@<role> ) pivot.head , pivot.arm_r , ... a marker object: its centre is the joint of that role pivot.eye , pivot.hand optional eye and held-item anchors (no name) merged into the torso Without a pivot.* marker the joint is the top centre of arms and legs and the bottom centre of head and torso. The model is moved so its feet touch y=0, centred on the origin, and scaled to 1.8 blocks (times the component scale ). character.SampleVoxHero() builds the bundled example; character.EncodeVoxParts writes it ( examples/characters/voxel_hero.vox ). A torso part is required. Body plans: quadrupeds A rig has a body plan, humanoid (default, everything above) or quadruped (wolf, deer, sheep, horse...). Same axes (faces -Y, the animal's right is -X). The plan is detected as soon as one of the four legs below exists, or forced with VoxOptions.Plan ( "humanoid" / "quadruped" ; forcing maps arm_r, arm_l, leg_r, leg_l to leg_fr, leg_fl, leg_br, leg_bl and back). name meaning torso (or body ), head as for humanoids; the head hinges at its back-bottom leg_fr , leg_fl , leg_br , leg_bl front/back, right/left legs ( leg_fr = front right). Aliases: front_leg_r , foreleg_r , back_leg_l , hind_leg_l , hindleg_l ... tail hinged at its front end, sways and lifts jaw (alias mouth , lower_jaw ) hinged at its back-top, child of head ; opens with the bite , eat , howl , rear clips neck optional; when present head hangs on it ear_r , ear_l optional, children of head , flick at idle A quadruped is 1 block tall by default (times scale ); the held item attaches to the mouth. Animate it with character.NewAnimatorFor(rig) (or set Animator.Plan = rig.Plan ): walk and crouch move the legs in diagonal pairs ( leg_fr + leg_bl against leg_fl + leg_br ), run is a bounding gallop with a lifted tail and panting jaw, idle sways the tail and breathes, jump and fall spread the legs. Head look is limited to +-55 degrees yaw and -35..+40 pitch. The attack and hurt triggers play bite and hurt_q on a quadruped. character.SampleVoxQuadruped() is the bundled reference fox (humanoid-only first-person arm code simply draws nothing for it). Animation character.Animator is a deterministic state machine with blending. Step(dt, Motion) advances it: m := character.Motion{Speed: 4.3 , OnGround: true , Yaw: 90 , Pitch: - 10 } // from the physics state + the camera an.Step( 1.0 / 60 , m) pose := an.Pose() States, chosen by character.Classify (priority top to bottom): swim (Swimming), fly (Flying), jump (airborne and rising), fall , crouch , run (speed above 5.6 or sprinting), walk (speed above 0.15), idle . Poses are blended linearly over 0.12 s. The gait phase advances with the distance travelled (2.3 rad per block), so feet do not slide. Look: the head follows the camera pitch and yaw relative to the body (yaw clamped to 75 degrees); the body yaw follows the look yaw with exponential damping while moving or acting, and only drags along once the head is turned more than 50 degrees when standing still. Clips are keyframed overlays (smoothstep between keys, fade in/out): attack (break), place , wave , hurt , cheer , nod ; the locomotion state names are also valid clip names (they force that state, walking in place: the editor's preview). Animator.Trigger(name) plays a one-shot, Play(name, loop, rate) loops at a rate, Stop() fades out. Animator.Rate scales time. Triggering from scripts and agents : set the anim field of the character component ( editor_set_component , a script's Insert ) to loop a named animation, "" to hand control back to the motion; Go hosts can also send the charplay.Trigger{Path, Name, Loop} engine event ("" path = the player). The player attack/place swings fire on the left/right mouse buttons. Water. Motion.Swimming selects the swim animation. The player adapter derives it from app.FrameState.HeadUnder , InWater while airborne, or a liquid voxel at chest height; charplay.Avatar.Swimming replaces that test (the hook for other water physics). Scene characters use the position deltas of their node plus physics.character 's on_ground / vy . Rendering render.extract builds an rworld.Input from the scene; engine.AddRenderInputHook lets a plugin edit it before rworld.Extract . The character plugin appends MeshInstance items (one per part, plus the held object) with the texture and alpha-mask material, and CastShadow set, so the existing soft and Vulkan paths draw them (sun shadows on the terrain and on themselves where the renderer supports them) without any shader or render/vulkan change . Part meshes and textures live in a character.Store layered over the project assets ( character.Overlay , keys start with char: ). Parity soft/Vulkan is measured by make character-test (Vulkan shot vs render/soft hybrid of the same frame, shaders off, mean abs RGB difference 0..255 over the pixels the character covers): third person walking 8.9, running from behind 6.2, voxel hero 4.7, first person 2.6 (the whole image, dominated by unrelated terrain differences, is 37 to 41: the soft frame has no load radius or fog). Tolerance 12. Views and camera charplay.Plugin{Player: true} (burrowplay and the games enable it; runtime.plugins.character: false turns it off) draws the player and moves the camera: First person : camera at the eyes; the right arm and the held object at the bottom right with a gait bob and the attack/place swing. The body and head are not drawn. Third person back / front : the whole body; the camera sits dist blocks behind (or in front of, looking back at) the eye, shortened by a voxel raycast so it never goes through terrain. Input actions (in the default input map; custom maps add them to opt in): camera_toggle (F5: first, back, front), camera_closer / camera_farther (PageUp/PageDown, = / - ), camera_zoom (Ctrl + wheel), crouch (C, visual only: the sandbox controller has no crouch physics). Rebind them in vox.project 's input map like any action. F5 used to toggle block textures in the window; while the avatar plugin is on it belongs to the camera ( engine.KeyReservations ). The held object is the selected hotbar block: a cube with the blocktex face textures and the same plains biome tint as the 3D hotbar icons ( blockicon.FaceImage ); a block without a texture uses its flat colour; a non-block item ( charplay.Avatar.Held = &character.Held{Kind: character.HeldItem} ) is a generic tool placeholder. The game hotbar keeps its 3D block icons. Project blocks ( runtime.custom_blocks ) show their own PNG faces too (a texture reload refreshes the held atlas). Precedence of the local player's held object, highest first: charplay.Avatar.Held (Go), held_model of the Avatar child's character component, a non-empty held of that component (a block name; a game with its own inventory sets it from a script, empty gives the hotbar back), the engine hotbar block. Walking sway: the speed that drives the walk cycle is measured over 0.2 s (0.5 s for scene characters), so the arm does not jitter at any frame rate. Your own character, from scratch Use data, never a script, for the body, the arm and the hand: Draw a .vox with named parts ( head , torso , arm_r , arm_l , leg_r , leg_l , optional pivot.hand ) or a 64x64 skin, and set it on the Avatar child of your player prefab variant ( model , skin , scale ). The first-person arm is that model's arm_r ; tune it with fp_offset , fp_rot and fp_scale . Hold a custom object with held_model (a .vox ), or leave the hotbar block (textured, tinted like the icons). From an empty project ( burrow new mygame --template empty ), write assets/prefabs/hero_player.prefab : { "version" : 1 , "nodes" :[{ "id" : 1 , "name" : "Player" , "components" :{ "prefab.instance" :{ "prefab" : "builtin:player.prefab" , "overrides" :[ { "path" : "Avatar" , "component" : "character" , "fields" :{ "model" : "assets/hero.vox" , "held_model" : "assets/tool.vox" , "fp_offset" :[ 0.3 ,- 0.25 ,- 0.3 ], "fp_rot" :[ 60 , 10 , 0 ], "fp_scale" : 0.8 }}]}}}]} then burrow config set runtime.player_prefab assets/prefabs/hero_player.prefab , check with burrow test and look at the arm and the held object with burrowplay -shot out.png -frames 30 -freeze (run in the project folder; the player starts in first person). The arm and the held object are drawn in the render hook with the interpolated camera, so they never jitter. A script updates a node at the simulation rate (20 Hz): do not move a node from a script to fake a viewmodel, and do not push blocks to the hotbar to show them in hand. The character component { "id" : 2 , "name" : "Hero" , "components" : { "transform" : { "pos" : { "x" : 0 , "y" : 9 , "z" : 0 }, "rot" : { "x" : 0 , "y" : 0 , "z" : 0 }, "scale" : { "x" : 1 , "y" : 1 , "z" : 1 }}, "character" : { "model" : "humanoid" , "skin" : "assets/skins/me.png" , "scale" : 1 , "held" : "stone" , "anim" : "" , "speed" : 1 , "hidden" : false }}} model : humanoid , humanoid_slim , voxel_hero or a .vox asset path; skin : a 64x64 PNG asset (empty = built-in); scale : 0.05..20 (0 = 1); variant : the layer set of a layered .vox / .bmodel model (antlers, a collar, shorn wool: each part is built from the variant's replacement model; empty or unknown = default); recolor : palette changes of a .vox model ( 3=#c02020,7=#2060d0 , see modeling.md ) for colour variants of one animal or villager without a new file; held : a block name; held_model : a .vox asset held instead of a block (its longest side is 1 block, times held_scale ); fp_offset / fp_rot / fp_scale : the first-person arm and held object in camera space (right, up, forward is -Z; rotation in degrees pitch, yaw, roll; all zero = the defaults 0.30,-0.20,-0.20 , 70,16,-6 , 0.7 ); fp_sway / fp_bob : multipliers of the first-person walking arm swing and bob (0 = 1, negative = off, max 3; the swing of an attack or place clip is not scaled); anim : see above; speed : animation rate (0 = 1); hidden . It is a normal schema component: saved in .voxscn , validated (unknown animation or a negative scale is refused), shown by the inspector with tooltips and ranges, undoable, and editable by the editor agent with the generic tools ( editor_create_node with components , editor_set_component , editor_remove_component ); no dedicated MCP tool is needed. Registering a component is part of the simulation configuration and changes StateHash . To keep the hashes of existing projects, a game registers character only when runtime.plugins.character is explicitly true or its default scene uses it (the editor always registers it). The avatar and the animation themselves never change the hash (test TestAnimationDoesNotTouchStateHash ). Fill light At low sun a character can turn into a black silhouette. env.post fill_light (0..2, see lighting.md ) adds a real light to the character meshes ( character.Subject.Fill ): a warm directional fill from the camera side (above and slightly left of the view) plus a cool rim (back light, fresnel-like edge, pow(1 - n.v, 3) ), both scaled by the strength and added to the lighting before albedo. It lives in the built-in mesh shaders ( mesh.frag , mesh_hdr.frag ; the strength travels in Material.Params[0] , so materials with a custom shader ignore it), costs a few ALU per pixel and does not touch the simulation. It applies to scene characters and to the player avatar (third person and the first-person arm). The soft renderer draws no characters. Pair it with exposure for a menu backdrop. Editor panel Tools > Character editor is a full-screen tool like the model editor. The header shows the node, undo/redo, the view (Orbit, First person, Back, Front), Turntable , Frame (F) and a menu. The rail on the left has Select a part (V: click a part of the preview), Pose (R: drag rotates the selected part; an editor-only pose, never saved, with a Reset pose chip), Paint the skin (P: opens the skin in the texture editor) and Attach a held item (H: pick the held block). The centre is the isolated 3D preview (left or right drag orbits, middle drag or Shift+right drag pans, wheel zooms, F frames it; drawn by the GPU at the panel's own pixel size, with the render/soft CPU renderer only for headless runs) above the Animations strip: a card per clip (length, loop, progress of the playing one), a click plays it, and Open in the animation editor . Character settings has three tabs: Body (model cards for the built-ins and the project's .vox assets, scale, height, eye height, preview walk speed, held items), Skin (64x64 thumbnail, Edit, New, Import) and Motion (walk speed, animation speed, loop). With no character node selected the preview still works and an empty-state card offers Create character node / Add to selection . Every change to a node is one undo step. Limits The first-person arm is depth tested against the terrain, so it clips into a wall you press against. No inverse kinematics, no foot planting on slopes, no cloth or secondary motion, no per-part tint, no capes. The sandbox controller has no crouch or swim physics of its own: crouch is visual, swim follows FrameState . Skins are 64x64 only (no 64x32 legacy skins) and are not downloaded. The player is rendered from the controller state of the frame: another player or NPC needs a character node. The Vulkan shadow of the character depends on the renderer's sun shadow settings (unchanged here). The player is an entity The first person player is a node of the scene, an instance of a prefab you can override. Defining the player (one path) A player is game.mode (what the scene wants) plus a player prefab (what the player is). Everything else is a fallback for projects without a game.mode ; first match wins. Question 1. Scene 2. Project 3. Engine Which prefab? explicit scene_spawn_player.prefab game.mode.player_prefab , then runtime.player_prefab builtin:player.prefab Where? game.mode.spawns + spawn_tag (picked by spawn_pick ), then game.mode.spawn runtime.start above the terrain at the origin scene.ResolveSpawn and scene.PlayerPrefabPath are the only implementations; the controller, a scene switch and a session join all call them. A node you build by hand with physics.character and a script is a creature, not a player: it gets no camera, input or capabilities. Give the scene a game.mode and a prefab variant instead. All three walkers (the player, physics.character and remote players) are one function, physics/walker.Step , with the same defaults: gravity 32, terminal speed 78, jump 1.25 blocks, sneak edge reach 0.6; a player steps 1.05 (only where shaped blocks exist), a creature takes its own step_height . Prefab. The player is spawned from builtin:player.prefab (engine prefab, shipped in the binary; builtinprefabs.List() ): a root Player with the player component ( id , mode walk/fly, eye ) and the tag player , and a child Camera with an active render.camera at eye height. A scene chooses another with the game.mode component ( player_prefab , spawn ); without one, runtime.player_prefab in vox.project applies, else the built-in. A project prefab is usually a variant : a file holding one node with a prefab.instance link to builtin:player.prefab and overrides (for example {"path":"Camera","component":"transform","fields":{"pos":[0,2,0]}} ); add scripts or children with add overrides. Spawn. The controller spawns player 0 on its first frame (journaled scene_spawn_player ) at game.mode.spawn (a node path; its position and yaw), else runtime.start , else above the terrain. In a session every PlayerJoin spawns one instance ( Player<id> , inactive camera) and a leave despawns it. A scene switch keeps the players and respawns them from the new scene's prefab and spawn point. In the editor, Play spawns the node and Stop discards it. Pose. In single player the controller mirrors its feet position, yaw, pitch and mode into the node with the journaled, quantized scene_player_pose command, so the node is hashed, replayed and snapshotted. In a session the pose stays frame domain (each peer owns its camera); the node stays at the spawn point. The view itself uses the controller's interpolated pose and FOV (the player camera node is rendered with app.FrameState ), so camera rigs keep working. The camera height comes from the prefab's Camera node. Scripts. burrowsdk.Player(id) / burrowsdk.LocalPlayer() return the node; FindTag("player", 0) finds all. Avatar. The prefab has a child Avatar with a character component (model, skin, scale). A variant changes the model with an override ( {"path":"Avatar","component":"character","fields":{"model":"voxel_hero"}} ). The character plugin draws the body from that node (mesh entities are the node, so the editor selects it), driven by the player's animator; first person hides it. A prefab without an Avatar child falls back to the frame-domain avatar at the controller's pose. The character component is registered by default ( runtime.plugins.character: false turns it off; the built-in prefab then loads without it). Capabilities What the player may do is data on the player node, read every frame by the controller (all hashed, so a replay agrees). The absent component means the capability is off ; builtin:player.prefab carries every one with today's behaviour, and a variant overrides fields or removes the component. A player without a node (bare simulations) keeps everything on. Component Fields player.move walk , fly , walk_speed , fly_speed , sprint , sprint_mul , crouch , jump , jump_height , step_height , gravity_scale , swim , fly_toggle ( both / key / double_tap / none ), no_climb (ladders and vines cannot be climbed). A zero number takes the controller default. Neither walk nor fly : the player cannot move. player.build break , place , reach , blocks (names that may be placed, empty = any), protect (names that cannot be broken), repeat (hold to repeat) player.interact block (doors, buttons, block logic), node (nodes with interact ), reach player.inventory slots (0..9 usable hotbar slots), creative (the creative panel), items (block names of the first slots at spawn) player.controls input_map (project path of an input map) player.impulse vel (m/s), seq ; not on the built-in prefab, a script adds it (see Impulses) Climbing. Inside a ladder, vine or rope cell (a non-solid block whose name contains ladder , vine or rope : the rule nav agents use with can_climb ) a walking player goes up at 2.35 m/s with forward or jump, down with back or the down key, holds its height while sneaking and otherwise slides down at 2 m/s at most, slower than a hard landing, so no landing hit or fall damage follows. player.move.no_climb turns it off. Entities. The controller collides with the voxels and, once wired with entcollide , with solid entities: physics.body (not triggers), physics.character creatures and physics3d rigid bodies and voxel bodies, each as an axis-aligned box (rotated bodies by their rotated extent). Sweeps stop at the first box face (no tunnelling), a box that overlaps the player is pushed out along the shortest axis (at most 0.15 m per physics step), and you can stand on a box. The player node and its children never collide with the player, nor does a node tagged player_passthrough . Wire it with ctl.SetEntityBoxes(entcollide.Source(engine, schema)) (package app/entcollide ; app itself cannot import physics). Impulses. player.impulse pushes the player: write vel (m/s, x y z) and a new seq and the controller adds vel to its velocity once per seq (knockback, jump pads). From Go scripts burrowsdk.PlayerImpulse(player, [3]float64{0, 9, 0}) bumps the seq for you. The component is hashed and replayed like the other player data, and a project that never writes it keeps its state hash. A controller that first sees a node only records its seq , so a loaded game does not replay an old push. Controls. The input map in use is the local player's player.controls.input_map , else the scene's game.mode.input_map , else the project's input_map . Switching scene or player prefab switches the map ( input/controls , frame domain). Spawn points ( game.mode ): spawns (node paths) and spawn_tag , spawn_pick ( round_robin by player id | random , seeded by the engine seed | farthest from the other players). Health, death and respawn are the game's rules, not the engine's. The engine has no hit points, lives, respawn delay or kill plane ( player.health and the lives , respawn_delay , respawn_at , kill_plane and kill_y fields of game.mode were removed, along with the scene_player_hurt / die / respawn / checkpoint / rules commands and the player.died and player.respawned events). Keep the values in the game's own state (a Go game: Ctx.State ), decide in your tick, and put the player back with a pose ( scene_player_pose , Ctx.SetPos ). Scenes and prefabs saved with the removed component or fields still load: they are dropped on load, and burrow migrate removes them from the files. The level settings.kill_y and bounds of the levels plugin return an actor that leaves the level to the level's default spawn (a plain teleport). Scene switch. Players survive a switch. A scene root with the same name as a kept player (for example Player ) is renamed Player_scene (then Player_scene2 , ...) when it loads; the player keeps its name. Hooks for sound and effects (frame domain, on app.Controller ): OnFootstep(pos, ground, sprinting) every ~1.9 voxels walked, OnJump , OnLand(pos, ground, speed) , OnBreak , OnPlace . Player id 0 is the local player; in a session it is the netsim player id ( Controller.PlayerID ).

Concepts Two domains frame domain (variable dt) simulation domain (fixed 20 Hz, deterministic) OS input, window, render, UI, editor, sim.Engine: ECS world, voxel chunks, block registry, agents, chunk streaming workers seeded RNG, journal, snapshots, undo | Commands (queue) ---------------> Do(cmd): journaled, hashed, replayable | read-only View <--------------- StateHash, blocks, components The simulation is everything that defines the game state: components, voxels, scripts, physics. It advances in fixed ticks of 50 ms ( FixedUpdate systems). StateHash summarises it. The frame domain reads the simulation through a read-only View and changes it only by queueing Commands (set a block, spawn a node, set a component). Commands are applied between ticks and recorded in the journal . Input is frame-domain data. To affect the game it must become a journaled command or component: the controller turns clicks into SetBlock commands; script.Plugin turns changed input actions into a script_set_input command that scripts read. Determinism rules Inside the simulation (FixedUpdate systems, commands, scripts): no wall clock, no global math/rand (use Sim.Rand() / the script rand_u64 ), no map-iteration order, no goroutines, no I/O; all state lives in registered components and voxels (components must be hashable); anything else is a derived cache; register the same components, commands and systems on every engine: they are part of the replay configuration; scripts run only in FixedUpdate , with no clock, files or network, deterministic gas metering and a reset memory image for every call (see scripting.md ). The engine enforces most of this (frame code cannot reach sim state; a failing tick rolls back completely). The result: same seed + same journal + same systems = same StateHash , for any GOMAXPROCS . Across machines it holds on macOS Apple silicon and Intel (tested). Windows and Linux are checked by the CI workflow against a golden hash, which has not run yet. The simulation uses integer math or explicitly rounded floats with a deterministic math library; rendering is not covered. See Determinism . Journal and replay Every applied command is appended to the journal ( tick , kind , JSON data ). app.VerifyReplay() rebuilds a fresh engine from app.ReplayConfig() , re-applies the journal and requires the same hash. This is how undo history, editor sessions, agent sessions and burrow test prove they are exact. burrowplay -headless -ticks 200 -journal j.json -hash mygame # tick=200 StateHash=ab12... burrowplay -replay j.json -expect ab12... mygame # exit 0 only if the replay matches The journal also carries the world identity (seed + generator parameters), so replaying it against a different world is an error instead of a silent divergence. Terrain: base + overlay The world is a pure base terrain , a function (seed, generator, chunk position) -> chunk that is never stored, plus a sparse overlay of edited chunks. Reads see the overlay, then the base, then air. Writes copy a chunk into the overlay. The base lives in an evictable cache and is not state; the overlay is what is hashed, snapshotted, journaled and saved. Streaming ( VoxelWorldPlugin ) only warms the cache and meshes chunks for the GPU, so the load radius cannot change a hash. A .voxworld file is the overlay plus the base identity: "VXWORLD" , header (seed, generator hash, block names), zlib chunks, SHA-256. Loading one onto a different seed or generator is refused. Each scene has its own ( scenes/x.voxscn uses scenes/x.voxworld , written by the editor's Save); runtime.world in vox.project is the older project-wide file. The generator comes from runtime.generator : heightmap (fBm hills, optional caves, trees) or flat . Scenes and components A scene ( .voxscn , JSON) is a forest of nodes. Each node has an id, a name, an optional parent and components: { "id" : 2 , "name" : "spinner" , "parent" : 1 , "components" : { "transform" : { "pos" : [ 8 , 11 , 8 ], "rot" : [ 0 , 0 , 0 ], "scale" : [ 1 , 1 , 1 ] }, "render.mesh" : { "mesh" : "cube" , "cast_shadow" : true }, "script" : { "module" : "assets/scripts/spin.wasm" , "props" : { "speed" : 90 } } } } Components are described by a schema (name, fields, types, ranges, tooltips), which drives validation, the editor inspector and scripts. Built-ins: transform , script , physics.body , physics.velocity , physics.character , render.camera , render.dirlight , render.pointlight , render.mesh , render.sprite , render.voxmodel , render.material . Register your own with burrow.RegisterComponent (simulation state) and burrow.RegisterSceneComponent (schema entry). Prefabs are scene documents instantiated with overrides. Node tree changes are scene commands ( scene_spawn , scene_set_component , ...), so they are journaled like voxel edits. Plugins and stages A game is an App plus plugins. Systems run in stages: Startup , then per frame PreUpdate , FixedUpdate (N ticks), Update , PostUpdate , Render , then Shutdown . Ordering inside a stage uses Before / After names. The built-in plugins are ScenePlugin , WindowPlugin , VoxelWorldPlugin , ControllerPlugin , RenderPlugin , RenderWorldPlugin , SoftRenderPlugin , DebugPlugin , physics.PhysicsPlugin , input.InputPlugin , assets.Plugin and script.Plugin ; burrowplay assembles them from vox.project . The complete rules are in ARCHITECTURE.md . A complete headless game with one FixedUpdate system, run twice, shows the guarantee: package main import ( "fmt" "os" "burrow-engine" ) func build() *burrow.App { app := burrow.NewApp(burrow.Options{Seed: 42 , StrictCommands: true }) app.AddFixedSystem( "tower" , func (c *burrow.FixedContext) error { if c.Tick < 8 { c.Commands.SetBlock(burrow.IVec3{X: 0 , Y: int32 (c.Tick), Z: 0 }, "stone" ) } return nil }) return app } func main() { a, b := build(), build() for _, app := range []*burrow.App{a, b} { if err := app.RunHeadless( 20 ); err != nil { fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err) os.Exit( 1 ) } } if a.StateHash() != b.StateHash() { fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "not deterministic" ) os.Exit( 1 ) } if err := burrow.VerifyReplay(a); err != nil { fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err) os.Exit( 1 ) } fmt.Printf( "tick=%d StateHash=%016x\n" , a.Tick(), a.StateHash()) }

Dedicated server burrow-server is a headless server for Burrow multiplayer : it hosts one game, keeps the world on disk and runs until you stop it. Players join with burrowplay -connect , exactly as for burrow serve , but nobody has to keep a game window open. Contents What it is Quick start Data directory server.json Commands Admin control Large servers Saves and game changes Lobby mode Deploying Firewall and ports Backups and restore Upgrading the game Security notes Limits What it is Headless. No window, no GPU, no audio. It runs on any small Linux VPS. cgo-free. A single static binary ( CGO_ENABLED=0 ); it cross-builds for Linux, macOS and Windows with make server-dist . Persistent world. The world is restored from world/world.snap at start and saved on a timer, on save and on shutdown. Same protocol as burrow serve . Clients need nothing special; see Networking . Quick start burrow-server init --data ./srv --project ../mygame # writes srv/server.json and the TLS certificate burrow-server run --data ./srv # starts the server on :7777 burrow-server ctl --data ./srv link # prints the join link (from another terminal) --project is a path relative to the data directory: a project directory or a .voxpak . Give the join link to your players. Data directory Everything the server writes lives in one directory ( --data , default . ): path content server.json the configuration ( below ) join.key the generated join password, mode 0600 (only when no password is set) cert/ server.crt and server.key (mode 0600 ): the TLS identity, created by init world/world.snap the current world snapshot world/meta.json metadata of the world: seed, tick, save time, engine version, project name and content hash world/backups/world-<UTC timestamp>.snap rotated backups players.json roster {"players": {"<key>": {"id": N, "name": "last name"}}} . The key is the player's identity id (anonymous players: name:<lowercased name> ), so a player keeps its id after renaming and a name owned by one identity is refused to others. The old {"ids": {...}} format is migrated on start bans.json banned names, identities ( identities ) and addresses whitelist.json allowed names or identity ids control.sock unix socket of the admin control, mode 0600 server.json burrow-server init writes the defaults. Unknown fields are an error. field default meaning project none game to host, path relative to the data directory: a project directory or a .voxpak world "world" directory of the world, relative to the data directory addr ":7777" listen address (TCP, TLS) advertise "" host:port written in the join link; set it to the public name when it differs from addr password "" join password. Empty and open false: a random key is generated once and kept in join.key open false true accepts players without any password max_players 16 players connected at the same time: at most 1024 view 0 (default) view distance in chunks of each player ( Replication ) bytes_per_second 0 (default) bandwidth budget per player migrate false start a saved world after the game lost a component, dropping its saved values (see Saves and game changes ) seed 0 world seed; 0 means the project's. Ignored once a world exists: the world's seed wins autosave_minutes 5 autosave period; 0 disables it backups 5 rotated backup copies kept motd "" chat line sent by the server whenever a player joins (at most 200 bytes) whitelist false only names or identities in whitelist.json may join mode "persistent" "persistent" : the world is restored, autosaved and saved on shutdown (a survival-style server). "lobby" : matches (see Lobby mode ). claim_anonymous false let the first identity that joins with a name take the anonymous roster entry of that name. Off by default, because anybody could claim someone else's past; use the claim command instead require_identity true from init ; false when absent reject clients without an identity key ( <config dir>/burrow/identity.key , created by the client) The environment variable BURROW_SERVE_PASSWORD overrides password . Commands burrow-server init [--data DIR] --project PATH write DIR/server.json with defaults (fails if it exists), create cert burrow-server run [--data DIR] [--config FILE] [--addr A] [--advertise H:P] [--password P | --open] [--max-players N] burrow-server ctl [--data DIR] <command...> send an admin command to the running server burrow-server version --data defaults to . ; --config defaults to DIR/server.json . The flags of run override the file. init fails if server.json already exists. ctl talks to the unix socket DIR/control.sock . Signals: SIGTERM and SIGINT save the world, then stop. On start the world is restored from world.snap , and players still marked connected (after a crash) are marked left. The journal is trimmed before each save so snapshots stay small. Admin control The same commands work on the console (stdin, when the server runs in a terminal) and through burrow-server ctl : command effect list connected players status JSON: project, tick, players, max players, uptime, last save, motd, whitelist, require_identity, connected players with their identity ids, certificate fingerprint, engine link print the join link say <text> message to every player kick <name> [reason] disconnect a player ban <name> [reason] ban the identity of the known player with that name (an anonymous one: the name) and kick it ban-ip <addr> ban an address pardon <name|identity|addr> lift a ban claim <name> <identity id> bind an anonymous player's roster entry (its id, so its per-player state) to an identity; the player sees the exact command when the server refuses its name whitelist on|off|add <name|identity>|remove <name|identity>|list manage the whitelist lobby the lobby state as JSON (games with runtime.lobby ) lobby start|cancel|return start the countdown, cancel it, go back to the lobby after a match (the server acts as player 0, always an authority) lobby end [results JSON] end the running match lobby set <key> <value> change a game setting voice mute <name> mute a player's voice chat for everyone; kept across reconnects until lifted ( voice chat ) voice unmute <name> lift a voice mute voice status voice relaying on/off, frame counters (in, out, dropped, refused, malformed) and muted players, as JSON save save the world now (persistent mode only) stop save and stop control.sock is mode 0600 : whoever can open it is an admin, so only the user running the server (and root) can use ctl . Large servers The server alone simulates ( Replication ), and each player receives only the chunks and entities around it, so a server holds up to 1024 players and a big world. Tune view and bytes_per_second ; roughly 300 busy players per core at 20 ticks per second, about 100 KB/s per player in a busy area and a few hundred bytes per second in a quiet one. Lobby mode works the same way: the lobby state is replicated to every client. Saves and game changes The world restored at start must fit the game. A component the game gained is added empty (logged). A component the game lost would lose its saved values: the server refuses to start with the saved world holds component data the game no longer has: <component> (<n> values) . Restore the previous component name, set "migrate": true in server.json to drop that data (the previous save stays in world/backups ), or move the world directory away for a new world. A plugin turned on or off (lobby, weather, fluid) cannot be converted and is named in the error. Lobby mode With "mode": "lobby" the server hosts matches instead of a lasting world, for games with a lobby ( runtime.lobby , see Lobby ): players gather, pick teams and colours, get ready, and the host starts the match. Nothing is saved or restored: every server start is a fresh world. The journal is still trimmed every autosave_minutes . While a match runs (countdown or playing), new players are refused with "a match is running" unless the lobby sets late_join ; players who lost their connection may still come back. A full lobby ( max_players of the lobby, without spectators) refuses new players too. With "host": "server" in the lobby configuration, only the server changes settings and starts matches: use lobby set , lobby start and lobby end (from ctl , or from a script of your own). With "host": "first" the first player hosts. The world is not reset between matches by the server: the game does it when the match starts (load the map level, see Loading the chosen map ). Deploying systemd deploy/install.sh (also in the server-dist archives) does it all, on Linux as root: sudo sh deploy/install.sh ./burrow-server ./mygame # or ./mygame.voxpak It creates the system user burrow , /var/lib/burrow-server (mode 0750 ), copies the binary to /usr/local/bin , the game to /var/lib/burrow-server/game , runs init if server.json is missing, then installs, enables and starts burrow-server.service . It is safe to run again (to update the binary or the game). The unit is hardened ( ProtectSystem=strict , no capabilities, restricted address families) and reads optional settings from /etc/burrow-server.env , for example BURROW_SERVE_PASSWORD=... . sudo systemctl status burrow-server sudo journalctl -u burrow-server -f sudo runuser -u burrow -- burrow-server ctl --data /var/lib/burrow-server link Docker make server-image # docker build -f deploy/docker/Dockerfile -t burrow-server . mkdir -p data && cp -R ./mygame data/game && sudo chown -R 65532 data docker compose -f deploy/docker/compose.yaml run --rm burrow-server init --data /data --project game docker compose -f deploy/docker/compose.yaml up -d The image is distroless, runs as nonroot (uid 65532), keeps everything in the /data volume and exposes 7777/tcp . The game goes to /data/game , either copied into the volume as above or mounted: -v /path/to/mygame:/data/game:ro (or a single file, -v /path/mygame.voxpak:/data/game.voxpak:ro with --project game.voxpak ). The compose file gives the server 30 s to save on docker stop . Admin commands: docker compose exec burrow-server /burrow-server ctl --data /data status . Plain binary Run burrow-server run --data DIR under any supervisor (tmux, launchd, a Windows service wrapper). The server-dist archives contain builds for Linux amd64/arm64, macOS arm64 and Windows amd64. On Windows (10 1803 and later) the control socket works too, so ctl is available everywhere. Firewall and ports The server listens on one TCP port, 7777 by default ( addr ). Open it inbound: ufw allow 7777/tcp , or the equivalent on your cloud provider's security group and any router in front of the machine. Set advertise to the public host:port so the join link is right behind NAT or a proxy. Backups and restore Autosave rotates backups copies in world/backups/world-<UTC timestamp>.snap . To back up by hand, run save then copy the data directory (or only world/ , players.json , bans.json , whitelist.json , server.json , cert/ and join.key ). To restore: stop the server, copy the chosen world/backups/world-<timestamp>.snap over world/world.snap , start the server. Upgrading the game A world snapshot must match the project that loads it. If you change the components of the game (new, removed or reshaped components), restoring the old snapshot fails with a clear error and the server does not start. Before replacing the game in game/ : stop the server, make a backup of the data directory, replace the game, start. If the start fails, put the previous game back (and the backup if needed). Changes that do not touch components (scripts logic, assets, text) restore normally, but clients must have the same game version to join ( Networking pins). Security notes Identity is a key, a name is only a label. With require_identity (the default of init ) every player proves it owns an ed25519 key, bans and the roster follow the key, and nobody can take a name another identity uses. Anonymous clients (identified by name only, so anyone knowing a name can join as it) are admitted only when require_identity is false, as in a server.json written before this option. Protect the server with the password (the default: a random key in join.key ) and, for a closed group, the whitelist. list and status show identity ids. Treat the join link as a secret. It carries the key; anyone with it can join. Rotate it by changing password (or deleting join.key ) and restarting. TLS. The connection is encrypted with the certificate in cert/ ; clients pin it by fingerprint, which the join link contains. Keep server.key private; if you regenerate the certificate, previous links stop working. --open accepts anyone: use it only on a private network. The admin control is the unix socket only; nothing admin is reachable over the network. Limits Server cost. The server runs the whole simulation and builds one stream per player; clients only draw it, so the weakest player's machine does not limit the game. The player registry keeps up to 1024 players at the same time. Roster ids go up to 65535 : players.json assigns a new id to each new player (identity or anonymous name), so a public server with many one-off identities eventually exhausts them. max_players counts connected players only.

h: Script module bytes must not depend on the build machine
x: Determinism Burrow's central promise: the same project, the same seed and the same inputs give the same StateHash . Same project, seed and inputs give the same StateHash, on macOS Apple silicon and Intel (tested). Windows and Linux are checked by the CI workflow against a golden hash, which has not run yet. The simulation uses integer math or explicitly rounded floats with a deterministic math library; rendering is not covered. The design target is every desktop system and 64-bit CPU (Windows, Linux, macOS; amd64, arm64); what is verified today is stated above and in Platforms . Replays, journals multiplayer and golden tests depend on it. This page says what the promise covers, how it is kept and tested, and the rules that contributors and script authors follow so it stays true. What is covered The simulation domain : everything that runs inside a fixed tick (20 ticks per second) or writes state that StateHash covers. That is the voxel world and world generation, water, weather, the block rules, 2D ( physics ) and 3D ( physics3d ) physics, navigation and AI, animation players, scene components, levels and saves, the input mapping that turns devices into journaled commands, WebAssembly scripts, and the engine and app layers that drive them. It holds bit for bit, not "close enough": the hash covers the exact bits of every integer and float in the state. How the simulation gets there: Integer and fixed-point first. Voxel coordinates, block ids, water levels, timers and counters are integers. Randomness comes from seeded integer hashes (splitmix64), never from math/rand without a seed or from the clock. Fixed order. No goroutines inside a tick, no iteration over Go maps where order matters, ascending entity order, explicit sorts with total keys. Floats only with explicit rounding. IEEE 754 addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and square root are correctly rounded on every CPU, so float math is portable as long as each operation is rounded on its own. Go allows the compiler to fuse x*y + z into one fused multiply-add instruction (FMA) with a single rounding; it does so on arm64 (and ppc64, s390x, riscv64, and amd64 built with GOAMD64=v3 ) but not on default amd64, so the same source gives different bits on two machines. The Go specification forbids fusion across an explicit conversion, so simulation code writes float64(a*b) + c (or float32(a*b) for float32 operands): every product, and every division by a constant (the compiler turns x/2 into x*0.5 ), is rounded before it meets an addition. Deterministic math library. math.Sin , Cos , Tan , Atan2 , Exp , Log , Pow , Hypot and friends are not bit-identical across architectures: some have assembly versions on one CPU only, and the pure Go ones are compiled with fused multiply-adds on arm64. Simulation code calls burrow-engine/mathx/detmath instead: the standard library's own algorithms, ported with every product rounded and no assembly. Results are within 2 ulp of package math (Acos within 4e-16 absolute, Pow within 1e-15 relative), and on amd64 the trigonometric functions are bit-identical to package math . math.Sqrt , Floor , Ceil , Trunc , Round , Abs , Min , Max , Mod , Frexp and Ldexp are exact everywhere and stay. Simulation rate The simulation runs at 20 ticks per second by default. A project can choose 30, 40 or 60 with runtime.tick_rate in vox.project ; the rate is a property of each engine ( sim.Config.TickRate , engine.Options.TickRate , built from the project by internal/simplan for the game, the dedicated server and the editor alike) and cannot change afterwards. There is no process-wide rate and no environment variable in a shipped game. A rate is part of a recording. A journal written at a rate other than 20 carries tick_rate on its first entry and ReplayWith refuses a different rate with an explicit error. A journal without the field is a 20 Hz journal. Snapshots and StateHash of a world are only comparable at the same rate. Everything per tick follows it: the Dt and TickRate of the system context ( sim.Context , engine.FixedContext , App.FixedDt() ), the wall-clock tick of a network session ( netbase.TickInterval(rate) ), the lobby countdown, the thunder delay, the day length of env.time and the movement of replicated players. A duration in seconds keeps its meaning; a count of ticks does not (a timer of 20 ticks is one second at 20 Hz and a third of a second at 60 Hz). Scripts should use AfterSeconds , EverySeconds , Wait(sec) of a Seq and TickDt() . Cost is linear: 60 Hz is three times the simulation work per second of 20 Hz, so the per-tick budget drops from 50 ms to 16.7 ms. Dense rigid-body scenes are the first to exceed it. runtime.physics_substeps refines physics inside a tick without raising the rate of scripts and gameplay, and frame-domain visuals ( OnFrame , visual.* ) smooth what is drawn at any rate. Authored durations are seconds. Behavior-tree wait / cooldown / timeout seconds and state machine after , runtime.saves.autosave_seconds , environment.json day_length and the weather_set day_length are seconds, converted to ticks once at load with the engine rate: mathx.SecondsToTicks rounds half up to the nearest tick and never gives a positive duration less than one tick (0.5 s is 10 ticks at 20 Hz, 30 at 60 Hz). The weather smoothing rates, front durations, wind period and lightning gap are defined at 20 Hz and rescaled the same way (rates to the nearest tick, at least 1: a ramp may differ by about 2 % at 60 Hz); fine-water evaporation is per second of simulated time. Fields named in ticks ( interval , memory , sleep_ticks ) are still ticks. The network handshake pins the rate: sim.tick_rate is one of the pinned rules, so a client at another rate is refused. Tests: BURROW_TICK_RATE=60 go test -tags ratematrix ./... runs the suite at another rate (the tag is the only way the variable is read; it moves the default of engines that do not choose a rate). A test tied to 20 Hz constants declares it with ratetest.Only20(t) (package internal/ratetest ); the others are written in durations. What is not covered The frame domain : rendering, the camera rigs, particles, the in-game UI layout, audio, the character avatar animator, the editor and the Hub. They read the simulation but never write it, so their float math can differ between machines without changing a hash. Two machines show the same world; the pixels may differ by a rounding. Outside the promise as well: NaN bit patterns. A NaN produced on arm64 and on amd64 can carry different payload bits. The simulation keeps state finite (physics clamps and drops non-finite values); a game that lets a NaN into hashed state can diverge. Converting a NaN or an out-of-range float to an integer ( int(x) ) gives different values on amd64 and arm64. Clamp first. Different engine versions. A new version may change the simulation on purpose (the changelog says so); replays are checked with the engine that recorded them. How it is tested Portability golden. scripts/portability-hash.sh ( make portability ) creates the eight templates, runs each headless for 200 ticks and compares the StateHash with scripts/portability-golden.txt . Every CI job runs it, so each operating system and CPU of the matrix is compared with the same golden. On an Apple silicon Mac it runs both the arm64 build and the amd64 build under Rosetta 2. Fused multiply-add guard. internal/detguard compiles the simulation packages for linux/arm64 and for linux/amd64 with GOAMD64=v3 , reads the assembly listing and fails on any fused multiply-add instruction ( FMADDD , FMSUBD , FNMADDD , FNMSUBD , VFMADD231SD , ...) whose source line is in a simulation package, inlined code included. Source guard. The same package type-checks the simulation packages and fails on a float product that is not explicitly rounded and on a call to an architecture dependent function of package math . Math library tests. mathx/detmath is tested for accuracy against package math and against a table of result bits recorded on arm64 and verified on amd64. Finding a divergence. burrowplay -headless -ticks N -hash-every 1 <project> prints the hash after every tick: run it on two machines and diff the output to find the first tick that differs. Rules for contributors In a simulation package (the list is SimPackages in internal/detguard ): Round every float product before it is added or subtracted, and before it is stored, returned or passed on (after inlining, a product stored in a variable can still be fused with an addition elsewhere): float64(a*b) + c , V3{float64(v.X * s), ...} . A product that only feeds another product, a division, a comparison or a conversion needs nothing. Write x = float64(x * s) instead of x *= s . Do the same for a division by a constant: float64(x / 2) . Use detmath.Sin , detmath.Atan2 , detmath.Pow , ... instead of the math functions. Never iterate a map where the order reaches the state; sort with a total key. A line that is provably safe can opt out with a reason: //burrow:fma-ok exact: both factors are small integers . Use it rarely; the reason is reviewed. A new package that runs in the tick goes into SimPackages . go test ./internal/detguard checks rules 1 to 3 in a few seconds. Rules for script authors WebAssembly scripts are deterministic: the WebAssembly specification forbids fused multiply-add and the runtime follows it. Avoid NaN in values you keep, and clamp before converting floats to integers. Go scripts that the engine compiles to WebAssembly get the same guarantee. A Go program that embeds the engine and adds its own simulation systems follows the contributor rules above for those systems. Never read the wall clock, the machine or unseeded randomness from simulation code: use the tick and the seeded burrowsdk.Rand family. Script module bytes must not depend on the build machine The script RNG is seeded from the content hash of the wasm module, so the module bytes are part of the determinism contract. script/guestbuild therefore builds with -trimpath , -X=runtime.modinfo= and -buildid= : the linker build id otherwise hashes the checkout path of a replace d engine, and two machines building the same project got different modules and different StateHashes. make portability builds the templates on each host to catch this.

t: Reading the docs in the editor
h: Reading the docs in the editor
x: Reading the docs in the editor The whole documentation ships inside the editor binary, so it works offline and in exported editor builds. Open it with F1 or Help > Documentation . The Help window area what it does Sidebar the pages in five groups (Start here, Tutorials, Guides, Scripting, Reference); the page you are reading unfolds its second-level headings Page headings, paragraphs, bold, italic and code spans, lists, tables, block quotes, images and fenced code blocks Search box full-text search over every page; results are ranked and the matching words are highlighted in the result and on the page you open Back and forward Alt+Left and Alt+Right ; each page remembers its scroll position Links a link to another page or a heading opens it inside the window; an http or https link opens in your browser Code blocks have a Copy button and a simple colour tint for Go, shell, JSON and TOML. The window follows the dark or light theme of the editor and wraps to its width: resize it freely. Keys inside the window: Ctrl+F focuses the search box, Enter opens the best result, Esc clears the search, Page Up , Page Down , Home and End scroll. Contextual help F1 with the pointer over a panel opens the page that explains that panel; over a component title in the Inspector it opens that component in the component reference . With nothing under the pointer it opens the index. Shift+F1 is the shortcut cheat sheet. Every panel header has a ? button that does the same. Hover a component title or a field name in the Inspector for its description, field type, range and default. Descriptions come from the schema, then from the doc comments of the Go types, so the tooltip and the reference always agree. The generated reference Eight pages under docs/reference/ are produced from the code, never edited by hand: page source components the scene component schema (fields, types, ranges, defaults) and the doc comments of the component types script API the host function table of script/ABI.md and the exported functions of sdk/burrowsdk MCP tools the tool registry of the editor server (parameters, enums, ranges) command line the command table and flag definitions of burrow , burrowplay and burrowedit project file the structs of assets/project , including every runtime.* section input actions input/core.DefaultMap blocks the block set ( blockset/blocks.json ) render options shader levels, anti-aliasing, upscalers, ray tracing and look presets After changing any of those sources run: make docs-gen go test ./docs fails with the list of stale pages when a committed page no longer matches the code, and also checks that every link, heading anchor and image of every page resolves. For AI agents The same pages are served by two read-only MCP tools, available in every editor mode: editor_docs_search {query, limit} returns ranked sections: page, heading, anchor, snippet. editor_docs_read {page, anchor} returns a page, or only the section under one heading, as Markdown. Without arguments it lists every page. Writing documentation Pages are Markdown files in docs/ ; tutorials live in docs/tutorials/ and are listed in the index . Write original text and keep one idea per page. Link with relative paths: [levels](levels-saves.md#the-level-file) . An anchor is the heading in lower case with spaces turned into hyphens and punctuation dropped. Images go to docs/img/ . Only editor-* , tut-* and help-* PNGs are embedded in the binary (large renderer galleries stay on disk and show a placeholder in the editor), so name tutorial screenshots tut-<topic>.png and keep them small. Produce them with the editor self-test or the soft renderer and look at each one before you commit it. Go code blocks in the top-level docs/*.md files must compile; mark an illustrative snippet with go nocheck . Never edit docs/reference/*.md . Not done yet The documentation is English only. A French translation (a docs/fr/ tree and a language switch in the Help window) is future work; the library already treats a page path as its identity, so a second tree fits without changing the renderer.

Every edit is a journaled ApplyVoxels command, so strokes are deterministic, undoable and replayable; agents reach all of it through editor_tool_apply ( tool raise, lower, flatten, smooth, ramp, surface, replace, extrude, scatter; strength , hardness , surface_only , radial , seed , density , kind , from , level , amount , invert , dry_run to get the count and bounds without writing) and editor_selection_op replace .
