A body must have a layer bit ( rigidbody.layer ) that the query mask includes, or it is invisible to queries; mask 0 = every layer LoadLevel(id, spawn) , CurrentLevel() , LevelSpawns() , LevelZoneAt(x, y, z) , LevelSettings() hand-built levels (needs plugins.levels ). LoadLevel is a request: the file is read in the background and applied by a journaled command when ready, so the level changes a few frames later, not in the same tick. Positions are in world blocks BlockData(x,y,z) , SetBlockData , DeleteBlockData , ScheduleBlock(x,y,z, delay, every) , UnscheduleBlock , DueBlocks() a string bound to a cell (fuel of a furnace, content of a chest) and cells delivered on a schedule (needs plugins.blocks ). The data belongs to the block the cell holds when written and is hashed and saved with the world; DueBlocks returns the cells due this tick, once, in due-tick then position order. Block change/break/use events are not delivered to Go games yet PlayAnim(node, clip, AnimOpts{Mode, Queue, Fade}) , StopAnim , SetAnimSpeed , SetAnimParam , TriggerAnim , AnimTime the node's anim.player (simulation state, journaled). Queue waits behind a playing clip; Fade > 0 crossfades and keeps the queue, Fade == 0 cuts and clears it. An unknown clip name plays nothing NavGoal(node, x, y, z, slack) , NavStop , NavState , NavPath , SetBlackboard , Blackboard , DeleteBlackboard , NavSensed navigation and AI of a node ( nav.agent , ai.brain , ai.perception ; plugin nav ). A goal is a journaled component write; the path is computed inside later ticks from a queue with a budget, so the node starts moving a few ticks after NavGoal . The blackboard holds numbers here (the typed values of the WebAssembly call are not exposed) Parent(node) , ScenePath(node) , FindWith(component, root) scene tree reads; FindWith scans depth first (root 0 = whole scene, at most 65,536 nodes) and fails the run for an unknown component Field(node, component, path) , FieldNum , SetField(node, component, path, v) one field of a component by path ( pos[0] , bodies[2].mass ); writes send the whole component back through the schema, so it is validated like Set BlockEvents() block events since the last call (a cell changed, or a player used a block); the first call turns collection on, so call it in the first tick. Needs plugins.blocks ; fluids do not produce events FloodBlocks(x,y,z, through, ends, max) the network of conductor cells connected to a start cell (cables, pipes), breadth first in a fixed order; needs no plugin SetLevelZone(name, min, max, props) , DeleteLevelZone(name) zones made by the game in world blocks (simulation state, cleared by a level load); LevelZoneAt finds them after the level's own ParticleEmit(node, count) , ParticleStop(node) extra particles from a node's emitter; stop one emitter (0 = clear all) FluidAmount , FluidPour , FluidDrain ( FluidUnitsPerBlock = 64) water volume of a cell (needs plugins.fluid ); the water then flows by the automaton's rules SetBlackboardValue , BlackboardValue ( BBNum , BBVec , BBNode , BBStr ) typed blackboard values SwitchScene(path) replace the whole running scene (nodes and voxel world) by another .voxscn of the project; served at the end of the tick, one per tick WorldInfo() (WorldInfo, bool) slot, name, free-text mode, seed, generator of the world the game was started on Light.Level(skyDim) the one brightness a rule such as "mobs spawn in the dark" reads Tags(e) , HasTag , AddTag , RemoveTag , Children(e) , Has(e, component) scene tree helpers State(key, &v) , SetState(key, v) , StateOf[T](c, key) , StateBytes/SetStateBytes/DeleteState the game state, see below Frame (OnFrame): Dt , Frame , Tick , Alpha (0..1 between ticks), Find(name) , VisualSet/VisualAdd(node, target, v) (render-only overlay, targets of visual.bind ; write it every frame), Key(name) , FreeCursor() , Quit() , Context() . While the immediate-mode UI holds the mouse, mouse-button actions read as false in Ctx.Action (the flag is journaled, so replays agree). Game state Package variables are not saved or rolled back, so a game keeps its rules (inventory, timers, quests, health, hunger) in Ctx.State : named values stored in one simulation component. They are hashed, snapshotted, saved, rolled back and replayed with the world, with no node and no script. Values are JSON ( SetState / State / StateOf ) or raw bytes ( SetStateBytes / StateBytes , for a binary format of your own). Limits: 256 keys, 1 MiB per key, 4 MiB in all; unchanged writes cost nothing. Use structs, not maps, in JSON you hash. The engine gives the state no meaning: health, death and respawn are rules of the game, written in OnTick . Multiplayer note: the whole state is one component value, and a server sends a component value only when its JSON is at most 64 KiB ( wire.MaxCompData ; bytes are base64, so about 48 KiB of blobs). A game whose state is larger works the same in solo and on the authoritative side, but its state is not mirrored to remote clients; keep what a client must read small. type Vitals struct { HP, Food int } OnTick: func (c *gogame.Ctx) { v := gogame.StateOf[Vitals](c, "vitals" ) if c.ActionPressed( "eat" ) { v.Food++ } _ = c.SetState( "vitals" , v) } Network games A Go game can run as a dedicated server and be played from the game's own window. There is no listen server: nobody hosts from a window. ./game -init-server ./srv # writes srv/server.json and the TLS certificate (Game.Dir is the project) ./game -serve ./srv # prints "join link: burrow://host:7777?fp=...&key=..." ./game -connect "burrow://..." -name ana Game.NetScene is the scene the server runs and the clients follow. The server alone runs OnTick ; a client runs only frame systems ( OnFrame , UI ) on the replicated copy, and a dedicated server runs neither. So: Loop over c.Players() in OnTick (one player, id 0, when the game is played alone), read a player's input with c.ActionOf(p, name) (in a session an action is a button bit: move gives the axes, the scroll wheel reaches the server in one direction only; at most 30 bit actions), and keep per-player data in c.SetPlayerBytes(p.ID, key, b) . Per-player data is replicated to its owner only (component gogame.pdata , tag owner:<id> , at most 64 KiB of JSON per player in all) and saved with the world. A client reads its own with Frame.PlayerBytes(key) . What a player must see (HUD values, lists, screens) is written by OnTick into the player's data and played by OnFrame with Frame.UISet , UISetItems , UIShow , UIHide , CameraShake , CameraCut , ParticleBurst . UIEvents() events carry Player : the server stamps the sender on every gameui_event . The world seed pins the handshake: the client's -seed (default the project's) must match the server's. Terrain: Game.Generator runtime.generator in vox.project picks one of the engine terrains ( biomes , heightmap , flat , empty ). To add features of your own (ores that are not in the engine, ruins, a village) or to replace the terrain, set Game.Generator : a function that receives the generator the project describes and returns the one the world uses. gogame.Main(gogame.Game{ Generator: func (base worldgen.Generator) worldgen.Generator { return &worldgen.Decorated{ Base: base, ID: "mygame-ores/v1" , // bump it when Decorate changes what it generates Decorate: func (ctx worldgen.DecorateCtx, c *voxel.Chunk) { tin, ok := ctx.Reg.ID( "tin_ore" ) // resolve names here, on the first chunk, not earlier if !ok { return } // write only voxels of this chunk, from a hash of (ctx.Seed, ctx.Pos) c.Set( 5 , 12 , 5 , tin) }, } }, // ... }) worldgen.Decorated keeps what the base terrain offers (chunk layers, registry binding, far-terrain sampling, the biome tint) and adds DecorateCtx.Surface(x, z) , the base terrain height in a column, for placing something on the ground from every chunk it overlaps. Rules: the generator is a pure function of (seed, chunk position) , safe for concurrent use, with no clock, global state or other random source; a feature wider than a chunk is computed by each chunk it overlaps, from a position hash, and each writes only its own voxels. ID (and ChangesSilhouette , true for a feature that changes the ground seen from afar) are part of the world identity: change the ID whenever the decoration changes, because a saved world would otherwise mix two versions. A generator of your own works too: implement Generate(seed, chunkPos) *voxel.Chunk , WorldID() string and, to receive the registry, WithRegistry(*voxel.Registry) worldgen.Generator . base is nil when the project has no runtime.generator section. imui reference ( burrow-engine/gameui/imui ) Immediate-mode UI drawn on a render/canvas.Canvas : call widgets every frame, get their result back at once. gogame runs it for you after the declarative game UI; for other hosts call Begin and End yourself. API Meaning New(theme *gameui.Theme) *UI nil theme = "dark" Begin(cv, in Input, w, h) , End() frame bracket; Input{MouseX, MouseY, Down, Pressed, Released, Text, Backspace, Enter, Escape} Window(title, fn) centered, dimmed backdrop, sized to content (a first-frame measure pass runs the body once, idle) Panel(id, rect, fn) fixed screen rectangle; captures the mouse Row(fn) , Column(fn) , Spacer(px) layout; the default flow is a column Label(text) , Image(path, w, h) , ProgressBar(frac) display ( UI.LoadImage resolves image paths; gogame wires the project files) Button(label) bool , ButtonID(id, label) bool true on click (press and release on it) Checkbox(label, *bool) bool , Slider(label, *float32, min, max) bool , TextInput(id, *string) bool true when the value changed Captures() bool , Open() bool mouse over the UI / a Window is shown (gogame frees the cursor then) Emit(name, value) send a signal to OnTick (journaled, next tick): the only way UI code should change the game Widget identity is the label (or id) plus its place in the container; use ButtonID when labels repeat or change.

Burrow Hub Burrow Hub ( BurrowHub.exe , burrowhub ) is the native launcher: it keeps your projects in one list, installs several engine versions side by side, opens each project with the version it pins, and optionally checks for updates. It is drawn with the engine's own UI toolkit over Vulkan (no web view). The Hub works fully offline. make hub-run # build and start the Hub (macOS: with the MoltenVK environment) make hub-test # vet, gofmt, -race tests, soft screenshots of every panel, one GPU capture per tab What it does tab content Home Play the Sandbox ; continue the last project; a folded Learn and documentation section with Documentation , What's new and Download buttons that open the website in your browser, plus the local GETTING-STARTED, docs, examples and templates of the active engine kit); What is new: the signed news and the release notes of the newest release. A Update available button next to the tabs jumps to Updates Projects recent first, pinned on top, search; New project (pick a template, a name, a folder and an engine version) and Import (a folder explorer with Home / Desktop / Documents / Downloads shortcuts, breadcrumbs and a marker on folders that hold a vox.project ; the same explorer locates a moved project folder and, behind Browse... , picks the location of a new project); per project: Open in editor and Run , and a More menu with Build / Export ( burrow build -o ), Duplicate, Upgrade engine, Show folder, Pin, Remove from list, Delete files. Revert upgrade and the fixes for a broken project stay in the panel Updates one summary (what is new, one Update all button, Check now ) that installs the newest engine and downloads the new Hub in one job, with progress and cancel. A folded Advanced section holds the installed engines (set default, show folder, uninstall, adopt the kit the Hub lives in), the engine releases of the channel with release notes and the update source Settings automatic check on/off, automatic Hub download on/off (default on with automatic checks; the new Hub replaces the running one at the next start), channel (stable, beta), manifest URL, website URL (editable in developer mode only), new project folder, UI scale (auto or 100 to 300 percent), privacy notes A project that cannot be opened shows why and offers a fix: folder missing (locate the moved folder or remove the entry), broken vox.project (restore the last upgrade backup), engine not installed (install that version when the manifest lists it, or re-pin to an installed one). "Remove from list" never touches files. "Delete files" is separate, needs a first confirmation, then the project name typed again, and refuses anything that has no valid vox.project . Play the Sandbox The primary button on Home and Templates plays the ready-made sandbox template without the editor: No engine installed: the Hub first uses the kit next to it (full installer, nothing contacted). Otherwise it asks before downloading the latest engine from the update source (same signed manifest and sha256 checks as the Updates tab); declining leaves a message and creates nothing. The project is created once as Sandbox in the projects folder (Settings; default BurrowProjects in your home folder). A later click reuses it and never overwrites or duplicates it; a non-empty folder of that name that is not a Burrow project is left alone and reported. It starts burrow run of the project's engine, detached (no console window on Windows). A failure in the first seconds is shown under the button with the tool's own text, for example the "no Vulkan driver" help from the graphics check. Other messages: no engine and download declined, install failed, template missing, could not start. Window frame The Hub window has no system frame: it draws its own title bar (logo, name and version on the left; minimize, maximize/restore and close on the right, each at least 24 logical px and scaled with the UI scale). Only the Hub does this ( window.Config.Frameless ); the editor and games keep native frames. Drag the empty bar to move the window; double-click it to maximize or restore; drag a maximized window off the bar to restore it. Resize from any edge or corner (minimum 800x480 logical px). F11 toggles fullscreen and hides the bar. Maximized state and placement are remembered. Alt+F4 (and Cmd+W on macOS) closes. The bar buttons are reachable with Tab and have accessible labels (Minimize, Maximize/Restore, Close). BURROW_HUB_FRAME=native keeps the system frame. Limits, because GLFW has no native move/resize request: the window follows the cursor frame by frame (slightly less smooth than a native drag); on Windows the Aero Snap gestures (drag to an edge, snap layouts under the maximize button) are not available, while maximize, restore and minimize work; diagonal resize cursors are custom images; macOS gets the window shadow through a small Objective-C runtime call; on a native Wayland session GLFW cannot position windows, so use BURROW_HUB_FRAME=native there. The Windows, Linux and Wayland paths are compiled but have not been tried on a real display. Storage what where config ( hub.json , projects.json , manifest-cache.json ) %APPDATA%\Burrow , ~/Library/Application Support/Burrow , ~/.config/burrow engines, downloads, backups, staged Hub updates %LOCALAPPDATA%\Burrow , ~/Library/Application Support/Burrow , ~/.local/share/burrow BURROW_HUB_HOME= puts both under /config and /data (portable installs, tests). Engines live in /engines// with the layout of the creator kit zip ( BurrowEditor.exe , burrow.exe , burrowplay.exe , sdk\ , docs\ , templates\ , licences\ , engine.json ). The kit's own engine.json ( {"version": "..."} , written by scripts/dist-engine-windows.sh ) lets the Hub adopt an unpacked kit in place: the first-run wizard and the Updates tab (Advanced) offer "Use the engine next to this Hub"; for a portable folder nothing is copied and uninstalling only forgets it. A kit that an installer owns (inside Burrow.app/Contents/Resources/engine , an AppImage, the folder of the Windows installer or install.sh , a .deb : recognised by the app bundle path, $APPIMAGE , or an Uninstall.exe , uninstall.sh or .managed file next to the Hub) is copied into the engine store instead, because that folder is replaced when the app is updated and an AppImage is mounted somewhere else on every start ( hub.Store.AdoptCopy , hub.KitDirOf ). Platforms The Hub runs on the six desktop targets: Windows, macOS and Linux, each on x64 ( amd64 ) and ARM64. Manifest assets are keyed - ( windows-amd64 , windows-arm64 , darwin-amd64 , darwin-arm64 , linux-amd64 , linux-arm64 ; hub.AssetKey ) and a Hub offers only the engine and Hub releases that have an asset for its own key. Release asset names are Burrow-Engine-- and Burrow-Hub-- with = windows , darwin or linux and = x64 / x86_64 / amd64 or arm64 / aarch64 ; the archive is a .zip on Windows and a .tar.gz on macOS and Linux (a tarball keeps the exec bits; burrowrelease manifest rejects the wrong format, an unknown OS or CPU, and two files for one key). Installers ( BurrowSetup-*.exe , *.dmg , *.AppImage , .deb ) are not engine assets and are ignored by burrowrelease manifest ; they are attached to the release as plain files ( Releasing ). The Hub reads the archive format from its content ( PK or gzip magic), never from the name, and .tar.gz gets the same protections as the zip: no absolute path, .. , drive letter, alternate stream, symlink, hard link, device or fifo; no duplicate or case-colliding name; entry, per-file and total caps counted while writing; modes reduced to 0644/0755 (no setuid, setgid or sticky bit). Tool names: BurrowEditor.exe , burrow.exe , burrowplay.exe , BurrowHub.exe on Windows, burrowedit , burrow , burrowplay , burrowhub elsewhere. Data folders per OS are in the Storage table above. Hub self-update by layout ( Service.SelfUpdateSupport ): Windows , a Linux install folder you can write ( install.sh ) and a macOS app bundle you can write ( /Applications/Burrow.app installed by the owner) swap the executable as described below. On macOS the swap changes the main binary of a sealed bundle, so right after every swap, and after every rollback, the Hub signs the bundle again with the system's codesign (ad-hoc, the same three steps as scripts/pack-macos.sh : the executable, the bundle with --deep , then codesign --verify --deep --strict ). If signing or verification fails, the previous executable is put back and signed again, the version is not offered again, and the Updates tab shows the problem. A macOS Hub without codesign (no Xcode command line tools) or in a folder the user cannot write, an AppImage (a read-only mounted image) and a folder the user cannot write (a .deb in /opt ) do not replace themselves: those Hubs still update the engine versions, and when a newer Hub exists the Updates tab says so and how to get it (new disk image, new AppImage, apt ). Nothing is staged, so there is nothing to roll back. Engine pins and upgrades vox.project has an engine field ( "0.3.0" , pre-releases such as "0.4.0-beta.1" are accepted). It is the version burrow new wrote; the Hub rewrites it. Absent: the Hub uses its default engine, else the newest installed. "Open in editor" starts /BurrowEditor.exe -project , Run starts burrow run , Build starts burrow build -o , all from the pinned engine's folder with BURROW_BIN_DIR and BURROW_SDK pointing at it. Upgrade engine (only to an installed newer version): shows the release notes between the two versions (from the cached signed manifest), writes a backup zip /backups/--.zip , runs burrow migrate of the target engine when it exists ( "migrate": true in its engine.json , or burrow help migrate answers), then writes the pin. The migration of this engine turns the fine water on for a project that never chose ( runtime.plugins.fine_water absent; an explicit false stays): the water of the project behaves differently, its StateHash changes and saves taken with the coarse water do not load, so keep the backup if you need to go back. If migration or the pin fails the project is restored from the backup automatically. The backup stays registered: Revert last upgrade swaps the project folder back (the current folder is kept aside until the swap succeeded). A project that contains symbolic links is not upgraded (a zip backup cannot restore them faithfully; the message says which one). Restore uses its own lenient validator for the Hub's backups (file names that are legal on this machine, such as a:b , are restored; downloads keep the strict one) and unpacks into a unique temporary folder next to the project. The state a restore replaces is kept as .before-restore- until you press "Delete the kept copy"; this includes the failed state after an automatic restore. Settings has "Keep per project" (default 5): older backups of the same project are pruned after a successful upgrade, never the one Revert needs. An engine pinned by a listed project cannot be uninstalled. Upgrading never runs the engine on the UI thread: the migration flag comes from engine.json ; burrow migrate runs in the background job after you confirm. "Delete files" moves the folder to the trash on macOS and Linux ( gio ), deletes it on Windows, and refuses the home folder, Desktop, Documents, Downloads and the other standard folders, every folder that contains your home, and drive roots. Launched tools always get BURROW_BIN_DIR of the pinned engine and either its sdk\ as BURROW_SDK or no BURROW_SDK at all (an inherited one is removed). Updates (no telemetry) The Hub fetches one signed manifest.json . Source, in order: BURROW_MANIFEST_URL , manifest_url in hub.json , the compiled-in default, and finally manifest.json when a website is compiled in (see Website and news ). The compiled-in default is a marked placeholder ( https://example.invalid/PLACEHOLDER/... ) that counts as "no update source configured"; the Hub then says so and does nothing else. The first run asks "Check for updates automatically?" and says exactly what a check fetches: manifest.json (the release list and the news) from the update host, nothing else. Off means nothing is contacted until you press Check now . No request is made before you answer. A request carries User-Agent: BurrowHub/ () and nothing else: no identifier, no cookie, no body. Proxies follow HTTPS_PROXY , HTTP_PROXY , NO_PROXY . HTTPS only, at most 5 redirects, never https to http. http://127.0.0.1 / localhost is accepted only when BURROW_HUB_ALLOW_INSECURE_LOCAL=1 (tests). The last verified manifest is cached, so release notes and the engine list work offline. A manifest whose generated time is older than the cached one is rejected (replay of an old file). flowchart TB C["Check for updates

for a compiled-in key?"} V -- no --> X["Rejected"] V -- yes --> G{"generated newer than
the cached manifest?"} G -- no --> X G -- yes --> K["Cache it"] K --> O["Offer releases for the channel,
if Hub version >= min_hub_version"] Manifest { "schema" : 1 , "generated" : "2026-05-01T10:00:00Z" , "channels" : [ "beta" , "stable" ], "news" : [{ "title" : "Burrow 0.2.0" , "date" : "2026-05-01" , "summary" : "plain text" , "link" : "https://.../news/index.html#020" , "version" : "0.2.0" , "severity" : "info" }], "releases" : [ { "version" : "0.2.0" , "date" : "2026-05-01" , "channel" : "stable" , "notes" : "markdown" , "min_hub_version" : "0.1.0" , "assets" : { "windows-amd64" : { "url" : "https://.../0.2.0/Burrow-Engine-windows-x64.zip" , "size" : 123456 , "sha256" : "<64 hex>" }}}, { "version" : "0.2.0" , "kind" : "hub" , "date" : "2026-05-01" , "channel" : "stable" , "assets" : { "windows-amd64" : { "url" : "..." , "size" : 1 , "sha256" : "..." }}} ], "key_id" : "a1b2c3d4" , "signature" : "" } news is optional (see below). kind is engine (default) or hub (Hub self-update packages). Asset keys are - . The beta channel also sees stable releases. A release is offered only when the running Hub is at least min_hub_version . Unknown JSON fields are rejected, so nothing can hide outside the signature. Signing Signatures are Ed25519 over the canonical JSON of the manifest with an empty signature . The Hub verifies with the public key set compiled in ( -ldflags "-X burrow-hub/hub.DefaultPublicKey=[,]" ); a manifest names its key in key_id (first 8 hex digits of the sha256 of the public key), so during a rotation the Hub ships both keys for one release. The compiled keys are the only trust root: public_key in hub.json and BURROW_HUB_PUBKEY_FILE are honoured only in developer mode ( BURROW_HUB_DEV=1 ) and are added to the compiled ones, never replace them. With no key every manifest is rejected: updates are off, everything else works. The public key is committed as release/burrow-release.pub (one line, 64 hex digits; HUB_PUBKEY overrides it); the dist scripts and scripts/publish-release.sh read it from there. Its key id , the key_id of every manifest it signs, is the first 8 hex digits of the sha256 of the 32 raw key bytes ( hub.KeyID ; a test checks the committed key against this convention). No private key is stored in this repository. It exists only where you created it. # once, on a trusted machine, OUTSIDE the repository (keygen refuses a folder under a go.mod or .git) burrowrelease keygen -priv /secure/burrow-release.key -pub burrow-release.pub # every release: build the zips, then sign export HUB_PUBKEY= $ (cat burrow-release.pub) HUB_MANIFEST_URL=https://downloads.example.org/burrow/manifest.json # HUB_SITE_URL is optional, see below make dist-engine-windows dist-hub-windows # dist/Burrow-Engine-windows-x64.zip, dist/Burrow-Hub-windows-x64.zip burrowrelease manifest -dist dist -version 0.3.0 -channel stable -base-url https://downloads.example.org/burrow \ -notes-file notes.md -priv /secure/burrow-release.key -out dist/manifest.json \ -merge old-manifest.json -pub burrow-release.pub \ -news-file news.json -tag-prefix v # keeps earlier releases; signed news; asset URLs /v/ (GitHub release tags) burrowrelease verify -manifest dist/manifest.json -pub burrow-release.pub # upload the archives to // and manifest.json to the manifest URL (all six platforms: see Releasing) Both dist scripts build BurrowHub.exe through the single dw_build_hub step of scripts/lib-dist-windows.sh , which fails without HUB_PUBKEY and an https HUB_MANIFEST_URL and checks that both strings are inside the binary (a Hub without the key can never update, and an update without the key would turn every installed Hub into one). HUB_DEV=1 allows a keyless development build with a loud warning; never ship it. Freshness: generated (RFC 3339) is required and a manifest older than the newest one ever accepted is rejected; that time is kept in state.json , separately from the cache, so deleting the cache does not reset the protection. burrowrelease manifest also signs an expires (180 days, ValidDays in hub/release ); past it the Updates panel warns that the source looks abandoned or frozen (it does not block). Release versions must be canonical ( 1.2.3 , 1.2.3-beta.1 ), dates YYYY-MM-DD , asset URLs https. Publishing a release (zips, signed manifest, website, README of the public repository) is scripted: see Releasing . Key custody: keep the private key in a password manager or on an encrypted offline volume with a second backup; never commit it, never put it in a zip or a CI log, give it mode 0600 (the tool refuses a group or world readable key on Unix). If it leaks, ship a new Hub with a new public key (old Hubs cannot update across a key change: publish it through the normal download page). The public key is not secret. Website and news The public website ( https://burrow-engine.github.io/burrow-releases/ , generated by cmd/burrowsite , see releasing ) also serves manifest.json . A release Hub carries its address, set at build time like the key: -ldflags "-X burrow-hub/hub.DefaultSiteURL=https://.../" ( HUB_SITE_URL in the dist scripts, default https://burrow-engine.github.io/burrow-releases/ , https only, no query or fragment, a missing trailing slash is added). The Hub derives manifest.json (when no other manifest source is set), docs/ , news/ and download/ from it. Without a compiled-in site the website buttons are disabled and nothing else changes. The website can be overridden (Settings, BURROW_HUB_SITE_URL , site_url in hub.json ) in developer mode only , like the keys. The buttons only open your browser; the Hub itself never fetches a page. Links are opened only through hub.OpenSiteURL , which refuses anything that is not https on exactly the site's origin (scheme, host and port; no credentials). News ride inside the signed manifest (a news array of at most 20 items: title 120 characters, summary 400, date , link , optional version , severity none, info or security). We chose this over a separately signed news.json because the signature, the key rotation, the rollback protection ( generated ), the freshness ( expires ) and the one-request-after-consent rule then cover the news for free, with no second file, no second request and no second verification path to get wrong. The cost is that a Hub older than this change rejects a manifest that has a news field (unknown fields are refused on purpose), so publish the first news-carrying manifest knowing that. burrowsite news writes news.json from the changelog ( burrowrelease manifest -news-file news.json embeds and signs it; the website also serves it as a plain file for readers). News is still untrusted display data : the signature proves who published it, not that the text is safe to render. The Hub shows plain text only: markup tags, markdown links and images (the label stays), emphasis marks, control and bidirectional characters are removed ( hub.PlainText ), the text is length capped, no image is ever fetched, and a link is shown as a button only when it is on the site's own origin. Oversized or malformed news makes the whole manifest invalid. Downloads Resume with Range from a .part file; the size in the manifest is a hard cap (a server that sends more is cut off); the sha256 is checked before anything is unpacked and a mismatch deletes the partial file. The archive (zip or tar.gz) is unpacked into a temporary folder next to the destination with these limits: no absolute path, .. , drive letter, alternate stream, symlink or special file; no duplicate or case-colliding name; at most 20000 entries and 6 GiB, counted while writing (not from the headers). The folder must contain the editor and the CLI, then it is renamed into place atomically; an existing install of that version is kept aside and restored if the rename fails. Nothing from the archive is executed during install. Hub self-update The new Hub is downloaded, verified and unpacked into /hub/staged// . At the next start it replaces BurrowHub.exe (the old one is kept as BurrowHub.exe.old ) and restarts. The swap is crash safe: the new executable is copied to BurrowHub.exe.new and fsynced, a journal entry is written, then exe -> exe.old , exe.new -> exe ; a start that finds the journal repairs an interruption between the renames, and hub.ResolveHubExe (for whatever launches the Hub) moves .new / .old back when the executable is missing. The state is bound to the executable path it was staged for, and a single-instance lock keeps two Hubs from racing it. The new Hub confirms 3 seconds after start (wall clock, so a minimised window counts). If a start never confirms, the next start restores the old executable and stops offering that version. A swap problem found at start is shown in the Updates panel and as a toast, not only on stderr. Concurrency: installs, uninstalls and clean-up take an OS file lock in the data folder ( hub.lock ), each download a lock of its own; partial downloads are named after the sha256 of the archive. An engine replaced by an install is kept as .old-~... until the new one is in place (a failed rollback never deletes it; the next start moves it back). Packages package role hub logic with no UI and no cgo: paths, versions, manifest, signature, client, download, unzip, engine store, registry, project upgrade, launcher, self-update hub/ui the panels ( App.Build ), tested headless with ui.Harness hub/release , cmd/burrowrelease manifest builder and signer, key generator hub/hubtest fixtures: fake kit zips, key pairs, a local Range-capable server cmd/burrowhub the window (cgo), -shot out.png -tab N for a hidden capture Known limits: the Hub has no native folder picker (paths are typed); signed manifests are the only update path; the Windows build is cross-compiled and untested on real Windows; the macOS Intel, Linux and ARM64 Windows builds are untested on real hardware until CI or testers confirm them.

Installing Burrow One download per system. You get the Burrow Hub ; the Hub installs and updates the engine versions (editor, burrow command line, documentation, templates) side by side and opens your projects. Pick the file for your system on the download page . system file what it is Windows 10/11 x64 BurrowSetup-<version>-x64.exe installer: Hub and the whole engine, works offline (recommended) BurrowHubSetup-<version>-x64.exe small installer: the Hub only; it downloads the engine after you agree Windows 11 ARM64 BurrowSetup-<version>-arm64.exe , BurrowHubSetup-<version>-arm64.exe same as x64 macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel) Burrow-<version>-macos-universal.dmg disk image with Burrow.app (or -arm64.dmg / -x86_64.dmg , one CPU each, smaller) Linux x86_64 Burrow-<version>-linux-x86_64.AppImage one file, no install Burrow-<version>-linux-x86_64.tar.gz install.sh : user install, menu entry, no root burrow_<version>_amd64.deb system install (Debian, Ubuntu) Linux ARM64 the same three files with aarch64 / arm64 The builds are not signed yet. Windows and macOS show a warning the first time; that is expected and the steps below get past it. Check the SHA-256 of the file against the download page before you run it ( burrowrelease verify and the Hub's own signature check cover the Hub's updates, see Hub ). Status, honestly. The Windows x64 build and the macOS Apple Silicon build have been run by the maintainers. The Windows ARM64, macOS Intel, Linux and .deb /AppImage packages are built by the same scripts but have not been tried on real hardware yet ; treat them as preview until testers confirm them, and please report what happens . Windows Run BurrowSetup-<version>-x64.exe . Windows SmartScreen says "Windows protected your PC": click More info , then Run anyway . The installer asks for nothing special: it installs for you only in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Burrow and needs no administrator rights. "Install for all users" (Program Files) asks for administrator approval. Tick or untick the Start menu and desktop shortcuts, then Finish. Burrow Hub starts. Silent install: BurrowSetup-<version>-x64.exe /S (add /allusers for all users, /D=C:\Tools\Burrow as the last argument for another folder). Uninstall: Settings > Apps > Burrow, or Uninstall Burrow in the Start menu. Your projects are never touched. The Hub's settings, project list and downloaded engines ( %APPDATA%\Burrow , %LOCALAPPDATA%\Burrow ) are kept unless you tick the box on the uninstaller page (silent: Uninstall.exe /S /PURGE ). There is no file association: a Burrow project is the file vox.project , and Windows associates extensions, not names. Open projects from the Hub. macOS Open the .dmg and drag Burrow.app onto Applications . The first launch is blocked ("Burrow can't be opened because Apple cannot check it for malicious software"). Open System Settings > Privacy & Security , scroll down and click Open Anyway next to the Burrow message. On macOS 14 and older you can instead right click the app, choose Open , then Open . From Terminal: xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Burrow.app . Nothing else to install: the Vulkan runtime (MoltenVK and the Vulkan loader, Apache-2.0) is inside the app. Needs macOS 11 or newer. The app is ad-hoc signed (its files are sealed as a set) but not notarized by Apple. Updates : the Hub updates the engine versions itself, and itself too: with automatic checks on, a new Hub is downloaded in the background, replaces the one in Burrow.app the next time you start it and the app is signed again with the system's codesign . If the app folder is not writable or codesign is missing, the Updates tab says so: download the new disk image and replace Burrow.app . Uninstall: drag Burrow.app to the Trash; delete ~/Library/Application Support/Burrow to remove settings and engines. Linux You need a Vulkan driver ( libvulkan.so.1 and the driver for your graphics card). The app tells you what to install when it is missing: Debian/Ubuntu sudo apt install libvulkan1 mesa-vulkan-drivers , Fedora sudo dnf install vulkan-loader mesa-vulkan-drivers , Arch sudo pacman -S vulkan-icd-loader vulkan-radeon (or vulkan-intel , nvidia-utils ). AppImage : chmod +x Burrow-<version>-linux-x86_64.AppImage && ./Burrow-<version>-linux-x86_64.AppImage . It needs FUSE 2 ( sudo apt install libfuse2 on Ubuntu 22.04+). Without FUSE, run ./Burrow-...AppImage --appimage-extract-and-run . An AppImage updates the engine versions but not itself: download the new file to update the Hub. tar.gz : tar xzf Burrow-<version>-linux-x86_64.tar.gz && cd burrow-<version>-linux-x86_64 && ./install.sh . It installs in ~/.local/share/burrow/app , adds "Burrow Hub" and "Burrow Editor" to the application menu and the commands burrow-hub and burrow in ~/.local/bin (add that folder to your PATH if needed). This install can update the Hub itself. Uninstall: ~/.local/share/burrow/app/uninstall.sh ( --purge also deletes settings and engines). .deb : sudo apt install ./burrow_<version>_amd64.deb installs in /opt/burrow with burrow-hub and burrow in /usr/bin . Update the Hub with the package; the Hub updates engine versions. Remove: sudo apt remove burrow . After installing Start Burrow Hub . The first run offers to use the engine that came with it (or to download the newest one). Then either press Play the Sandbox to try the Sandbox game (the Hub installs it for you), or create a project from a template ( Getting started ). Settings and downloaded engines live in %APPDATA%\Burrow and %LOCALAPPDATA%\Burrow (Windows), ~/Library/Application Support/Burrow (macOS), ~/.config/burrow and ~/.local/share/burrow (Linux). Advanced: portable archives You do not need these to use Burrow. The Hub itself uses the per-platform archives ( Burrow-Engine-<os>-<arch> and Burrow-Hub-<os>-<arch> , .zip on Windows, .tar.gz elsewhere) to install engine versions and updates, and you can unpack one by hand for a portable folder where nothing is installed (for example Burrow-Engine-windows-x64.zip ). The Sandbox and the templates are installed from the Hub, not from a separate download.

Items A project gives its scripts a small item registry : names, stable ids and stack limits. The engine owns the identity and the 6-byte stack format; the content is the mod's. There is no built-in item list, no recipe, no inventory, no dropped item and no item rendering in the engine. Machines, crates, conveyors and inventories keep counts in block data, Script.State or the save store, and draw them with the game UI. runtime.items The registry is one JSON file named by runtime.items in vox.project (project relative, under an asset directory so burrow build packs it; the build adds the file itself). { "items" : [ { "name" : "mymod:gear" , "display" : "Gear" , "max_stack" : 16 , "block" : "mymod:gear_block" }, { "name" : "mymod:wire" , "display" : "Wire" }, { "name" : "mymod:hammer" , "max_stack" : 1 } ] } field meaning name registry name, [a-z][a-z0-9_]* with an optional namespace: (at most 20 + 28 characters); air is reserved display readable name for tooltips and GUIs (default: the name) max_stack stack limit 1..65535 (default 64; uint16 , so 65535 is the maximum) block optional registry name of the block the item stands for or places; the engine only reports it, it never places anything Ids. Items are numbered in file order starting at 1; id 0 is the empty stack. Appending items keeps every id, while reordering or removing one renumbers the following items, so append only. The ids are project data, not simulation state: adding an item does not change the StateHash , and a replay or multiplayer peer must use the same project file to agree on them. Limits. At most itemset.MaxItems = 4096 items. The game refuses a file over 1 MiB. Parsing rejects unknown fields, duplicate or invalid names, and a block that is not a plain block registry name (no [state] ). One project per process. Like the project block registry, the item registry is global to the process ( itemset.Set ), which is what a game or an editor session is. Engine programs call itemset.Parse , itemset.Set , itemset.ID , itemset.ByID , itemset.All and itemset.Count directly. Stacks An item stack is 6 bytes, little endian: offset size field 0 2 item id ( u16 , 0 = empty) 2 4 count ( u32 ) A stack with an id and no count, or a count and no id, is invalid. The engine does not store stacks, it only defines the format so block data, bus payloads and saves are portable between scripts and languages. itemset.Stack and the SDK burrowsdk.ItemStack implement it: package main import "burrow-engine/sdk/burrowsdk" func init() { burrowsdk.OnBlockUse( "mymod:crate" , func (self burrowsdk.Entity, ev burrowsdk.BlockEvent) { id, err := burrowsdk.ItemIDByName( "mymod:gear" ) if err != nil { return } info, err := burrowsdk.ItemInfo(id) if err != nil { return } stack := burrowsdk.ItemStack{Item: id, Count: info.MaxStack} b := stack.Encode() _ = burrowsdk.SetBlockData(ev.X, ev.Y, ev.Z, string (b[:])) }) } func main() {} The Go API mirrors the engine: Encode , DecodeItemStack , Split(n) (removes up to n and returns them) and Merge(src, maxStack) (fills the receiver up to maxStack and returns what is left of src ). The engine has itemset.Stack.Encode , itemset.DecodeStack , Split , Merge and Validate (which also checks the registry and the stack limit). Scripts The host functions work without a plugin; a project without runtime.items reports 0 items. All ids are 1..item_count . function what it does errors ItemCount() number of registered items none ItemName(id) registry name of an id NOT_FOUND ItemIDByName(name) id of a name; case and the burrow: prefix are ignored NOT_FOUND ItemInfo(id) ItemProps{ID, Name, Display, MaxStack, Block} NOT_FOUND Always resolve items by name at on_start (or from a project data file) and keep the id in block data or Script.State : ids are stable only while the item file is appended to. What the mod writes the items themselves (the engine ships none), their recipes and crafting stations; inventories and containers (counts in block data or the save store, shown with the game UI); dropped items (a prefab spawned by a script), pickup and placement; item icons and rendering, tooltips, durability, enchantments or any other per-item behaviour; the machine logic that moves stacks between cells ( blocks , scripting ).

Levels and saves Two building blocks for games that are not sandboxes, both off by default ( runtime.plugins.levels: true / saves: true enable them): fixed levels (hand-built voxel regions with spawn points, trigger zones and settings, switched by a journaled command) and a generic save system (slots holding a sim snapshot, the level id and the game's own key/value data). Both are deterministic: a level switch replays from the journal, a restored save has the exact StateHash it was saved with. Packages: level (format, codec, library; no engine dependency), level/levelplug (engine plugin), save (format, slot store), save/saveplug (engine plugin). Example: examples/level_demo , make levels-test . Quick start vox.project : { "runtime" : { "plugins" : { "levels" : true , "saves" : true }, "levels" : { "dir" : "levels" , "initial" : "hall" , "actors" : [ "/player" ] }, "saves" : { "game" : "my_game" , "version" : 1 , "autosave_seconds" : 60 , "autosave_slots" : 2 } } } Both plugins add simulation state, so they are off unless asked for (existing projects keep their hashes). In Go: a.AddPlugin(&engine.ScenePlugin{}) a.AddPlugin(&engine.VoxelWorldPlugin{Generator: gen}) a.AddPlugin(&levelplug.Plugin{Dir: "levels" , Read: readProjectFile, Actors: [] string { "/player" }, Initial: "hall" }) a.AddPlugin(&saveplug.Plugin{Dir: saveDir, Game: "my_game" , GameVersion: 1 }) The .level file A level is one file, levels/<id>.level (id: letters, digits, _ . - , at most 64 bytes; also the file stem). Layout: BLVL , format version (u16, newer is rejected), the deflated body, then the SHA-256 of everything before it. The body is the metadata JSON plus the stored chunks ( voxel.Chunk run-length blobs, positions relative to the region's minimum chunk). Blocks are stored by name through a per-level palette, so a level loads into any registry that has those blocks and fails with the name of a missing one. part content region size in chunks (1..64 per axis, at most 4096 chunks), default origin chunk, stored chunks (empty chunks are not stored) mix replace (default): the whole box is the level, generated terrain inside it is carved away. keep : only stored chunks replace terrain, so the level can be a fixed building in a generated world spawns {name, pos, yaw, tags} , level-local blocks (relative to the region's minimum corner) zones `{name, kind: zone nodes , prefabs scene nodes (and prefab instances; the prefab documents are embedded, so a load reads no other file) spawned under the node /level settings sky , weather , weather_intensity , fog , gravity , kill_y , bounds Procedural worldgen stays the base layer: a level is an overlay on top of it ( mix decides how), unloading restores the generated terrain. Hostile input: file at most 64 MiB, body at most 192 MiB after inflating (a decompression bomb is cut at the limit), metadata at most 1 MiB, unknown JSON fields, bad names, non-finite or huge coordinates, chunks outside the box, bad palette ids and trailing bytes are all rejected ( level.ErrCorrupt ); ids and paths never contain separators or .. and symbolic links are refused. Level.Hash() (SHA-256 of the canonical body) is the content identity. Loading and switching level_load is a journaled sim.Command carrying {id, hash, origin?, spawn?, teleport?} . Apply unloads the current level (its region goes back to the generated terrain, /level is despawned), places the new region, spawns its nodes, moves the teleport nodes to the spawn point and records the new levelplug.State (id, hash, origin, size, spawn, loads). The state is a tracked fixed resource: rolled back with a failed tick, in StateHash, snapshotted. The hash is pinned in the journal : replaying against an edited level fails with a clear error instead of diverging. Apply is atomic (the engine rolls everything back on error) and bounded (at most 4096 chunk writes). Same level, same seed: same StateHash after the load, whatever the thread timing. Everything slow happens outside the tick. level.Library reads and decodes files on worker goroutines ( Prefetch ); a switch request waits in Manager until the level is ready and only then queues the command, so no frame blocks on disk or inflate ( Manager.Pending ). m := engine.Res[*levelplug.Manager](app) m.Request(levelplug.Request{ID: "garden" , Spawn: "from_hall" }) // async, from frame code m.Switch(levelplug.Request{ID: "garden" }) // sync, between frames (tools, tests) m.Current() // *level.Level of the loaded level Requests from the simulation never mutate the sim: a fixed system or script sends levelplug.Request with engine.SendFixed , the manager turns it into the command, so a replay (which has the command in its journal) is identical and the script saw a deterministic result. Transition hooks : Plugin.OnTransition(from, to) runs before a switch is queued (return an error to veto); Plugin.OnLoaded(m, level, state) runs on the frame after any load, unload or snapshot restore (apply sky, weather, fog, gravity there); the same moment is the levelplug.Loaded event. Zones and the kill plane : with Plugin.Actors set, a fixed system ( levels.zones , at most 16 actors x 256 zones per tick) sends a switch request when an actor stands in a trigger, and returns an actor below kill_y or outside bounds to the default spawn (a plain teleport). Actors should be root-level nodes (the position is the local translation plus ancestors' translations; rotation of ancestors is ignored). Saves A slot file ( <slot>.sav , slot [a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]{0,47} ) holds metadata (game id, game data version, level id, tick, StateHash, seed, label, wall-clock stamp for display only), the key/value data and sim.Engine.Snapshot() . Layout: BSAV , format version, deflated body, SHA-256 trailer. Limits: file 128 MiB, inflated body 512 MiB, 1024 keys, key 128 bytes, value 64 KiB, key/value total 1 MiB. Atomic : written to a temporary file in the same folder, fsynced, renamed over the slot (mode 0600). A crash leaves the old save or the new one. Rejected cleanly : bad magic, newer format, checksum mismatch, truncation, bombs, lying section lengths, invalid metadata, another game's id, a slot name that does not match the file, a save from a newer game version. A rejected load changes nothing. Same state : Manager.Load restores the snapshot (atomic Restore ), compares the StateHash with the saved one and restores the previous state if they differ (a changed engine configuration). Versions and migration : Plugin.GameVersion is the version of your own data; a save with an older version goes through Plugin.Migrate(from, *save.Data) (rewrite keys, the level id, ...). The file format has its own version. Game data : saveplug.KV is part of the simulation state (a tracked fixed resource): fixed systems use saveplug.FixedKV(c) , scripts save_set / save_get , hosts the journaled commands save_kv_set / save_kv_delete . Since it lives in the sim it is hashed, rolled back and restored with the snapshot, never out of sync with the world. Autosave : Autosave{EveryTicks, Slot, Slots} snapshots on the main goroutine every N simulation ticks (never the wall clock) and compresses and writes on a worker; a write in flight skips the tick instead of queueing. Slots > 1 rotates autosave-1..N . Requests from scripts and fixed systems ( saveplug.Request ) are served at the start of the next frame, between ticks; saveplug.Result reports the outcome. sm := engine.Res[*saveplug.Manager](app) sm.Save( "slot1" , "before the boss" ) sm.Load( "slot1" ) metas, bad, _ := sm.List() // bad lists unreadable slots with their errors Scripts and SDK Host functions (module vox , see script/ABI.md ): level_load , level_current , level_spawn_count , level_spawn , level_zone_at , level_settings , save_set , save_get , save_del , save_slot (save, load, delete). Requests return 0 whatever the host does later, so scripts stay deterministic; without the plugins they return unavailable. Go SDK ( sdk/burrowsdk/level.go ): LevelLoad , LevelCurrent , LevelSpawnCount , LevelSpawnAt , LevelZoneAt , LevelSettings , SaveSet , SaveGet , SaveDelete , SaveSlot , LoadSlot , DeleteSlot . To switch scenes (menu -> game) without a .level binary, use scene_load / burrowsdk.SceneLoad("scenes/game.voxscn") instead: it instantiates a .voxscn project file under the root at commit, pinned by content hash so replays load the same document (see script/ABI.md ). Editor and agents Tools > Levels is a full-screen tool: a tool rail (Select V, Spawn point S, Zone Z, Door D; Esc drops a half-drawn zone; every change of the draft is one undo step), the levels of levels/ as cards (click to select, double-click to open), and the world in the centre (top view by default) with the zones drawn as coloured boxes with their names and the spawn points as pins. The Spawn tool puts a spawn point where you click the ground; Zone and Door take two ground corners. Level settings holds the name, the region (grown to chunk boundaries on save) and the optional node root such as /level , the zone list, and the selected zone: a door's target level and target_spawn , the spawn point of that level the actors arrive at when they travel through it (chosen from the target level's spawn points; empty = its default spawn). Play from here saves the level if it changed and runs the game in its own window starting in this level at its first spawn ( burrowplay -level <id> [-spawn <name>] ). Mark spawn at the focus, mark zone from the region, save region as level and clear the draft are still there. MCP tool editor_level ( state , list , info , save , open , spawn_add , zone_add , remove , settings , clear ). Open places the region into the document as a journaled editor_open_level edit (pinned by hash) and spawns the nodes under /level ; saving converts the draft's world coordinates to level-local ones. The editor does not install the runtime level plugin (it would add state to every document), so scripts calling level_load in the editor's Play mode get "unavailable"; run the project with burrowplay for the real switch. Limits One level is loaded at a time; the region of the next level replaces the previous one (stacking several is not modelled). Player edits inside a level region are lost on unload (the region is reset to the generated terrain). gravity , sky , weather and fog are data (queries, OnLoaded , Loaded event); only kill_y and bounds are enforced by the plugin. Levels are .level files; the folder form is not implemented. Prefabs are embedded in the level, so a prefab edited later does not update existing levels until they are saved again. The library keeps at most 64 decoded levels within a 256 MiB estimated budget (plus registered ones); levels the sim loaded are pinned by content hash (the last 4), so zones, scripts and Manager.Current never read a file inside a tick. A level file edited while the game runs must be invalidated ( Library.Invalidate ); a journal made before the edit then fails its hash check on replay. A failed decode is reported once ( Manager.LastError ) and the request dropped. Loading a save whose level file has changed since is refused and rolled back ( Manager.EnsureCurrent ); a restore also drops switches queued before it. With several ticks per frame a save_slot request from a script is served after all of them, so the saved tick can be later than the requesting tick. The editor's editor_open_level is journaled but not undoable; saving a level that was opened in the document replaces the journal by a checkpoint so the hash pin cannot break replay. Saves restore into an equally configured engine (same plugins, blocks, world generator and seed): the snapshot checks it and refuses otherwise. A save does not contain assets. Worlds A world is a save slot plus two files next to <slot>.sav in the save folder: <slot>.world.json (name, mode, seed, generator, created and last played times) and <slot>.png , a 256x144 thumbnail written by windowed runs each time the world is saved (captured without the game UI overlay, so the UI never blinks) (needs runtime.plugins.saves ). The game UI "worlds" list, world:play , world:create , world:delete and the script calls WorldPlay / WorldCreate use them. Creating a world applies its seed (0 = random) and generator ( flat , biomes , heightmap , empty = all air; others keep the project's) and writes the sidecar; playing it rebuilds the game with the stored seed and restores the save if one exists. mode is free text kept for the game. The world a game starts on is a start parameter like the seed : it is held in simulation state ( app.world , hashed, immutable), so scripts can branch gameplay on the mode with ReadWorldInfo() ( world_info : slot, name, mode, seed, generator; UNAVAILABLE when the game is not on a known world) and the game UI sees it as the values world_name and world_mode . Because it is hashed, a replay must be started on the same world (same mode and seed) or its hash diverges, and a save only restores into a game started on the same world (a save of another world is refused). Games not started on a world have no such state and keep their hashes. Deleting a world removes the three files. Settings of the settings menu (applied live: volumes, fov through the controller, fullscreen, locale, and render distance through VoxelWorld.SetRadius ; the far plane and fog end follow it live unless the project sets an explicit Far . All are read again at the next start) are kept in settings.json in the user config directory. Switching scenes at runtime Every scene is a world of its own ( scenes/x.voxscn + scenes/x.voxworld : seed, generator, voxel edits). A script can move the game to another scene with burrowsdk.SceneSwitch("scenes/x.voxscn") (see scripting: entities and scene ): the roots are despawned, the base terrain is rebuilt for the target's seed and generator, its edits are loaded (or cleared) and the document is instantiated, as one journaled game_scene_switch command that carries the document and the world file. Save slots are scene aware: a save made in another scene than the start one records it in the slot's sidecar ( scene , scene_seed in <slot>.world.json ), and loading the slot starts the game in that scene and its world (the slot's own seed and generator stay for its start scene).
