x: Lighting: block light and skylight Burrow lights the voxel world with a propagated, coloured light field: block light (red, green and blue channels, 4 bits each) from emitters such as torches, lava and glowstone, and skylight (4 bits) from the open sky. It is derived data: a pure function of the blocks and the registry, never part of StateHash , a snapshot or a journal. What was there before voxel.Block.Emit and the default emitters by name ( voxel/light.go ) existed, and the mesher flood-filled a 64^3 window around every chunk to give each vertex a coloured light ( mesh.Opts.BlockLight ). There was no skylight (caves were lit by the hemispheric ambient, so a cave at night looked like the night outside), no attenuation by block, no persistent field (every edit re-meshed the 26 neighbours and recomputed the window), no query API, no soft renderer light and only 3 blue bits. Ambient occlusion existed (per-vertex AO in the mesh, SSAO or ray traced AO in the post stack) and is unchanged. The rules A light level is 0..15 per channel. Entering a non-opaque block costs one level per channel plus the block's filter; opaque blocks stop light (an opaque emitter lights its neighbours). Block light: Block.Emit (0..15) and a colour. Known names ( torch , soul_torch , redstone_torch , lava , glowstone , sea_lantern , lantern , the froglights, ...) have a default level and colour ( voxel.Block.Emission , state suffixes such as torch[wall=true] are ignored). Block.EmitColor overrides the colour. The colour is mixed 30% toward white so every channel holds levels for most of the range (a saturated colour would burn its weak channels close to the source and leave only a thin tail). A warm light still turns redder with distance because every channel loses the same number of levels. Skylight: 15 at the top of the topmost chunk layer, straight down it loses nothing , sideways one level per block. A roof therefore makes a dark room whose edges are lit. Filters ( Block.LightLoss = extra levels per channel; default by name, Block.LightFilter ): leaves 1/1/1, water 2/1/1 (red goes first), non-opaque ice 1/1/0, stained glass keeps its own colour and absorbs the others (a red pane passes red). Shaped blocks do not block light (a slab does not shade). Chunk borders are transparent to the algorithm; cells next to unloaded chunks are lit as if the unloaded space were solid until it loads. voxel.LightField Per chunk, 16 bits per cell (r | g<<4 | b<<8 | sky<<12), uniform chunks (open sky) store one value. Updates are incremental breadth-first searches per channel: Add : an emitter or a freed cell queues its neighbours; a cell brighter than a neighbour minus the cost raises it. Remove : removing a block or an emitter queues the old value; neighbours that could only have been lit through it are cleared and the brighter neighbours around the hole are queued again to refill it (the classic two queue algorithm, also for skylight columns). Edits are detected by diffing a chunk against the classes it was lit with ( Chunk.Version ), so undo, redo, restore, fluid and script edits all work without a hook. Chunk load / unload: a loaded chunk pulls from its loaded neighbours and pushes into them; an unloaded chunk removes the light that flowed out of it. The result is the fixpoint of max-propagation: independent of load order, edit order and budget slices (tests compare random edit sequences with a from scratch flood fill, cell by cell). Step(budget) does at most budget cell visits and keeps its queues; removals always run before additions. A torch placed and removed in a 85x27x85 cave costs about 0.6 ms ( BenchmarkLightCaveUpdate ) and TestLightUpdateBudgetBigCave bounds the visits. Where it runs (frame domain, off the main thread) The streamer ( engine/lightrun.go ) owns one LightField on its own goroutine, fed by columns loading and unloading and by chunk touches ( markDirty , plus a sweep of a few columns per frame for edits that bypass the controller). It reads blocks through the world read lock ( ChunkMap.View ). The main thread only sends commands and applies results, so propagation costs the main thread nothing (frame time p99 with light on equals light off, see Measurements). Mesh workers copy a padded light snapshot of their chunk ( LightField.Snapshot , under a read lock held for at most one 8192 visit slice) and the mesher reads it ( mesh.Opts.Light , per-vertex smooth light = the mean of the four open cells around each corner, exactly as before, now with the sky channel). Meshes are not delayed: a chunk meshed while the field is still settling uses a provisional estimate computed by the mesher ( mesh/lightest.go , Opts.EstimateLight ): the field's own rules run on the padded chunk (skylight falls down every column, from the sky or through the layers above the chunk read from the world, attenuated by leaves and water, nothing under a solid block, then spreads sideways; emitters inside the window flood). Each mesh records a hash of the light it read ( Result.LightHash , solid cells zeroed, like LightField.Snapshot ); when the field settles the runner re-meshes only the chunks whose hash differs (sources beyond the one-cell border), so a good estimate costs nothing and a change on a chunk border reaches only the neighbours that read it. Reports are flushed when the field is idle or every 4 s of continuous work; loads are sent nearest first. Simulation queries ChunkMap.LightAt(reg, p) (also on voxel.Access , sim -side code, nav and scripts) is the deterministic query: a separate sim-side field that lights the 3x3 columns around the queried cell synchronously, re-reads edited chunks and returns the exact value of the infinite world (light cannot travel 32 blocks, so a neighbourhood is enough). It depends on the blocks only: not on streaming radius, camera, frame rate or call order. It is never hashed. Light{R,G,B,Sky} .Block() = max(R,G,B) .Level(skyDim) = max(Block, Sky - skyDim) skyDim 0 at noon .. 15 at night Scripts: host import light_at(x,y,z) -> packed r|g<<4|b<<8|sky<<12 (ABI.md), Go SDK burrowsdk.LightAt(x,y,z) (Light, error) . It sees the committed blocks, not the writes buffered by the running call. Nav / AI: behaviour tree condition dark{max=7, sky_dim} ( nav.Builtins ) and nav.View.LightAt ; ai.Dark(light, skyDim, max) is the pure rule. "Mobs spawn in darkness": dark on the cell a spawner picks, with sky_dim taken from the (deterministic) day clock. MCP: vox_light {pos, sky_dim} (burrowd) and editor_light {pos, sky_dim, view} . Layers: skylight enters through the top of the highest generated chunk layer ( engine sets it from the generator, default 0..1). Chunks outside the layer range (edits far above the terrain) are not lit; blocks there neither shade nor emit. Rendering The vertex stays 16 bytes. Position uses bits 0..9 of x, y, z (0..512 in sixteenths), so the high bits of x carry the skylight and those of y the blue light (red and green stay above the AO bits of the vertex word). Dynamic voxel bodies keep raw positions ( pc.b.x = 2 ). An unlit vertex ( mesh.Vertex.Lit false) reads as open sky. Shaders ( voxel_body.glsl , water.glsl , water_hdr.frag , all shader levels including off , and -look classic ): ambient is multiplied by skyOcc(sky) (1 in the open, 0.012 + 0.988 * sky^1.7 below), direct sun by skyVis(sky) : caves are dark by day and at night (the existing sky/sun/moon cycle already scales the ambient, so "skylight scaled by time of day" is the ambient times the skylight); block light adds blockRadiance = 2.4 * light^2.2 (HDR levels, per channel) or 0.95 * light^1.7 (display space looks) times the albedo and AO; the environment reflection is scaled by the sky occlusion. Smooth lighting and AO: the corner light is the mean of the open cells (an occluded corner averages fewer, brighter-or-darker cells), the AO factor multiplies ambient and block light in the shader. Quads merge only when their four corner lights are equal. The soft renderer has the same terms ( render/soft/light.go , render.Options.Light ; the engine passes an on-demand voxel.DemandLight ), so headless renders and the parity tests match: make view-test parity 5.3 / 4.9 / 8.0, shadows off 4.1, classic 6.5 (thresholds 7.0 / 6.6 / 8.8 / 5.4 / 8.0). Ray tracing. Emitters already bounce light through the GI ray ( RTBlockInfo.Emit , now with the emission colour instead of the block colour). The traced passes scale the ambient share of the lit pixel, and the baked block light is added by the raster shader, so GI keeps working; the tracer does not trace the block light field itself (documented limit: no traced shadows from torches, no GI from block light onto other surfaces beyond the emitter bounce). Environment components: time, sun, sky, weather, fog, post The look of a scene's sky and air is made of ordinary components on ordinary nodes. New projects and templates put one Environment node in their first scene ( builtin:environment.prefab , scene.DefaultEnvironmentPrefab : env.time starting at 0.35, env.sun , env.sky ). Fog and post can also sit on zone nodes. component what it sets domain env.time the day clock: start (day fraction, 0 midnight, 0.25 sunrise, 0.5 noon, 0.75 sunset), day_length in seconds (0 = 1200), frozen . The time of day is a pure function of the simulation tick ( EnvTime.Fraction ), so it replays identically. hashed (sim) env.weather a held front: kind (clear, cloudy, fog, light_rain, heavy_rain, storm, snow), intensity , wind ( wind_dir , wind_speed , wind_auto ), frozen . The clock and the front reach the weather module as journaled weather_set commands ( weather.md ). hashed (sim) env.sun intensity (sunlight multiplier, 0 = 1), color (tint multiplier, 0,0,0 = the clock's), fixed + azimuth / elevation (degrees; 0 azimuth = +X, 90 = +Z) instead of the clock's direction, no_shadows . frame env.sky zenith and horizon colours (0,0,0 = from the clock), stars ( auto or off ), clouds ( auto follows the weather, on uses cloud_cover , off clears the sky). frame env.fog color (0,0,0 = the sky horizon) and density 0..1, in a volume. frame env.post exposure (EV), bloom (strength multiplier 1 + bloom , -1 = none), saturation , contrast , fill_light , distortion (air distortion multiplier 1 + distortion ), in a volume. frame What is hashed. Only env.time and env.weather are simulation state (they drive the clock and the weather, so they are in the StateHash and the journal like any component). env.sun , env.sky , env.fog and env.post are renderer-only: never hashed, never journaled, never read by a FixedUpdate system. Adding them to a scene changes no hash. The blended result lives in the frame-domain engine.EnvState resource. Volumes and blending. env.fog and env.post carry a volume: shape global (everywhere), box (half extents size in the node's space, follows its transform) or sphere (radius size.x ). Inside the volume the weight is 1 (times weight ), and it fades to 0 over blend blocks outside, measured from the active camera. Volumes blend in priority order, higher last so it wins, ties by node order: fog density and the post offsets interpolate toward each volume by its weight ( scene.BlendFog , scene.BlendPost ; a zero fog colour keeps the colour below). env.time , env.sun , env.sky and env.weather are global: the first node in tree order that carries one wins. scene.ResolveEnv(nodes, cam, tick) does all of it; internal/game calls it every frame for the game camera and the editor for the editor camera. What the renderer does with each field. field Vulkan (HDR levels) Vulkan (level off, classic) soft env.time sun, atmosphere, ambient sun, sky gradient sky time env.sun.intensity Look.SunGain Look.SunGain Look.SunGain env.sun.color tints the sun light, its transmittance and the disc tints the sun light tints the sun light env.sun.fixed direction override; the atmosphere uses a clock whose sun has the same elevation same same env.sun.no_shadows shadow map off same shadows off env.sky.zenith / horizon recolours the procedural sky and what reflects it ( atmo.glsl , weights in the w of horizon / zenith ) replaces the sky gradient ends same env.sky.stars off no stars (no stars) (no stars) env.sky.clouds cloud cover none none env.fog density folds into the weather fog ( WeatherFX.Fog ); colour replaces the distance fade colour density as in HDR; one colour for fog and sky horizon colour replaces the horizon env.post.exposure / saturation / contrast the colour pipeline, exposure pinned same same env.post.bloom bloom strength x 1 + bloom (levels with bloom) no bloom no bloom env.post.distortion air distortion strength same none Scene frames drawn through rworld (the hybrid mesh pass, character and model previews) take the same fields from rworld.ApplyEnv : a clock without a DirectionalLight node drives the sun, a DirectionalLight keeps its direction and colour but takes the gain, tint and shadow switch, env.sky and env.fog replace the sky and aerial perspective colours. The editor resolves the same components for the editor camera each frame ( editor/core/env.go , pushed to the renderer by editor/gpu through engine.EnvApplier ): the viewport shows the time of day, the sun, the sky, the fog volumes around the camera and the post grade of the open scene exactly like the game, and a change shows on the next frame (the scene is re-read every few frames). Nothing of it is an undo step. Old scene.settings fields time_of_day , exposure , fill_light and music no longer exist in scene.settings (a scene that still has them is rejected). burrow migrate turns them into an Environment node ( env.time frozen at that time, env.sun , env.sky , env.post ) and a Music node ( audio.music ); the scene looks and sounds the same. Scene settings: controller and hud A node of the scene (a root or a direct child of a root) can carry the scene.settings component; the running scene applies it (start scene, and again after a scene change, checked a few times a second by internal/game/scene_settings.go ). All fields are optional, absent means "project default": "scene.settings" : { "controller" : false , "hud" : false } field effect controller false suspends the first-person controller and the player avatar for this scene only (no movement, hotbar, break/place; the app paces the ticks itself). true or absent leaves the project setting. The scene also frees the mouse cursor (menu mode, clicks go to the UI) while it runs and takes it back when the next scene turns the controller on; a game UI modal keeps managing the pointer itself. With runtime.plugins.controller: false , any scene that says true makes the project install the controller plugin anyway (found by scanning the scene and prefab files for scene.settings with "controller": true ); it stays suspended in every scene that does not say true . A project with no such scene is unchanged (nothing is installed, StateHash identical). hud false hides crosshair, hotbar and text overlay, true forces them. Settings precedence: command-line flag, then BURROW_* environment variable, then vox.project , then the engine default. scene.settings is not a fourth source of the same values: it only switches the controller and the HUD while its scene runs (the project value applies again in the next scene). Everything except controller is frame domain (the engine.SceneRuntime resource): never hashed, never journaled. The component is registered in the default schema and not hashed, so adding it to a scene does not change the StateHash . Scene-stored voxel edits ( world.edits ) "world.edits" : { "boxes" : [{ "min" : [ 10 , 64 , 10 ], "max" : [ 14 , 70 , 14 ], "block" : "" }, { "min" : [ 12 , 64 , 12 ], "max" : [ 12 , 64 , 12 ], "block" : "campfire" }]} Boxes are applied in order, once, when the scene is first seen as the running one, as ordinary journaled fill_box commands (so they are part of the StateHash , replay and undo like any edit). block empty or air clears. Corners may be in either order. Limits: 64 boxes, 1,048,576 cells per box, 4,194,304 in total, coordinates within +-1,048,576; violations are rejected when the scene is decoded. An unknown block name skips that box with a warning. Blocks name level colour torch, lantern, glowstone, jack_o_lantern, redstone_lamp, sea_lantern, shroomlight, froglights, campfire, fire, beacon, lava 14-15 warm yellow / orange, cyan sea lantern, pearlescent froglight pink soul_torch, soul_lantern 10 cyan redstone_torch 7 red magma, end_rod, crying_obsidian, amethyst, candle 3-14 see voxel/light.go The extended block set has no lava block. A project (or the lavalake demo) registers one: voxel.Block{Name: "lava", Solid: true, Opaque: true, Emit: 15} . Debug view, switches BURROW_LIGHT=off or RenderSettings.NoLight turn the light off (meshes carry no light, shaders read open sky). Light debug view (frame domain): RenderSettings.LightView / RenderPlugin.SetLightView / editor View menu "Light view" / editor_light {view} : block (colour of the block light), sky (skylight), level (brightness heat map). The soft renderer has it too ( render.Options.LightView ). Demos: examples/voxel_sandbox -demo lightcave|lightcolors|lavalake -shapes -tick 18000 (night; -tick 6000 for day). Measurements (M2 Max; the machine was shared, load average about 11, so absolute numbers are indicative) Mesh memory: the GPU vertex stays 16 bytes. Default heightmap terrain radius 3: 176 280 -> 190 356 opaque vertices (+8.0%) ( TestLightMeshGrowth , limit 25%). 1440p, radius 8, -gen v2 , medium: GPU 5.82 ms with and without light, 1.064 M vs 1.045 M triangles in view (+1.8%). Frame time while flying and sprinting ( -novsync , 1280x720, p99 of 1380 frames): 9.7 and 12.3 ms with light, 13.0 and 13.3 ms without; walking 11.7 / 12.2 vs 11.3 / 11.8. Uploads while flying 73.8 MiB with light vs 37.0 MiB without (2.0x; 3.9x with the open-sky provisional light, 5-6x before the hash filter). Initial load at radius 16 (2 layers): settled after 2.35 s vs 1.24 s without light (was 11.9 s); TestLightStreamingUploadsStayLow keeps the upload ratio under 1.8x (1.4x measured). Light field cost ( BenchmarkLightCaveUpdate ): place plus remove a torch in a big cave 0.58 ms; the initial light of a chunk is a column fill plus seeds from the cells that can still brighten a neighbour (uniform open-sky chunks cost nothing in memory). Limits Shaped blocks do not partially block light; skylight does not model partial occlusion by slabs and stairs. Light is not shadowed by entities, and scene meshes / dynamic voxel bodies do not emit or receive propagated light (bodies read open sky). A class table holds 255 distinct (opaque, filter, emission) behaviours; beyond that further ones read as air. Registry.Update of a light property needs LightField.Reset . Cells at the edge of the streamed area are lit as if the unloaded space were solid (block light) or open (the provisional estimate in meshes). Voxel size Light is measured in metres, not voxels. The field keeps each channel in units of 1/ Scale level ( LightConfig.Scale = the world's voxels per metre: 1, 2, 4 or 8): an emitter holds level * Scale units, every cell step costs one unit (plus the block's filter), and sky enters at 15 * Scale . Queries, snapshots, light_at and the renderer still read the levels 0..15 (units floored to whole levels), so a torch lights the same radius in metres at every voxel size. At scale 1 a unit is a level and the field is byte-identical to before. The cost is memory: a materialised chunk of light holds four 8-bit channels (128 KiB per 32^3 chunk, was 64 KiB), and the on-demand sampler loads ceil(15 * Scale / 32) chunks around the cell (1 up to scale 2, 2 at scale 4, 4 at scale 8).

h: Loading the chosen map when the match starts
x: Lobby An Age-of-Empires-style lobby for multiplayer games: players connect, sit in the lobby, pick a team and a colour, toggle ready; the host changes the game settings and starts; a countdown runs; the match plays; scripts end it with a verdict and everybody returns to the lobby. The lobby is simulation state of the server ( networking ). There is no extra network protocol: its commands travel as ordinary whitelisted commands, the state is hashed with the simulation, saved in snapshots, and replicated to every client with the other extra states ( replication ). Package: net/lobby . Contents The model Turning it on Configuration Phases Commands Slots, host and countdown Script API Loading the chosen map when the match starts Lobby screen Match results convention Go API Limits The model State ( sim.Extra net.lobby , hashed): phase, host, match counter, countdown ticks, start tick, one slot per player (team, colour, ready, spectator, absent), the settings chosen so far and the results of the last match. Commands (journaled, validated again by every Apply ): lobby_ready , lobby_slot , lobby_setting , lobby_start , lobby_cancel , lobby_end , lobby_return . A command that is refused leaves the state untouched. A fixed system ( lobby.sync ) keeps the slots, the host and the countdown consistent with the player registry of net/netsim : it gives new players a slot, drops the slots of players who left, migrates the host and counts the countdown down. It runs first in every tick, before the game's systems and scripts, so scripts always see a synchronised lobby. The player registry changes only through commands applied between ticks, so the order against netsim is the same on every peer. Authority. Clients may submit every kind except lobby_end ; the whitelist rules ( lobby.Rules() ) force the player field of the payload to the sender, so a client cannot act for another player. Player 0 is the server. Settings, start, cancel and return need the host (or the server); lobby_end is the server's (scripts end matches through lobby_end_match ). Turning it on Add a runtime.lobby section to vox.project . runtime.plugins.net must be true (it is off by default): the lobby reads the player registry. { "runtime" : { "lobby" : { "min_players" : 2 , "max_players" : 8 , "teams" : 2 , "team_names" : [ "Red" , "Blue" ], "countdown_seconds" : 5 , "host" : "first" , "spectators" : true , "settings" : [ { "key" : "map" , "label" : "Map" , "choices" : [ "meadow" , "canyon" ], "default" : "meadow" }, { "key" : "speed" , "label" : "Game speed" , "choices" : [ "1x" , "2x" ] } ] } } } The section is part of the simulation identity: it is inside the runtime hash the handshake pins ( game.NetPins ), so a peer with a different lobby configuration is refused at the handshake. With the section present the game installs lobby.Plugin right after netsim.Plugin . Configuration key type default meaning min_players int 2 non-spectator connected players needed to start (1 to max_players ) max_players int 8 non-spectator slots, 1 to 64 teams int 0 number of teams, 0 to 16; 0 is free for all (everybody is team 0) team_names list Team 1 ... optional display names, exactly one per team (so teams must be set), printable UTF-8, at most 32 bytes each; part of the pinned configuration, returned by lobby_info ( config.team_names ) colors int max_players number of colours, max_players to 32; colours are unique among players countdown_seconds int 5 1 to 60, counted in ticks (20 per second) late_join bool false players connecting during a match get a player slot spectators bool false players may watch instead of playing; also where overflow players go host string "first" "first" : the first connected player hosts and the role moves to the lowest connected id when the host leaves. "server" : only the server (player 0) changes settings and starts (dedicated servers, matchmaking) settings list none up to 16 game settings: key (letters, digits, _ - . , 32 bytes), label (64 bytes), choices (1 to 32 values of at most 64 bytes), default (one of the choices, else the first) Zero fields take the default; invalid values fail vox.project validation ( runtime.lobby ). Phases stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> lobby lobby --> countdown: lobby_start (host/server, enough players, all ready) countdown --> lobby: lobby_cancel, a player leaves or un-readies, a new player joins countdown --> playing: countdown ends (match counter +1, start tick set) playing --> results: lobby_end (server) or lobby_end_match (script) results --> lobby: lobby_return (host/server) phase id what happens lobby 0 players change team, colour, spectator and ready; the host changes settings countdown 1 countdown_ticks counts down; any change that makes the start invalid returns to lobby playing 2 the match runs; ready flags are cleared; slots of players who leave are kept and marked absent results 3 results holds the verdict; lobby_return reopens the lobby Commands All payloads are JSON objects with a player field. On the wire the server overwrites it with the sender's id. kind payload accepted when lobby_ready {player, ready} lobby or countdown phase; the player has a slot and is not a spectator. Un-readying during the countdown cancels it lobby_slot {player, team, color, spectator} lobby phase; team and colour in range and the colour free (a spectator sends 0 and 0 and needs spectators ); a change clears the player's ready flag lobby_setting {player, key, value} host or server, lobby phase; value is one of the setting's choices. A change clears every ready flag lobby_start {player} host or server, lobby phase, at least min_players connected non-spectators and all of them ready; goes to countdown lobby_cancel {player} host or server, countdown phase lobby_end {player: 0, results} server only, playing phase; results is JSON, at most 4096 bytes after compaction lobby_return {player} host or server, results phase; clears ready flags and drops the slots of absent players Rates per player: lobby_ready , lobby_slot , lobby_setting 5 per second (burst 10); lobby_start , lobby_cancel , lobby_return 2 per second (burst 4); payloads are at most 512 bytes and decoded strictly (unknown fields are refused). Add them to a server whitelist with: for kind, rule := range lobby.Rules() { wl.Allow(kind, rule) } Slots, host and countdown New player. The first tick after a player connects gives it a slot: team = the least populated team (lowest index on ties; always 0 in a free for all), colour = the lowest free colour. When all max_players slots are taken, or a match is running without late_join , the player becomes a spectator if spectators is on, else gets no slot (the server decides what to do with a connected player the lobby has no place for). Leaving. In the lobby and the countdown the slot disappears (a leave during the countdown cancels it). During a match and in the results phase the slot is kept with absent: true ; the player's return clears the flag; lobby_return drops what is still absent. Host. With host: "first" the host is the lowest connected player id; when the host leaves, the next lowest connected id takes over (a lower id that connects later does not take it back). With host: "server" the host is always 0. Countdown. lobby_start sets countdown_seconds * 20 ticks. Each tick the system re-checks the start condition (enough connected players, all ready) and decrements; at 0 the phase is playing , match increases and start_tick is the tick the match began. Script API Host functions of module vox (also in script ABI and the Script API reference ); without runtime.lobby they return UNAVAILABLE : function result lobby_phase() i32 0 lobby, 1 countdown, 2 playing, 3 results lobby_info(out, cap) i32 JSON of the whole lobby: phase , phase_id , host , match , countdown_ticks , start_tick , slots , settings (key to value), results , config lobby_end_match(results, len) i32 0. Ends the running match with a JSON verdict (empty = none, at most 4096 bytes); INVALID , REJECTED when no match is running Go SDK: burrowsdk.LobbyPhase() , burrowsdk.ReadLobby() (a LobbyInfo ), burrowsdk.LobbyEndMatch(results) . How scripts end a match. A script runs inside the tick, where nothing can be journaled, so lobby_end_match does not create a command. Like save_set it queues an operation that is applied when the script call commits, and the commit calls lobby.EndMatch on the lobby state. Every peer (and every replay) runs the same script on the same state, so every peer makes the same transition on the same tick; the lobby_end command is the equivalent for the server's own code. func OnTick() { l, err := burrowsdk.ReadLobby() if err != nil || l.Phase != "playing" { return } if winner, done := checkVictory(l); done { res, _ := json.Marshal( map [ string ] any { "winner" : winner}) burrowsdk.LobbyEndMatch(res) } } Loading the chosen map when the match starts Settings are plain strings; the game decides what they mean. Detect the start by the match counter (it changes exactly once per match, on the same tick everywhere), read the setting, and load the level: var lastMatch uint32 func OnTick() { l, _ := burrowsdk.ReadLobby() if l.Phase == "playing" && l.Match != lastMatch { lastMatch = l.Match // keep it in State if the script can be reloaded burrowsdk.LevelLoad(l.Settings[ "map" ], "" ) // the server's request becomes a journaled level_load for everyone // spawn each slot's player at its team's start: l.Slots[i].Team, .Color } } level_load is served by the server's frame and reaches clients inside a tick batch ( networking ); on clients the request is dropped, so call it from the script on every peer without special-casing. Keep the "last match" in State (not in a Go global) when the module can be reloaded or a late joiner restores a snapshot. Lobby screen The game UI template Lobby (File > New > Start from > Lobby in the Game UI designer, gameui.Template("Lobby") ) is a ready-made lobby: a scrolling player list with aligned columns (name, team, colour, ready, under a header row that stays above the scrolling list), a list of spectators, Ready, Team, Colour and Spectate / Play buttons (only the ones that apply to the local player), a scrolling settings list (the host clicks a row to cycle its value; for everybody else the rows are disabled list items: dimmed, no highlight, no command), Start / Cancel start for the host, a countdown, and a results panel (winner or draw, the placements by name in order and, with teams, the team placements: the best place among a team's members, teams named after team_names , else "Team 1", "Team 2"...) with Back to lobby (host). The lists scale to any lobby (up to 64 players and 16 settings). The lobby_match project template ships it wired to a script ( burrow new mygame -template lobby_match ); its ui/lobby.ui.json is the compact JSON of the template. How UI events become lobby commands. Scripts cannot submit commands (they run inside the tick), so the buttons do it on the frame side. A button or list whose action starts with lobby: is turned by gameui/uiplug ( LobbyCommand ) into the matching command, queued like any frame command; a client's network layer forwards it to the server ( netapp.ClientKinds already holds the lobby kinds), the whitelist forces player to the sender and the simulation validates it again. A listen server's own player submits as itself (not as the server). No script code is needed for input: action command lobby:ready lobby_ready with the flag toggled lobby:team lobby_slot with the next team lobby:color lobby_slot with the next free colour lobby:spectate lobby_slot that makes the player a spectator, or back a player on the least populated team with the first free colour lobby:setting (a list; lobby:setting:<n> names the row) lobby_setting with the value of lobby_set<n>_next , n being the clicked row (the host only, the simulation refuses others) lobby:start , lobby:cancel , lobby:return lobby_start , lobby_cancel , lobby_return What the script publishes. The screen shows UI values; the script ( burrowsdk.UISetStr/Num/Bool/Items , only on change) fills them from ReadLobby . lobby_me (the local player id) is set by the network layer; what depends on it (host buttons, the Ready / Team / Colour / Spectate texts and visibility, the visible panel) is derived by the engine every frame ( uiplug.DeriveLobby ), so the same script serves every peer. value meaning lobby_phase (num), lobby_host (num) phase id 0 to 3 and host player id: required, nothing is derived before lobby_phase is set lobby_slots (str) id,team,color,state entries separated by spaces (state 0 not ready, 1 ready, 2 spectator; 1024 bytes hold 64 players): the data of the buttons lobby_teams , lobby_colors (num), lobby_color_names (str, space separated), lobby_team_names (str, tab separated, empty = "Team N"), lobby_spectators_on (bool) lobby configuration lobby_status (str), lobby_countdown (num, seconds) status line and countdown lobby_players , lobby_spectators (items), lobby_spectators_any (bool) one item per player or spectator; a player row is name<TAB>team<TAB>colour<TAB>status (the list's col_widths align it); the screen's fixed header row is a separate list above it lobby_settings_on (bool), lobby_settings (items, "Label: value"; the engine derives lobby_settings_view from it, disabled unless the local player is the host, and the screen's list binds that), lobby_set<n>_key , lobby_set<n>_next (str) settings list and, per row, the key and the choice a click selects lobby_result_title (str), lobby_result_list , lobby_team_list (items), lobby_team_results (bool) results panel (the team list only with teams): "Winner: x", "Tie for first: x, y" or "Draw", then one "place. name" line per placement The screen is modal: show it in the lobby and results phases ( UIShow("lobby") ) and hide it while the match plays ( UIHide("lobby") ), as scripts/lobby of the template does. The screen is data: rename widgets, restyle it or add widgets freely, as long as the values and lobby: actions it uses stay. Match results convention lobby_end_match accepts any JSON. Games that run on a dedicated server with a matchmaker should use { "placements" : { "<player id>" : 1 , "<player id>" : 2 } } where the key is the player id as a decimal string and the value the final place (1 is the winner; equal values are a draw or a shared place). This is the shape a dedicated server forwards to a matchmaker. The lobby_match template ends its matches this way. Go API lobby.Install(e *sim.Engine, cfg lobby.Config) error // needs netsim installed lobby.Plugin{Config: cfg} // engine.Plugin, add after netsim.Plugin lobby.Installed(e *sim.Engine) bool lobby.ViewOf(x sim.Extra, ok bool ) (lobby.View, bool ) // from FixedContext.Extra(lobby.ExtraName) lobby.ViewOfEngine(e *sim.Engine) (lobby.View, bool ) lobby.Rules() map [ string ]netbase.Rule // whitelist rules for the client kinds lobby.ServerOnly(kind string ) bool // lobby_end lobby.EndMatch(x sim.Extra, ok bool , results [] byte ) error // used by the script host View has Config , Phase , Host , Match , CountdownTicks , StartTick , Slots , Slot , Settings , Setting , Results and InfoJSON . Limits limit value players per match 64 slots (players and spectators) 256 (the player registry bound) teams / colours 16 / 32 settings / choices per setting 16 / 32 key / value / label 32 / 64 / 64 bytes results 4096 bytes of compact JSON countdown 1 to 60 seconds command payload 512 bytes The decoder of the state is strict (bounds, sorted slots, ranges, unique colours, settings equal to the configured keys and choices, compact JSON results, canonical varints), so a corrupt or hostile snapshot is refused. A snapshot restores only under the same lobby configuration, which the handshake pins already guarantee. See also Dedicated server : "mode": "lobby" hosts matches on a real machine, with lobby start|end|set admin commands. Networking : the whitelist, pins and limits. Multiplayer scripting . Determinism .

Materials A material asset ( materials/<name>.material.json ) chooses a shader and sets its parameters and textures. render.mesh ( material_ref ) and render.voxmodel reference one; the node's render.material component stays as a per-node override merged on top. On a render.voxmodel node with no material asset, a render.material on the node tints ( base_color ) and lights ( emissive ) that instance. { "shader" : "builtin:standard" , "parent" : "materials/base.material.json" , "params" : { "glow" : 0.5 , "tint" : "#ff8800" }, "textures" : { "albedo" : "textures/a.png" }, "base_color" : [ 1 , 1 , 1 , 1 ], "emissive" : [ 0 , 0 , 0 ], "render" : { "alpha" : "blend" , "alpha_cutoff" : 0.5 , "double_sided" : true , "cast_shadow" : true } } shader : builtin:standard (the engine's lit shading, no parameters) or a project *.shader (see assets.md, "Shader assets"). parent : another material (project path or builtin: name). A child inherits everything and overrides per key: params and textures merge, each render field and base_color / emissive / shader replace when set. Chains are limited to 8, cycles are errors. params values: number, bool, [x,y,z] array or "#rrggbb" colour string; unknown names, wrong arity and values outside range(...) are errors. Built-in materials (Engine folder, usable as builtin:<name> or as a parent): standard , emissive , glass , foliage . A file in the older format ( base_color , texture , array params , shader base path) still loads unchanged. Go: shadersys.Resolve(loader, ref) flattens and maps a material onto rworld.Material ; dbassets.Assets.Material does it for a project. Editing The material editor (double-click a .material.json , or Tools) lists the project's materials on the left; the body shows the shader and parent, the shader's parameters (sliders with their range(...) , colour pickers, vector fields, toggles), the texture slots and the surface state (base colour, emissive, alpha mode and cutoff, double sided, casts shadow). A material with a parent is a variant: every field it sets is marked, and the reset arrow of a marked field removes it so the parent's value shows again. Changing the parent checks the chain (cycles and more than 8 parents are refused). The preview sphere on the right (drag turns it, the wheel zooms, Ctrl+drag turns the sun, a combo picks sphere / cube / plane) is the real renderer with the material's compiled shader. Edits save 0.6 s after the last change; Undo / Redo (Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y; a slider drag is one step) and Revert (back to the state when opened) are in the header. The shader editor edits .shader files; the shader graph editor builds one from nodes and writes the same annotated GLSL. Graph nodes: inputs: uv normal position time view_dir vertex_color sun_dir param_float param_color param_vec4 const_float const_color texture math: add subtract multiply divide min max power sin cos abs fract floor saturate one_minus smoothstep dot length normalize split_x/y/z/w combine_vec2/vec3 colour and texture: mix fresnel desaturate contrast noise output : albedo , emissive , alpha , normal (the graph is lit with the sun, shadows and ambient). A float, colour or vec4 parameter node and a texture node become @param / @texture lines; unconnected input pins use the constants shown on the node. Graph canvas. The wheel zooms at the pointer ( + / - around the centre, 0 resets, F frames the whole graph, Shift+F the selection); middle, right or Space + left drag pans. A drag on empty space is a rubber band (Shift / Ctrl adds), Shift / Ctrl click toggles a node, and the selection moves, deletes ( Delete ), copies ( Ctrl+C / X / V , new ids, links among the copies kept) and duplicates ( Ctrl+D ) as one undo step each. Ctrl+G (or the Group button) frames the selection in a group : a titled, coloured frame (title, note and colour in the inspector, resize from the corner) that moves the nodes inside it; it is saved in the graph file ( groups ) and ignored by the generator. A comment is a free text box (library entry Comment, palette comment ): no header, it never moves nodes, its text is edited in the inspector or in place (double-click the box on the canvas and type, Enter makes a new line, Esc or a click elsewhere ends it; the whole session is one undo step) (stored as a group whose id starts with comment ). Title, note and comment text edits are one undo step per edit session of a field, and a library entry dragged onto the canvas lands at the drop point (a click still adds it near the view). Right click, double click or Tab opens the node search: type a name, Enter adds it. A minimap at the bottom right pans the view. Saving and leaving. The shader, shader graph and material editors autosave shortly after the last edit. Back to world (Ctrl+Space), Quit and switching file save a pending edit first and only prompt (Save again / Discard / Cancel) when that save fails; a failed save is not retried until the next edit. Each header has Undo / Redo and Revert (the shader editor also uses the text's own undo, Ctrl+Z). The graph file is plain JSON ( nodes with id , type , x , y , name , const , in ; optional groups with id , title , note , x , y , w , h , color ); shadersys.ParseGraph(...).Generate() returns the shader text. Limits 16 floats and 4 textures per material ( shadersys.PerMaterialFloats , TexturesSupported ); the extended block is a per-draw dynamic uniform sliced from one host buffer, up to 4096 custom-shader draws per scene pass (the remaining draws reuse the last slice). Textures of slots 1..3 are sampled with the repeat sampler. A shader the renderer cannot build keeps the built-in lit shading for that draw (the error is in Renderer.ShaderError ). render/soft ignores custom shaders. Shadows and motion vectors A material is drawn again in the sun's shadow pass and in the object velocity pass of the temporal anti-aliasing, so a vertex stage that moves vertices (wind, swell, dissolve) and a fragment stage that discards act there too. The compiler ( shadersys , variants.go ) writes the variants beside the pair: <base>.shadow.vert.spv , <base>.shadow.frag.spv , <base>.vel.vert.spv , <base>.vel.frag.spv (an rworld.ShaderVariants Assets serves them; a variant a material does not need is removed on recompile). Shadow vertex : made when the material has a vertex stage (or is a cut-out). It is the same stage with S.vp read as the sun's matrix, so write gl_Position = S.vp * wp; (or use BW_VP in the variant only) and the displaced mesh casts the displaced shadow. Shadow fragment : made when the fragment stage contains discard or the file says // @shadow cutout . It runs in the depth-only pass with BW_SHADOW defined ( sunShadow() returns 1 there, the pass writes the map) and cuts the shadow where it discards. // @shadow opaque keeps the solid shadow of a material that discards. Velocity : the vertex stage runs twice, with the shader clock F.misc.y read as the previous frame's time and then the current one (the previous model matrix and time reach the variant through the material block), so the vectors include the vertex animation's own motion (wind, swell). Animation driven by another clock ( S.qual.w , S.wind.w ) is evaluated at the current time in both runs and contributes no motion. The vertex stage must declare inPos and write vWorld (the displaced world position), the fragment stage must write outColor , as the templates do. A material with neither a custom vertex stage nor a discard keeps the built-in depth-only shadow pipeline; cast_shadow: false skips the shadow pass altogether. A variant that does not compile is a warning in the compile result and the built-in path serves that material. Pipelines are cached per material and version like the colour pipelines. Hot reload of pipeline overrides A change of a project shader override ( shaders.OverrideGeneration ) rebuilds, at the next frame and only for the modules that changed: the classic and HDR post pipelines (offscreen post states of the editor viewport are recreated), the scene pipelines (custom materials included), the anti-aliasing and velocity pipelines (TAA, FXAA, SMAA, FSR 1, post_vel ), the FSR 2 compute passes, the particle, particle trail and mesh particle pipelines, and the ray tracing compute passes ( render/vulkan/shaderreload.go , moduleFamilies ). The device is idle while pipelines are replaced; a pipeline that fails to build keeps the previous one and logs the error.

x: Modelling and texturing Burrow has built-in tools to make voxel models and pixel-art textures, for humans in the editor (Tools > Model editor and Tools > Texture Editor: each opens as a full-window docked panel, or in a separate window from the asset's right-click menu) and for AI agents through MCP ( editor_model , editor_texture ). Both are declarative and deterministic : you send a list of operations (ops), the same ops always give a byte-identical result, and the op list is stored with the asset so it can be edited later. Packages: model/ (voxel models), texedit/ (textures); windows editor/ui/model_ws.go , editor/ui/texture_ui.go , editor/ui/toolwin.go ; tools editor/agent/modeltools.go . Everything an agent needs is in the tool descriptions and this page. The loop is: send ops, look at the returned image , fix, repeat, save. Textures also get surface relief: the texture editor's Relief section derives a height from the colours (dark = deeper), or reads a painted one ( Painted : a grey layer named height , white = surface, darker = sunk; it is not part of the colours), builds a normal map from it and a constant specular map, and writes <name>_n.png / <name>_s.png next to the texture (see rendering.md , "Parallax relief"). Voxel models ( .bmodel ) A .bmodel is versioned JSON ( "format":"burrow.bmodel","version":1 ): name, grid size (up to 256 x 256 x 256), a palette of materials ( color #rrggbb , emissive 0..255, gloss 0..255, alpha 0..255), named parts (a part is a rigid bone: parent , pivot ), attachment points ( attach : a hand, a socket, a light position), the voxel grid (run-length encoded, gzip, base64, with a SHA-256) and the op list that built it. Decoding is strict: unknown fields, a bad version, a wrong checksum, oversize grids and corrupt runs are rejected ( model.Decode never panics, fuzzed). Axes: x right, y up, z toward the viewer (Burrow axes). A cell (x,y,z) fills [x,x+1) . Box corners are inclusive cell coordinates; centres, pivots and attachment points are corner coordinates ( center=[8,8,8] is the corner shared by the eight middle cells, so sphere center=[8,8,8] radius=3 is symmetric in a 16 grid). Two ways to send ops JSON list ( ops ) or the text DSL ( dsl ), one op per line, op key=value ... ; values are JSON or bare words ( mat=wood , min=[0,0,0] , colors=[a,b] ); repeat count=4 offset=[2,0,0] { ... } opens a block; # starts a comment. model.ParseDSL and model.FormatDSL round-trip; editor_model {action:get} returns the stored recipe as DSL or JSON. editor_model {"action":"ops","dsl":"size size=[16,16,16]\nmaterial name=wood color=#a67c45\nbox min=[2,0,2] max=[9,5,9] mat=wood"} ops is all or nothing (one undo step; on error nothing changes and the error names the op index and the valid values). build replaces the model by building it from scratch. verify replays the stored ops and compares the result (the determinism check). Ops op what it does size {size:[x,y,z]} grid size, <= 256 per axis (content kept, cropped). First op of a model. material {name,color,emissive,gloss,alpha} defines or updates a palette entry (index order = definition order, max 255). mat of any op also accepts #rrggbb , auto-added. material {name,rename:new} renames an entry (index kept); material {name,remove:true} deletes it (its voxels are cleared, higher indexes shift down). material {name,move:n} moves an entry to the 0-based palette index n (voxels are remapped, the model looks the same; drag a swatch in the Palette panel). use {mat} default material for the next ops. part {name,parent,pivot} creates or selects a part; new voxels belong to the active part. parent must exist already. part {name,rename:new} renames a part (children and attachments follow); part {name,remove:true} deletes it (its voxels are cleared, children re-attached to its parent; the root cannot be removed). attach {name,pos,part,dir} a named point. attach {name,remove:true} deletes it. box {min,max} , sphere {center,radius} , ellipsoid {center,radii} , cylinder {center,radius,height,axis} , cone {center,radius,height,axis} , torus {center,radius,r2,axis} , capsule {a,b,radius} primitives. A cone's base is at center , its apex height away (negative flips); a cylinder is centred on center ; a torus ring lies in the plane perpendicular to axis ( radius = ring, r2 = tube). voxel {pos} , line {a,b,radius} single cell; 3D line between cells (radius > 0 makes it a capsule). mode on every shape add (union, default), sub (subtract), and (intersect: keep only what is inside), paint (recolour existing voxels inside). Aliases union , subtract , intersect . fill {pos,mat} flood recolour of the connected region of equal material ( mode:sub erases it). extrude {pos,dir,count} pushes the face under pos out along dir (negative count carves in). clear {} empties the active part ( all:true : everything). mirror {axis,at,side,name} copies one side onto the other (default plane: middle of the grid). With name the copy becomes a new part (mirrored pivot): left arm to right arm. array {count,offset,min,max} copies the (boxed) content count times. repeat {count,offset,ops} runs nested ops count times, each shifted by offset more (depth <= 4). translate , rotate {axis,turns,center} , flip {axis} , scale {factor} move, rotate by 90 degree turns, mirror in place, grow (2..8) or shrink (-2..-8). Target: active part, part:"name" , or all:true ; min / max restrict to a box. hollow {thickness} , erode {iter} , dilate {iter} , smooth {iter} remove the inside, shrink, grow, round off (majority filter). displace {amp,scale,seed,noise,octaves} noise displacement of the surface ( noise value or perlin). paint {rule,...} all , gradient {colors,axis,jitter,seed} (height bands, low to high), `speckle {mat stamp {pos,size,mats,data} writes a copied box of voxels at pos (into the active part): size is the box, mats its material names, data the cells as run-length (count, material index) pairs (x fastest, then y, then z; index 0 = empty) base64 url-encoded. StampOp builds it; it is what Ctrl+C of the editor's model window captures. layer {name,rename,move,hidden,locked,copy,remove} creates a layer on top ( copy:other starts it as a duplicate; move:n puts it at index n , 0 = bottom), or renames, reorders, hides, locks or deletes it (the last layer cannot be deleted; variants follow renames and deletions). Every other op takes layer:"name" to draw into that layer (default: the first); on repeat it applies to the body. See Layers and variants . variant {name,layers,rename,move,remove} creates a variant or sets the layers it shows; move:0 makes it the default. Determinism: all geometry is integer arithmetic on 1/32-voxel coordinates, noise is fixed-point hashed noise with an explicit seed ; nothing reads a clock, a global random generator or map order. Limits (hostile input): grid <= 256^3, 4096 executed ops, repeat depth 4, a global evaluation budget (an op over the whole grid costs the grid volume), 255 materials, 64 parts, 64 attachments, 1 MiB of ops text, 64 MiB files; floats must be finite and within 512 voxels. Layers and variants A model has ordered layers (up to 32, bottom first), each its own voxel grid of the model's size with a material and a part per voxel. They are composited bottom to top: a filled voxel of an upper layer replaces the one below. Layers are independent of parts (bones): one part can have voxels in several layers. A layer has a name, a hidden flag (editor visibility only: the game ignores it) and a locked flag (tools and ModelApply refuse edits to it). A variant (up to 64) is a named list of layers shown together. With no variants every layer is shown; the first variant is the default. A campfire: size size=[8,8,8] material name=wood color=#6b4423 material name=fire color=#ff8a1e emissive=200 box min=[1,0,1] max=[6,1,6] mat=wood layer name=flame box layer=flame min=[3,1,3] max=[4,4,4] mat=fire variant name=off layers=[base] variant name=on layers=[base,flame] All variants share one frame (the union of their bounds), so switching variant does not move the model. Draw into a layer with layer: on the ops. Old files are one layer called base ; a model with just that layer is still written in the original format ( version 1 ), others as version 2 (voxels stored per layer, plus variants ); both versions are read. .vox export ( export_vox {variant} ) flattens the chosen variant; the asset loader gives render.voxmodel every variant. Pick the variant a node shows with render.voxmodel.variant (empty or unknown = the default variant). A script switches it at run time, for instance field_set(node, "render.voxmodel", "variant", "\"on\"") (or entity_set_component ) when a campfire is lit; the new variant is meshed once and cached. In the modeler, the Layers tab of the settings panel lists the layers (eye = hide in the editor, lock, click to make one active; add, duplicate, move up/down, rename, delete) and the variants (a checkbox per layer, rename, make default, delete, and a Preview selector that composites only that variant in the viewport). Tools paint, erase and fill into the active layer; every layer or variant change is one undo step. editor_model {action:layer_list} lists them for an agent ( layers is the ASCII slice dump). Recolor: colour variants without a new file render.voxmodel.recolor (and character.recolor ) changes palette entries for one instance: index=#rrggbb[aa] entries separated by commas, with the 1-based palette indices of the .vox , for instance "3=#c02020,7=#2060d0" makes the red team and the blue team from one model. The recoloured mesh is built once per combination and cached, so there is no per-frame cost. A script sets it at run time with field_set(node, "render.voxmodel", "recolor", "\"3=#c02020\"") . In the editor the inspector shows one colour row per colour the model uses (the 16 most used), with Reset colours . It composes with variant . A character with a built-in model ( humanoid ...) ignores it; use skin there. Which way a .vox faces MagicaVoxel's front is its -Y side (what its default camera sees). render.voxmodel puts that side toward the engine forward (-Z, yaw 0), the same as a character made from the same file. There is no option: it is the only convention. A project made before it ( vox_front absent or "legacy" ) is converted by burrow migrate , which turns its render.voxmodel nodes by 180 degrees about Y (and their direct children back) so they look the same. Bounds and editor picking follow the same front. The model editor's own viewport keeps its fixed view. Feedback an agent gets editor_model returns stats (voxel count, bounds, colours with counts, per-part counts, mirror symmetry per axis for shape and colour, connected pieces and floating/disconnected voxels with their positions) and, for ops / build / load , a montage image : front (F), side (S), top (T) and isometric (I) views. preview {view,part,yaw,pitch} renders one view ( part dims the others: the onion view). layers prints the voxels as ASCII layers (top layer first). Read the image after every batch : stats cannot tell you a nose is on the wrong side. Scale and size references A block is one world voxel edge: 1 m at the default world voxel size 1, 0.25 m in a world with 0.25 m voxels. A model stores its target scale , voxels_per_block (default 16, so one model voxel is 6.25 cm and render.voxmodel scale is 1/16), optionally with a kind hint ( prop , character , vehicle , building , item ). Both are optional fields of the .bmodel (absent = 16 and no kind) and Model.PreferredScale() is the scale the model asks for when placed. Metres per model voxel = world voxel size / voxels_per_block . The player is 1.8 m tall (28.8 model voxels at 16 per block), eye line 1.62 m, shoulders 0.6 m; a door is 1 m wide and 2 m high. Typical sizes: character height 1.2-2.5 m, item largest side up to 1 m, prop 0.1-4 m, vehicle 1.5-12 m, building 3-64 m; a model outside its kind's range gets a warning. In the editor, the Advanced tab of Model Settings has a Scale section: voxels per block (drag or 8/16/32/64), the kind, the size in metres, blocks and voxels, the ratio to the player, a "fits a 1 x 2 m door" check and the warnings. Its toggles (also in the viewport menu, Scale references) draw over the viewport: a player silhouette, a one-block cube, a block grid on the floor, rulers along the bounds (metres, blocks, voxels), and a doorway with the 2 m door and 3 m ceiling lines. Changing the scale or the kind is one undo step. Agents: editor_model results carry dimensions (voxels, blocks, metres, player_ratio , fits_door , warnings ) and dimensions_text ; the montage draws a blue player figure and a red one-block cube left of and behind the model at the same scale ( no_reference turns them off). action: scale with voxels_per_block and/or kind sets the target scale; a rebuild keeps it and spawn uses it when scale is 0. Assets, instances, bones save {path} writes assets/models/<name>.bmodel (project relative, confined to the project). export_vox / load handle MagicaVoxel .vox (parts become scene-graph nodes and come back as parts with their pivots; palette colours become materials c<index> ; emissive and gloss have no .vox equivalent here). .bmodel loads through the asset system as the same value as .vox , so it works wherever a .vox does: the render.voxmodel component (props, entities: editor_model {action:spawn} adds the node, saving again hot reloads it), character models ( "model":"assets/x.bmodel" ) and the animation skeleton ( anim.SkeletonFromVox : each part is a bone with its pivot, parent gives the hierarchy, the root part is the skeleton root; docs/animation.md). Model 0 of the loaded file is the whole model merged (what render.voxmodel draws), models 1.. are the parts. Dynamic voxel bodies (physics3d): model.SolidMask() gives the dense occupancy array for physics3d.VoxelBody . Block custom shapes : a 16 x 16 x 16 model gives BlockBoxes() / editor_model {action:block_shape} : boxes in sixteenths of a block with the axes and units of package shape ( shape.Box ). Registering a new shape family still means appending to the frozen shape.Models table (a source change); the boxes are the geometry to put there. Scripts (read access only): burrowsdk.SpawnModel("assets/models/crate.bmodel", 0, burrowsdk.SpawnOpts{...}) spawns a node showing the asset by name. It is sugar over Spawn with a render.voxmodel component: no new host call, the script reads nothing, the sim is unaffected. In the editor the model editor is a docked panel (Unreal-style asset editor): Tools > Model editor, or double-click a .bmodel / .vox in the Content browser, opens the Model panel in the dock (a tab next to the Viewport), with Model settings on the right and the Content browser below as the content browser. The panel has one header row (document name with an unsaved dot, Save, undo/redo, the Iso / Front / Side / Top views, Frame, and the ⋯ menu), the tool rail on the left with each tool's key on its button (B place, E erase, C paint, X box, O sphere, L line, F fill, T extrude, S select) and the viewport in the middle. Model settings has three tabs: Palette (the material grid with number keys, double-click a swatch for its colour picker, a Recent row, the selected material's name, colour, emissive and gloss, then the options of the active tool: Add or Carve for the shapes, brush size, mirror, Stay on the start plane , slice), Parts and Advanced (file, selection, modifiers, recipe, model info). The viewport is a real 3D render (perspective by default, orthographic with the header's Persp / Ortho switch or P; the picking uses the same camera; daylight lighting) when a GPU is available, with the software render as fallback. Save writes the asset path directly (Ctrl+S); New and Save-as are inline forms in Model settings (New also offers the embedded templates crate / lantern / tree / creature), Open is the Content browser — no modal dialogs. A separate OS window is still available (right-click the asset > "Open in a separate window", or Window > New window; burrowedit -tool model -project <dir> -asset <file> , a second process that saves into the project and the editor picks the saved file up). input action left click, left drag use the tool (place, erase and paint drag as one stroke, held to the plane it started on unless Stay on the start plane is off); a ghost voxel in the material colour shows where a voxel will land, and with brush > 1 the real brush sphere is drawn drag (box, sphere, line, select) draw the shape live from one end to the other, its size shown next to the pointer; it is placed when the pointer is released. In the docked panel a Box on a flat footprint takes a second step : move the pointer up to set the height, click to place, Esc cancels. A click without dragging sets the first corner of the two-click workflow instead. Hold Shift (or choose Carve) to carve instead of add right drag, Alt + left drag orbit (Alt + drag for trackpads); the preset views animate P switch between the perspective and orthographic camera orientation cube (bottom left) click X, Y or Z to look along that axis; click it again for the opposite side middle drag, Shift + right drag, Space + left drag pan wheel zoom toward the pointer 1 to 9 pick a material (or click a swatch; Alt + click a voxel picks its material) Home isometric view (also Front, Side, Top, Back, Left, Right, Bottom in the View menu) Shift+F frame the selection (or the hovered cell) in the viewport Shift+X / Y / Z toggle the mirror plane of that axis Ctrl+A select the whole grid Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V copy the selection; then a ghost of the copy follows the pointer and the next click drops it (Esc cancels) Esc cancel the first click of a two-click tool, a paste or a gizmo drag, clear the selection Delete delete the selection + / - brush size Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Y, Ctrl+S, Ctrl+Shift+S, Ctrl+O, Ctrl+N undo, redo, save, save as, open, new Menus: the tool window's menu bar has File (New..., New from template ▸ crate/lantern/tree/creature, Open, Save, Save as, Export .vox), Edit (undo/redo, Select all, Copy/Paste/Delete selection, brush size +/−), View (presets, Frame selection, Reset zoom and pan, mirror, slice, onion, hide part) and Help (keyboard shortcuts). The docked panel exposes the same entries in its ⋯ header menu , and the viewport opens the same menu on a right click without drag (a right drag still orbits). In the main editor, Tools > Model editor opens the panel and also offers New from template and Open in a separate window; the Content browser's right-click menu on a .bmodel / .vox adds Spawn in scene at focus and Export .vox , and New > New voxel model from template starts from a template. With the Select tool, the selection shows a move gizmo : drag one of its three coloured axes to translate the selection (one undo step). The Modifiers panel applies the engine's procedural ops to the selection (or the whole model without one), each one undo step: Hollow (thickness), Smooth / Erode / Dilate (iterations), Displace (noise amp, scale, seed), Paint gradient (from/to material, axis) and speckle (density), mirror fix (copy one half onto the other), and Array (duplicate the selection N times with an offset). The Palette panel shows the usage count of each material, renames (name field) and deletes (Delete button or right-click a swatch) entries. The Parts panel renames and deletes parts and edits the attach points (add one at the hovered cell). The Model panel resizes the grid (content kept, cropped if smaller) and shows the stats; the Recipe panel shows the stored op list (DSL) that rebuilds the model byte for byte. The status bar shows the active tool, brush, mirror planes, selection and zoom at a glance, and an empty model shows its shortcut hints in the viewport itself. Mirror X, Y and Z (the tool options) mirror every edit across the middle plane of the grid; the planes are drawn in the viewport while they are active. The Slice buttons (the tool options or View menu) cut the model along an axis to reach the inside: the slider keeps the first N layers, the cut plane is drawn in the viewport and picking ignores the cut cells, so you edit the exposed interior directly. The view draws the floor grid and axes, and renders at half resolution while you orbit, pan or stroke so the view stays smooth on big models. Every stroke is one step of the window's undo history and appends an op to the recipe. The view draws the floor grid and axes, and renders at half resolution while you orbit, pan or stroke so the view stays smooth on big models. Every stroke is one step of the window's undo history and appends an op to the recipe. Model edits are not part of the simulation hash. Textures editor_texture edits one texture at a time: block textures 16 x 16 .. 128 x 128 (square or not), item icons, with layers. Ops are JSON: op what it does size {count} or {w,h} texture size (4..128). First op. palette {name,color} names a colour; any colour field accepts #rrggbb , #rrggbbaa , transparent or a palette name. lock {colors} palette lock: every later op snaps its result to these colours (no colors = unlock). fill , clear , `erase {rect points}` gradient {from,to,dir,count} dir v, h, d (diagonal) or r (radial); count > 1 makes bands. `noise {kind,seed,scale,colors from,to,octaves,count,strength}` `dither {from,to,kind,dir strength}` speckle {colors,density,seed} random pixels. pattern {kind,colors,mortar,seed,...} bricks (bw, bh, gap), planks (bh), cobble (cell), ore (count, depth), grass_edge (depth), checker , stripes . Sizes must divide the texture to tile (the error tells you which). ascii {grid,legend,pos} draw from a character grid; . and space are transparent unless the legend says otherwise. editor_texture {action:ascii} dumps the current pixels in the same format. pixel , line , rect {hollow} , ellipse {hollow} , flood {pos,color,tolerance} , replace {from,to,tolerance} pixel tools. outline {kind,color} outer , inner , both or border (tile edge). shade {kind,amount} edges (light from the top left), bevel (tile border), relief (luminance steps read as height). hue {deg,sat,light} hue shift and saturation / lightness percent. seamless {amount} cross-fades the shifted copy so the borders match. quantize {colors,kind:bayer,strength} nearest-palette (optionally dithered). offset {dx,dy} , flip {dir} , rotate {count} wrap shift, mirror, quarter turns. layer {action,name,opacity,visible,locked,kind} new , duplicate , select , delete , merge_down , opacity , visible , lock ( locked : a locked layer refuses drawing ops), blend ( kind : normal , multiply , screen , overlay ). Ops draw on the active layer. Limits: 128 x 128, 2048 ops, 8 layers, 1 MiB PNG, 128 x 128 ASCII cells. The same ops always give the same PNG bytes. Feedback: ops returns the texture tiled 3 x 3 (read the seams), a block-in-world render (3 x 3 blocks with a pillar, isometric; give top / side / bottom texture names to see a real block), the mip chain , and stats: colours and counts, transparent pixels, wrap-around steps ( seam_error_h/v ) against the largest interior step and tileable_h/v . A grass side texture is meant to tile horizontally only. Saving: the project override layer save {kind:block,name:"cobblestone"} or save {block:"grass_block", face:"side"} writes <project>/textures/block/<texture>.png (and the recipe <texture>.texops.json beside it). block + face resolves the pack texture name that face samples, so the override replaces exactly it (a texture shared by several blocks changes all of them). The bundled third-party pack (Pixel Perfection CC-BY-SA) is never modified : overrides live in the project, win over the pack, and are resampled to the pack size (16) because the layer table has one size (the PNG keeps its resolution). The running game (editor Play, burrow run ) rebuilds its block texture layers on the next frame ( blocktex.OverrideGeneration ); burrow build packs only the folders listed in asset_dirs of vox.project : add "textures" there to ship the overrides. Item icons go to textures/item/ . Tinted textures (grass top, leaves) are gray luma in the packs and biome tinted at render time. In the editor the texture editor is a window of its own (Tools > Texture Editor, or double-click a .png in the Content browser; burrowedit -tool texture -project <dir> -asset <file> ). Tools are on the left (B pencil, E eraser, L line, R rectangle, O ellipse, F fill, A replace colour, I picker, G gradient, plus the Hollow toggle for rectangle and ellipse, mirror left-right and top-bottom and the primary / secondary colours), the canvas takes the middle and the colours, layers, previews, generators and relief maps are on the right. A block texture has three faces : the side is the main picture, the top and the bottom are drawn only when they differ (the header's Face selector; a new face starts as a copy of the side). Save writes <name>.png , <name>_top.png and <name>_bottom.png (the packs' naming), open reads them back, and undo goes back to the face it was made on. Layers can be hidden, locked (drawing tools refuse a locked layer) and blended (normal, multiply, screen, overlay) with an opacity. input action left button, right button draw with the primary, the secondary colour Alt + click pick the colour under the pointer (any tool) wheel zoom toward the pointer (the pixel grid shows from 6x) middle drag, Space + drag pan 0 or Home, + / - fit to the window, zoom X swap the primary and secondary colours Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Y, Ctrl+S, Ctrl+Shift+S, Ctrl+O, Ctrl+N undo, redo, save, save as, open, new One-click styles (Generate panel): pick a style (Stone, Planks, Bricks, Cobble, Metal, Grass, Sand, Ore, Fabric), a seed and a base colour, press Generate: the layer is cleared and rebuilt by a curated op stack (pattern, periodic noise, speckle, shading, seamless) as one undo step, the whole "patron" of a block texture. From a 3D model : pick a .bmodel or .vox of the project and press Import: its material palette (most used first) fills the swatches and the primary / secondary colours, so the styles match the model they will sit next to. The pattern steps always divide the texture size, so the tiled styles tile by construction; texedit.StyleOps builds the same stacks programmatically. Strokes are filled in between mouse samples, so a fast drag leaves no gaps, and each stroke is one undo step. The brush size (pencil and eraser) goes up to 8. A texture made with New saves to textures/<block|item>/<name>.png (the override layer above); a .png opened from the Content browser saves back to that file. File > Save to a block face writes the texture over the one a block uses on a face. The status bar shows the pixel and colour under the pointer. h: Behaviour trees and state machines ( nav/ai )
x: Navigation and AI Package nav (graph, pathfinding, steering, plugin) and nav/ai (behaviour trees, state machines, utility scoring, perception geometry). Genre neutral: a profile describes the body, the voxels describe the world. It is off by default in vox.project ( runtime.plugins.nav: true enables it: its components and request queue are hashed state), or add &nav.Plugin{} after ScenePlugin , the voxel world and PhysicsPlugin . Behaviour definitions load from <name>.bt.json (or ai/<name>.bt.json ) in the project. Try it: go run ./examples/nav_demo -shot out.png (CPU renderer, no window). Design Graph. A node is the voxel holding an agent's feet (for width 2, the lowest corner of its 2x2 footprint). Per profile ( Height 1-8, Width 1-2, StepHeight , JumpHeight <= 4, DropHeight <= 31 (a region reads at most one chunk below a node), CanSwim , CanClimb , CanFly , NoDiagonal ) a node is ground (solid floor, body clear), water (feet in liquid, or floating on it), climb (ladder, vine and rope blocks, World.Climbable ) or air (flyers: any clear cell). Moves: 4/8 neighbours with step up, jump up, drop down (fall column clear), unit moves through water and ladders, 26 neighbours without corner cutting for flyers. Costs are tenths of a block: 10 / 14, +4 per stepped block, +14 per jumped block, +2 per dropped block, 15 swimming, 20 climbing. The heuristic is admissible, so flat A* is optimal (tests compare it with BFS and Dijkstra). Micro-voxels. A cell holding a brick (docs/blocks.md "Micro-voxels") is neither solid nor air: its solid micro voxels (registry Solid ) are reduced to a mask of sixteenths of the cell height inside the agent's footprint band (the whole cell, or the centred 2 * RadiusM band for a one-cell wide agent with RadiusM , so a doorway carved 8/16 wide passes a 0.5 m wide agent and not a 1 m one). An agent stands at the lowest feet offset f (0..15 sixteenths) with a solid layer right under its feet (the cell below for f = 0) and its body, Height cells tall, free above them: on a micro slab or half-step it stands at f = 8, under a lintel only if it fits. Moves compare floors in sixteenths: a rise up to the step height ( StepHeight , or StepM in sixteenths of a voxel after Scaled ) is a step (cost +4 per voxel, rounded up per micro step), up to the jump height a jump, a micro step down is a walk, a longer fall a drop. TestWalkerCrossesMicroStepsAndEndsOnTheSlab drives a nav agent that is a physics.character over a micro quarter step and a micro slab and checks it ends at the slab height; the character reads the world through sim.Chunks ( voxel.Access ), which exposes the bricks, the shape registry and the fine water like the map itself. A world without bricks classifies and costs exactly as before (navmesh results unchanged). String pulling only joins nodes with the same feet offset. The follower aims at the micro floor: the waypoint height is the node's cell plus its feet offset ( feetY ), so the arrival test, the final approach, the jump decision (a rise above the controller's step height) and the kinematic height all use the sixteenths, and an agent steps up micro steps smoothly and stands on a micro slab. Water in bricks: a brick cell counts as liquid for the swim, avoid and surface-float rules when any of its micro voxels holds a liquid block ( liquidAt ; the layer does not matter, the body of an agent in the cell is wet), so a swimmer treats it as water and a walker cannot stand in it. Fine water: when the source carries the fluid automaton's fine bricks ( voxel.FineReader : a ChunkMap with SetFine , or voxel.Access ), a cell whose fine brick holds a mean depth of at least World.FineWaterDepth (a fraction of the cell, default 0.5, negative disables) is liquid too. It is live state read on each liquidAt query, not cached with the chunk, so cached region paths are not invalidated when the water moves. Derived, never state. World classifies each chunk into solid/liquid/climbable bit planes (12 KB per chunk) and validates it against voxel.Chunk.Version (changes on every write, undo restore and decode; new, additive accessor) on first use per request. A stale answer is impossible, with or without an observer, after undo and after snapshot restore. The voxel.Observer feed ( World.Attach , chained behind an existing observer such as fluid's) only queues changed chunks: World.Update(budget) rebuilds at most budget of them per call in ascending chunk order. Tests prove incremental update == fresh rebuild (classification and regions) and that undo is noticed. The caches are bounded ( MaxCachedChunks 2048, MaxCachedRegions 1024, least recently touched dropped at the start of the next request: wall time only, charges are unchanged). Detach is chain-aware (an observer installed after ours stays in the chain); install fluid before Attach , since fluid refuses a map that already has an observer. Hierarchy. For goals farther than 48 blocks, each chunk is split per profile into regions (components of the mutual moves inside the chunk) with portals (moves leaving the chunk). An abstract A* over regions gives a corridor, then every chunk segment is refined by a small A* confined to that chunk (HPA ). The abstract search, the refinement and a fallback flat A share one unit budget (an unreachable goal in a big loaded world costs the budget, not hundreds of region builds), and every portal move is re-checked before it is used. Any failure falls back to flat A . On a 200x200 field with pillars and walls the corridor search expanded 746 nodes against 2275 for flat A at 5 % longer paths. Smoothing. String pulling: look-ahead 24 nodes, a straight sweep of the body (corner cells included) must be free; ground profiles only smooth within one level, flyers and swimmers in 3D. Flying and swimming. Flyers use 3D flat A* (no hierarchy: long flights are partial paths that re-plan). Swimmers switch between walking and swimming nodes; a swimming physics.character gets the swim intent ( Move.Y ). Dynamic obstacles. nav.obstacle entities block a box each tick (not cached, not in the hierarchy). Moving or removing one changes the answer on the next request; agents revalidate the next four waypoints every ValidateEvery ticks and re-plan when a node vanished. Crowds. Steer is RVO-lite: 28 candidate velocities (7 headings at 3 speeds + stand still) scored by deviation and time to collision against up to Neighbours nearest agents (spatial hash, fixed order, pure function), plus a personal-space push. Neighbour velocities are the previous tick's, so entity order never matters. Following. Agents with a physics.character get Move / Jump intent (jump when the next waypoint is above the step height, swim up/down in water); others are moved by the plugin (flyers, simple creatures). Stuck for 3 s: re-plan. Determinism and budgets Paths are computed inside the fixed tick by the system nav (before physics.character ) from a FIFO queue ( Queue , a hashed fixed resource: entity + goal sequence). Requests run to completion, never across ticks, so there is no half-done search to snapshot. The cost of a request is counted in units (one unit is about one node expansion; first touch of a chunk = 4, of a region = 100, per request) and charged whether or not the data was cached, so which tick a path completes in never depends on the cache. engine.VerifyCacheNeutrality passes with the plugin. cap default meaning TickUnits 4000 units spent on requests per tick (one request may overshoot by its last step, <= ~1000) ReqUnits 2500 cap of one request; beyond it the best partial path is returned MaxPerTick 48 requests started per tick MaxQueue 4096 queued requests; agents beyond stay pending and retry the next tick ValidatePerTick , ValidateEvery 256, 8 path revalidations ScanPerTick , ThinkPerTick 96, 256 perception scans and brain thinks per tick: the agents whose next time is oldest go first, so nobody starves ScanChunks 32 chunks re-verified per tick by the prewarm Neighbours 6 crowd neighbours per agent Per agent and tick the plugin always does O(1) work (follow, steer, write back changed components only). Measured on this machine: 10k agents with every request queued: worst tick 7 ms; 3000 walking agents with crowd avoidance: mean tick 3.5 ms (see nav/scale_slow_test.go , go test -tags slow ./nav ). A far request (170 blocks) costs ~1800 units, about 1.4 ms warm and 20 ms the first time the chunks are seen. Agents under a parent node use their world position ( WorldAffine ); nav writes back the local position. Limits: coordinates within +-1048575; a stored path holds at most 512 waypoints (longer ones are partial and re-planned); unloaded space counts as air (no floor, so not walkable, but flyers may enter it).
