Components component purpose nav.agent profile , speed , radius , goal ( goal , has_goal , slack ), feet and face (agents without physics.character : the node's origin is its feet, where a .vox model has its base, instead of its body center; the node turns toward where it walks, yaw 0 facing -Z); state: state , path , idx , partial , ... nav.obstacle half : box blocked around the node position nav.target makes an entity perceivable: tag , height , noise , hidden ai.perception sight , fov , hear , eye , targets (tag filter), memory , interval ; state: seen ai.brain asset ( wolf loads wolf.bt.json ), interval ; state: blackboard, node memory Commands (journaled, in the agent session act list and engine.RegisterCommand ): nav_set_goal {path, goal, slack} , nav_stop {path} . nav.SpawnAgent(name, pos, agent, extra...) returns the commands that create an agent node. nav.Res(app).Stats() reports the last tick (agents, requests, units, queue, scans, thinks, builds). a.AddPlugin(&nav.Plugin{Config: nav.Config{ Profiles: []nav.Profile{nav.Walker, nav.Flyer, {Name: "tank" , Height: 3 , Width: 2 , StepHeight: 1 , JumpHeight: 1 , DropHeight: 2 }}, Assets: func (name string ) ([] byte , error ) { return os.ReadFile( "ai/" + name + ".bt.json" ) }, }}) cmds := nav.SpawnAgent( "wolf" , mathx.Vec3{X: 4.5 , Y: 1.9 , Z: 4.5 }, nav.NewAgent( "walker" ), nav.Comp{Name: physics.CompCharacter, Value: physics.NewCharacter()}, nav.Comp{Name: nav.CompBrain, Value: nav.NewBrain( "wolf" )}) Without the physics plugin agents are moved by nav itself, so a headless game needs nothing else. With it, give the character StepHeight >= profile.StepHeight + 0.05 . Voxel size Everything an author writes is in metres; the graph is built in voxels. At the default one metre voxel the two are the same, so existing profiles and components read unchanged. In a world of n voxels per metre (0.5 m, 0.25 m, 0.125 m voxels: n = 2, 4, 8) the plugin converts at Build ( Profile.Scaled(n) ): the whole-number fields ( Height , Width , StepHeight , JumpHeight , DropHeight ) multiply by n , and the optional fractional fields HeightM , RadiusM , StepM , JumpM , DropM (JSON height_m , radius_m , step_m , jump_m , drop_m ) win over them. Rounding keeps the body honest: height and footprint ( 2 * RadiusM in cells) round up, so a 1.8 m agent never fits a gap lower than itself; step, jump and drop round down, so it never claims a ledge or fall beyond its ability; drop is capped at 31 voxels. Body limits scale with n (height 8 m, width 2 m, jump 4 m). A 1.8 m / 0.4 m agent ( HeightM 1.8, RadiusM 0.4 ) is 2x1 voxels at scale 1 and 8x4 at scale 4, and passes the same 2 m doors in either. Build graphs by hand with NewWorldAt(n, profile.Scaled(n)) . nav.agent speed , radius and slack , ai.perception sight , hear and eye , nav.target height , and the behaviour tree arguments ( wander radius , chase stop , flee dist , dist_lt / dist_gt ) are metres; sensed distances ( seen[].dist , target_dist ) are reported in metres. Path costs are tenths of a voxel of walking and the ratios between move kinds are per voxel, so paths have the same shape at every size; nav.CostMetres(cost, n) converts a result cost to metres. goal and path stay voxel cells. Behaviour trees and state machines ( nav/ai ) A definition is JSON ( .bt.json ) or Go ( ai.Def ). Node types: sequence , selector (both resume the running child; "reactive": true re-evaluates from the first child every think and resets the child it pre-empts), parallel ( policy all or any ), inverter , succeeder , failer , repeat {n} , retry {n} , cooldown {seconds} , timeout {seconds} , wait {seconds} , condition {name,args} , action {name,args} , utility (each child has a score naming a registered scorer; the best child runs until it finishes). Limits: 512 nodes, depth 32, 1 MiB. { "type" : "bt" , "name" : "wolf" , "root" :{ "type" : "selector" , "reactive" : true , "children" :[ { "type" : "sequence" , "children" :[{ "type" : "condition" , "name" : "has_target" },{ "type" : "action" , "name" : "chase" , "args" :{ "stop" : 1.6 }}]}, { "type" : "sequence" , "children" :[{ "type" : "action" , "name" : "wander" , "args" :{ "radius" : 9 }},{ "type" : "wait" , "seconds" : 1 }]}]}} {"type":"fsm","fsm":{"initial":"graze","states":[{"name":"graze","on_tick":[{"name":"stop"}],"transitions":[{"to":"alert", "if":[{"name":"can_see"}]}]}, ...]}} is a state machine: on_enter and on_tick calls run, then the first transition whose conditions ( not negates) all succeed and that is at least after seconds old fires. examples/nav_demo/ai/ has a tree and a machine for each creature. Built-in conditions: has_target , can_see , heard , arrived , path_failed , moving , in_water , bb_true {key} , bb_lt / bb_gt {key,v} , dist_lt / dist_gt {v,key} , chance {p} . Actions: wander {radius} , move_to {key,slack} , look_home , chase {key,stop} , flee {key,dist} , stop , set {key,value} , idle . Scorers: const , random , target_near , target_far . Register your own with nav.Config.AI ( ai.NewRegistry().Func(name, f).Scorer(...) ); a function gets an *ai.Ctx (blackboard, tick, Rand , Local scratch) and nav.ViewOf(ctx) for the agent. Everything an agent remembers is in ai.brain : the blackboard (sorted, at most 64 keys; numbers, vectors, entities and short strings) and mem , so snapshots, undo and replay cover an agent in the middle of an action. ctx.Rand is a pure function of agent, tick and salt. The blackboard keys target , target_pos , target_dist , can_see , heard , arrived , failed , moving , self_pos and home are refreshed before every think. A bad asset name or definition leaves the brain inert (a failed read is retried after 60 ticks, a failed compile after 600; the tick never fails). The brain stores the content hash of its asset ( ai.brain.hash ): a changed asset restarts the brain, and an asset that differs between a live run and its replay shows as a StateHash difference. Config.Assets must be a pure function of the name during a run. State machines are capped at 256 calls/transitions and 8 conditions per transition; forged mem values never crash a tick. .bt.json files are project files and asset database assets (importer behaviour , validated at load); the plugin compiles them on first use through Config.Assets . Perception. ai.perception scans every interval ticks (at most ScanPerTick per tick): targets within max(sight, hear) from a spatial hash, nearest first, at most 12 checked. Sight: inside the cone ( fov , facing follows movement), within sight , and a voxel.Raycast from the eye to the target's height is not blocked. Hearing: distance <= hear * noise (through walls). Seen targets are remembered memory ticks, nearest first, at most 8. Utility scoring. ai.Option{Considerations: [...]} with ai.Curve response curves (linear, quadratic, sqrt, inverse, logistic, step) scored with a compensation factor; ai.Best picks the first maximum. Scripts Additive host calls (module vox , see script/ABI.md) and sdk/burrowsdk/nav.go : NavSetGoal , NavStop , NavSetGoalPos (world position), NavGetState , NavPath , NavSetBB , NavGetBB (numbers), NavPutBB , NavReadBB , NavDelBB (typed values: number, vector, entity, string), NavSensed . They edit the nav components like entity_set_component (applied at the end of the invocation, journaled). Debug overlay and tools engine.DebugLines ( engine/debuglines.go ) is a frame-domain list of world lines in named layers ( Layer("nav") ; a user only ever clears its own layer). nav.Res(app).SetDebug(nav.DebugOptions{Paths: true, Graph: true, Center: c, Radius: 12}) makes the plugin fill its layer every frame: paths (green, white waypoints, red goal box), the walkable graph (yellow ground, blue water, magenta ladder, cyan air), obstacles (orange). The CPU renderer and -shot captures draw the lines with engine.OverlayLines ; the Vulkan renderer draws them live ( render/vulkan/lines.go , shaders dbgline.* , up to 4096 lines per frame, depth tested) in the game window and in the editor viewport ( make nav-demo-gpu writes a GPU frame). The editor and the editor MCP server have it too: the Project settings dialog has a nav checkbox ( runtime.plugins.nav ; burrowedit -nav ), and the tool editor_nav {action state|path|goal|stop|debug} queries a path over the current world, sends a nav.agent node to a goal (journaled nav_set_goal ), stops it and toggles the overlay. Tests go test ./nav/... : mazes against BFS and Dijkstra, incremental update against a fresh rebuild, undo and stale caches, hierarchy validity and cost, step/jump/drop/headroom, swim/climb/fly, obstacles, steering, behaviour tree semantics, JSON loading, twin runs, snapshot mid path, journal replay, cache neutrality, perception, path floods (600 agents fast, 10k with -tags slow ), fuzzing ( go test ./nav -fuzz FuzzFindPath , ./nav/ai -fuzz FuzzLoad ).

h: What a game author must know
Joining and hosting from the game
x: Networking Burrow multiplayer is server-authoritative replication : the server alone runs the simulation (scripts, physics, water, block logic, weather) and streams to each client the part of the state around its player. Clients run only frame stages (rendering, UI, audio, prediction) on the replicated copy and send whitelisted commands. There is one network model; burrow serve , burrow-server , the lobby and the matchmaker, burrowplay -connect and the editor's host session all use it. How the state is selected, encoded and budgeted is in Replication . This page describes the connection layer shared by every server: the protocol ( net/wire ), the transports ( net/transport ), the handshake, security and limits ( net/gate , net/netbase ), the simulation side ( net/netsim ), the engine integration ( net/netapp , internal/netplay ) and how to play. For an always-on headless server see Dedicated server ; for matches between players, the Lobby . The player registry is off by default; runtime.plugins.net: true installs it. Contents What a game author must know Playing: host, join, editor Engine integration Remote player movement Using the API Protocol Security and threat model Limits How it is tested What is not covered FAQ Joining and hosting from the game What a game author must know The server simulates, clients show. Fixed systems and scripts run on the server only. A client never steps its copy of the simulation, so its StateHash and journal mean nothing. Keep client-visible state in components, not in script State. Script State (inventories, furnaces, skills kept in a table) stays on the server. What a client must display or read goes in a component, replicated to everyone, to the owner only or to nearby clients: see Component visibility . All state changes are commands. A frame system that changes the simulation from local input (keyboard, mouse, UI clicks) must submit a command instead of applying it: the engine's command router ( App.SetCommandRouter ) takes such commands away and sends them to the server. Read player input from the registry. netsim.Lookup(e, id).Input is the input the player sent for this tick: quantized integers (movement axes in thousandths, yaw and pitch in millidegrees, a button bit field). Use netsim.Quantize to build one from floats. Client commands are whitelisted. By default a client may submit net_player_input , set_block , block_use (a right click on an interactive block), fill_box (at most 4096 voxels), fill_sphere (radius at most 8) and micro_edit (at most 16 edits and 128 listed voxels, no raw put ), each with its own rate limit. Anything else is rejected and counted. A game adds its own kinds with Whitelist.Allow , with a validator that checks the payload and rewrites it into its canonical form; the simulation validates every command again when it applies it. Do not trust a command's claim of who sent it. The default validator of net_player_input forces the player id to the sender. Chat is not simulation state. It travels next to the frames. Moderation (kick, ban, whitelist), passwords, identity and TLS pinning are the same on every server. Pins. The server rejects a client whose engine version, project content hash, configuration hash, seed or pinned rule versions (for example the fine water rules) differ. netbase.HashFS computes the project content hash. World scale. A world with a voxel size other than one metre (or texture_scale metre ) adds the pin rules world.voxel_size and world.texture_scale . A client with another size is refused with CodeProject and "world voxel size: server 0.25 m, client 1 m"; the player installs the matching project. Playing: host, join, editor Add "net": true to runtime.plugins in vox.project . Players need the same project files and engine version. Host: burrow serve [dir | game.voxpak] . It listens on :7777 with TLS 1.3 ( --addr ), creates its certificate on first run in <user config dir>/burrow/server ( server.key mode 0600), and prints join link: burrow://host:7777?fp=<certificate fingerprint>&key=<password> The key is random unless you pass --password (or the BURROW_SERVE_PASSWORD environment variable) or --open . --advertise host:port writes your public name in the link. Treat a link with a key as a secret. Chat lines arrive on stderr. Join: burrowplay -connect <link> [-name ana] [project] . The link's fingerprint pins the certificate; without one the first connection trusts the certificate and remembers it in <user config dir>/burrow/known_servers , and a changed certificate is refused. The reconnect token of each server is kept in <user config dir>/burrow/tokens.json (mode 0600): after a lost connection the client redials for about 30 s and takes its slot back. Lines typed on stdin (and -say text ) are chat. -headless -ticks N follows the server for N ticks (for tests). Editor: Play > Host multiplayer session runs the open project as a listen server whose first player is the editor user. While the session runs, editing, undo, redo and manual stepping are disabled ( ErrNetLocked ): the session owns the simulation. Stop ends the session and restores the document exactly as Play does. Engine integration The plugin. runtime.plugins.net installs netsim.Plugin (the player registry and the net_player_* commands). Server ticks. A tick is App.StepFixed : flush the queued commands, run the plugins' pre-tick hooks ( App.OnPreTick ), run exactly one fixed tick, flush again. Frames (input, UI, rendering) run on their own with App.Frame ; the app is in manual step mode ( netapp.Attach ), so a frame never ticks. A host loop is: Poll the server, then App.Frame . The command router. netapp.Link installs App.SetCommandRouter , so commands that frame systems queue never change the simulation on their own: command server (dedicated or listen) client script_set_input , script_bind , script_module_changed dropped dropped gameui_event , set_block , block_use , fill_box , fill_sphere , micro_edit , net_player_input Server.Submit Client.Submit (whitelisted) any other (for example level_load ) Server.Submit dropped: the server's own frame produces it script_set_input is replaced by the per-player input of the registry ( net_player_info , scripting ). A game adds client-submittable kinds to netapp.ClientKinds and to the server whitelist ( netplay.WhitelistFor shows how gameui_event is added). The controller. With a session the first-person app.Controller sends its block edits through the link ( Controller.SetNetwork ) instead of Do , stops stepping the simulation, and its undo/redo are off. Restore. App.RestoreSnapshot runs App.OnRestore hooks so each plugin rebuilds its frame-domain state (a dedicated server restoring its world, the editor stopping a session). The lobby. runtime.lobby adds lobby.Plugin after netsim.Plugin : players, teams, colours, ready flags, settings, the countdown and the match results as simulation state replicated to every client ( lobby_* commands go through the whitelist, lobby.Rules() ). See lobby . Pins. game.Game.NetPins fills the handshake pins: toolchain version ( game.Version ), the content hash of the project files ( netbase.HashFS ; saves/ and dot files are skipped), the hash of the runtime section without its presentation fields, the seed, the tick rate and the fine water rule version when fine water is on. Remote player movement Every applied net_player_input also moves the player's node ( netsim/move.go ): yaw on the node, pitch on its camera, and one tick of walking along the move axes at player.move speeds against solid blocks. Jump, sprint and crouch follow the local controller's rules from fixed button bits ( netsim.ButtonJump , ButtonSprint , ButtonCrouch ); internal/netplay.InputFromState sets the bits from the input actions named jump , sprint and crouch (or sneak ). A player without player.move does not move. A joining player appears at the game.mode spawns unless the server placed it with net_player_spawn . The local avatar is predicted on the client ( replica.Smoother ) and corrected by the server; the other players are interpolated. Using the API // server (dedicated): a listener, the authoritative simulation, the pins ln, _ := transport.ListenTCP( ":7777" , transport.TCPOptions{TLS: transport.ServerTLS(cert), Notify: wake}) srv, _ := replica.NewServer(replica.ServerConfig{Sim: &netapp.AppSim{A: app}, Listener: ln, Pins: pins, Password: "optional" }) for { srv.Poll(time.Now()); app.Frame(dt) } // client: dial with the fingerprint of the join link, then poll from the frame loop c, _ := replica.Connect(ctx, link.Addr, netbase.ConnectOptions{Fingerprint: link.Fingerprint}, replica.ClientConfig{Target: app, Pins: pins, Name: "ana" , Password: link.Key}) for running { c.SubmitInput(netsim.Quantize(moveX, moveY, yaw, pitch, buttons)) c.SetView(camX, camY, camZ) c.Poll(time.Now()) } Server and Client are poll-driven: Poll(now) does a bounded amount of work and never blocks, so a host can drive them from its frame loop and a test can drive a whole session from one goroutine on a virtual clock. Callbacks ( OnPlayerJoin , OnPlayerLeave , OnChat , OnEvent , and OnFrame , OnReconcile on clients) run after the Poll's work, outside the session's lock. The shared types are in net/netbase . Host controls: Submit , AddLocalPlayer and SubmitAs (a listen server's own player), Kick , Chat , Metrics , Peers , Close ; hooks AllowConnect (ban list by address) and AllowJoin . A join link looks like burrow://host:7777?fp=<certificate fingerprint>&key=<password> ( netbase.JoinLink , netbase.ParseJoinLink ). Treat a link with a key as a secret. Protocol Framing The transport carries frames. On TCP each frame is a 4-byte big-endian length followed by the payload; a length of 0 or above the limit (1 MiB by default) closes the connection before anything is allocated. A frame is one message: a type byte, then the fields. Field encodings: uv is an unsigned LEB128 varint (minimal encoding only), u8 one byte, u64 eight bytes little endian, [n] n raw bytes, str a uv length then UTF-8 bytes, bytes a uv length then raw bytes, bool one byte 0 or 1. Decoding is strict: every length and count is checked against its limit and against the bytes that remain, trailing bytes are an error, and a value has exactly one encoding. Messages type name direction fields 0x01 Hello C→S [4] magic BRWN , uv protocol version, str engine version (≤64), pins, str name (≤32), [32] client nonce, [8] token id (zero: new player), [32] identity (ed25519 public key, zero: anonymous) 0x02 Challenge S→C [32] server nonce, [16] salt, uv PBKDF2 iterations, u8 flags (1 password, 2 token, 4 replication server) 0x03 Auth C→S [32] password proof, [32] token proof, [64] identity signature (zero when anonymous) 0x04 Welcome S→C uv player id, [32] reconnect token, [32] server proof, uv start tick, tick length (µs) 0x05 Reject S→C u8 code, str detail (≤256) 0x10 Input C→S uv seq (strictly increasing), uv count (≤16), then per command str kind, bytes JSON payload (≤4 KiB) 0x40 Ping both uv seq, u64 sender time, uv ack 0x41 Pong both uv seq, u64 echoed time, uv server tick 0x50 Chat C→S str text (≤256) 0x51 ChatMsg S→C uv from, str text 0x60 Kick S→C u8 code, str detail 0x61 Bye both u8 code 0x70 - 0x74 RepSchema, RepFrame, RepAck, RepView, RepFrameZ both the replication stream, see Replication 0x80 VoiceUp C→S bytes voice frame (1..256, voice chat ): the sender's own voice 0x81 VoiceDown S→C uv speaker (≥1), bytes voice frame (1..256), forwarded unchanged 0x82 VoiceBlock C→S uv player (≥1), bool blocked: a personal mute the server applies to the sender's copies Pins: [32] project content hash, [32] configuration hash, uv seed, uv rule count (≤32), then sorted unique str key and str value pairs (≤64 bytes each). Reject and kick codes: 1 version, 2 project, 3 authentication, 4 full, 5 banned, 6 timeout, 7 protocol, 8 rate limits, 11 shutdown, 12 kicked, 13 busy, 14 connected elsewhere, 15 quit, 16 identity required. The golden test in net/wire pins these bytes: a change is a protocol change and bumps the protocol version. (The wire package still defines the messages of the removed lockstep model; the server kicks a client that sends one.) Handshake and authentication sequenceDiagram participant C as Client participant S as Server C->>S: Hello (nonce, versions, pins) S-->>C: Challenge (nonce, salt, iterations, flags) C->>S: Auth (proof) Note over S: Welcome at the next tick boundary S-->>C: Welcome (player id, start tick) The client sends Hello with a fresh nonce. The server checks the protocol version, the engine version and the pins (a mismatch is a Reject that names the field), and the player count. The server answers with a Challenge: its own nonce, the salt and iteration count of the password key, and flags. The client answers with Auth. With a password, the shared key is PBKDF2-SHA256(password, salt, iterations) and the proof is HMAC-SHA256(key, "burrow-net v1 client proof" ‖ 0 ‖ SHA-256(Hello ‖ Challenge)) . A reconnecting client proves its token the same way; the Hello only carries the token id. Neither the password nor the token is ever sent again; proofs are compared in constant time. A client with an identity key (ed25519) names its public key in Hello and signs "burrow-net v2 identity proof" ‖ 0 ‖ SHA-256(Hello ‖ Challenge) in Auth. The server always verifies the signature when the key is not zero and keeps the key on the player's record; a reconnect must present the same key. A server with RequireIdentity rejects anonymous clients with code 16. With a password the Welcome carries the server proof, so the client knows the server has the password too. Client side states: connecting → handshake → syncing → playing → closed . Reconnect moves a lost client back to connecting with its token; the server keeps the slot for the reconnect grace period. Security and threat model Network input is hostile until proven otherwise. What the core defends against: Malformed and oversized input. Every length and count is bounded before allocation; a frame over the limit closes the connection; a malformed message ends that connection. Message handling recovers from panics at the connection boundary and counts them; no other peer is affected. Flooding. Per connection: messages per second, bytes per second, commands per kind per second, pending commands, chat lines per 10 seconds. A rejected message or command is a violation; too many violations in the window disconnect the client. At most 64 messages per connection are read per Poll. Forbidden or forged commands. Only whitelisted kinds pass, each with a size limit and a validator; the simulation validates again. Older Input sequence numbers are rejected. A client cannot submit joins, leaves, seeds, steps or editor commands, nor act for another player. Slow clients and slowloris. Handshakes time out (10 s, 3 s while the Hello is still missing); the number of handshakes in progress is bounded (32 in total, 4 per address group); 5 failed authentications from one address group lock it out for 30 s; idle connections time out (15 s); TCP limits connections per address group (8) and in total (64); the TLS handshake runs off the accept loop with its own deadline. Information. A client receives only its interest and the component values its visibility rules allow ( Replication ). Passwords. Challenge-response with PBKDF2 and HMAC: the password never crosses the wire, even without TLS. A client that has a password refuses a server that does not ask for it, and refuses an iteration count outside [10 000, 4 000 000]. Without TLS an eavesdropper can still try passwords offline against a recorded handshake, and the reconnect token in the Welcome is visible: use TLS on untrusted networks. TLS. TLS 1.3 only. The server generates a self-signed ECDSA P-256 certificate on first run. The client pins the certificate's SHA-256 fingerprint: from the join link, or trust on first use stored in <user config dir>/burrow/known_servers ; a changed certificate is refused. There is no mode that accepts any certificate. Logs. Events, logs and errors never contain passwords, keys or tokens. Identity. A player is its ed25519 key, not its name: names are display only unless the server maps names to keys (the dedicated server refuses a name already owned by another identity). The key never leaves the client ( <config dir>/burrow/identity.key , mode 0600). Keys are not certified: a new key is a new player. Not defended against: a malicious server (play on servers you trust), denial of service by bandwidth exhaustion below the transport, and an active attacker on a plaintext TCP connection after authentication (use TLS). Limits limit default where players per server 256 (max 1024) ServerConfig.MaxPlayers tick rate 20 Hz (50 ms) sim.TickRate ; TickInterval only for tests frame size 1 MiB transport.Limits.MaxMessage send budget / receive budget per connection 4 MiB / 2 MiB transport.Limits commands per Input message 16 wire.MaxCmdsPerInput client command payload 4 KiB (default rules: 256 bytes) wire.MaxClientCmdData , Rule.MaxBytes commands of one player per tick 8 (the rest wait for the next ticks) MaxCmdsPerTick pending commands per player 64 MaxPendingCmds messages per connection per Poll 64 MsgsPerPoll message rate / byte rate per client 200 /s, 256 KiB/s MsgRate , ByteRate violations before disconnect 50 in 10 s ViolationsToKick , ViolationWindow chat 256 bytes, 5 lines per 10 s wire.MaxChat , ChatPer10s handshakes in progress 128, 4 per address group MaxHandshakes , MaxHandshakesPerIP failed authentications 5 per address group, then 30 s lockout AuthFailuresToLock , AuthLockout timeouts hello 3 s, handshake 10 s, idle 15 s *Timeout reconnect grace 60 s ReconnectGrace TCP connections 64 total, 8 per address group, 2 TLS handshakes per address group, 32 waiting TCPOptions password key PBKDF2-SHA256, 600 000 iterations (clients accept 10 000 to 4 000 000) Iterations , MinIterations , MaxIterations The replication limits (view distance, bandwidth, entities per client) are in Replication . How it is tested net/wire : round trip of every message, every truncation rejected, golden bytes, limit violations, and FuzzDecode . net/transport : the in-memory fault injector is reproducible from its seed; budgets, oversized frames, close, break and partition; TCP framing, a forged 1 GiB length, per-address limits; TLS pinning with the expected fingerprint, a wrong one, trust on first use and a changed certificate. net/replica : see Replication : joins, leaves, chat, kicks, authentication, hostile clients, component visibility. net/netapp , internal/netplay , internal/dedicated , cmd/burrowplay : the command router policy, the networked controller, a host and guests built from the sandbox template over loopback TCP with TLS, pins, the token store, the lobby and matchmaker modes, a dedicated server restarting from its save, and burrowplay -connect -headless against a running host. make net-test runs the fast suite (net and internal/netplay) with -race . What is not covered Chat has no on-screen box yet: it is a terminal line ( burrowplay , burrow serve ) and a log in netplay.Host.Chat / Guest.Chat . UDP, LAN discovery and relays. The in-memory transport models a reliable ordered stream, like TCP. The engine draws remote players only when the game gives their avatars the character component; otherwise a game draws them from the replicated avatars and net_player_info . FAQ Why server-authoritative replication and not lockstep? One model has to serve both a four-friend session and a persistent public world: the server holds the truth, a client downloads only what is around it, cannot read what a visibility rule withholds, and a slow or modified client cannot desynchronise anyone. Can a client cheat by sending commands? Only whitelisted commands, within limits, validated twice. A client can always lie about its own input (like in any game); it cannot act for someone else or change the rules. Does a slow player slow everyone down? No. The server ticks on time and each client has its own bandwidth budget. Is my password safe on a LAN without TLS? It is never sent, but a recorded handshake allows offline guessing: use a long password, or TLS. Joining and hosting from the game A windowed game does not need burrowplay -connect . Its menus ( net:join:<link> , net:host , net:server_add , see game UI ) and its scripts ( NetJoin , NetHost ) ask the launcher, which ends the current run and then: join : plays on the server of the link, as -connect does. If the connection fails the launcher prints the error and returns to the title screen. host : builds the game, starts the embedded server ( runtime.plugins.net is required, same as burrow serve ) with you as its local player, prints join link: burrow://... on the console and plays on it. Saved servers of the "servers" list live in servers.json in the user config directory ( <config>/burrow/servers.json , at most 64 burrow:// links).

h: Events from the simulation and scripts
x: Particles Burrow's particle system is frame domain : it never reads or writes simulation state, so it can never change a StateHash . The simulation only requests effects ( particles.Event , deterministic per tick) and the optional particle_emitter scene component is ordinary scene data. Packages: particles (parameters, assets, library, simulation; no engine dependency), particles/partplug (the engine plugin) and, for drawing, render ( ParticleBatch ), render/vulkan (GPU) and render/soft (CPU). Quick start It is off by default ( "runtime": { "plugins": { "particles": true } } enables it). This installs the system and registers the particle_emitter component (registering a component changes StateHash ; a default scene that already uses the component registers it too, and particles: false with such a scene is a build error). In code: a := engine.New(engine.Options{Seed: 1 }) a.AddPlugin(&engine.ScenePlugin{}) a.AddPlugin(&partplug.Plugin{Component: true }) // a deterministic gameplay system asks for effects; the frame domain shows them a.AddFixedSystem( "fx" , func (c *engine.FixedContext) error { if c.Tick% 20 != 0 { return nil } return partplug.Burst(c, "builtin:sparks" , mathx.Vec3{X: 3 , Y: 20 , Z: - 4 }, 0 ) }) // a continuous effect is a node with a component c.Commands.Spawn( "" , "campfire" , &t) c.Commands.AddComponent( "/campfire" , particles.CompName, particles.Emitter{Asset: "builtin:fire" , Enabled: true }) examples/particles_demo shows the six presets on a flat stage plus simulation-driven bursts: go run ./examples/particles_demo , or make particles-test for the captures (classic pipeline, HDR pipeline, the CPU twin, a stress run) with the validation layer on. The emitter component particle_emitter (all fields appear in the inspector): asset ( builtin:<name> or a .particles.json path; empty = use the inline fields), enabled , seed , scale (size, spawn volume and speed multiplier), then the inline effect (the same fields as the asset): group fields emission rate (per second), burst , burst_interval , duration (0 = forever), max (live cap of this emitter) shape and motion shape ( point , sphere , box , disc ), extent , direction , cone (half angle, 180 = every direction), speed [min,max], lifetime [min,max], gravity , accel (wind), drag , spin over life size [min,max], size_over_life (4 stops), color (4 RGBA stops, RGB above 1 glows) look texture (empty = soft disc, `builtin:puff distortion distortion (strength 0..8, default 0 = off) and distortion_only : the particles also bend the image behind them (heat haze from smoke, fire or exhaust; see rendering.md "Air distortion"); with distortion_only they draw no colour. Shader level medium and up on the GPU renderer; the CPU renderer ignores distortion and skips distortion-only emitters space space : world (particles stay where they were born) or local (they follow the node as a whole) collision collide , bounce , friction , kill inheritance inherit_velocity (0..1): fraction of the node's velocity (measured between frames, teleports ignored) added to world-space particles at birth forces forces , up to 4 of {kind, pos, axis, strength, radius, scale} in the emitter frame: vortex (swirl around axis through pos ), attract / repel (toward / away from pos ), turbulence (smooth noise, scale = noise cell size in blocks, changes slowly with time). strength is an acceleration (blocks/s^2, -100..100), radius the reach with linear falloff (0 = unlimited) sub-emitters sub , up to 4 of {event, asset, count, inherit_velocity, chance} : at a particle's spawn , collide (impacts faster than 0.5 blocks/s) or death (end of life, or kill impact) another effect ( builtin:<name> or .particles.json ) is spawned there as a one-shot burst of count particles (0 = the effect's burst , or 8), inheriting inherit_velocity of the parent particle's velocity, with probability chance (0 = 1) trail trail {length, width, color_over_trail, min_dist, texture} : a ribbon behind each particle; length seconds of history 0..2 (0 = off), width [head, tail], color_over_trail 2 RGBA stops, min_dist between points, texture like texture . Drawn by the renderers ( render.ParticleTrail ) mesh mesh {model, scale, align} : a voxel model ( cube or a .vox path) per particle instead of a billboard; align is velocity , random or none ( render.ParticleMesh ) light light {color, radius, intensity, max} : the particles emit point lights (colour zero = the particle's own, max lights per emitter, render.ParticleLight ) Toggling enabled (a journaled component change) starts or stops emission identically in every replay; turning it off lets live particles finish. Gravity and wind are world accelerations; for local emitters they go through the inverse of the node's full transform, so a non-uniform scale (or a shear) still makes particles fall straight down in the world. Zero-valued extras ( forces , sub , trail , mesh , light , inherit_velocity ) are omitted from the JSON, so older assets and emitter hashes are unchanged. Lists and groups appear in the inspector as JSON objects. In the editor, the emitters of nodes hidden by the Outliner's eye or a hidden layer stop emitting in the viewport ( partplug.Plugin.Skip , set by the editor; nil in the game); particles already in flight run out. .particles.json A document is the inline fields plus version (1) and an optional name ; omitted fields take defaults. particles.Decode rejects unknown fields, trailing data, documents over 64 KiB, non-finite or out-of-range numbers and newer versions, then sanitizes. Hot reload: the library re-reads four loaded files every 15 frames and compares content hashes; a changed file replaces the effect for every emitter using it, a broken save keeps the last good version and the error shows up in editor_particles state ( errors ). Start from a preset: editor_particles {action:"get", asset:"builtin:smoke"} # sanitized params editor_particles {action:"save", path:"fx/chimney.particles.json", asset:"builtin:smoke", params:{"rate":30}} Built-in presets builtin:smoke (rising puffs, soft, alpha), sparks (additive, velocity stretched, bouncing), dust (a burst of soft puffs, drag), splash (water droplets, gravity), fire (additive flipbook flames), soul_fire (the cyan twin of the fire), debris (block-break chips with voxel collision; a break event names the block and its texture, block:<name> , replaces the sprite, each chip showing a random quarter of a face). Sprites are generated procedurally ( particles.BuiltinTextureNames ): no third-party material. Every preset and sprite is also a read-only engine asset (package builtinassets ): the effects ship as embedded .particles.json files, so "Copy to project" in the editor's Engine folder gives an editable variant, and partplug.Plugin.Overrides ( {"builtin:debris": "assets/particles/debris.particles.json"} ) makes a project file replace the builtin everywhere it is named (block break debris included). See Builtin assets . Fire on the burning blocks partplug.Plugin.BlockFX keeps an effect alive on top of every loaded block of a type (torch fire): map[block name]partplug.BlockFX ( {"torch": {Asset: "builtin:fire", Scale: 0.45}} ). Every state variant of the name counts ( torch covers torch[wall=true,facing=east] ); the flame sits on the shape (0.65 above the cell for a floor torch, 0.82 for a wall one; Height overrides). The emitters follow the loaded chunks around the camera within blockFXRadius chunks (a chunk is rescanned only when its content version changed; scanning one without a watched block costs a palette lookup per watched name), at most BlockFXMax alive, nearest the camera first, and the fire dies with the block or the chunk. Frame domain, never hashed: the StateHash and replays are unchanged. Events from the simulation and scripts partplug.Emit(fixedCtx, particles.Event) sends the event with engine.SendFixed : one ordered list per tick, byte identical across replays, dropped on rollback and while a replay verifies. Kinds: EvBurst (one-shot effect at a position; the effect lives on its own), EvEmit (extra particles from the emitter component of an entity), EvStop (clear an emitter, or everything with entity 0). Helpers: partplug.Burst(c, entity, asset, offset, count) , partplug.BlockBreak(c, entity, "stone", offset) . Effects come from an entity: a burst from the simulation names the entity that emits it ( particles.Event.Entity , the position is that entity's world position plus X, Y, Z as an offset); a burst without one is refused ( particles.Event.ValidateSim , particles.ErrNoEmitter ) and the frame domain drops it. Only host code (the editor, tests) may queue an absolute burst ( Particles.Queue with entity 0). The debris of the blocks the player breaks is emitted by the player entity, at the block. Scripts (module vox , ABI additive, see script/ABI.md ): particle_burst , particle_emit , particle_stop ; Go SDK in sdk/burrowsdk/particles.go : burrowsdk.ParticleBurstOn(self, "builtin:sparks" , burrowsdk.ParticleOpts{Offset: &[ 3 ] float32 { 4 , 20 , - 3 }, Count: 24 }) burrowsdk.ParticleBlockBreakOn(self, "stone" , 4.5 , 20.5 , - 2.5 ) Determinism The frame domain owns everything visual. Replays look the same because the requests are the same: seeds are splitmix(emitter id, spawn index) for emitters and splitmix(tick, index of the event in the tick) for events. There is no math/rand , no wall clock in the random streams. A particle is a closed-form trajectory p = p0 + v0 f1 + a f2 ( f1 = (1 - e^-kt)/k , f2 = (t - f1)/k , series for small kt because the naive form cancels in float32): no integration state, so the position at time t is independent of the frame rate and identical on the GPU and the CPU ( render.ParticleBatch.Eval and particle_update.comp are twins). Spawning and collision advance in fixed 1/60 s substeps (at most 15 per frame, delta clamped to 0.25 s), so 30 and 60 fps runs spawn the same sequence; a collision rebases the trajectory segment. Force fields break the closed form, so they are integrated in the CPU substep: each substep the acceleration of the fields at the particle is added to its constant acceleration and the segment is rebased at that substep (the shader and Eval just see more segments; no GPU change, twin parity kept). Turbulence is a hash lattice noise of (emitter seed, cell, time), no state. Collision is the same: the segment of a substep is walked voxel by voxel (DDA) and only an impact rebases it. Sub-emitter seeds are splitmix(parent emitter seed, particle spawn index, event, impact count, index in the list) ; the effect lives in a one-shot pool of the next substep. Depth is bounded (emitter, then two generations; a third is ignored), and Config.MaxSubPerFrame (256) plus the one-shot cap bound the rest. Particles.Queue (the editor, editor_particles burst ) plays an effect from host code; it is never journaled. Rendering GPU ( render/vulkan/particles.go ). Per frame the CPU copies the live records (80 bytes: position, spawn time, velocity, life, acceleration, drag, size, rotation, spin, emitter/frame/variant, segment start) and the emitter table (176 bytes each) into the frame slot's buffers; a compute pass ( particle_update.comp ) evaluates every record at the batch time into one billboard instance (current and previous position, size, colour over life, atlas uv, rotation). In the main pass, after the glass and the rain, the pass is split once (like the water scene copy): the depth buffer becomes linear view depth in an R32F image ( particle_depth.frag ), then every emitter draws its range of instances with an instanced quad ( particle.vert / particle.frag ): soft fade clamp((sceneZ - z) / soft) , alpha ( src_alpha, 1 - src_alpha ) or additive ( src_alpha, one ) blending, depth test without depth write. It works in the classic pipeline ( -shaders off , display colours through toLinear ) and in the HDR levels (exact sRGB decode, so RGB above 1 feeds bloom). Order across emitters : every colour particle of every emitter (alpha and additive together) is sorted far to near by view depth, so overlapping emitters interleave correctly. The sort runs on the CPU ( render.ParticleOrder , a radix sort of at most 32768 keys: the record positions are at hand and the sprites are separate textures with no bindless array, so a GPU sort would still need one draw per run); particle_sort.comp then copies the instances into that order and the list is cut into runs of one emitter, one draw each (at most 1024 runs; with more interleaving than that the frame falls back to one draw per emitter, emitters in batch order, particles far to near inside each). Particles of equal depth keep emitter and spawn order. Lighting and fog (emitter lit , default on for alpha blending and off for additive ): at the particle centre particle.frag multiplies the colour by the ambient light and the sun ( sunShadow , the same shadow map and filter as the terrain) in the classic pipeline, by the sky/ground ambient and the sun radiance in the HDR levels. One lookup per fragment, so a dense lit emitter costs more than an unlit one. Block light is not applied (it lives in the chunk meshes only). In the voxel passes the fog (classic) or the aerial perspective (HDR levels) applies to every particle: alpha particles take the haze colour, additive ones lose strength. The CPU renderer draws particles unlit and unfogged. Depth collision (emitter depth_collide : off , bounce , kill ): particle_collide.comp tests every instance against the previous frame's linear depth image and camera. A particle that lies behind the surface seen at its pixel (up to 4 blocks behind it) is killed, or mirrored back out of the surface along the normal rebuilt from the depth neighbours ( bounce is the restitution: 0 sticks to the surface, 1 is a perfect mirror). It is stateless (the trajectory is closed form and keeps no velocity), so it only sees surfaces the camera saw last frame: nothing behind the camera or behind other geometry, nothing on the first frame or right after a resize, and a bounce is the mirror image of the free path, not an impulse. The voxel collision of collide is unchanged and exact; use depth_collide for what voxels do not know (meshes, characters, dynamic bodies). Scene-only path : RenderToTarget and the swapchain frame without a voxel world draw the batch too (after the transparent meshes and sprites, before the canvas), lit by the scene sun and shadow map, without fog. A frame with no meshes or sprites (the editor's UI frame) draws none. The editor viewport (hybrid target) always drew it; the model and animation viewports no longer show the world's particles. Motion vectors : blended particles are not written to the temporal anti-aliasing velocity target (they would overwrite the background velocity of the pixel). They are drawn after the scene copy, which makes the temporal passes treat them as reactive (history is not trusted there); the previous position only drives the velocity stretch of sparks. CPU ( render/soft/particles.go ). render.Options.Particles splats the same batch over the image after the markers: far to near, depth tested against the ray distance, same soft fade, alpha or additive, bounded by a pixel budget. It serves headless runs, examples/particles_demo -cpu , and the editor preview ( soft.PreviewParticles ). The two paths agree visually (see make particles-test ); the CPU does not stretch sparks. Budgets and robustness budget default hard cap live particles, all emitters ( Config.MaxGlobal ) 16384 32768 ( render.MaxParticleRecords ) live particles per emitter ( max ) 1024 16384 emitters drawn per frame ( MaxEmitters , nearest kept) 128 256 ( render.MaxParticleEmitters ) spawns per frame 4096 65536 live one-shot effects 128 1024 collision voxel lookups per frame (every voxel a segment crosses, and a re-test of resting particles every 8 substeps) 40000 1048576 sub-emitter effects per frame ( Config.MaxSubPerFrame , they count as one-shot effects too) 256 4096 host events per frame / queue 256 / 256 sprite textures resident on the GPU 48 (LRU, at most 4 uploads per frame) Spawns beyond a budget are dropped and counted ( dropped in editor_particles state ), never queued. Every number of a component, asset, event or script call is clamped or rejected ( Params.Sanitized / Validate , Event.Validate ); NaN and infinities become defaults, non-finite records evaluate as dead particles on both renderers, textures are limited to 1024 px and 4 MiB, asset files to 64 KiB, texture and effect names to 256 bytes without .. . A failing GPU setup disables only the particle pass ( Renderer.ParticleStats().Error ). Measured (M2 Max, MoltenVK, 1280x720, examples/particles_demo , vsync-bound 8.3 ms frames): scene main pass GPU CPU simulation 6 presets, about 180 particles +0.2 to +0.4 ms (classic and HDR, near the timer noise) below 0.01 ms 4 emitters of soft smoke, 20 000 to 26 000 live +0.4 to +0.9 ms (large overdraw) 0.2 ms ( BenchmarkStep20k , 32 768 live) 10 000 live colliding chips not run on the GPU 0.39 ms ( BenchmarkStepCollide5k ) Editor and agents Tools > Particle editor (a docked full-screen panel: Particles with Particles settings ; a double-click on a .particles.json in the Content browser opens it there; burrowedit -tool particles -project <dir> -asset <file> still gives a separate window): the library of presets and project effects on the left (presets open as an unsaved copy), an animated CPU preview on a plain backdrop in the middle (Space plays or pauses, R restarts, a time slider scrubs, a loop length and a camera distance in the ... menu), and every parameter on the right in Emitter / Appearance / Advanced tabs, as flat sections of label-and-field rows (units in the fields, min and max side by side, x y z with axis colours): appearance (sprite, blend, space, flipbook), emission, shape and motion, size over life (a curve with four draggable points) and colour over life (a gradient with four stops), collision. A slider drag is one undo step; invalid values are refused. File > Save as writes the .particles.json , and every emitter that uses it reloads. Double-click a .particles.json in the Content browser to open it. The inspector shows the particle_emitter fields; drop a .particles.json on asset . MCP tool editor_particles ( state , list , get , validate , save , burst , stop , preview ): preview {asset | params, seconds, width, height} simulates one effect alone and returns a CPU render as an image block, so an agent can check an effect without a window; validate reports why params are rejected; save writes a .particles.json and hot reloads it. Trails trail ({ length , width [head, tail], color_over_trail [head, tail RGBA], min_dist , texture }) drags a camera-facing ribbon behind every particle of the emitter. No history is stored: the trajectory is closed form, so the ribbon is p(t - k*dt) for k*dt over length seconds (up to 24 samples). Samples older than the current trajectory segment (a collision or force rebase, ParticleRecord.Seg ) clamp to the segment start, so the ribbon ends at the last bounce instead of crossing the wall. Points closer than min_dist are merged. The ribbon colour is the particle colour times the color_over_trail ramp (head to tail); u runs along the ribbon (head 0), v across; without a texture the ribbon is solid with soft edges. It blends (or adds) like the emitter and is depth tested. Emitters with forces (and collisions) rebase the segment every substep, so the closed form only reaches back one substep: the Vulkan renderer then keeps a render.TrailHistory (head position per frame, keyed by a hash of the particle's immutable fields, at most 24 samples per trailing particle) and TrailPoints reads older samples from it; the ribbon ends at the oldest recorded sample. The CPU renderer has no history (previews show the short ribbon). partplug loads the .vox of mesh emitters into ParticleBatch.Meshes itself ( particles/partplug/meshes.go ). GPU ( render/vulkan/particle_trails.go , particle_trail.vert/.frag ): the CPU samples the ribbons ( render.ParticleBatch.TrailPoints ) into a storage buffer and the vertex shader expands one quad per segment. CPU ( render/soft/particle_fx.go ): the same points, rasterised. Cost: up to render.MaxTrailPoints (24576) points per frame, about 17 Eval -like samples per particle; one draw per trail emitter. The ribbon is not soft-faded against the depth buffer and gets no motion vector. Mesh particles mesh ({ model "cube" or a .vox path, scale , align velocity | random | none }) draws every particle as a lit mesh instead of a billboard (the emitter then draws no sprite). The mesh is normalised to a unit cube, so the size curve gives its edge in blocks. velocity points the model's +Z along the velocity (and spins it by the particle rotation), random gives each particle a fixed random orientation that tumbles with the rotation, none keeps the world axes and spins about the vertical. The renderer finds the geometry in ParticleBatch.Meshes[model] (build it with rworld.ParticleMeshFromAssets ); a missing entry draws the cube. GPU ( particle_meshes.go , particle_mesh.vert/.frag ): de-indexed vertices of all distinct meshes in one storage buffer (re-copied only when the set changes), one 80 byte instance per particle, one instanced draw per emitter, opaque with depth write. Lit by ambient, the sun, the terrain shadow map and the particle lights; the HDR levels use the atmosphere light and aerial perspective. Limits: render.MaxParticleMeshes (8192) instances per frame, 16384 vertices per mesh, 65536 across meshes; the tint alpha is a cutout (below 0.5 discards), there is no blending, no velocity vector and the meshes cast no shadow. CPU renderer: flat-shaded triangles with a fixed sun direction and its own z buffer. Particle lights light ({ color , radius , intensity , max }) makes the particles point lights. Terrain had no dynamic point light path (only block light; scene meshes use Frame.Points ), so the scene UBO now carries render.MaxParticleLights (16) lights after the swell block ( sceneUBOSize 1536). Each frame ParticleBatch.Lights takes at most max particles per light emitter (the nearest to the camera), then the 16 nearest of all; radiance is color * intensity * particle alpha . particleLights() in shaders/plights.glsl adds a smooth quadratic falloff to radius with wrapped diffuse to the voxel shading ( voxel_body.glsl : terrain, glass), scene meshes ( mesh.frag , mesh_hdr.frag ) and mesh particles. Cost: one Eval per particle of light emitters on the CPU; on the GPU a loop that stops at the first unused slot, so nothing is paid without lights. The light is not shadowed, does not propagate through blocks, ignores the sky occlusion, and lights popping in or out at the 16 light limit follow the camera. The CPU renderer and the scene-only path ( RenderToTarget ) apply no particle lights. GPU checks: BURROW_GPU=1 BURROW_GPU_ONLY=trail go test ./render/vulkan -run TestGPUChecks -v (trail, mesh and light shots in vk_pfx_*.png ). Limits Voxel collision runs on the CPU only (a few lookups per particle and substep; collide is not free). It is continuous (no tunnelling through thin walls), but a particle stops sliding after three impacts in one substep, and a local emitter moving through a wall is not tested (only the motion of the particles relative to the node, at the node's current pose). Resting particles are re-tested against their support voxel every 8 substeps (cost and a 0.13 s delay), and a block placed on top of a resting particle does not move it. Blended particles are sorted by their centre, not per pixel: large particles that intersect each other, or a big quad around a small one, can still swap. More than 1024 order changes between emitters in one frame fall back to one draw per emitter. The sort is by view depth of the batch time, so a particle crossing another within one frame can pop. Lit particles use the sun shadow map and the ambient light only (no block light, no point lights, no occlusion by the terrain's sky light), the same value over the whole quad. The CPU renderer and the editor's effect preview draw them unlit. The scene-only path has no fog and skips frames with an orthographic camera or a viewport rectangle. depth_collide sees the visible surfaces of the previous frame only (see Rendering), tests one point per particle, and does not run in the CPU renderer. Force fields and impacts rebase the closed-form segment every substep, so a trail (history before the segment start) of a particle in a force field is at most one substep long; sub-emitter effects are CPU one-shot pools (no GPU path) and nest two levels deep. MoltenVK: dynamic indexing of a vec4 component in the compute shader crashed pipeline creation, so the curves are written with explicit branches.

Rigid-body physics (physics3d) physics3d is the engine's deterministic rigid-body layer: boxes, spheres, capsules and voxel bodies (small voxel grids that move, rotate, collide and break apart). It is a plugin, off unless you add it, and is meant for destruction games, vehicles and physics puzzles. The older physics package (AABB bodies, character controller, triggers) is unchanged and independent; use physics3d when you need rotation, stacking, joints or destruction. a.AddPlugin(&engine.ScenePlugin{}) a.AddPlugin(&physics3d.PhysicsPlugin3D{}) // project setting: runtime.plugins.physics3d = true Try it: go run ./examples/physics3d_playground -shot playground.png (stack of ten boxes, a destructible voxel tower, a hinged door, a rope bridge; it runs twice, compares the StateHash , verifies the journal replay, and writes PNG captures). Model Everything is ECS state, so StateHash , Snapshot / Restore , undo, journal replay and failed-tick rollback are the engine's own. component role physics3d.rigidbody kind ( static / kinematic / dynamic ), mass, material, layers, damping, CCD flag, and the state: pos (centre of mass), rot (quaternion), vel , ang_vel , sleeping, derived inverse mass/inertia physics3d.collider box (half extents), sphere (radius), capsule (radius, half height along local Y) physics3d.voxelbody voxel grid ( sx,sy,sz , block id per cell, 0 = empty), density scale, cell (edge of one cell in world units, 0 = 1 block), derived centre of mass physics3d.joint fixed , hinge (limits, motor), ball , distance (rope or rod); on its own node, referencing two bodies ( b = 0 is the world) All four are described in the scene schema (ranges, tooltips), so the inspector edits them. A body also writes its scene.Transform (position, Euler degrees) every tick it moves, for the scene tree and the render. Render voxel bodies from physics3d.voxelbody + rigidbody (see Rendering), not from the Euler angles. Create bodies with journaled commands: SpawnBody , SpawnVoxelBody , SetJoint (return []sim.Command of scene commands) and ApplyImpulse , RemoveVoxels , Explode , Detach , CarveBody (custom commands: physics3d_apply_impulse , physics3d_remove_voxels , physics3d_explode , physics3d_detach , physics3d_carve_body ). For a voxel body, Pos of a new body is the world position of the grid corner; the first step moves it to the centre of mass. Mass comes from the collider volume or, for voxel bodies, the sum of cell densities ( Config.Densities by block name, default 1 per cell); Mass > 0 overrides it (a split clears the override and uses density). Determinism One FixedUpdate system pair ( physics3d.split , physics3d.step ), no goroutines, no Go map iteration, ascending entity order, explicit sorts. Math is float64 with a fixed operation order; the state is hashed and snapshotted as exact float64 bits. Platform stance. Same seed and inputs give bit-identical results on the arm64 and amd64 builds, verified on macOS (Windows and Linux are checked by the CI workflow, which has not run yet) (tested: twin engines, mid-simulation snapshot, journal replay, failed-tick rollback, fuzzed impulses, and the templates hashed by the arm64 and the amd64 builds at 200 and 2000 ticks). Every float product is explicitly rounded ( float64(a*b) + c ) so the Go compiler cannot fuse it into a multiply-add (it does on arm64 and with GOAMD64=v3 , not on default amd64), and the trigonometry comes from mathx/detmath , not from package math . Guards: internal/detguard (no fused instruction in the arm64 and amd64-v3 assembly, no unrounded product, no banned math call). See Determinism . Fixed-point was rejected: quaternions, inertia tensors and the sequential-impulse solver need a wide dynamic range, and IEEE 754 float64 with explicit rounding is already exact and portable. Pending impulses, contact warm-start impulses ( State.Warm ), touching pairs (for events) are state, so a restored snapshot continues exactly. Worlds that do not add the plugin hash exactly as before. With the plugin and no bodies the extra state is empty. Simulation Per tick: broadphase (sweep and prune on swept AABBs, layers/masks, joints exclude their pair), narrowphase once per tick with a speculative margin derived from the speeds (speculative contacts that cannot be reached this tick are dropped, manifolds are reduced to 4 points per convex pair), contacts sorted bottom-up, then Substeps of: gravity and damping, buoyancy, warm start, soft contact + joint iterations, integrate, RelaxIterations (1) relax pass. Quality follows the work budget : SolverBudget (200000 contact solves per tick) is spent as substeps x iterations: a few contacts get up to MaxSubsteps (24) substeps and doubled Iterations (4), which makes stacks of 20+ boxes stable at the defaults; thousands of contacts get down to 4 substeps. Contacts are soft constraints ( ContactHertz 80, ContactDamping 3) with a speculative term, Coulomb friction (geometric mean of the materials, 2 tangents), restitution applied after the substeps for impacts faster than BounceThreshold . Over MaxContacts the lowest contacts are kept (upper layers fall onto them instead of through the floor). runtime.physics_substeps ( vox.project , 1..32, 0 = default) sets Substeps of both physics engines for a game, so contacts and character movement can be finer without raising runtime.tick_rate . Shapes. Capsules decompose into spheres, voxel bodies and terrain into unit boxes (only exposed cells). Contacts into a solid neighbour cell are dropped, so flat terrain and flat voxel bodies produce no edge ghost contacts. Non-cubic blocks collide as cubes. Terrain. Bodies collide with solid voxels when mask has LayerTerrain (bit 31). A fast body (more than half its radius per substep, or ccd ) also ray-casts its centre against the terrain every substep, so bullets do not tunnel. Water. In liquid blocks (coarse levels and fine water, read with voxel.LiquidTable.Sample ; the fluid state is never written) a body gets Archimedes lift Water.Density x submerged fraction x volume x g , drag toward the current ( Water.Drag , Water.FlowPush ) and angular drag. Bodies near a liquid are re-sampled every substep, others cost nothing. A box of density 0.4 floats with 40% submerged; a dense one sinks. Characters. With physics.PhysicsPlugin added before PhysicsPlugin3D , the system physics3d.character (after physics.character and physics3d.step ) lets physics.CharacterController characters stand on and be carried by moving bodies (platform velocity plus rotation at the feet), be held up by platforms and stopped by solid bodies, and push dynamic bodies up to CharacterConfig.MaxPush mass (30) toward the walking direction at PushSpeed . Sleeping. A body sleeps when its island (contacts and joints) is quiet for SleepTicks (30). A sleeper wakes on a pending impulse, on contact with a body faster than WakeSpeed , when a jointed partner wakes, and when the terrain around it changes (signature check every 4 ticks), so removing a block under a sleeping crate drops it. Events (frame domain, engine.Read ): ContactBegin , ContactEnd (body pairs), TriggerEnter , TriggerExit (bodies with trigger set). Exits first, then enters, in ascending entity order. Body-terrain contacts have no events. Joints. Sequential impulses with Baumgarte-style position error; hinge angle limits ( min / max , degrees) and motor ( motor_speed , degrees per second; the angle state is in radians); distance joints are one-sided ropes when min < max ; break_force (a force: constraint impulse per second, independent of the substep count) removes a joint above it; a joint whose body was deleted is removed. Joint-connected bodies do not collide unless collide . Queries (the FixedScene used by scripts and the character system shares the end state of the previous step: no per-call copies; components written by other systems in between are seen after the next step) ( Scene : FrameScene , FixedScene , EngineScene ): Raycast (box, sphere, capsule, voxel-body cell walk, terrain), Overlap , ShapeCast (sphere, box, capsule; conservative advancement + bisection to ~1e-3 blocks). Scripts: physics3d_raycast , physics3d_apply_impulse , physics3d_body_get , physics3d_remove_voxel , physics3d_water_at ( script/ABI.md , burrowsdk.Physics3D* ). Buoyancy A body in liquid (coarse levels or fine water, read-only) is cut into displacement cells: a sub-grid of about Water.Spacing (0.5) blocks for a box, sphere or capsule, the cells of a voxel body plus its sealed cavities (empty cells the outside cannot reach through faces), merged into clusters above Water.MaxPoints (96) cells. Every second substep each cell reads the liquid surface under its centre and gets a submerged fraction; the body receives the lift rho * V_sub * g at the centre of buoyancy (not at the centre of mass), so it rights itself, trims by its load and can capsize, and a sealed hollow hull floats on its whole inside. Drag and angular drag scale with the displaced fraction, and the body is pulled toward the current. A body that cannot reach liquid during the tick (its swept box is dry) skips the sampling, and one fully under water takes the whole displaced volume without reading the surface. Open hulls. In a voxel body the +Y axis is up. An empty cell that has to climb to get out (a boat's inside) is a pocket : it displaces like a solid cell while the air holds it, i.e. while its rim (the highest cell of its lowest way out) is above the water and above the cell. When the rim goes under water the pockets fill ( Water.FloodRate , 2 per second, state RigidBody.Flood ) and stop displacing, which is exactly the buoyancy of a hull full of water: an overloaded or swamped boat sinks, and it empties again ( Water.FloodDrain , 0.5 per second) once the rim is dry. Tilted past its rim, a pocket spills at once. RigidBody.Displace (default 1) still multiplies the displaced volume. Sleeping: a body asleep on water wakes when the immersion of its box changes by 1/32 (the water rises, drains or moves). Swell. Water.Swell ( Amp blocks, Length , Speed , Dir ; off at Amp 0; in a project runtime.plugins.swell: {"amp": 0.4, "length": 12} ) lifts and lowers the water with three travelling waves, a pure function of position and tick (package swell , detmath ): deterministic, and the same for the solver, the scripts and the renderer. The renderer draws the very same waves ( shaders/swell.glsl , checked against the Go table by a test): the smooth water surface ( water2.vert , the HDR levels and the linear look) moves its top vertices and the upper edge of its sides by the swell, the normals take its slope, and the eye under the surface follows it, so a floating body sits where the water is drawn. Bodies bob on it and replays stay exact ( go run ./examples/swell_demo -shot out.png floats a hull, a boat, a log and a rock on a swelling lake and writes captures). Scripts read the water with physics3d_water_at ( burrowsdk.Physics3DWaterAt : surface height with swell, depth of the point, flow); the buoyancy knobs of a body are its components ( displace , gravity_scale , flood ). Limits: the fraction of a cell uses the vertical extent of its box (exact for a flat surface); air pockets open downward (a diving bell) are not modelled, and a flooded hull does not move its centre of mass; the classic cube water ( -shaders off ) does not draw the swell (its greedy quads would crack), only the smooth surface does; the foot effects of waterfalls do not follow it; the surface is displaced at the block corners, so keep Length at 6 blocks or more. Destruction Splitting. RemoveVoxels (or an explosion) marks a voxel body dirty; the next tick flood-fills it (6-connectivity) and the largest island stays on the entity while each other island becomes a new root node frag_<entity>_<tick>_<k> with the correct centre of mass, inherited linear and angular velocity and its own inertia. Voxels are conserved exactly (fuzz-tested). Empty bodies are despawned. Budget: SplitBudget (16384 grid cells flood-filled per tick, oldest first; the rest waits), and no split is made while it would exceed MaxBodies . World chunks. Detach{Seeds} (and Explode{Detach: true} on the crater rim) runs a bounded structural support check on the solid terrain: a flood fill over solid voxels, at most SupportBudget (4096) voxels per piece, at most 16x that per command. A piece that touches y <= Bedrock (default 0) or outgrows the budget counts as ground; a smaller piece is floating and becomes a VoxelBody (grid at most 64 per axis, 32768 cells; larger pieces stay in the world; at most 64 pieces per command). CarveBody cuts a chosen box out of the world. Explosions. Explode{Center, Radius<=48, Impulse, Destroy, Detach} removes voxels (terrain and voxel-body cells) inside the radius and pushes every dynamic body within 2 radii with a linear falloff. Caps (DoS) and measured cost cap default what happens beyond it MaxBodies 2048 extra bodies (highest entity ids) are not simulated; Stats.Dropped MaxJoints 2048 extra joints ignored MaxPairs 8192 extra broadphase pairs dropped MaxContacts 8192 per tick; the lowest contacts are kept SolverBudget 200000 substeps shrink above it (min 4) MaxPrimTests 600000 primitive pairs (and a quarter of the grid cells walked) per tick; the rest of the pairs is skipped terrain scan 32768 cells an oversized body only collides with terrain within 32 cells of its center per long axis ApplyImpulse / Explode 1e12 per component refused above; the step also clamps speeds and sanitises non-finite state, so a bad input never wedges the tick Detach 16 bodies per command, MaxBodies pieces that do not fit stay in the world MaxPrimsPerPair , MaxTerrainCells 128, 1024 prims/cells examined per pair / per body MaxPairContacts 48 per pair, reduced by farthest-point sampling voxel body 64 per axis, 32768 cells Validate rejects SplitBudget , SupportBudget 16384, 4096 see Destruction physics3d.Res(app).LastStats() reports bodies, awake, pairs, contacts, substeps, cap hits and splits of the last tick. Measured on an Apple M2 Max ( BURROW_PERF=1 go test ./physics3d -run PerfNumbers -v , -bench Dense ; the machine was shared with other jobs, so numbers vary). Cost is the narrowphase (once per tick) plus contacts x (Iterations + Relax) x substeps soft-contact solves (about 100 ns each): scene (dense piles dropped as 20x20 columns) per tick stack of 10 boxes under 0.5 ms 500 boxes, impact ticks (3.6k contacts) average about 6 ms, worst about 16 ms; asleep afterwards (about 1 ms) 1000 boxes, impact (6.3k contacts) average about 20 ms, worst about 23 ms; asleep afterwards (about 2 ms) 2048 boxes (the cap), impact (cap of 8192 contacts) average about 25 ms, worst about 29 ms voxel body 32x16x32 (16384 cells) resting on terrain 5-8 ms splitting a 32x32x32 grid (32768 cells) into 8 islands 5 ms for the flood fill (two ticks at the default budget) A tick is 50 ms (20 Hz). Piles of up to about 1000 boxes fall asleep; 2048 boxes in 5 layers exceed the contact cap, so the lower layers are solved and the pile keeps shifting (it stays awake and costs about 25-30 ms per tick) instead of sleeping. Rendering mesh.BuildDynVoxel meshes a grid once (same vertices, culling and AO as chunks) and mesh.DynModel gives the object matrix. For the Vulkan renderer, physics3d/p3render.Plugin (add it after engine.RenderPlugin ) blends the previous and current tick state with App.TickAlpha() (smooth motion at any frame rate), bakes the transform into the mesh (positions in sixteenths of a block, face index = the world axis nearest the rotated normal) and calls Renderer.UploadDynVoxel : the body is drawn by the terrain pipelines (opaque pass and sun shadow cascade), so it is lit, fogged, shadowed and shadow-casting like world blocks, with the flat block colours. Primitive colliders are drawn as scaled cubes (spheres and capsules by their bounding box). go run ./examples/physics3d_playground -gpu -shot out.png . The bodies also write motion vectors ( Renderer.RegisterVelocityPass , shader vel_dynvox.vert : previous pose = current pose moved by the rigid delta of the last two uploads), so TAA/FSR 2 do not ghost behind them ( -aa taa capture sequence of the explosion in the playground). GPU keys carry the entity generation, removals run before uploads, and each body has its own culling cube (bounding radius), so 64-cell grids and large boxes are not culled at the screen edge. Not done: textured block faces and normal-mapped lighting on rotated bodies, and a true instanced pipeline (the per-frame bake costs one upload per moving body; PackDynVoxMesh / PackDynVoxInstances hold the data layer for it). Limits and untested areas Soft contacts sag under load (a stack of 10 unit boxes settles about 0.1 blocks lower in total); stacks of 14, 20 and 30 boxes hold at the defaults (tested for 14 and 20 with random 0.01-block offsets). Voxel body collision uses surface cells only: a body fully inside another overlap is not resolved; very large overlapping grids are limited by MaxPrimsPerPair . Terrain contacts are cubes only; a body pushed deep inside terrain (more than a few cells) is not pulled back out.

h: How the Vulkan loader is found
x: Platforms Burrow v1 targets the desktop: Windows, macOS and Linux, on x64 and ARM64, all through Vulkan (MoltenVK on macOS). Web and mobile are out of scope for now. This page states what is verified and what is not, because "it builds" and "it runs" are different claims. Support matrix Status words: tested = run by a developer on that machine; CI = built and checked on a native GitHub Actions runner (the workflows are in the repository); cross-compiled = the binary was produced from another machine and never run; untested = not built yet. OS CPU Renderer Windowed engine Headless tools ( burrow , burrowplay -headless , burrowd ) macOS 11+ arm64 (Apple silicon) Vulkan on Metal (MoltenVK) tested (developer machine); CI on pushes to main tested; CI macOS 11+ x64 (Intel) MoltenVK cross-compiled from arm64; never run; optional CI runner cross-compiled; the simulation hash matches arm64 under Rosetta Windows 10 1809+ / 11 x64 Vulkan 1.3 driver cross-compiled with mingw from macOS; never run on real hardware; CI on pull requests cross-compiled; CI Windows 11 arm64 Vulkan 1.3 driver untested: no toolchain here; optional CI runner cross-compiled (Go only) Linux (glibc, X11 or XWayland) x64 Vulkan 1.3 driver (Mesa, NVIDIA) never compiled before this work; CI native build plus a software-Vulkan (lavapipe) smoke cross-compiled; CI Linux (glibc, X11 or XWayland) arm64 Vulkan 1.3 driver untested; optional CI runner cross-compiled; optional CI Honest reading: today only macOS arm64 has ever shown a frame. The CI configuration exists so that the other five rows get a real answer; until its first green run, treat them as untested. Not supported: 32-bit systems, FreeBSD and other Unix systems, Android, iOS, the web, native Wayland (Wayland desktops run Burrow through XWayland). Requirements All platforms: a GPU and driver exposing Vulkan 1.2 or newer with the 1.3 features dynamicRendering and synchronization2 (the engine asks for 1.3, falls back to 1.2 with those features, and refuses a device without them). Rough guide, not a tested list: a GPU from roughly 2015 or later with a current driver (NVIDIA Maxwell and newer, AMD GCN and newer, Intel Skylake and newer), every Apple silicon Mac. If vulkaninfo --summary shows a Vulkan 1.3 device, Burrow should start. OS What to install Notes Windows The graphics driver (NVIDIA, AMD, Intel) from the vendor, which provides vulkan-1.dll . The loader is opened from System32 only. Remote desktop and virtual machines without a GPU driver have no Vulkan. macOS Nothing for a packaged app: the Vulkan loader and MoltenVK are inside the .app ( Contents/Frameworks , driver manifest in Contents/Resources/vulkan/icd.d ). A development build uses Homebrew ( brew install molten-vk vulkan-loader ). Needs a Metal-capable GPU; virtual machines without Metal cannot run the windowed engine. Linux libvulkan1 plus a driver: mesa-vulkan-drivers (AMD, Intel, and the lavapipe software renderer), or the NVIDIA proprietary driver. An X11 or XWayland session. Fedora: vulkan-loader mesa-vulkan-drivers . Arch: vulkan-icd-loader plus vulkan-radeon , vulkan-intel or nvidia-utils . Check with vulkaninfo --summary . Sound uses PulseAudio or PipeWire (through its PulseAudio server) first, then ALSA ( libasound.so.2 ); without either the game runs silent. Building from source on Linux needs the GLFW development packages: libx11-dev libxrandr-dev libxinerama-dev libxcursor-dev libxi-dev libxxf86vm-dev libgl1-mesa-dev pkg-config (Debian and Ubuntu names) and a C compiler. On Windows x64 use MinGW-w64 gcc (MSYS2); on Windows arm64 use clang from MSYS2 CLANGARM64. On macOS, Xcode command line tools. How the Vulkan loader is found The lookup runs before the loader starts ( internal/vkenv , used by window.Init ). macOS, first match wins for the loader ( libvulkan.1.dylib ) and the MoltenVK driver manifest ( MoltenVK_icd.json ): BURROW_VULKAN_LIB (absolute path of the loader file) and an already set VK_ICD_FILENAMES or VK_DRIVER_FILES (never overridden). BURROW_VULKAN_DIR (a folder laid out like one of the places below). The app bundle: Contents/Frameworks , Contents/Resources/vulkan . Next to the executable, and lib/ beside it. System: /opt/homebrew/lib , /usr/local/lib , ~/VulkanSDK/macOS/lib . When a driver manifest is found the engine exports VK_ICD_FILENAMES and VK_DRIVER_FILES for the process; when only libMoltenVK.dylib is found it writes a manifest into a private temporary folder. Executables do not link MoltenVK: nothing in a shipped binary points at /opt/homebrew . The loader is opened by absolute path only (a bare name would let dyld search the working directory). Linux: the system loader libvulkan.so.1 (no bundled copy). BURROW_VULKAN_LIB can point at another loader. Windows: System32\vulkan-1.dll only, overrides are ignored on purpose (DLL search-order hijacking). When no driver is found the editor, the Hub and burrowplay print the install hint to stderr and, on Windows and macOS, show a message box. On Windows the same text lands in the log file. burrow doctor runs the same checks ahead of time (loader, driver, display server, platform). Environment variables Variable Effect BURROW_VULKAN_LIB Absolute path of the Vulkan loader to open first (macOS, Linux). BURROW_VULKAN_DIR macOS: folder holding libvulkan.1.dylib and the MoltenVK manifest or library. VK_ICD_FILENAMES , VK_DRIVER_FILES Standard Vulkan variables; honoured and never overridden. On Linux, point at lvp_icd.json to force the software renderer. BURROW_NO_DIALOG=1 Never show a message box (used by CI and tests). BURROW_BREW_PREFIX macOS development: Homebrew prefix when it is not /opt/homebrew or /usr/local . BURROW_SOUNDS , BURROW_SDK , BURROW_ROOT , BURROW_CACHE_DIR , BURROW_HUB_HOME See Audio , Getting started and Security . Where things live What Windows macOS Linux Hub settings, projects, engine versions ( BURROW_HUB_HOME overrides) %AppData%\Burrow (settings), %LocalAppData%\Burrow (engines) ~/Library/Application Support/Burrow ~/.config/burrow (settings), ~/.local/share/burrow (engines), XDG variables honoured Editor layout, appearance, autosave %AppData%\burrow-editor (from os.UserConfigDir ) ~/Library/Application Support/burrow-editor $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/burrow-editor or ~/.config/burrow-editor Tool cache $BURROW_CACHE_DIR , else the user cache folder ~/Library/Caches/burrow $XDG_CACHE_HOME/burrow or ~/.cache/burrow Your sound packs %USERPROFILE%\.burrow\sounds ~/.burrow/sounds ~/.burrow/sounds Log Burrow.log , BurrowEditor.log next to the program (else %TEMP% ), only when there is no console the terminal (no log file is written) the terminal (no log file is written) Project cache and thumbnails <project>/.burrow-cache same same Linux file systems are case sensitive: asset names in a project must match their case exactly ( Stone.png is not stone.png ). Windows and macOS usually are not, so a project can work there and fail on Linux: keep names consistent. Display scaling (HiDPI) The Hub, the editor and runtime windows follow the display scale of the system, so the interface has a normal physical size on a 4K monitor. Automatic (default). The window asks the system for its content scale (Windows display scaling per monitor, Xft.dpi on X11, the output scale on Wayland, the Retina factor on macOS), rounds it to the nearest step (100, 125, 150, 175, 200, 250 or 300 percent) and lays out and rasterises text, icons and borders at that size, so glyphs stay sharp. Moving a window to a monitor with another scale re-lays it out at once. Setting. Hub: Settings, Display, UI scale ( ui_scale in hub.json ). Editor: Preferences, UI scale. A fixed value is a percentage of the platform's logical size: 100 is normal on a 1x display and on macOS (where the Retina factor is added on top), 150 is one and a half times larger than that. Shortcuts. Ctrl and plus, Ctrl and minus, Ctrl and 0 (Cmd on macOS) in the Hub and the editor: larger, smaller, back to automatic. The choice is saved. Environment.
