BURROW_UI_SCALE ( auto , 150 , 150% or 1.5 ) overrides the setting. On Linux, when the window system reports no scaling at all, GDK_SCALE and QT_SCALE_FACTOR are used as a hint. The scale never goes so high that the window holds less than 800 by 480 logical pixels. Window size. A window without a requested size covers about 70 percent of the work area of the primary monitor (at least 960 by 600 logical pixels), centred. Position and size are remembered per window in <user config dir>/burrow/window/ and restored only when the window is still on a connected monitor. Windows. Every executable embeds an application manifest that declares per-monitor DPI awareness v2, long path support and the requested execution level asInvoker (no administrator rights), together with a version resource (company, product, description, version, copyright). Without the DPI declaration Windows would stretch the window as a bitmap. The sources are in assets/winres/ . Game HUD. gameui scales with the window height (reference 720 px), so it grows with the resolution; its Scale option multiplies that. Determinism across platforms StateHash is meant to be the same on every OS and CPU; verified today on macOS Apple silicon and Intel (Rosetta), while Windows and Linux are checked by the CI workflow against the golden hash, which has not run yet. The simulation (voxel world, water, the standard game rules, 2D and 3D physics, navigation, animation, weather, scripts) uses integer math where it can, and its float math rounds every product explicitly and takes its trigonometry, exponentials and logarithms from a deterministic library instead of the platform's. scripts/portability-hash.sh runs the eight templates for 200 ticks and compares the hashes with the committed golden ( scripts/portability-golden.txt ); every CI job runs it. On one Mac the arm64 and the amd64 (Rosetta) binaries give identical hashes for all eight templates at 200 and 2000 ticks; the other operating systems are verified by CI once it has run. Rendering and other frame-domain code is not covered and does not need to be. Details, guards and rules for contributors: Determinism . Known limits Graphics: the windowed engine has been run on one GPU family (Apple M2 Max through MoltenVK). Other drivers (NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, Mesa) may expose driver bugs or missing features the renderer has not met. Windows binaries are not code signed and Microsoft SmartScreen warns on first run; macOS apps are ad-hoc signed and not notarised, so Gatekeeper asks for confirmation. Clipboard: macOS uses the system clipboard through pbcopy / pbpaste ; Windows and Linux use GLFW's clipboard (new in this version, untested on those systems). Audio on Linux needs PulseAudio, PipeWire-Pulse or ALSA at run time. Wayland sessions run through XWayland (X11 build of GLFW). Software rendering (lavapipe, WARP) works for smoke tests but is far too slow to play.

h: A campfire with on and off
Using a node: the interact component
x: Linked prefabs A prefab is a reusable subtree saved as a .prefab file (the .voxscn format with exactly one root). Placing one from the Assets panel creates a linked instance : the nodes are expanded in the scene, and the instance remembers its prefab and the few things you changed on it. Edit the prefab once and every instance follows; each keeps its own settings. Example, a campfire: a voxel model node, a particle_emitter (fire), an audio_source (crackle) and a script with props. Build it once in the scene, then reuse it in ten places, one of them with {"on": true} in the script props and another with the smoke turned off. Using prefabs in the editor Create prefab... (Hierarchy right-click): saves the selected node and its children as a .prefab (path inside assets/ , extension added, existing files are never overwritten), with the root reset to the identity transform, and replaces the selection by a linked instance with the same name and transform. One undo step (the file stays). Place : drag a .prefab into the viewport or the hierarchy. A single-rooted prefab becomes a linked instance; a scene ( .voxscn ) or a multi-rooted prefab is still copied under a holder node. Instance roots show the prefab icon in the Hierarchy. The Inspector of an instance (or of any node inside it) shows the prefab, the number of overrides and Open / Apply / Revert . Under each component card, the fields you changed are listed as buttons: click one to revert that field to the prefab (undoable). Open prefab (Hierarchy menu, Inspector header, or double-click the .prefab asset): opens the prefab editor , a full-screen tool like the model editor. Apply to prefab : writes the instance's current content into the prefab (the instance keeps its own name and transform) and updates every other instance, which keep their overrides. It is one undo step in the scene: undo restores the previous prefab file, the other instances and the applied instance's own overrides. Revert to prefab : drops all the overrides of the instance (one undo step). Unpack : removes the link and keeps the nodes (one undo step). The prefab editor The prefab editor edits a .prefab in isolation. The prefab is its own document: its own scene, selection, undo history and viewport, a small studio with a grid floor and day lighting. Nothing it does touches the open scene (nodes, voxels, history, dirty flag) until you save. The scene stays where you left it behind Back to world . Tabs : several prefabs can be open at once; each tab keeps its own camera, selection and undo history, and a tab with unsaved edits asks before it closes (the x refuses; Revert drops the edits). Header : Save (Ctrl+S), Revert (asks twice), Undo and Redo (Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Y: the prefab's own history only, never the scene's), the gizmo mode (W move, E rotate, R scale), Frame (F selection, Shift+F everything), Back to world. Hierarchy (left): the prefab's nodes. Click to select (Ctrl+click adds), double-click or F2 renames, drag a row to reorder or reparent (top and bottom edge place it before or after, the middle moves it inside; the node keeps its place in the world), right-click for Duplicate, Add child and Delete (Del). Add creates a cube, sphere, sprite, light or empty node, an interact box, a particle emitter, a sound or a script under the selection. A prefab has one root: it cannot be deleted or duplicated, and a second root is refused on save. Viewport (center): drag on empty space to orbit, right or middle drag to pan, wheel to zoom, double-click a node to frame it, click a node marker to select it. The gizmo moves, rotates or scales the selection (hold Ctrl to snap); one drag is one undo step. Drop an asset from the Content panel to add it at the floor point under the cursor: a voxel model, mesh, PNG (sprite), .particles.json (emitter), .wav / .ogg (spatial looping sound), .wasm (script) or another prefab or scene (copied in as plain nodes). A prefab cannot be dropped into itself. A voxel.group node shows its box and its blocks (meshed with the block colours of the project); the blocks are only drawn, they are written to the world of whichever scene places the prefab, never to this tool's. Inspector (right panel): the selected node's transform (the root's transform is not saved: every instance has its own) and component cards with the same field editors as the main Inspector (asset pickers, ranges, colours), Add a component, Reset and Remove in each card's menu. Status line : how many instances of the prefab are in the open scene, and whether the tab is saved. Save writes the .prefab and rebuilds every instance of it in the open scene (also those that contain it through another prefab), keeping their names, transforms and overrides. In the scene this is one undo step, "Update prefab instances" , that also holds the file write: Ctrl+Z in the world puts back the previous file and the previous instances, and Redo writes the new one again. A prefab nothing in the open scene uses is just written. A prefab that would contain itself, directly or through other prefabs, or that is not single-rooted, is refused, and nesting is limited to 8 levels. A tab without unsaved edits follows the file when it changes on disk (an undone Apply, git). Previews (header): the particle button plays or pauses the live preview of the particle_emitter nodes (enabled ones only, from their asset or inline params, local or world space, at their place in the prefab; default playing) and the restart button replays it from time zero, with the same particles every time. The speaker button (default off) plays the audio_source nodes that have an asset, autoplay and are not muted: spatial sources sit at their node and are heard from the viewport camera (with their min/max distance, rolloff and model; the sound pans and fades as the camera orbits), the others play as plain stereo; they stop when it is switched off, when the tab changes or the tool closes; a looping source repeats, a one-shot plays once per start. Particles with collide bounce on the grid floor (y = 0) and on the cells of the voxel.group nodes (a rotated or scaled group is tested exactly: the particle's cell box against the blocks in the group's own frame), a spatial source with the Occlusion option is muffled and attenuated like in the game when a voxel.group stands between the viewport camera and the node (0.35 per solid cell crossed, fully blocked at three), grass and foliage blocks of a group take the default biome tint, and mesh emitters draw their .vox / .bmodel model. voxel.group blocks draw with their block textures and shapes (slabs, stairs, plants, transparency; flat colours when textures are off). Neither preview touches the prefab file or the open scene. When a .prefab changes on disk (another tool, git, Apply) the open scene's instances are rebuilt in place, keeping their name, transform, position among siblings and overrides. That is not an undo step and marks the scene modified. Opening a scene also refreshes its instances from the current prefab files. A node inside a prefab that is itself an instance (a campfire inside a camp) is part of the outer instance: edit, apply and revert always work on the outermost link, and the inner one is refreshed through it. Variants A variant is a .prefab of one node whose prefab.instance links a base prefab (a project file, a built-in such as builtin:player.prefab , or another variant) with overrides. The engine resolves it as the base plus the overrides, so it follows the base for everything it does not change. Variants nest: a variant of a variant works, up to 8 levels. Create variant : right-click a prefab in Content (or in the Engine folder for a built-in one), or the Create variant... button of the game.mode player prefab. It writes <base>_variant.prefab (next to a project base, in assets/prefabs for a built-in one) and opens it in the prefab editor. The prefab editor opens a variant expanded (the base's nodes with the overrides applied) and shows a bar under the header: the base, how many fields differ, Open base , Apply to base and Revert all . Each component card lists its overridden fields as buttons; a click reverts that field to the base (undoable in the tab). Save writes the variant back as the diff against its base. Apply to base writes the variant's content into the base prefab (other users of the base follow) and leaves the variant with no overrides. It is only offered when the base is a project prefab: a built-in base is read-only (a built-in prefab opens for viewing; Save is refused). The tab of a variant follows its base when the base is saved and the tab has no unsaved edits. A campfire with on and off Model it in the modeler with layers base , logs , charred , flames , embers and two variants: off (base, charred) and on (base, logs, flames, embers). See modeling . In a scene, make a node campfire with three children: model ( render.voxmodel of the .bmodel ), flames ( particle_emitter , builtin:fire ) and crackle ( audio_source , loop, autoplay, spatial). Script panel > New script from a template > state , name campfire , on the campfire node. Props: {"on": false, "group": "camp"} . Add an interact component on model (or on the root) with a box around the fire, e.g. {"size": [0.5, 0.4, 0.5], "prompt": "Light the fire"} : the player's right click on it toggles the fire. Hierarchy right-click > Create prefab... . Place as many as you like; set on to true on the instances that start lit (a per-instance override). The state script applies its state when it starts and whenever a message reaches it: every render.voxmodel under the node gets the on_variant / off_variant variant, every particle_emitter is enabled or not, every audio_source is muted or not. Another script lights them: burrowsdk.Publish( "state.toggle" , [] byte ( "camp" )) // every state script whose group is "camp" burrowsdk.Emit(fire, burrowsdk.BusKind( "state.on" ), nil ) // one node A message without a payload reaches the state scripts whose group is empty. Set no_click to ignore right clicks. Using a node: the interact component A node with interact ( size half extents and offset in the node's space, so the box follows its transform; range , prompt , disabled ) can be right clicked by the player, before the block behind it. The first person controller sends the journaled scene_use command (multiplayer: allowed by the default gate whitelist, 10 per second, the player id forced to the sender); the script runtime delivers a node.use event to the nearest script at or above the clicked node, so a script on a prefab root hears clicks on any part. In Go: burrowsdk.OnUse( func (self burrowsdk.Entity, ev burrowsdk.UseEvent) { /* ev.Node, ev.Player */ }) While a usable node is aimed the HUD shows its prompt ( FrameState.UseNode , UsePrompt ) and no block outline. The state is kept in the script's state, so it survives save and load. The prefab.instance component The link is a scene component on the instance root, saved in the .voxscn : { "id" : 4 , "name" : "campfire_north" , "components" : { "transform" : { "pos" : [ 12 , 3 , - 4 ], "rot" : [ 0 , 90 , 0 ], "scale" : [ 1 , 1 , 1 ] }, "prefab.instance" : { "prefab" : "assets/prefabs/campfire.prefab" , "overrides" : [ { "path" : "Smoke" , "component" : "particle_emitter" , "fields" : { "enabled" : false } }, { "path" : "Logic" , "component" : "script" , "fields" : { "props" : { "on" : true } } }, { "path" : "Crackle" , "remove" : true } ] } } } prefab is the project-relative path (renaming the file in the Assets panel rewrites it like any other reference). The instance's nodes follow in the file, fully expanded, so the runtime needs no prefab lookup : a game loads the scene as usual and the link is only data (the component is registered in the default schema, so every build reads it). Overrides store only the differences from the prefab, in order: key meaning path node relative to the instance root ( "" = root, "arm/hand" = descendant) component + fields merge these JSON fields into the component (adds it when absent). A key is a field path: "intensity" replaces that top-level field, "props.on" sets a nested field (numbers index arrays) and leaves its siblings alone component + drop remove the component remove delete the node and its subtree (never the root) add graft a subtree document ( {"version":1,"nodes":[...]} ) as children of the node rename rename the node (a renamed node whose components and descendants are unchanged is one rename , not a remove plus an add) order child names of path in the wanted order, written when the instance's sibling order differs from the prefab The root's name, transform and parent belong to the instance and are never overridden. The editor recomputes the overrides by diffing the instance's nodes against the prefab, field by field (nested objects down to the changed field; arrays are replaced whole), when it saves the scene and before it re-syncs from a changed prefab; the saved list is therefore always current. Limits: EntityRef fields inside grafted ( add ) or nested subtrees are not remapped, and a key removed from a nested object replaces that object whole, and one removed at the top level replaces the whole component (a merge cannot unset a key); field names containing a . cannot be addressed by a path. Older files whose fields hold whole top-level values apply unchanged. In the Inspector, clicking an overridden field path reverts just that path. Go API Package scene : PrefabInstance , Override , ResolveLinked (prefab + overrides to an instance document), DiffOverrides , ExpandLinks , CheckPrefabCycle , SameContent , OverriddenFields , RevertOverride . Package editor/core : CreatePrefabFromSelection , PlacePrefab , PrefabApply , PrefabRevert , PrefabRevertField , PrefabUnpack , SyncPrefabInstances , PrefabLinkOf , RefreshPrefabLinks , and the prefab editor's workspace: PrefabWS , OpenPrefabDoc , ClosePrefabDoc , PrefabInstanceCount and, on a PrefabDoc , Spawn , SpawnAsset , SpawnPart , Delete , Duplicate , Rename , Reparent , Reorder , SetTransform , SetComponent , AddComponent , RemoveComponent , Undo , Redo , Revert , Save . ( EnterPrefabEdit , SavePrefabEdit and ExitPrefabEdit , the older way of swapping the open scene for the prefab, stay as an internal fallback with no UI.)

h: Measurements (M2 Max, MoltenVK, 2560x1440, radius 12, -shaders high -aa taa , no validation, GPU ms of the RT passes, one consistent run after the a-trous filter became 3x3)
x: Ray tracing Render-only (frame domain): nothing here touches the simulation or StateHash . It applies to the HDR shader levels of the Vulkan renderer; -shaders off , -look classic , the soft CPU renderer and offscreen editor targets ignore it. The tracer is software: a hierarchical voxel DDA in compute shaders, so it runs on MoltenVK. No hardware ray tracing is required (see Hardware path ). Settings flag (env) values default -rt ( BURROW_RT ) off , shadows (sun shadows + AO), full (+ GI + reflections), or a list of sun,ao,gi,reflections the shader level: low and medium off, high shadows and ultra full enable ray tracing by default ( -rt off turns it off) Flags exist on examples/voxel_sandbox and burrowplay . engine.RenderPlugin.RT and the live engine.RenderSettings.RT take the same strings (applied the next frame); vulkan.Renderer.SetRayTracing(render.RTSettings) is the renderer API. Switching on from off rebuilds the HDR target once (it gains the storage usage) and the engine re-meshes the resident chunks once so the acceleration structure is complete. BURROW_RT_DEBUG=1..5 shows one signal instead of the lit image (sun visibility, AO, normal, GI, reflection). Frame layout UploadChunkVoxels / RemoveChunk -> acceleration structure (copied at the start of the frame) main pass -> HDR target + depth rt-trace half resolution: sun shadow ray (cone jitter), AO ray, GI bounce ray, reflection ray rt_trace.comp rt-temporal reprojection (previous view-projection), per pixel history count, disocclusion test rt_temporal.comp rt-atrous 3 edge-avoiding wavelet iterations (3x3, steps 1, 2, 4) rt_atrous.comp rt-composite depth aware upsampling, applied in place to the HDR target (and the scene copy) rt_composite.comp -> velocity, TAA / FSR 2, bloom, exposure, composite, LDR stage (all unchanged) Ray traced AO replaces the screen space AO (its passes are skipped while the effect is on; the AO textures are initialised once so the composite never samples garbage). Ray traced sun shadows replace the shadow map of the world; the map is still rendered, without the world chunks, when something the tracer does not know can cast a shadow: dynamic voxel bodies, scene meshes and avatars (hybrid frames). Both shadows then multiply. Particles cast no shadow. Under water the whole chain is skipped (the HDR frame is left as rendered). Acceleration structure ( render.RTChunk , vulkan.rtAS ) Per chunk (32^3): an occupancy bitmask (4 KiB, only light blocking blocks: opaque blocks and solid cubes such as leaves; glass, plants and shaped blocks do not occlude), a water bitmask, a material byte per voxel (a class of colour / emission / gloss, at most 255 classes, colours are quantised when a registry has more) and the coarse level: one bit per 8^3 brick that holds an occluder. A chunk without occluders and water takes no slot. A toroidal index of 256 x 32 x 256 chunks (16 MiB) maps a chunk coordinate to its slot. It covers the largest streaming radius ( engine.MaxRadius = 96, plus 2 columns each side: 197 of the 256 entries) without aliasing; beyond 32 chunk layers in Y two layers would share an entry (the key check then gives a missing chunk, never a wrong one). Empty chunks and empty bricks are crossed in one DDA step, so open sky and caves are cheap. Incremental: the mesh workers ( engine/rtvoxels.go ) distil every meshed chunk; an edit re-meshes the chunk and uploads only its data. A cache keyed by chunk pointer and Version avoids rebuilding the neighbours that are re-meshed next to an edit. At most 48 chunks per frame go through a per-frame staging buffer; the copies are ordered against the compute passes by memory barriers. Removal frees the slot and clears the table entry. Capacity: 5 x columns slots from the renderer's far plane (512..3584, 40 KiB each). When it is full the nearest chunks to the camera win: a farther resident chunk is evicted, or the new one waits in the queue with its data until a slot frees; evictions are reported ( Renderer.TakeRTMisses ) and the streamer re-sends them, so there is no permanent hole ( RayTracingStats.Overflow counts them). Switching ray tracing on re-sends every resident chunk through an RT-only queue (no re-mesh). After 240 frames with ray tracing off the structure, the pipelines and the half resolution images are freed (the storage usage of the HDR target stays). If the setup fails, the engine stops building chunk data. Denoising and history The trace takes one sample per effect per half resolution pixel per frame. The temporal pass reprojects with the unjittered previous matrix, rejects taps by view depth and normal, and blends with max(1/count, 0.04) . The a-trous filter stops at depth planes (linear in the tap offset, voxel normals are axis aligned) and, on the shadow / AO channels, at luminance edges that are trusted more as the history grows. Renderer.ResetHistory() , app.FrameState.CameraCut , a resize, a preset change and the automatic detection of the anti-aliasing stage (24 blocks, 75 degrees, 25 degrees of FOV) drop the history; the GPU test rt-cut checks it. The composite applies the same linear transform to the scene copy so the reactive mask of the temporal anti-aliasing does not light up. Hardware path (stub) vulkan.RTBackend is the traversal interface ( Name , TraceModule , Setup , Close ). softwareRT is the only working backend. rayQueryRT is selected by a capability check ( VK_KHR_ray_query , VK_KHR_acceleration_structure , VK_KHR_deferred_host_operations on the device) but its Setup returns ErrRTUnavailable and the renderer prints one line and keeps the software tracer. It cannot be tested on MoltenVK, so it is not implemented: a real backend builds BLAS / TLAS from the chunk data and ships an rt_trace_rq.comp using rayQueryEXT . Measurements (M2 Max, MoltenVK, 2560x1440, radius 12, -shaders high -aa taa , no validation, GPU ms of the RT passes, one consistent run after the a-trous filter became 3x3) mode trace temporal a-trous composite RT total effect on the rest of the frame sun shadows 0.77 0.24 1.74 0.59 3.3 shadow map pass 0.5 -> 0.03 AO only 0.22 0.18 1.84 0.57 2.8 screen space AO passes (1.5) skipped GI only 2.69 0.36 1.94 0.65 5.6 reflections only 0.48 0.29 1.92 0.54 3.2 shadows (sun + AO) 0.61 0.31 1.85 0.60 3.4 shadow map -0.5, AO passes -1.5 full 3.00 0.70 3.05 0.93 7.7 Whole frame (GPU total, ms): off 18.6, shadows 19.4, full 23.4 (the machine is shared; runs repeat to about 1 ms). Memory: about 100 MiB of half resolution images at 1440p plus the structure (140 MiB at 3584 slots). Idle machine, -gen v2 -shaders high (preset shadows , spawn view, 2560x1440, native TAA): trace 0.48, temporal 0.34, a-trous 0.49, composite 0.55, RT total 1.9 ms of a 7.5 ms frame. The tables above were taken while the GPU was shared with other jobs and read about 3-5x higher; the a-trous pass is already below 1 ms when the GPU is idle, so it was left as is. At 75% render scale the RT passes cost 0.53 / 0.19 / 0.28 / 0.28 (1.3 ms). Tests render ( rt_test.go ): parsing, presets, RTChunk bits, material classes; engine : TestBuildRTChunk ; render/vulkan ( make render-test , validation on): every effect changes the frame, the denoised static scene is stable, ResetHistory drops the history, an edit of the structure shows, switching off restores the classic frame, a teleport runs clean, a glossy floor reflects the tower ( rt-gloss ), a structure with two slots keeps the nearest chunk and reports the others ( rt-capacity ); vulkan unit tests: the table never aliases a loaded region, the shadow map plan; engine : the RT-only rebuild re-meshes nothing and re-sends a dropped chunk; render : the material table never maps a block to air. Limits Block light: emitters bounce light through the GI ray with their emission colour; the propagated block light and skylight (docs/lighting.md) are baked into the raster shading and are not traced. Glass, plants, shaped blocks (stairs, fences) do not occlude; dynamic voxel bodies and scene meshes are not in the structure. Surface normals come from the depth buffer checked against the voxels (axis aligned): smooth water and non-cube meshes get an up / depth normal; water waves in the reflection are a small analytic ripple, not the water shader's waves. GI is one bounce with the hemispheric ambient at the hit and one sun shadow ray; it is applied as a ratio to the flat ambient of the lit shader, so it adds occlusion and colour bleeding, not new energy. Effects fade with the aerial perspective and the far fog. By design: unloaded chunks and chunks beyond the structure are empty space (rays leave the loaded world; light can enter through unstreamed terrain). Rays have step caps (shadow 96 steps / 160 blocks, AO 24 steps / 2.5 blocks, GI 64 / 64 blocks, reflection 128 / 160 blocks, hit shadow rays 40-48 steps): a longer path counts as a miss. Fine (sloped) water is not in the structure (the water-only re-mesh does not rebuild it): only whole water blocks mark the surface for reflections. The composite applies the water surface's reflection weight to the already refracted colour behind it, so the water tint of a reflective pixel is replaced together with the base reflection. The composite never writes a NaN / Inf into the HDR frame (it skips the pixel), so the TAA / FSR 2 history cannot be poisoned. Untested on AMD, NVIDIA, Intel and Windows; the hardware path is untested everywhere.

Recipes Complete programs for the most common game features, each compiled by go test ./docs/ . Replace the string literals by the burrow_gen.go constants ( burrow gen ) in a real project. Recipe Flavors Main menu gogame Pause menu gogame Pickup and score HUD gogame, WASM script Enemy that chases the player gogame, WASM script Door and trigger zone gogame, WASM script Cards for agents: llms-gogame.txt , llms-script.txt .

Recipe: door and trigger zone A wall of three blocks at x=10, z=10, y=9..11 opens (air) while the player stands inside the box around it and closes (stone) when they leave. Stateless: the voxels are the state, so it is deterministic and survives saves. gogame package main import "burrow-engine/gogame" func inZone(x, y, z float32 ) bool { return x >= 7 && x <= 13 && y >= 8 && y <= 13 && z >= 7 && z <= 13 } func main() { gogame.Main(gogame.Game{ OnTick: func (c *gogame.Ctx) { player, ok := c.Player() if !ok { return } p, _ := c.Pos(player) want := "stone" if inZone(p.X, p.Y, p.Z) { want = "air" } for y := 9 ; y <= 11 ; y++ { if c.Voxel( 10 , y, 10 ) != want { _ = c.SetVoxel( 10 , y, 10 , want) } } }, }) } WASM script On any node (for example the player). Resolve block ids once per call with BlockByName . package main import "burrow-engine/sdk/burrowsdk" func init() { burrowsdk.Register(burrowsdk.Script{ OnTick: func (self burrowsdk.Entity, dt float64 ) { player, ok := burrowsdk.LocalPlayer() if !ok { return } t, err := burrowsdk.GetTransform(player) if err != nil { return } x, y, z := t.Pos[ 0 ], t.Pos[ 1 ], t.Pos[ 2 ] open := x >= 7 && x <= 13 && y >= 8 && y <= 13 && z >= 7 && z <= 13 name := "stone" if open { name = "air" } want, err := burrowsdk.BlockByName(name) if err != nil { return } for by := 9 ; by <= 11 ; by++ { if cur, err := burrowsdk.Voxel( 10 , by, 10 ); err == nil && cur != want { _ = burrowsdk.SetVoxel( 10 , by, 10 , want) } } }, }) } func main() {}

t: Recipe: enemy that chases the player
h: Recipe: enemy that chases the player
x: Recipe: enemy that chases the player Enemy nodes are tagged enemy . They walk straight toward the player on the XZ plane and stop within 1.2 blocks. There is no pathfinding here: for walls and slopes add a nav.agent component and NavSetGoalPos ( navigation ). gogame package main import ( "math" "burrow-engine/gogame" ) const ( speed = 3.0 // blocks per second stop = 1.2 ) func main() { gogame.Main(gogame.Game{ OnTick: func (c *gogame.Ctx) { player, ok := c.Player() if !ok { return } pp, _ := c.Pos(player) for _, e := range c.FindByTag( "enemy" ) { ep, ok := c.Pos(e) if !ok { continue } dx, dz := float64 (pp.X-ep.X), float64 (pp.Z-ep.Z) d := math.Hypot(dx, dz) if d < stop { continue } step := float64 (speed * c.Dt()) ep.X += float32 (dx / d * step) ep.Z += float32 (dz / d * step) _ = c.SetPos(e, ep) } }, }) } WASM script On the enemy node, with props {"speed": 3} . package main import ( "math" "burrow-engine/sdk/burrowsdk" ) type props struct { Speed float64 `json:"speed"` } func init() { burrowsdk.Register(burrowsdk.Script{ OnTick: func (self burrowsdk.Entity, dt float64 ) { p, _ := burrowsdk.Props[props]() player, ok := burrowsdk.LocalPlayer() if !ok { return } pt, err1 := burrowsdk.GetTransform(player) me, err2 := burrowsdk.GetTransform(self) if err1 != nil || err2 != nil { return } dx, dz := float64 (pt.Pos[ 0 ]-me.Pos[ 0 ]), float64 (pt.Pos[ 2 ]-me.Pos[ 2 ]) d := math.Hypot(dx, dz) if d < 1.2 { return } me.Pos[ 0 ] += float32 (dx / d * p.Speed * dt) me.Pos[ 2 ] += float32 (dz / d * p.Speed * dt) _ = burrowsdk.SetTransform(self, me) }, }) } func main() {}

t: Recipe: main menu that loads the game scene
h: Recipe: main menu that loads the game scene
x: Recipe: main menu that loads the game scene vox.project default scene is scenes/menu.voxscn (camera, sky, one root node named MenuRoot ). Play despawns it and loads scenes/game.voxscn . The button emits a UI signal ( ui.Emit ); it reaches OnTick on the next tick through a journaled command, so the run replays exactly. package main import ( "sync/atomic" "burrow-engine/gameui/imui" "burrow-engine/gogame" ) var ( quit atomic.Bool // frame side only (closing the window is not simulation) inGame atomic.Bool ) func main() { gogame.Main(gogame.Game{ OnTick: func (c *gogame.Ctx) { if !c.UIClicked( "play" ) { return } if root, ok := c.Find( "MenuRoot" ); ok { _ = c.Despawn(root) } _ = c.LoadScene( "scenes/game.voxscn" ) inGame.Store( true ) }, OnFrame: func (f *gogame.Frame) { if quit.Load() { f.Quit() } }, UI: func (ui *imui.UI) { if inGame.Load() { return } ui.Window( "My Game" , func () { if ui.Button( "Play" ) { ui.Emit( "play" , 0 ) } if ui.Button( "Quit" ) { quit.Store( true ) } }) }, }) } Keep "runtime":{"plugins":{"scripts":true}} in vox.project .

Recipe: pause menu P toggles the menu. SetPausedBy freezes the simulation while it is open. The key is read raw in OnFrame (cosmetic input only, no simulation change). package main import ( "burrow-engine/gameui/imui" "burrow-engine/gogame" ) var ( paused bool // frame side only (OnFrame and UI run on the same goroutine) quit bool held bool volume = float32 ( 0.8 ) ) func main() { gogame.Main(gogame.Game{ OnFrame: func (f *gogame.Frame) { now := f.Key( "P" ) if now && !held { paused = !paused } held = now f.Context().SetPausedBy( "menu" , paused) if quit { f.Quit() } }, UI: func (ui *imui.UI) { if !paused { return } ui.Window( "Paused" , func () { if ui.Button( "Resume" ) { paused = false } ui.Slider( "Volume" , &volume, 0 , 1 ) if ui.Button( "Quit" ) { quit = true } }) }, }) }

Recipe: pickup and score HUD Scene nodes tagged coin (component "tags" ). Touching one (within 1.5 blocks of the player) removes it and adds 1 to the score. gogame package main import ( "fmt" "sync/atomic" "burrow-engine/gameui/imui" "burrow-engine/gogame" ) var score atomic.Int64 // read by the UI, written by OnTick func main() { gogame.Main(gogame.Game{ OnTick: func (c *gogame.Ctx) { player, ok := c.Player() if !ok { return } pp, _ := c.Pos(player) for _, coin := range c.FindByTag( "coin" ) { cp, ok := c.Pos(coin) if !ok { continue } dx, dy, dz := cp.X-pp.X, cp.Y-pp.Y, cp.Z-pp.Z if dx*dx+dy*dy+dz*dz < 1.5 * 1.5 { _ = c.Despawn(coin) score.Add( 1 ) } } }, UI: func (ui *imui.UI) { ui.Panel( "hud" , imui.Rect{X: 12 , Y: 12 , W: 160 , H: 40 }, func () { ui.Label(fmt.Sprintf( "Score: %d" , score.Load())) }) }, }) } WASM script Put the script on the player node. The score lives in State (memory resets every call) and goes to the HUD with UISetNum . ui/hud.ui.json holds a label {"type":"label","text":"Score {score}"} and plugins.gameui is on. package main import "burrow-engine/sdk/burrowsdk" type state struct { Score int `json:"score"` } func init() { burrowsdk.Register(burrowsdk.Script{ OnTick: func (self burrowsdk.Entity, dt float64 ) { me, err := burrowsdk.GetTransform(self) if err != nil { return } coins, _, _ := burrowsdk.FindTag( "coin" , 0 ) st, _ := burrowsdk.LoadState[state]() before := st.Score for _, coin := range coins { t, err := burrowsdk.GetTransform(coin) if err != nil { continue } dx, dy, dz := t.Pos[ 0 ]-me.Pos[ 0 ], t.Pos[ 1 ]-me.Pos[ 1 ], t.Pos[ 2 ]-me.Pos[ 2 ] if dx*dx+dy*dy+dz*dz < 1.5 * 1.5 { _ = burrowsdk.Despawn(coin) st.Score++ } } if st.Score != before { _ = burrowsdk.SaveState(st) _ = burrowsdk.UISetNum( "score" , float64 (st.Score)) } }, }) } func main() {}

Work in this order: footprint and circulation, then masses and heights, then roof, then palette, then depth and detail, then lighting and surroundings. Starting from the facade or from random blocks gives boxes that cannot be fixed with decoration. theme-first. Pick one style (see styles) and its palette before placing the first block; every later choice follows from it. Local materials win over taste: a stone castle needs a quarry, a desert town is sandstone. Mixed styles and out-of-place materials read as noise. fill-then-carve. Block out each volume with fill_box (or hollow boxes), then carve openings and add detail. Prefer a few big fills to many single blocks. Single-block placement is slow, error-prone and runs into per-call limits. review-loop. After each stage look at the result (screenshot) and run the build review on the area; fix what it flags before adding more. Problems compound when detail is added on top of a bad base. palette palette-size. Use 3 to 5 building blocks: a base (about half of the surface), a secondary (about a third) and an accent (about a fifth). More than 5 materials looks messy; one material looks flat. Too many materials: chaos. One material: a featureless box. palette-contrast. Give frame and infill different tones or textures: a darker or lighter frame (logs, dark oak) on lighter walls, or stone below and wood above. Similar blocks look fine up close but vanish at a distance. Walls and frame of the same block have no readable structure. palette-gradient. Use dark below and light above (plinth darker than walls, walls darker than trim). Grade 3 or 4 blocks of one hue from light to dark instead of a single block. Light-on-top draws the eye up and gives weight to the base. palette-texture-mix. Mix variants of one family in small, justified amounts: stone bricks with a few cracked or mossy ones near the ground and the corners. Never 50/50 random noise; keep the odd variant to roughly one block in ten, grouped where weathering would happen. Evenly scattered variants read as static, not age. palette-rare-accent. Rare or loud blocks (gold, emerald, diamond, quartz, coloured glass, glowstone) are accents at doors, corners, ridges and focal windows, never the bulk. Whole walls of shiny blocks look cheap. palette-whole-building. Roof, ceiling, floor and furniture follow the same palette as the walls. A ceiling in a clashing wood or a glass floor breaks the interior. silhouette silhouette-not-box. Break the cube: use an L, T or U footprint, two or three volumes of different heights, a porch, a tower or a wing. One dominant volume, smaller ones subordinate. A plain rectangle with a roof is the signature of a first attempt. silhouette-asymmetry. Keep an ordered frame but add controlled asymmetry: an offset chimney, a lean-to, a door off the centre line. Use odd widths when something must sit exactly in the middle (single door, ridge). Perfect symmetry everywhere is sterile; random asymmetry is sloppy. silhouette-heights. Vary floor and ceiling heights between rooms and wings; do not put every wall at the same height. depth depth-relief. No facade is a single plane. Every 3 to 5 blocks change the depth by one block: recess a window bay, push out a pillar or a corner, add a bay window or a balcony. Flat walls catch no shadow and look painted on. depth-windows. Set windows one block back from the wall face (or push them out as a bay), frame them with trapdoors, stairs or slabs, and give them a sill and a lintel. Glass flush with the wall disappears. depth-trim. Add a cornice (upside-down stairs or slabs) under the roof, a plinth where the wall meets the ground, and vertical pillars at the corners and every 3 to 5 blocks. depth-3d-texture. Detail with small shaped blocks: trapdoors as shutters, fences as railings and posts, walls as columns, stairs and slabs as ledges, buttons or ladders as texture. Never leave a large wall of one flat block. walls walls-thickness. Exterior walls are 2 to 3 blocks thick for stone and castle styles (window reveals need it); light timber walls are one block over a frame. Interior partitions are one block. A one-block stone wall cannot be recessed. walls-two-tone. Decorate plain walls with one of: two tones (dark low, light high), a band of another material, a wavy boundary between two materials (one block step), or 3D texture. Pick one to four wall elements and use them everywhere in the room or facade. walls-taper. Large castles and churches get thicker at the bottom: step the base out by one block or add buttresses (stairs-capped piers) at regular spacing. Small houses keep a constant thickness. walls-battlements. For crenellations alternate a full block and a gap along the top edge; add corner towers that stand out from the wall. roof roof-slope. Pitched roofs are the default: 1:1 (stairs, 45 degrees) is the standard, 1:2 (alternating slabs) is flatter, 2:1 (two blocks per step) is steep. Use a flat roof only for the modern style, and give it a parapet or an edge of a different block. A flat roof with no edge looks unfinished and lets mobs spawn. roof-overhang. Let the roof overhang the walls by one block (two for big roofs); it throws a shadow line and protects the facade. roof-height. A roof is one to two storeys tall. Past about 5 to 7 blocks per section, split it into several roofs, put a storey in the attic, or turn the volume into a tower. A single plain gable wider than about 12 to 15 blocks looks like a barn: use several gables (T, L, cross-gable) or a hip roof. roof-parity. Odd span: the ridge is a single block row centred over the middle (and over a single door). Even span: two stairs back to back, or two top slabs, form the ridge. Mismatched parity leaves a one-block gap or a lopsided ridge. roof-gables. Close the gable ends with wall material (a triangle), put one window in the middle of it, and break big roofs with dormers or a chimney. roof-joins. When joining roofs build the tallest one first as if alone, then the next, down to the lowest; finally remove the blocks that ended up inside another roof. roof-contrast. Make the roof a contrasting material from the walls (dark stairs on light walls), still within the palette. windows windows-size. Windows start one to two blocks above the floor. Vary their size and spacing; avoid a perfect grid. A tall 1x2 window gets trapdoor shutters; big openings (3 wide) suit halls. windows-glass. Use glass panes for thin, framed windows and full glass blocks for modern walls; tint glass to match the mood (blue near water, white for a cloudy look). Leave an opening rather than a glass wall in styles that would not have glass. windows-doors. Few doors, framed with a lintel, a step and a lamp. A door is two blocks tall and sits flush with the wall or in a recess. interior interior-height. Ceilings are 3 to 4 blocks in a house (a slab ceiling gives about 2.5), 4 to 5 in a small room, 5 to 6 in a medieval hall, 10 to 12 in a castle great hall. Vary heights from room to room. A 2-block ceiling cannot be jumped under and feels cramped. interior-halls. Corridors are 2 blocks wide in a small house and 3 to 4 in a large one; add a carpet and a window. interior-floors. Floors are never bare dirt or grass. Alternate two blocks (planks and logs, polished andesite and diorite, a chequer of two concretes), vary by room (tile in kitchen and bathroom, wood in living rooms, cobblestone in cellars), and put a pattern in the middle of a room with a plain border. interior-furniture. Furnish with shaped blocks: a table is a fence with a pressure plate on top, a chair is a stair, a sofa 2 to 4 stairs, shelves are bookshelves, a cabinet is a barrel with trapdoors. Put a focal point in each room (hearth, table, bookshelf wall). interior-hearth. A fireplace is a stone or brick frame with a 1x2 opening, a campfire or netherrack as fire, and a chimney that rises through the roof. Keep wood out of the 4 blocks above a fire. Wood near fire burns. light light-plan. Light every room and the outside path at roughly one source every 6 to 8 blocks; hide sources in the structure (under carpets, in slabs, behind panes, in lamps) rather than torches stuck on walls. Dark corners spawn mobs and look dull. light-style. Match the light to the style: torches and campfires for rustic and medieval, glowstone, sea lanterns or redstone lamps for modern and underwater, shroomlight for the Nether, froglights for fantasy. terrain terrain-integrate. Fit the building to the ground: dig into slopes, step the foundation, never leave a flat square of grass at the foot. Add a path, a garden, a fence, hedges (leaves on a log), a well or a tree group of two or three trees. A building dropped on a lawn looks pasted. terrain-paths. Paths are 2 to 3 blocks wide, mix two or three path blocks (gravel, cobblestone, coarse dirt, andesite), wiggle slightly, and lead to the door. Village streets radiate from a centre (well, square) and buildings adapt to them. terrain-water. Water features need a rim: a fountain is a frame at least 5x5 with a column in the middle and a margin of 4 blocks around it; a cascade needs a barrier above its top and a trench at its foot; a pool is dug 1 deep everywhere first and deeper in zones. scale scale-reference. Reference sizes (width x height x depth): small starter house 7x5x7, medium house 11x6x9, large manor 17x8x15, barn 9x6x11, tower 5x12x5, bridge 5 wide with an arch every 7 blocks. Too small a building cannot hold detail. scale-hierarchy. In a settlement make landmarks bigger and taller, keep houses modest, leave open space between buildings, and keep industry away from homes. logic logic-materials. Choose blocks for what they would be in the world: stone or cobblestone for foundations, wood for frames and floors, brick or stone for chimneys and fireplaces, glass for windows, never glass or wool for a floor or a barn wall, never leaves or sand as walls. Illogical materials destroy believability faster than any other mistake. logic-fire. Wood, wool and carpet burn. Keep them away from fire, lava and campfires; use stone, brick or concrete around hearths. logic-loose. Dirt, grass, sand, gravel and snow are ground, not building blocks: they fall, can be carried off by endermen and read as unfinished. Use them for paths, gardens and terrain. logic-aging. Age follows story: new buildings use clean blocks, old ones add cracked and mossy variants, broken windows and vines, and overgrown ruins use mossy stone and holes. Add it deliberately and only where water and shade would put it. Common mistakes mistake fix Plain box: one block, smooth walls, flat roof. Break the footprint, add a pitched roof with an overhang, change materials by role and add relief. More than five materials. Reduce to a base, a secondary and one or two accents; use shades of the same family. Perfect symmetry on every face. Keep the plan ordered and add one or two deliberate off-centre elements. Wall one block thick with glass flush to it. Thicken to two or three where possible, recess glass one block and frame it. Flat roof with no edge, or a roof that is too big for the walls. Add a parapet or a pitched roof of 1 to 2 storeys, split big roofs into sections. Random scatter of cracked and mossy blocks. Group variants near the ground and corners, one block in ten. Glass, wool, dirt or sand where they are illogical. Use planks or stone for floors and walls; keep loose blocks for the ground. Torches on every wall. Hide light in the structure or use proper lamps; light the way to the door. Building pasted on a flat lawn. Dig into the slope, add a path, a plinth, hedges, trees and a garden. Too small to carry detail. Start from the reference sizes and scale up. Starting with the facade or with details. Footprint, masses, roof, palette, then relief and detail. Roof types roof use recipe gable The default pitched roof, two slopes meeting at a ridge; good up to about 12 blocks of span. Stairs on both long walls facing the ridge, shifted one block in and one up per layer; ridge block or two back-to-back stairs; fill the triangular end walls. Tool: build_plan kind=gable_roof. hip Slopes on all four sides; little attic volume; a pyramid on a square plan. Concentric rings of stairs facing inward, shrinking one block per layer, corner stairs shaped automatically; cap with a block or slab. Tool: build_plan kind=hip_roof. shed One slope, for lean-tos, porches and sheds. A single run of stairs all facing up the slope; tuck its high side against a wall. Tool: build_plan kind=shed_roof. flat Modern style only. A slab or block layer with a parapet one block high (or an edge of stairs or slabs of another material); light or cover it so mobs do not spawn. saltbox A gable with one slope much longer than the other, often over a rear lean-to. Two runs of different length; the long slope may be shallower. gambrel Barns and large volumes: steep lower slope, shallow upper slope. A steep run (2:1) then a gentle run (1:1 or 1:2); only above about 16x20. mansard Like a gambrel but on four sides, usually with dormers. Steep on all four sides to a shallow or flat top ringed by a parapet; needs a big plan. pyramid Towers and pavilions. Hip roof on a square plan up to a single block. cone Round towers. Disc layers shrinking one block of radius every one or two levels, edges of stairs or slabs. Tool: build_plan kind=cone. dome Domes, observatories, mosques. Upper half of a sphere layer by layer. Tool: build_plan kind=dome. thatch Rustic cottages. One uninterrupted steep slope in a single material (hay or yellow carpet); no valleys, eyebrow dormers only. Slope patterns Line patterns that approximate a slope: the run lengths repeat (1 is a 45 degree diagonal, 2 a slope of 1:2, 1, 2 one of 2:3). rise:run angle run lengths 1:1 45.0° 1 3:4 36.9° 1, 1, 2 2:3 33.7° 1, 2 3:5 31.0° 1, 2, 2 4:7 29.7° 1, 2, 2, 2 1:2 26.6° 2 2:5 21.8° 2, 3 1:3 18.4° 3 2:7 16.0° 3, 4 1:4 14.0° 4 Proportions what reference barn 9 x 6 x 11 with a gambrel or steep gable roof bridge 5 wide, an arch every 7 blocks building_floors storey 4-5 blocks; towns 2-4 storeys corridor_width 2 in a small house, 3-4 in a large one fountain_frame at least 5x5, margin of 4 around the column (3x3 column: 7x7 frame) gable_max_span about 12 blocks (15 for a barn look); beyond that use several roof sections light_spacing a light source about every 6-8 blocks manor 17 x 8 x 15 with wings; split the roof into sections above 15x15 medium_house 11 x 6 x 9 with a gable or hip roof path_width 2-3 blocks; village streets 3 roof_height 1 to 2 storeys; split above 5-7 blocks per section roof_overhang 1 block (2 for large roofs) room_height 3-4 in a house (2.5 with a slab ceiling), 4-5 small room, 5-6 medieval hall, 10-12 great hall starter_house 7 wide x 5 high x 7 deep (walls 4 high plus roof) tower 5 x 12 x 5; round towers 7 to 9 across with a conical roof wall_thickness 2-3 for stone, 1 for timber infill and interior partitions window_sill 1 to 2 blocks above the floor Furniture Built from shaped blocks the engine has. piece recipe table A fence post with a pressure plate on top (keep it off the wall so the fence does not connect), or two stairs back to back. long table A row of fence posts every 2 blocks with slabs on top, or slabs on a stair base at both ends. chair One stair facing the table (or a slab with trapdoor arms). sofa 2 to 4 stairs side by side facing the room, a stair turned inward at each end as arms. bookshelf wall Stacked bookshelves 2 to 3 high, a slab or trapdoor row as the top lip. cabinet A barrel (or bookshelf) with a trapdoor in front and one on top. lamp A fence with a torch on top, or a light block hidden under a carpet in the floor. counter A run of slabs or stairs of stone in front of a crafting table, furnace or smoker. hearth A stone or brick frame around a 1x2x1 opening with a campfire or netherrack, chimney to the roof. rug A 3x5 area of carpets in two colours with a border. shutter A trapdoor on each side of a window, opened flat against the wall. flower pot A trapdoor box around a block of dirt with a plant on top. Floor patterns: log and planks stripes (alternate rows) polished andesite and polished diorite chequer (kitchen, bathroom) two concretes in a chequer or concentric bands stone bricks mixed with a few cracked, mossy and cobblestone (cellar, ruin) smooth stone border around a central motif Limits of the block set Stairs, slabs, doors, trapdoors, fences, walls, panes, carpets, torches and ladders exist as shaped blocks (blockset shapes). Only about 38 materials have stairs and 40 have slabs: check the palette, not the vanilla list (no stairs for deepslate, tuff, mud brick, concrete, wool, cherry, bamboo, mangrove). There is no double slab: use the full block. No lantern, chain, candle, bed, sign, item frame, painting, chest, rail or crops; use glowstone, sea lanterns, redstone lamps, torches, barrels and bookshelves. Stair corners, fence, wall and pane connections are derived from the neighbours: never place corner states by hand. Orientable blocks (furnace, barrel, ...) always face +z (south). Stairs: facing is the direction you climb toward (the tall back is on that side). half=top flips them upside down (cornices, eaves). A bare name is the default state (facing north, bottom). Doors are two blocks (lower and upper half); use the bare name for the default state or name each half. Three programs ship with the engine: burrow (the project tool that drives the others), burrowplay (the game runner) and burrowedit (the editor). Flags may be written with one or two dashes. burrow <command> --help prints the same usage text as this page. burrow burrow <command> [flags] [args] . A Go game (root main.go importing burrow-engine/gogame) runs as "go run . -dir <dir>" instead; flags after -- go to it. Flags after -- go to burrowplay, e.g. burrow run -- -shot out.png -frames 60 or burrow run -- -headless -ticks 200 -hash flags: --validate enable the Vulkan validation layer (VK_LAYER_PATH is set) --no-scripts do not rebuild scripts first flag type default description -no-scripts bool skip building scripts -validate bool validation layer burrow edit Open a project in the editor (burrowedit). usage: burrow edit [dir] [--validate] [-- burrowedit flags] Opens the project in dir (default .) in the native editor (burrowedit -project). flag type default description -validate bool validation layer burrow serve Run a dedicated multiplayer server and print the join link. usage: burrow serve [dir | game.voxpak] [flags] Runs a dedicated multiplayer server for a project (docs/networking.md). The project must set runtime.plugins.net to true. The server listens with TLS 1.3 (a self-signed certificate created on first run in <user config dir>/burrow/server, private key mode 0600), checks that every client runs the same project, engine version and rules, and prints the join link: burrow://host:7777?fp=<certificate fingerprint>&key=<password> For a server that runs on a real machine (persistent world, autosave, bans, systemd or Docker), use the burrow-server executable instead (docs/dedicated-server.md). Give the link to the players (burrowplay -connect <link>, or the Hub). The key is the server password: treat the link as a secret. Without a password anyone who reaches the port can join. flags: --addr :7777 listen address --advertise host:p the address written in the link (default 127.0.0.1 and the listen port: pass your public name) --password text join key (default: a random one) --open no password --max-players N at most N players (default 16) --seed N world seed (every client must use the same project; the seed is pinned) flag type default description -addr string fmt.Sprintf(:%d, netplay.DefaultPort) listen address -advertise string address written in the join link -max-players int player limit -open bool no password -password string join key -seed uint world seed burrow build Pack a project into a single-file game or macOS .app. usage: burrow build [dir] -o <out> [--app] [--native|--wasm] [--target darwin-arm64] [--burrowplay path] [--no-default-textures] [--no-verify] [--json] burrow build [dir] --pak <file.voxpak> Packs the project into ONE self-contained executable: a copy of the prebuilt burrowplay with the game archive (.voxpak: vox.project, asset directories, scene, input map, world overlay, scripts; sorted, SHA-256 per file and overall) appended. ./game runs with no toolchain and no project directory. -o out output executable (default ./<project name>) --app write a macOS <out>.app bundle INSTEAD of the plain executable (Info.plist, MacOS/<exe>, Resources/game.voxpak, Frameworks/); the archive ships once, in Resources, and the bundle is ad-hoc signed once as a whole (codesign --verify --deep --strict passes); libvulkan.1.dylib and libMoltenVK.dylib (with an ICD manifest) are bundled when found in Homebrew with install_name_tool; otherwise the app needs Homebrew molten-vk and says so when it is missing. The app and the plain executable are ad-hoc signed (codesign -s -): they run on this Mac, but they are NOT notarised. The plain executable has the archive appended after the Mach-O, so strict code-signature validation and Gatekeeper need a proper Developer ID signature and notarisation (use --app for that). A copy downloaded by someone else carries the macOS quarantine flag and Gatekeeper blocks it ("cannot be opened because the developer cannot be verified"): the recipient clears it with xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine <app>, or you sign with a Developer ID (codesign --force --deep --options runtime -s "Developer ID Application: ..." <app>) and notarise (xcrun notarytool submit ... --wait; xcrun stapler staple <app>) --pak file write only the archive --target t only the native target is supported (darwin-arm64 on Apple silicon): burrowplay links cgo (GLFW, Cocoa) and MoltenVK, so cross-compiling needs the target's C toolchain and SDK --burrowplay path burrowplay binary to embed (default: next to Burrow, on PATH, or built from the checkout) --no-default-textures embed a burrowplay built with -tags novnr,nopp: the default block textures (Pixel Perfection CE, CC-BY-SA-4.0) are NOT bundled and blocks render flat. Needs the Burrow source checkout (go build); cannot be combined with --burrowplay. Without it, a game that bundles the default textures (runtime.texture_pack is not "none") gets their licence warning on stderr and in the build manifest --no-verify skip the load-and-run check before packing --native link the project's Go scripts into the game executable instead of shipping WebAssembly (like IL2CPP in Unity): faster, no .wasm in the archive, one executable. Compiles a player from the Burrow source checkout (BURROW_ROOT) with the Go toolchain; scripts then run without gas or a memory sandbox, and the editor/mods keep using wasm. burrow test --parity proves both runtimes simulate identically (docs/scripting/15-native.md). BURROW_BUILD_NATIVE=1 makes it the default. --wasm ship the scripts as WebAssembly in the archive (the default); the prebuilt burrowplay is used as is The build manifest <out>.build.json (also with --app: <out>.app plus <out>.build.json) records the pack hash, the texture bundling decision and the licence warning. flag type default description -app bool macOS .app bundle -burrowplay string burrowplay binary -native bool link the scripts natively -no-default-textures bool build burrowplay with -tags novnr,nopp (no embedded block textures) -no-verify bool skip verification -o string output -pak string write only the archive -target string target (native only) -wasm bool ship the scripts as WebAssembly burrow test Headless project check: load, run, replay, StateHash. usage: burrow test [dir] [--ticks N] [--runs N] [--parity] [--go-tests] [--json] Headless health check of the project in dir (default .). No window, no GPU: 1. load vox.project, the default scene, the world overlay and the input map 2. build stale scripts and verify every module the project lists 3. run N ticks (default 200) --runs times (default 3) with GOMAXPROCS = default, 1 and 8; the StateHash must be identical every time 4. check for failed commands and script faults, replay the journal and compare 5. with --go-tests only: run "go test ./..." in the project when it has its own _test.go files 6. with --parity only: link the project's scripts natively into a headless runner (the same linking as burrow build --native), run it for the same N ticks and require the very same StateHash as the WebAssembly run above; also runs the natives with BURROW_NATIVE_DEBUG=1, which faults any script that keeps state in package-level variables Prints the StateHash; exit 1 on any problem. Scene components Generated by make docs-gen from the source code. Do not edit this page by hand: change the code or its doc comments and regenerate. The scene schema registers 59 component types. A scene file stores each node's components by these names; the inspector, the editor_set_component tool and the script host functions entity_get_component / entity_set_component all use the same names and JSON fields. The default column is the zero value of the field's Go type, which is what a field takes when it is left out; where a component fills in a different value when it loads (the transform scale, for example) its description says so. Ranges are checked when a scene loads and by the inspector. Field types: bool , int , float , string , vec3 (three numbers), entity (a reference to another node) and object (a nested structure, edited as JSON). A project is a folder with a vox.project manifest (JSON). The sections below list every key. Keys under runtime configure burrowplay , the exported game and the editor's Play mode. Everything is additive: a missing key keeps the default in the description, and unknown keys are rejected with a message naming the valid ones. vox.project (top level) Project is the manifest. key type description schema int format int Format is FormatVersion (2): the content conventions of the project (opt-in plugins, the MagicaVoxel front, the environment components). Absent = a project from before them; burrow migrate converts it once and writes this field. name string engine string asset_dirs []string default_scene string input_map string scripts []string placeholder: script entry points icon string Icon is the game's icon: a PNG path relative to the project folder (default: none, the Burrow icon). It is the window icon at runtime and, in Windows exports, the exe icon (square, 256x256 recommended). settings map[string]json.RawMessage runtime *Runtime Runtime configures how burrowplay runs the project (additive; nil = defaults). runtime Runtime is the optional "runtime" section of vox.project: how the game runner (burrowplay) builds the app. Zero values select the defaults noted. key type description runtime.title string window title (default: project name) runtime.width int window width (1280) runtime.height int window height (720) runtime.radius int terrain load radius in chunk columns (8) runtime.mode string "fly" (default) or "walk" runtime.start *[3]float64 player start (feet); default above terrain at 0,0 runtime.yaw float64 start yaw, degrees runtime.pitch float64 start pitch, degrees runtime.player_prefab string PlayerPrefab is the prefab the player is spawned from when the scene has no game.mode: "builtin:player.prefab" (the default) or a project .prefab, usually a variant (an instance of the built-in one with overrides). runtime.seed uint64 world seed (default: the .voxworld seed, else 1) runtime.world string .voxworld overlay loaded at start runtime.texture_pack string TexturePack selects the block textures: "default" (embedded Pixel Perfection CE, may be absent), "pixelperfection" or "none" (flat colours). runtime.blocks string Blocks selects the block registry. "shapes" (the default, and the only supported registry) is the core blocks, the full-cube Minecraft block set of package blockset and the non-cubic shapes of package shape (slabs, stairs, plants, ...). New projects are created with "shapes" and "pixelperfection". runtime.custom_blocks string CustomBlocks is the project's own block file (JSON, project relative, e.g. "data/blocks.json"): its blocks are appended to the registry after every built-in block, in file order, and can carry textures, a palette entry and a right-click interaction (package blockset, Custom; docs/blocks.md "Project blocks"). Absent = no project blocks. runtime.block_packs []string BlockPacks enables optional block content packs on top of the neutral engine set, in order (blockset.PackNames: "minecraft" is the full Minecraft catalog, 338 full cubes and about 230 shaped items, which pairs with the "pixelperfection" textures). Ignored when BlockRegistry is set. Before 0.7 that catalog was built in, so burrow migrate enables it for older projects. runtime.block_registry string BlockRegistry is a project folder (e.g. "blocks") holding the project's own copy of the block registry: blocks.json and shapes.json in the format of the engine's block files, in id order. When set it REPLACES the engine's blocks and every pack, so the ids and properties of the project's blocks no longer depend on the engine version. burrow blocks export writes it and burrow new creates it; runtime.custom_blocks are still appended after it. See docs/blocks.md "Project registry". runtime.items string Items is the project's item registry file (JSON, project relative, e.g. "data/items.json"): the items scripts name and carry, with stable ids (package itemset, docs/items.md). Item 0 is the empty stack; the engine provides identity and stacks only, the mod writes recipes, inventories and dropped items. Absent = no items. runtime.script_limits *ScriptLimits ScriptLimits raises (or lowers) the limits of the scripting host for this project: gas per call, guest memory and the host call budgets, which a mod with thousands of machines needs more of. Render options Generated by make docs-gen from the source code. Do not edit this page by hand: change the code or its doc comments and regenerate. Set at the command line ( -shaders , -aa , -upscale , -render-scale , -rt ), in the runtime section of the project file, or live from the editor's View menu. Rendering is frame-domain only: none of these options changes the simulation or its StateHash . See rendering.md , anti-aliasing.md and ray-tracing.md . Shader levels -shaders off|low|medium|high|ultra (default medium , environment variable BURROW_SHADERS ). Level off is the classic renderer; the others render in HDR with tone mapping. Values per level: setting off low medium high ultra meaning HDR - yes yes yes yes HDR renders the world into an offscreen RGBA16F target and tone maps in a final post pass. AutoExposure - yes yes yes yes AutoExposure adapts the exposure slowly to the mean log luminance of the frame. Bloom - - yes yes yes Bloom is the mip-chain bloom: BloomLevels downsamples, BloomStrength added to the HDR colour, BloomThreshold/BloomKnee in exposed radiance units. BloomLevels - - 4 5 6 BloomStrength - - 0.07 0.08 0.09 BloomThreshold - - 1.1 1.1 1.1 BloomKnee - - 0.8 0.8 0.8 CloudSteps - 1 4 8 14 Clouds: 0 none, otherwise the number of ray-march steps through the cloud slab (1 = a flat 2D layer). CloudOctaves - 3 3 4 5 CloudOctaves is the number of noise octaves of the cloud density. CloudShadow - - yes yes yes CloudShadow lights the clouds with a second density tap toward the sun (self shadowing, silver lining). AO - - yes yes yes AO is the screen-space ambient occlusion pass (GTAO-style horizon search on the depth buffer, half resolution, depth aware blur): AOSlices directions with AOSte... AOSlices - - 2 3 4 AOSteps - - 5 6 8 AORadius - - 1.6 1.8 2 AOStrength - - 0.85 0.9 0.9 ShadowTaps - 8 12 16 24 ShadowTaps is the number of rotated-disk taps of the sun shadow filter (0 keeps the 3x3 box); ShadowSoft is the filter radius in shadow texels. ShadowSoft - 1.6 2 2.4 2.8 Stars - yes yes yes yes Stars draws the night stars. Aerial - yes yes yes yes Aerial blends distant terrain into the sky colour (atmospheric perspective) on top of the far-plane fog. Vignette - 0.12 0.14 0.15 0.16 Vignette is the corner darkening strength (0 none). Dither - yes yes yes yes Dither adds +-0.5/255 noise before the 8 bit quantisation (hides banding in the sky gradient). Refraction - yes yes yes yes Refraction copies the lit opaque scene (colour + linear depth) before the water pass so the water refracts the bottom with depth-based absorption, finds the rea... SSRSteps - - 16 24 40 SSRSteps is the number of screen-space reflection march steps on water (0: sky/atmosphere reflection only). WaveOctaves - 2 3 4 5 WaveOctaves is the number of procedural wave octaves of the water normal (wind and current driven). Caustics - - - yes yes Caustics adds the animated caustic pattern on the refracted bottom. Precip - 1500 3000 6000 10000 Precip is the maximum number of rain/snow streak instances (0: no particles); Wet enables wet surfaces and puddles. Wet - yes yes yes yes Sway - yes yes yes yes Sway moves leaves and cross plants with the wind in the vertex shader. GodRaySamples - - - 32 48 GodRaySamples is the number of radial samples of the screen-space sun shafts (0: off). DoF - - - - yes DoF and MotionBlur run the full-resolution depth of field / camera motion blur pass (off by default except ultra). MotionBlur - - - - yes DoF and MotionBlur run the full-resolution depth of field / camera motion blur pass (off by default except ultra). Distortion - - yes yes yes Distortion runs the air distortion pass (heat haze, shock waves; docs/rendering.md): medium and above. Custom - - - - - Custom marks a level changed setting by setting on top of its preset (WithGraphics); behaviour never depends on it. Anti-aliasing -aa off|fxaa|smaa|taa . off none, fxaa and smaa single-frame filters, taa temporal (game only: needs motion vectors). An empty value uses the shader level's preset. Upscalers -upscale off|fsr1|fsr2|dlss|xess . fsr1 spatial, fsr2 temporal, dlss and xess need vendor support and fall back with a log line. Combine with -render-scale ( native , quality , balanced , performance or a scale 0.5..1). Ray tracing -rt off|shadows|full|sun|ao|gi|reflections . shadows is sun shadows plus ambient occlusion, full adds global illumination and reflections, and sun , ao , gi , reflections combine with commas ( sun,reflections ). Needs hardware ray tracing support. Look presets -look natural|vivid|classic . Colour grading applied by the tone mapper.

Scripts are WebAssembly modules run by the deterministic scripting host. They talk to the engine through the host functions below (imported from the vox module; the module name predates the engine rename and is part of the ABI) and, for Go scripts, through the SDK that wraps them. The full execution model is in scripting.md . Host functions 137 rows from the ABI table ( script/ABI.md ). Pointers and lengths are i32 ; every function returns a value >= 0 or a negative error code ( -1 invalid, -2 memory, -3 not found, -4 buffer too small, -5 budget, -6 denied, -7 unavailable, -8 rejected, -9 limit). function signature result abi_version () -> i32 1 log (level, ptr, len) -> i32 0. level 0 debug .. 3 error; message cut at 1 KiB tick () -> i64 current fixed tick rand_u64 () -> i64 next value of the simulation RNG entity_self () -> i64 this script's entity event_from () -> i64 sender of the event being delivered last_required () -> i32 size needed after ERR_TOO_SMALL entity_exists (e i64) -> i32 1 / 0 entity_get_component (e i64, name_ptr, name_len, out_ptr, out_cap) -> i32 JSON length written (canonical, scene schema) entity_has_component (e i64, name_ptr, name_len) -> i32 1 / 0 entity_set_component (e i64, name_ptr, name_len, json_ptr, json_len) -> i32 0; validated against the schema immediately; the script component is DENIED (use state_set) entity_remove_component (e i64, name_ptr, name_len) -> i32 0 spawn (prefab_ptr, prefab_len, opts_ptr, opts_len) -> i64 handle usable in this call; node appears at commit. prefab "" = bare node, else a name from Plugin.Prefabs . opts JSON: {"name","parent","transform","components":{name:json}} despawn (e i64) -> i32 0; runs on_destroy hooks at commit find_by_name / find_by_path (ptr, len) -> i64 entity transform_get (e i64, out_ptr) -> i32 writes 9 x f32 LE: pos, rot (deg: pitch,yaw,roll), scale transform_set (e i64, in_ptr) -> i32 reads the same 36 bytes; NaN/Inf -> INVALID voxel_get (x, y, z i32) -> i32 block id voxel_set (x, y, z, id i32) -> i32 0; budgeted; id must be registered voxel_micro_res (x, y, z i32) -> i32 the resolution (2, 4, 8 or 16) of the micro-voxel brick in the cell as this call sees it, 0 for a plain block or air voxel_micro_get (x, y, z, n, mx, my, mz i32) -> i32 block id of micro voxel (mx, my, mz) of an n^3 grid (n = 2, 4, 8, 16) of the cell; a plain cell answers its block, a brick of another resolution is sampled. Sees this invocation's own writes voxel_micro_set (x, y, z, n, mx, my, mz, id i32) -> i32 0; budgeted (one voxel edit). Writes one micro voxel: a plain cell is subdivided into an n^3 brick first, a brick of another resolution is resampled; a brick that becomes one block collapses to it. Applied at commit through the rules of the micro_edit command voxel_micro_fill (x, y, z, n, x0, y0, z0, x1, y1, z1, id i32) -> i32 0; budgeted (one voxel edit plus one per 512 micro voxels). Fills the micro box [min, max) of the cell, clipped to the grid; id 0 carves light_at (x, y, z i32) -> i32 packed light r | g<<4 | b<<8 | sky<<12 (each 0..15) of the committed blocks, deterministic, see docs/lighting.md block_id_by_name (ptr, len) -> i32 id ("air" = 0) raycast (ox,oy,oz,dx,dy,dz,max f32, out_ptr) -> i32 1 hit / 0 miss. out (32 B): i32 x,y,z, nx,ny,nz, f32 dist, i32 block physics_raycast (ox..max f32, mask i32, out_ptr) -> i32 1 / 0. out (48 B): u64 entity (0 = terrain), i32 x,y,z, f32 point(3), normal(3), dist physics_overlap (minx..maxz f32 x6, mask, out_ptr, cap) -> i32 bodies found (may exceed cap). out: u64 flags (bit0 touches terrain), then <= cap u64 entities physics3d_raycast (ox..max f32, mask i32, out_ptr) -> i32 rigid bodies + voxels (needs plugin physics3d , else UNAVAILABLE ). 1 / 0. out (56 B): u64 entity (0 = terrain), u32 flags (bit0 terrain), i32 cell x,y,z, f32 point(3), normal(3), dist physics3d_overlap (minx..maxz f32 x6, mask, out_ptr, cap) -> i32 rigid bodies whose shapes overlap the box (needs plugin physics3d , else UNAVAILABLE ); bodies found (may exceed cap). out: u64 flags (bit0 touches terrain when mask has bit 31), then <= cap u64 entities, ascending. Mask 0 = every layer physics3d_apply_impulse (e i64, ix,iy,iz f32) -> i32 0. Momentum impulse on a dynamic body, applied next step, wakes it physics3d_body_get (e i64, out_ptr) -> i32 0. out (60 B): f32 pos(3), rot x,y,z,w, vel(3), angvel(3), u32 flags (bit0 sleeping, bit1 dynamic, bit2 kinematic), f32 inverse mass physics3d_water_at (x,y,z f32, out_ptr) -> i32 1 liquid / 0 none (needs plugin physics3d , else UNAVAILABLE ). Liquid at or up to 32 blocks below the point. out (24 B): f32 surface height (swell included), f32 depth of the point under it (negative above), f32 flow(3), u32 flags (bit0 under the surface) physics3d_remove_voxel (e i64, x,y,z i32) -> i32 1 removed / 0 empty cell. Voxel body cell; islands split next step input_action_value (name_ptr, name_len, out_ptr) -> i32 0; out: i32 x, i32 y in milli-units (1000 = 1.0) emit_event (target i64, kind i32, ptr, len) -> i32 0. target 0 = every script. Each group below is one source file of the SDK, listing its exported functions and methods with their doc comments; the types, constants and variables follow after. anim func AnimPlay(e Entity, clip string , o AnimPlayOpts) error AnimPlay starts clip on the entity's anim.player. Frame domain: it never changes simulation state, is not hashed or replayed, and is ignored by headless runs and servers. An unknown level returns INVALID. Use it for a graphics setting or to lower the quality in a heavy scene. func SetGraphics(name string , value float64 ) error SetGraphics changes one graphics setting at the next frame, on top of the shader level: "bloom", "ao", "god_rays", "cloud_steps", "shadow_taps", "ssr_steps", "dof", "motion_blur", "distortion", ... (docs/rendering.md lists them all with their ranges). A switch is 0 or 1 (see SetGraphicsOn). The setting stays when the level changes with SetShaders; ResetGraphics puts every setting back to the level's preset. Frame domain, like SetShaders. An unknown name or an out of range value returns INVALID. func SetGraphicsOn(name string , on bool ) error SetGraphicsOn turns a graphics switch ("bloom", "ao", "dof", "caustics"...) on or off. func ResetGraphics() error ResetGraphics puts every graphics setting back to the preset of the current shader level. func ReadWorldInfo() (WorldInfo, error ) ReadWorldInfo returns the world the game runs on.
