Water mesh. With an HDR level, VoxelWorld.SetWaterSurface makes the mesher leave the liquid blocks out of the cube mesh ( mesh.Opts.LiquidSurface ) and build Result.Liquid ( mesh.BuildLiquidSurface ): top faces with the corner heights of LiquidCornerHeights (flowing water slopes, no full cubes, no faces between two liquid cells), sides only toward open cells, bottoms over air. The fine water bricks ( mesh.Opts.FineWater , exported once per tick from the fluid state and re-meshed at most every 4 ticks per chunk) are appended; both use the mesh.FineVertex layout packed to 24 bytes ( waterStride , pipeline water2.vert ). On a block corner both meshes take the same height, so there is no crack. Falling fine water is carried by the automaton's streams (a debit per sub-column, no bricks in the air) and drawn from them ( mesh/cascade.go , see water-fine.md "Rendering"): a translucent curtain leaving the lip along the free-fall parabola, joined across lips, tapered and wobbling at its open ends, whose opacity, aeration and streak speed follow the debit and the fall (thin = glassy with the cliff refracted behind, thick = white), plus at the foot GPU-animated spray droplets, churning boils, rising mist and expanding foam rings on the water. Moving fine water re-meshes only the water of its chunks ( Mesher.BuildWater on the workers, UploadChunkWaterOnly ), and far chunks (> 96 blocks) draw their bricks as the coarse surface. Scene copy. When water is in view the HDR main pass is split: after the opaque terrain, sky and highlight, a full-screen pass copies the lit colour and the linear depth (alpha) into scene-copy (RGBA16F), then the pass resumes (load ops) for the water, glass, rain and hybrid transparents. The water writes alpha 1 and does its own compositing. Water shader ( water_hdr.frag , written from published descriptions, nothing copied): wave normals from octaves of travelling directional waves around the wind (deep-water dispersion), a slow domain warp, cross-current ripples along LiquidFlow / the fine Flow ; amplitude from the wind gust (calm water is nearly a mirror). Schlick Fresnel (F0 0.02). Reflection: screen-space ray march against the scene copy with a binary refinement and edge / distance fades, falling back to the sky model, a one-tap cloud layer and a normalised sun / moon glint. Refraction: the scene copy offset by the normal, Beer-Lambert absorption over the real path to the bottom (screen depth), in-scattering lit by the sky and the sun (shadowed). Caustics (high+): an animated ridged-noise pattern on the bottom, fading with depth. Foam: shore (the depth difference, i.e. the real distance to the bottom), current speed, the fine-water foam attribute and falling sheets (the shore fringe is subtle). Seen from below: Snell's window with total internal reflection, then the under-water fog. Look, after the Minecraft shader packs: the absorption is tinted by the biome / registry colour (low saturation: a swamp goes green, the default stays clear; red is absorbed first), the in-scattering is a teal in the shallows and a deep blue in the depth, the sky mirrored in the water is occluded under cliffs and canopies ( skyVis ), and the sun glint is GGX (sharp when calm, long tails in a breeze, shadowed by the sun shadow map). water.glsl (low / classic path) shares the palette and the sky occlusion. The classic render/soft renderer applies the same per-channel depth absorption (deep water is darker and bluer). Water level. Like vanilla, a free liquid surface stands below the block top: voxel.LiquidSurfaceFrac = 8/9 for a source, level/8 * 8/9 for flowing levels; a cell with liquid directly above stays full (1), so columns are continuous. LiquidTable.SurfaceHeight , SurfaceCorners ( mesh.LiquidCornerHeights ), BlockCornerHeight and LocalSurfaceHeight are the drawn surface: the coarse mesh, the fine-water bricks ( column scales a free column the same way, so both meet at a block corner), the terrace drop (to the lower surface, one block down minus 1/9) and the cascade lip / impact read them, and engine.HeadUnderWater compares the eye with it. Height , Submerged , LocalHeight , Sample (swimming, buoyancy, the simulation and its hash) keep the full cell. The classic cube water keeps its own 0.06..0.1 dip ( water.vert ). Under water. FrameState.HeadUnder (or, for free cameras and the editor, the eye inside a liquid surface: engine.HeadUnderWater ) fades every HDR surface and the sky into the water colour ( underwaterFog , per-channel extinction). Weather ( render.WeatherFX , filled by the weather plugin once per frame from weather.Res and State.At(camera) , weather.RenderFX ): cloud cover from State.Cover when -clouds is auto (the flag keeps priority), overcast clouds with fewer march steps, the sun scaled by SkyLightFactor , fog / humidity / precipitation thicken the aerial perspective, the sky follows the weather clock ( scene.NewSky(Clock) ), cloud drift integrates the wind. Rain and snow: instanced camera-relative streaks / flakes ( precip.vert , no vertex buffer, at most Precip instances scaled by the intensity), slanted by the wind, removed under a roof, a canopy or in a cave by the precipitation height map (64 m around the camera at every voxel size: 64 x 64 columns at 1 voxel per metre, up to 256 x 256 texels of several voxels, top of the highest solid or opaque block, engine.PrecipMapUnit , Renderer.SetPrecipMapGrid , set 2 binding 3). Lightning: FlashAt adds a cold fill light to the ambient and the sky; a jagged bolt is drawn in the sky at the strike bearing. Wet surfaces ( Wetness , open faces only by the same height map): darker porous albedo, glossier, puddles on flat tops (noise mask) that mirror the sky, raindrop rings while it rains. Wind sway: leaves and cross / tall plants ( vulkan.Options.Sway , flag in the tint byte, anchored at the ground for plants), deterministic in the frame tick. Atmosphere. Sun shafts (high+): half-resolution radial samples toward the sun over the sky mask of the depth buffer, added in the composite with the sun colour. DoF + motion blur (ultra only): one full-resolution pass, a 12-tap disk for the far field beyond 1.6x the focus distance (screen centre) and camera motion blur by reprojection with the previous view-projection (8 taps). TAA (not part of S3, added later, see anti-aliasing.md ): the SSR uses no per-frame jitter (fixed steps plus a binary refinement, faded at the edges), the AO is already blurred, and the remaining shimmer (far ripples, rain streaks) fades with distance; a history buffer would cost a pass and ghost the rain for no visible gain. Capture aids. examples/voxel_sandbox : -weather type[:intensity] (frozen front and clock, clock = -tick ), -wind deg:speed , -fluid off|coarse|fine , -demo waterfall|rill|sheet|breach ; BURROW_LIGHTNING= forces a bolt at that bearing (the real strikes are random and the shot freezes the sim). Budget (M2 Max, 2560x1440, radius 12, no validation, camera 172,25,250 facing a lake, storm 1.0 with wind 14 m/s and a forced bolt, GPU ms; the opaque half includes sky and clouds): off 2.4; low 5.6 (main 4.8, water half 1.1, post 0.6); medium 5.5 (main 4.5, water half 1.2, post 0.9); high 7.0 (main 6.0, scene copy 0.06, water half 1.4, post 0.9, sun shafts 0.02); ultra 8.9 (main 7.3, scene copy 0.05, water half 1.9, post 1.4, DoF + motion blur 0.33). Clear sky, same view: medium 5.5, ultra 9.9. All below 16.6 ms. Before capping the overcast cloud steps, ultra in a storm measured 13.5-15.4 ms. Water artefacts found. The line of small blue blocks across the river ( img/worldgen-meadow-shapes.png ) and the dark horizontal bands ( img/worldgen-river.png ) are generator terraces: worldgen/terrain2.go sets the river level per column to floor(sea + (hb - sea) / 2) , so the level drops by one block along level lines of the base height (65 steps in x 0..140, z -200..0 of seed 1). The base water never flows, so a one-block wall of source water stands across the river; the old cube water drew its side faces (and faces between different liquid ids) as translucent walls. The renderer now turns such a step into a short ramp ( BuildLiquidSurface pulls the corners next to an open cell standing on a full liquid cell down to that lower surface) with a little foam. The fix belongs in the generator (not changed here): make the river level monotone and constant along a river segment (for example quantise Lr along the river axis, or take the minimum of the neighbouring columns' levels), or place water_7..1 along the step so the surface slopes. Swell. With a swell ( runtime.plugins.swell , package swell , physics.md ) the smooth water surface rides three travelling waves: water2.vert lifts the top vertices and the upper edge of the sides (the pack marks them with the alpha of the vertex colour, waveWeights ; a zero-depth corner of a shore stays put), water_hdr.frag and water.glsl tilt the normal by the slope of the swell, and the eye under the surface follows it. The scene UBO carries the amplitude, wavelength, heading and the time phase of each wave in floats 224..231 ( S.swellA , S.swellB , shaders/swell.glsl ). The classic cube water does not move (its greedy quads would crack). BURROW_SWELL=amp,length,dir forces a swell for captures. Limits. SSR only finds what is on screen (the fallback is the sky); the clouds in reflections are a one-tap layer; no snow cover or ice; the shadow pass does not sway the leaves; the precipitation map is centred on the camera (64 blocks), beyond it every face counts as open; water lit by block light uses no per-vertex light (the fine vertex has no slot); the cascade's spray, boils and rings are drawn after the scene copy, so the water surface's SSR does not reflect them (nor the curtain). Flowing water ( water_1 .. water_7 , water-physics.md ) is ordinary blocks; mesh.LiquidHeight/LiquidCornerHeights/LiquidFlow give a renderer the surface height, smooth corner heights and flow direction of a water cell. Environment overrides of the sky ( scene.SkyLook ) The environment components ( env.sky , env.sun , env.fog , env.post ; fields and blending in lighting.md ) reach the renderers as engine.EnvState . The part that overrides what the clock computes is a renderer-neutral scene.SkyLook (zenith, horizon and fog colours, sun tint, fixed sun direction, stars off, bloom offset): vulkan.Renderer.SetEnvLook and soft.Renderer.Env take it, the zero value changes nothing. The grade (exposure, saturation, contrast, sun gain), clouds, shadows and fog density go through SetLook , SetCloudCover , SetShadows and WeatherFX.Fog as before. engine.envApplier (game) and engine.EnvApplier (editor viewport) push it once per change. Bloom: the post pass multiplies its strength by 1 + bloom (levels with bloom only). Stars: the star visibility of the atmosphere is zeroed. Sun tint and fixed direction: applied to the light the frame computes ( SkyLook.Light , SkyLook.Atmo ); a fixed direction replaces the clock sky by the one whose sun stands at the same elevation ( SkyLook.Sky ) so transmittance, twilight and ambient fit it. Sky and fog colours at the HDR levels: the procedural atmosphere ( shaders/atmo.glsl ) mixes atmoSky toward the given colours (display values, converted to linear radiance with gain 1.6) with the weights carried in the w of the horizon and zenith vectors of the scene uniform, and fogSky returns the fog colour carried in the w of camFwd , camRight and camUp (all zero = the sky). These components were unused; the uniform layout is unchanged. At the classic level the colours replace the sky gradient ends and the fog fades to the (fog or horizon) colour. Tests: scene ( TestSkyLookFixedSun ), render/soft ( TestEnvLookChangesImage ), and render/vulkan envLookChecks in the GPU suite ( BURROW_GPU=1 , BURROW_GPU_ONLY=env for just these): each field must move the image, and resetting the look must bring the base image back. Air distortion Heat haze above lava, fire and torches, shimmering volumes and shock waves, on the HDR levels medium and up ( render.ShaderQuality.Distortion ; off at low , in the classic pipeline and in the soft renderer, which ignores it). Frame domain only: nothing here reads or writes simulation state, the StateHash of a run is the same with and without the effect (the one exception is registering the fx.distortion component, which is opt-in like every component, see below). Passes ( render/vulkan/distort.go , shaders distort*.vert/frag , particle_dist.frag ). When a frame has sources, three post passes run right after the main pass, before anything else samples the HDR colour (TAA / FSR 2, DoF and motion blur, bloom, exposure, tone mapping): distort-map draws every source into a half-resolution RGBA16F buffer as a screen-space UV offset (one instanced soft volume per source, additive blending, fragments behind opaque geometry dropped by sampling the main depth); distort-apply offsets the HDR colour by that buffer into a scratch image; distort-copy copies it back, alpha kept. No source in view: no pass runs and nothing is drawn. The three passes appear by name in GPUTimes.Post ( vulkan.Stats().GPU.Post ), so they are in the per-pass GPU timings of the perf stats; the buffers are a half-resolution and a full-resolution RGBA16F image (about 20 MB at 1080p), allocated only at the levels that have the effect. Depth aware. distort-apply compares the depth of the pixel with the depth of the offset sample and fades the offset out when the sample is nearer (up to 0.6 blocks): a foreground object is never smeared into the background. The offset fades to zero within 5% of the screen edges (no samples from outside the image), and every source fades with distance (full near, gone past 112 blocks). Water. When the scene copy was taken this frame (water, glass or precipitation in view), pixels where water or glass lies in front of the opaque scene (the copy's depth differs from the depth buffer) are left alone: the water already refracts, no double distortion. Sources. (a) Hot blocks : voxel.Block.HeatLevel() (0..15; the block's heat field, else a default by name: lava 15, fire 12, campfire 10, magma 5, lit furnaces 6-8, torches 3). distortion.HeatScanner scans the loaded chunks within 3 chunks of the camera once per chunk version (the same cheap Chunk.Each scan as the torch fire effects), merges the hot cells into 4x8x4 buckets per chunk and HeatSources turns the nearest 48 into rising columns (height 1.2 to 5 blocks, strength 0.3 to 1.2 by heat). The columns are owned by an fx.heat entity ( scene.FxHeat : strength multiplier, disabled ; the Environment node of new projects carries one, found by a scene tree scan): none, no heat. runtime.distortion stays the global quality switch and multiplier. Projects whose scenes never mention fx.heat (and packed games) keep the always-on heat until a scene gets an fx.heat entity. (b) the fx.distortion scene component. (c) particle emitters with distortion ( particles.md ). (d) shock waves: expanding rings emitted by an entity ( fx_shockwave(entity, offset...) , centred on its position plus the offset; a wave from the simulation without an entity is dropped; distplug.Distortion.Shockwave is the host-code form with an absolute position), at most 16 alive. At most render.MaxDistortionSources (128) volumes per frame. fx.distortion ( distortion.Component ): shape ( sphere , box ), size (diameter or box sides, blocks), strength (1 is up to about 14 px at 1080p near the camera), speed , scale (ripple frequency), rise (how fast the pattern travels up; heat uses 1), disabled . Zero values mean the default (strength, speed, scale 1; size 2). It is schema-driven, so the inspector edits it, editor_set_component / entity_get_component and the Go SDK accessors ( FxDistortionStrength , ...) work. It changes the registry hash, so it is registered only when runtime.plugins.distortion is true or a scene or prefab of the project mentions it (the editor always registers it); projects that never use it keep their hashes. Settings. runtime.distortion in vox.project : true / "on" (default), false / "off" , or a strength multiplier 0..4 (JSON number or string). burrowplay -distortion off|on| overrides it. runtime.plugins.distortion: false removes the plugin altogether. Limits. The CPU renderer ( render/soft , headless screenshots) draws no distortion (distortion-only particles are skipped). The offset is not written to the TAA velocity buffer, so under heavy TAA / FSR 2 the shimmer is smoothed by the temporal history; translucent glass drawn before the passes is distorted with the rest of the frame. Heat columns are anchored to the top of the hottest cell of a bucket (lava lakes merge into 4 x 4 blocks patches); a lit furnace needs a block whose name or heat says so (the engine has no furnace state). Anti-aliasing and upscaling FXAA, SMAA 1x, TAA (Halton jitter, velocity buffer, YCoCg variance clipping, reactive mask), FSR 1 and FSR 2 on the HDR levels, -aa off|fxaa|smaa|taa , -upscale off|fsr1|fsr2 , -render-scale native|quality|balanced|performance|0.5..1 , a pluggable vulkan.Upscaler (DLSS and XeSS stubs: their SDKs are not bundled), HUD composited at native resolution after the upscale, no-op on the soft backend. The shader level picks the default (low fxaa, medium smaa, high and ultra taa). Everything is in anti-aliasing.md . Materials and custom shaders A draw with Material.Shader set uses a user vertex/fragment pair on the Scene3D contract ( shaders/scene3d.glsl ): sets 0 (scene), 1 (texture slot 0), 2 (frame) as for the built-in meshes, plus set 3 ( render/vulkan/matblock.go ): bindings 0..2 are the textures of material slots 1..3 and binding 3 is a 64-byte dynamic uniform with the 16 material floats of the draw. rworld.Material.Ext carries floats 4..15 and the slot 1..3 textures from a resolved material asset ( shadersys.Resolve ). Pipelines of built-in modules are rebuilt when a project shader override is applied or removed ( render/vulkan/shaderreload.go , also the anti-aliasing, upscaling, particle and ray-tracing passes); a material shader's pipelines follow its asset version, and a material with a displacing vertex stage or a discard also draws with its own stages in the shadow and velocity passes. See materials.md and assets.md .

Replication Burrow multiplayer is server-authoritative replication : the server alone runs the simulation and streams to each client the part of the state it needs, the chunks and entities around its player. There is one network model; every way of playing online ( burrow serve , burrow-server , the lobby, the editor's host session, join links) uses it. The shared parts (transports, handshake, authentication, identity, whitelist, rate limits) are described in Networking . Contents The model What runs where Interest management Replicated state Component visibility Dedicated server saves Protocol Bandwidth budget Client inputs, prediction and reconciliation Proximity chat Using the API Security Limits Measurements How it is tested What is not covered The model sequenceDiagram participant A as Client A (near) participant B as Client B (far) participant S as Server A->>S: Input (set_block, net_player_input) Note over S: applies the commands, runs the fixed tick,
scans what changed, builds one frame per client S->>A: RepFrame (chunk delta, entity updates) S->>B: RepFrame (only its own surroundings) A->>S: RepAck The server is authoritative. It applies the clients' commands (the whitelist of Networking ) and runs every fixed system: scripts, physics, water, block logic, weather. After every tick it scans the simulation once ( tracker ): each overlay chunk, each component value of each entity and each replicated extra state gets a version that changes with its content. For every client it compares those versions with what that client holds and builds one frame of what changed inside the client's interest, nearest first, within the client's bandwidth budget. The client writes the frame into its copy of the simulation and runs only frame stages on it. Nothing is deterministic on the client side and nothing has to be: the client never steps its simulation, its StateHash and journal are meaningless, there is no desync and no resync. What runs where server client fixed systems (scripts, physics, water, block logic, weather) yes no (the app is in manual step mode and never calls StepFixed ) frame stages (input, UI, audio, particles, rendering, the voxel streamer and mesher) yes (headless: no window) yes, on the replicated copy command validation (whitelist, rate limits, the commands' own checks) yes no base terrain generation yes yes (same seed and generator, pinned) overlay chunks (edits) owner copy, within the view distance entities and components owner copy, within the view distance local prediction no yes (frame domain) The base terrain is never sent: both sides generate it from the pinned seed and generator. Only the overlay (the chunks edited since the world was generated, which is what a snapshot stores) is replicated. The voxel streamer remeshes on the client exactly as after a local edit: App.ApplyReplica sends a CommandsApplied event after every frame and the mesher compares chunk versions. Interest management Each client has an interest center , in voxels. The authoritative position comes first: replica.ServerConfig.PlayerPos(engine, player) , the game's own rule; the player's avatar : the entity named avatar_ ( scene.name ) or tagged avatar_ or player: ( tags ), lowest entity index first ( replica.FindAvatar ). The multiplayer template's avatars script names and tags its avatars so: its servers are authoritative out of the box. Only when the game declares neither does the server use the view the client reports ( RepView , the camera position; netplay sends the voxel streamer's focus). That view moves at most ViewSpeed voxels per second (128) from the last accepted position and is held within ViewLeash voxels (256) of the player's last authoritative position, or else of its registry spawn point ( net_player_spawn ). Without any of them it is only speed limited; without a view, the center is the spawn point, else the origin. A game without avatars that wants the leash calls net_player_spawn . The interest is the chunks within View chunks horizontally (a disc, default 8, at most 32) and Vertical chunks vertically (default 4) of the center's chunk, and the entities and fine water inside. Leaving uses one chunk of hysteresis so a player walking on a border does not make chunks flicker. Replicated state What is replicated is a registry of names ( replica.Policy ); what is not listed is server-only. Components : every registered component except those in Policy.ServerOnly (the default keeps script , script.input on the server: clients do not run scripts, and script State is private; see Component visibility ). A component travels through its snapshot encoding (JSON), unless it has a codec : then, while the rest of the value (its cold part) is unchanged, only its hot fields travel, quantized, as a per-field delta against the value the client holds. See Component codecs . Extra states ( sim.Extra ): only those in Policy.Extras , each with a check interval and an optional encoder. The default replicates the player registry net.players through netsim.PublicState (the registry without the players' inputs, so it changes on joins, leaves and spawns, not on every input), the lobby net.lobby and the weather . Fluid state, block logic, animation libraries and the engine's fixed resources stay on the server. Fine water ( fluid.Config.Fine , runtime.plugins.fine_water ): the bricks of sub-cell water, which live in the fluid state outside the chunks. The server exports them once per tick, groups them by chunk and versions each chunk; a client receives the chunks of its interest whole, then as brick deltas (the bricks that changed and the cells that lost theirs), under the same budget as the voxels, and drops them when they leave its interest. The client draws them through its own voxel.FineSource , which the voxel streamer meshes like local fine water. Falling streams ( FineGrid.Streams ) are not replicated: a fall shows once its water lands. Chunks : the overlay chunks, sent whole on enter (deflate of voxel.Chunk.MarshalBinary , compressed once per version and shared by every client) and then as per-edit deltas (the voxels that changed between the version a client holds and the new one; more than 1024 edits and the whole chunk is cheaper). A removed overlay chunk is sent as base : the client shows the generated terrain again. Component codecs replica.RegisterCodec(name, replica.NewCodec[T](version, fields, hot, set)) gives a component a compact binary form: hot quantizes its hot fields into at most 64 integers, set writes them back; the rest of the value is its cold part. When the cold part changes the value travels as JSON followed by its hot fields whole (the baseline); otherwise only the hot fields travel, whole ( CompFull , zigzag varints) or as a delta from the version the client holds ( CompDelta : a varint mask of the changed fields, then their differences). The codec versions are announced in RepSchema and must match on the client. Built in: component hot fields quantization transform position, Euler rotation, scale (9) 1/256 voxel, 1/100 degree, 1/1024 physics3d.rigidbody position, rotation, velocity, angular velocity, sleeping (14) 1/256 voxel, smallest-three quaternion (15 bits per component), 1/256 voxel/s, 1/1024 rad/s A walking entity costs a few bytes per tick instead of about 70 bytes of JSON. Policy.NoCodecs sends JSON only. Versions are per item, not per client: one scan per tick, shared encodings, and per client only a version number per held chunk and entity. A component changes when its HashBytes changes (the same encoding as the state hash). Component visibility Clients do not run scripts, so a game's script State (the script component) never reaches them. Anything a client must show or read (inventory, furnace contents, skills, health) must live in a component , written by the script or a native system and replicated. Rule of thumb: keep client-visible state in components, not in script State. By default a replicated component goes to every client that holds the entity. A game narrows that per component with a visibility rule : rule who receives the value VisAll (default) every client that holds the entity replica.Owner ( VisOwner ) only the player that owns the entity replica.Nearby(r) ( VisNearby ) only clients whose interest center is within r voxels of the entity // next to the registration of the component, in the plugin that owns it (server and clients alike) sim.RegisterComponent[Inventory](e, "game.inventory" ) replica.RegisterVisibility( "game.inventory" , replica.Owner) replica.RegisterVisibility( "game.nameplate" , replica.Nearby( 24 )) // or per server: replica.ServerConfig{Policy: &replica.Policy{Visibility: map[string]replica.Visibility{...}}} The owner of an entity is the player named by the entity itself: a node named avatar_ , or an entity tagged avatar_ , player: or owner: ( tags ). Put the inventory component on the player's avatar, or tag a pet, a chest or a furnace owner: . An entity with no owner is owned by nobody, so an owner-only component on it is sent to no client. The entity and its other components stay visible to everyone in range; only the restricted component is withheld. Restricted values are never sent, so a modified client cannot read them. Visibility is re-evaluated every tick even when no value changes: a client that comes within r voxels, or an entity that changes owner, makes the server send the whole value; a client that moves away or loses the entity gets the component removed. The component is whole in the simulation and the saves: the rule changes the replication only. A script keeps its working data in State if it likes, but must write what clients show into the component each time it changes. Dedicated server saves A dedicated server restores its saved world on start. When the game changed since the save: a component the game gained is added empty , with a log line (always safe); a component the game lost (removed or renamed) would lose data: the server refuses to start and names each component with its number of values ( the saved world holds component data the game no longer has: game.mana (14 values) ). Restore the previous name, set "migrate": true in server.json to drop that data (the previous save stays in world/backups ), or move the world directory away for a new world; a plugin turned on or off (lobby, weather, fluid: a fixed resource state) cannot be converted; the error names it. Protocol The replicated model uses the transports and the handshake of Networking unchanged (Hello, Challenge, Auth, Welcome, Reject, Ping, Pong, Chat, ChatMsg, Kick, Bye, Input), protocol version 3. The Challenge flag 4 ( FlagReplicated ) announces the model. After the Welcome (whose snapshot fields are unused) the server sends one RepSchema , then one RepFrame (or RepFrameZ ) after every tick. sv is a zigzag varint (minimal encoding), pos three sv chunk coordinates within ±2^26. type name direction fields 0x70 RepSchema S→C uv tick length (µs), u8 view, u8 vertical, uv count (≤256) of component names, uv count (≤64) of extra names ( str ≤64 printable ASCII, unique), uv count of codecs, each uv component index (increasing) and u8 codec version 0x71 RepFrame S→C uv seq (from 1, +1 per frame), uv server tick, uv input ack, leaves ( uv count ≤4096, pos each), chunks ( uv count ≤4096, then pos , uv version, u8 kind: 0 full + bytes ≤128 KiB, 1 delta + uv from version + uv count ≤4096 of ( uv index ≤32767, uv block ≤65535), 2 base), despawns ( uv count ≤8192, uv entity), entities ( uv count ≤8192, then uv entity, uv count ≤256 of ( uv component index, u8 encoding: 0 JSON, 1 hot fields whole, 2 hot fields delta, bytes ≤64 KiB), uv count ≤256 of removed component indexes), extras ( uv count ≤64 of ( uv index, bytes ≤512 KiB)), fine water ( uv count ≤1024, then pos , uv version, u8 kind: 0 full, 1 delta, 2 drop; for 0 and 1 u8 N (2, 4 or 8), for 1 uv from version, uv count ≤4096 of ( uv cell ≤32767, N³ fill bytes ≤32), for 1 uv count ≤4096 of removed cells) 0x72 RepAck C→S uv last frame applied 0x73 RepView C→S three sv camera coordinates in thousandths of a voxel (±2^40) 0x74 RepFrameZ S→C uv raw size (≤1 MiB), bytes deflate of a whole RepFrame message (type byte included) 0x80 VoiceUp C→S bytes voice frame (1..256) 0x81 VoiceDown S→C uv speaker, bytes voice frame (1..256) 0x82 VoiceBlock C→S uv player, bool blocked The voice messages are shared with the other messages ( Networking , Voice chat ): the replicated server routes them on the interest centers and never lets them into a frame or the bandwidth budget. An entity is its 64-bit ECS handle (slot index and generation); the client mirrors the server's ids ( ecs.World.Revive ), so references between components stay valid. Within a frame, leaves and despawns apply first, then chunks, entity updates (an update of an unknown entity spawns it) and extras. The server keeps every frame under 960 KiB and compresses it ( RepFrameZ ) when that is smaller; JSON components compress about 3.5 times. Frames ride the reliable, ordered stream: a delta is computed against the version the server last sent to that client, which the client is guaranteed to have applied before the next frame. The acknowledgements are flow control: the server pauses a client's stream (it sends nothing and keeps the pending work) while MaxUnacked frames (40, two seconds) are unacknowledged or its send window is full, and resumes with the current state, not a backlog. Bandwidth budget Every client has a token bucket of BytesPerSecond (256 KiB/s by default, burst half a second) on the bytes actually sent (compression is refunded). Each tick the server sorts the pending items of a client and adds them until the budget or the frame size is spent; the rest waits: entities without a position first, then by distance to the interest center; an entity update that has waited age ticks has its distance divided by 1 + age² , so under a saturated budget far entities still move, less often; chunks and fine water chunks by distance (the chunk under the player first). Deltas and leaves are small; extra states are sent outside the budget (they are few and checked at most once per interval). A client never holds more than MaxEntities entities (2048). Client inputs, prediction and reconciliation Clients send Input messages with the whitelist ( net_player_input , set_block , fill_box , fill_sphere , block_use , gameui_event , the lobby_* kinds) and rate limits; the target tick is ignored. The server applies at most MaxCmdsPerTick commands per player per tick, in order, before the tick; server-only kinds ( net_player_join , net_player_leave , net_player_spawn ) are refused. Every frame carries the sequence number of the last Input the server applied for that client. The client keeps its sent commands in a prediction ring ( netbase.Pending ) and replica.ClientConfig.OnReconcile(tick, pending) runs after every frame with the commands still unapplied. Smoothing and prediction replica.Smoother (installed by netplay for a replicated guest; GuestOptions.NoSmoothing turns it off) works in the frame domain only: a PostUpdate system after scene.hierarchy recomputes the world transforms over replica.SmoothNodes (the replicated node tree with overriding local transforms). The replicated simulation is never written, so what the server sends stays exact. Remote entities are drawn Delay (100 ms, GuestOptions.InterpDelay ) behind a smoothed estimate of the server clock (the frames' arrival times, filtered so jitter does not show), interpolated between the two replicated transforms around that time (positions and scales linearly, angles along the shortest arc). Past the newest sample, when frames are late, the motion is extrapolated for at most MaxExtrapolate (250 ms), then held. The local avatar ( FindAvatar of the local player) is predicted: the unacknowledged inputs are replayed with a PredictFunc on top of the replicated avatar after every frame. The misprediction is the prediction made for the last input the server applied minus where the server actually put the avatar: a correct prediction gives no correction whatever the latency; an error is blended away over Correction (100 ms) and snapped beyond Snap (4 voxels: a teleport). The server's movement code runs in its scripts (WebAssembly in the simulation), which the frame domain cannot call, so the game provides the PredictFunc ( GuestOptions.Predict ); the default, replica.TemplatePredict , mirrors the walk of the multiplayer template's avatars script (4.317 voxels per second along the input yaw, ×1.3 with the sprint button 21). Vertical motion (gravity, jumps, steps) is left to the corrections. Root-motion dashes are predicted by wrapping the predictor: replica.RootPredict(base, root) runs base , then adds the local-space velocity returned by the RootFunc for that input step (a clip's root.move sampled at a time the game derives from the input), rotated by the input yaw exactly as the animation system does; ok == false leaves the step to base . Proximity chat runtime.proximity_chat (a radius in voxels; HostOptions.ChatRange ) makes chat local: a player's line reaches only the players within that distance, measured between interest centers ( replica.ServerConfig.ChatRange ). Lines of the server reach everyone, the sender always gets its own line, and the host's chat log ( OnChat ) sees every line. The server also takes a generic ChatFilter(from, to) hook. This is text chat; voice chat uses the same server-side positions ( Voice chat ). Using the API // server (a dedicated server, or a listen server polled from the game loop) srv, err := replica.NewServer(replica.ServerConfig{Sim: &netapp.AppSim{A: app}, Listener: ln, Pins: pins, Password: key, Whitelist: netplay.WhitelistFor(), View: 8 , BytesPerSecond: 256 << 10 }) for { srv.Poll(time.Now()); app.Frame(dt) } // client c, err := replica.Connect(ctx, addr, netbase.ConnectOptions{Fingerprint: fp}, replica.ClientConfig{Target: app, Pins: pins, Name: "ana" }) for { c.SetView(camX, camY, camZ); c.Poll(time.Now()); app.Frame(dt) } internal/netplay does all of this: Host.Srv is the netplay.Server interface (the host API of *replica.Server : Submit , SubmitAs , AddLocalPlayer , Kick , Chat , Peers , Tick , Close ), Guest.Client the *replica.Client . The hooks of the dedicated server ( AllowConnect , AllowJoin , PlayerID , RequireIdentity , OnPlayerJoin ) are HostOptions fields. replica.Server.Metrics and Clients report the scan size and time, chunk and entity counts and the frame bytes of every client. Security The threat model is that of Networking : clients are hostile, the server is trusted. The handshake, the authentication lockout, the identity, the whitelist, the per-kind command rates, the message and byte rates and the violation budget are the shared code of net/gate . Specific to this model: Information. A client receives only its interest: it cannot see chunks, entities or fine water beyond its view distance (no wallhack beyond it, no world download). With an authoritative position ( PlayerPos or an avatar) the center is the server's and the client's view is ignored; a client-reported view moves at ViewSpeed at most and stays within ViewLeash of the player's authoritative or spawn position. Server-only components and extra states are never sent. Forged acknowledgements. An ack beyond the last frame sent or going backwards is a violation; too many kick the client. Acks only gate the stream, so a lying client can only slow its own stream down. Floods. Inputs, views, acks and chat are counted by the message and byte buckets; commands by the whitelist rates; pending commands are bounded per client. Memory per client is bounded: held chunks by the view distance, entities by MaxEntities , pending commands by MaxPendingCmds , queued bytes by the transport's send window (the stream pauses instead of queuing). Hostile server (client side): decoders are strict and bounded (fuzzed), inflation is bounded (a chunk to 70 KiB, a frame to its announced size within 1 MiB), block ids are checked against the registry, entity slots against ecs.MaxReviveIndex (4 Mi), the entity count against ClientConfig.MaxEntities ; a frame that contradicts what the client holds (a delta from another version, a leave of an unknown chunk) ends the session. Limits limit default where players connected (plus those within their reconnect grace) 256, at most 1024 ServerConfig.MaxPlayers player registry records 4096 netsim.MaxRecords view distance 8 chunks (at most 32), vertical 4 View , Vertical bandwidth per client 256 KiB/s BytesPerSecond entities held by one client 2048 MaxEntities unacknowledged frames before pausing 40 MaxUnacked send window before pausing 2 MiB SendWindow client view speed 128 voxels/s ViewSpeed client view distance from the authoritative or spawn position 256 voxels ViewLeash frame workers GOMAXPROCS Workers fine water chunks in a frame, bricks per chunk 1024, 4096 wire.MaxFineChunks , wire.MaxFineBricks voxel edits of one delta 1024 MaxDeltaEdits frame 960 KiB wire.MaxRepFrameSize one component value 64 KiB wire.MaxCompData one extra state 512 KiB wire.MaxExtraData handshakes in progress 128 (4 per address group) MaxHandshakes , MaxHandshakesPerIP The other limits (rates, timeouts, reconnect grace) are those of the shared limits table in Networking . Measurements go test ./net/replica -run TestBandwidthReport -v and go test ./net/replica -bench BytesPerClient -benchtime 1x on an Apple M2 Max (12 cores), 20 ticks per second, clients walking over a 512×512 area with edits every half second and mobs whose transform changes every tick. "Before" is the first version (JSON components, frames built on the server loop), "after" the current one (component codecs, frames built in parallel): scenario bytes/client/s before after server tick before after 8 clients, 200 mobs, view 4 13.5 KB/s (max 20 KB/s) 4.6 KB/s (max 6.2 KB/s) 0.4 ms 0.35 ms 16 clients, 500 mobs, view 8 99 KB/s (max 141 KB/s) 28.7 KB/s (max 39.8 KB/s) 2.8 ms 1.0 ms 64 clients, 500 mobs, view 8 99 KB/s (max 146 KB/s) 28.8 KB/s (max 41.1 KB/s) 9.4 ms 1.8 ms 256 clients, 500 mobs, view 8 93 KB/s (max 146 KB/s) 27.2 KB/s (max 41.1 KB/s) 33.7 ms 4.4 to 4.8 ms A view of 8 chunks over that area holds about 390 mobs that all move every tick: the stream is dominated by their transforms, now about 4 bytes of position delta each instead of 70 bytes of JSON. A quiet world (8 walking clients and an edit every half second, no mobs) costs about 235 bytes per client per second. Capacity at 20 ticks per second (a 50 ms tick): the first version spent 0.13 ms per client per tick on one core, about 380 clients per server. With codecs the serial cost is 0.11 ms per client ( Workers: 1 : 27.7 ms for 256 clients), about 460 clients per core; with 12 workers 256 clients take 4.8 ms, about 2600 clients per server within the tick (about 220 per core: the scan, the views and the sends stay serial). The scan itself costs 0.06 to 0.6 ms per tick here (a codec component's cold part is hashed when its value changes). How it is tested net/wire : round trip, golden bytes, limits and the decoder fuzz target cover the replicated messages, the codec encodings and the fine water entries. net/replica : chunks enter, leave, deltas and removal; entities enter, leave, single-component updates (binary) and death; the registry without inputs; the budget (bytes over two seconds within the budget, nearest first, everything arrives eventually); inputs applied and the prediction ring confirmed; reconnect with the same player; frames identical with 1 and 8 workers ( TestParallelFramesDeterministic , every byte on the network); the codecs (smallest-three quaternions within 0.0002 rad, field deltas); fine water replicated under interest with brick deltas; interpolation (midpoints, shortest arc, capped extrapolation, held entities), reconciliation with 0 to 7 ticks of latency (no correction on a steady walk, a snap on a teleport) and the render overrides that leave the simulation untouched; proximity chat; hostile clients (forged acks, ack floods, input floods, forbidden commands, malformed and server-only messages, view teleport, view walking away from its leash, an avatar overriding the view); a fuzz target that feeds arbitrary frames (binary components, fine water) to a client; a 64-client soak ( -tags slow ) and the bandwidth benchmark. The package runs under -race (the parallel frames). internal/netplay : a dedicated replicated server built from the sandbox template with three guests over loopback TLS: only the near guests receive an edit, moving reveals it, a lost connection resumes with the same player and its state, the smoothing system is installed. Component visibility (owner-only, nearby, entering and leaving the radius) is tested in net/replica ; the lobby and lobby mode and a restart from a save, including a game that gained or lost a component, in internal/dedicated . What is not covered Vertical prediction. The default predictor walks on the horizontal plane; jumps, gravity and steps come from the server's corrections (blended, or snapped beyond 4 voxels). A game with its own movement passes its own PredictFunc . Interpolation of children. Only replicated local transforms are interpolated; a parent's motion carries its children through the recomputed world transforms. Falling streams of fine water are not replicated (the bricks are). Unreliable transport. Over TCP a delta against the last sent state is safe; a UDP transport would move the baseline to the last acknowledged frame (the acks already exist). Serial parts. The scan, the views, the reference counts and the sends stay on the server loop; beyond a few thousand clients they dominate.

Scripting Scripts are WebAssembly modules that run inside the deterministic simulation. You write them in Go with the guest SDK burrow-engine/sdk/burrowsdk (Go 1.24+, GOOS=wasip1 , no TinyGo needed), or in any language that targets the ABI . Everything a script does is journaled, so a game replays bit for bit. This category has one page per topic. Getting started with scripts A script is a Go program compiled to WebAssembly that runs inside the deterministic simulation; this page takes you from nothing to a spinning cube and lists the project layout, the script hooks and every burrow script command. What a script is One Go package ( scripts/<name>/ ) = one .wasm module = one behaviour. Attach it to any number of nodes with the script component; each node has its own props and state . It is called by the engine, never the other way round: the host calls OnStart , OnTick , OnEvent and OnDestroy inside a fixed tick (20 per second). A script has no loop of its own, no window, no files, no network, no clock. Guest memory is reset before every call, so a script keeps nothing in globals. It remembers things in components: Props and State . The Go SDK is burrow-engine/sdk/burrowsdk . Any other language that targets the ABI works too ( script/ABI.md ); this documentation covers Go. Quickstart (5 minutes) Requirements: Go with the wasip1 port ( Go version ), and burrow on your path. burrow new mygame --template empty # or open any project folder cd mygame burrow script new spin # scripts/spin/main.go (+ go.mod when the project has none) burrow script build # scripts/*/ -> assets/scripts/*.wasm burrow script check # re-verify the modules scripts/spin/main.go is a complete script that turns its node around the Y axis: package main import "burrow-engine/sdk/burrowsdk" // props is the designer configuration: JSON from the script component, read-only. type props struct { Speed float32 `json:"speed"` } func init() { burrowsdk.Register(burrowsdk.Script{ OnTick: func (self burrowsdk.Entity, dt float64 ) { p, _ := burrowsdk.Props[props]() t, err := burrowsdk.GetTransform(self) if err != nil { return } t.Rot[ 1 ] += p.Speed * float32 (dt) burrowsdk.SetTransform(self, t) }, }) } func main() {} Attach it, then run: Editor: select a node (for example Edit > Create > Cube ), Add component , pick script , set module to assets/scripts/spin.wasm and props to {"speed": 90} . Press Ctrl+Shift+P (Play). The node turns at 90 degrees per second. Esc stops and restores the scene exactly. Outside the editor: burrow run (rebuilds stale scripts, then plays) or burrow test (headless, prints the StateHash ). Edit the code, run burrow script build again: the editor re-registers a changed .wasm within about a second and bound scripts keep their State. The editor never compiles Go: build with burrow script build (or let burrow run , burrow test and burrow build do it). The script component Attach the same data from a scene file ( .voxscn ) instead of the inspector: "script" : { "module" : "assets/scripts/spin.wasm" , "props" : { "speed" : 90 } } field type meaning module string Required. A name registered on the runtime, an asset GUID, or a project-relative path of the .wasm . Resolved in that order. A game registers every .wasm under the project's asset folders and the scripts list of vox.project by project-relative path (at most 256 modules). entry string Optional. Selects a RegisterNamed script inside the module. Empty = the Register script. props JSON object Optional designer configuration, at most 16 KiB. Read-only for the script. state , hash , cfg , started , disabled , faults , inbox , subs , timers , reads Managed by the engine. Do not write them in scenes. hash pins the module by content on first run. Full schema: components reference . An unresolved module is not an error: the node is retried every frame and its script never runs (see debugging ). The burrowsdk.Script struct type Script struct { OnStart func (self Entity) OnTick func (self Entity, dt float64 ) OnEvent func (self Entity, ev Event) OnDestroy func (self Entity) } type Event struct { From Entity // sender (the script's own entity for timers) Kind int32 Payload [] byte } A nil hook is skipped. Every hook runs inside the node's transaction ( execution model ). hook called notes OnStart(self) once, in the first transaction of the node after the script is bound Runs again if that transaction faulted (the started flag is saved only on success). Not re-run after hot reload or restore. OnTick(self, dt) every fixed tick dt is 1 / rate , 0.05 (50 ms) at the default 20 Hz ( runtime.tick_rate can raise it). Use Tick() for time. OnEvent(self, ev) once per event emitted on an earlier tick, in emission order Events come from Emit , Publish and timers. A matching OnMessage or OnTimer handler consumes its event first, so OnEvent does not see it. Keep your own kinds below 0x40000000 : 0x40000000..0x7fffffff is reserved for bus topics and timers. OnDestroy(self) when a script's Despawn of the node (or of an ancestor) commits Not called for editor deletion or scene unload. Runs as its own transaction; effects commit with it. Its own Despawn calls do not cascade. Registration rules: Register from init() (or package-level variable initialisers). init() runs once; the host snapshots memory right after it, so what init() set up is restored before every call. Anything registered later, inside a hook, is lost at the next reset. Register(s) sets the default script; calling it twice keeps the last. RegisterNamed(name, s) adds scripts selected per node with the component's entry . If a module has named scripts and entry is empty, the default runs; if entry names something unknown, no hook runs (silently). OnMessage(topic, fn) and OnTimer(id, fn) are also registered from init() (see the API reference ). Do not call host functions from init() : they return ERR_UNAVAILABLE ( Rand() would return a garbage value). Pure Go set-up is fine. The SDK exports all four entry points whatever hooks you set, so burrow script check always lists on_destroy on_event on_start on_tick . This script uses every hook: package main import "burrow-engine/sdk/burrowsdk" const kindPing int32 = 1 func init() { burrowsdk.Register(burrowsdk.Script{ OnStart: func (self burrowsdk.Entity) { burrowsdk.Logf( "started at tick %d" , burrowsdk.Tick()) }, OnTick: func (self burrowsdk.Entity, dt float64 ) { if burrowsdk.Tick()% 20 == 0 { _ = burrowsdk.Emit( 0 , kindPing, [] byte ( "hi" )) // target 0 = every script, delivered next tick } }, OnEvent: func (self burrowsdk.Entity, ev burrowsdk.Event) { if ev.Kind == kindPing { burrowsdk.Logf( "ping from %#x: %s" , uint64 (ev.From), ev.Payload) } }, OnDestroy: func (self burrowsdk.Entity) { burrowsdk.Log(burrowsdk.LevelInfo, "bye" ) }, }) } func main() {} Project layout mygame/ vox.project manifest (optional "scripts": ["assets/scripts/spin.wasm"]) go.mod go.sum require burrow-engine, replace burrow-engine => checkout or kit sdk scripts/ spin/main.go one package per module (more .go files allowed) shared/... helper packages are fine, they compile into every module that imports them assets/scripts/spin.wasm build output: commit it or ignore it, but it must exist to play scenes/main.voxscn nodes with the script component burrow script build treats each directory scripts/<name>/ that holds a .go file as one script and writes assets/scripts/<name>.wasm . A module is about 4 MiB (the Go runtime), about 1 MiB inside a .voxpak . That cost is per module: prefer one module with several named entry points ( RegisterNamed , Script.Entry ) to many small ones. For release, burrow build --native links the scripts into the game executable instead ( Native scripts ). Go toolchain and script templates You do not have to install Go. When burrow script build (or the editor's build button, burrow run , burrow build ) finds no go of at least Go 1.27.2 (the version in Burrow's go.mod ), it downloads the official release for your OS and CPU into <user cache>/burrow/go/go1.27.2 (about 70 MB, once, with a progress message). The archive comes from https://go.dev/dl/ over HTTPS, its SHA-256 is checked against the release list before anything is unpacked, and the unpacking refuses absolute paths, .. , links that leave the folder and oversized archives. Only one process downloads at a time. Variable Effect BURROW_GO Use this go binary (or GOROOT folder) and never download. BURROW_OFFLINE=1 Never download: build fails with a clear message when no suitable Go is installed. BURROW_CACHE_DIR Move the cache (default: the OS user cache directory + burrow ). burrow doctor shows which Go the scripts compile with, or that one will be downloaded. Ready-made behaviours: burrow script templates lists them, burrow script new <name> --template <t> starts a script from one. Each is a complete script with its Props documented in the header. Template Does rotate turns the node around an axis bob floats up and down door opens and closes on the door.open , door.close , door.toggle bus events (AnimPlay when the node has an anim.player , else slides) pickup collected when a tagged node (the player) comes close: publishes pickup.collected , disappears platform moves between its start and a second point zone publishes zone.enter / zone.exit for tagged nodes inside a box spawner spawns a prefab on a timer follow walks toward the nearest tagged node and faces it state on/off state for a prefab: switches the model variant ( render.voxmodel.variant ), the particles ( enabled ) and the sounds ( muted ) under the node on the state.on , state.off , state.toggle bus events; prop on sets the start state, group limits which messages reach it (see Linked prefabs ) In the editor, the Script panel has a "New script from a template" button (sparkle icon): choose a template, type a name, and the editor writes scripts/<name>/main.go , attaches a script component with sensible Props to the selected node (one undoable step), opens the file and builds it in the background. The zap button rebuilds all scripts; changed modules hot-reload. Go version and the SDK The guest needs GOOS=wasip1 and //go:wasmexport : Go 1.24 or newer (Burrow fetches Go 1.27.2 itself when needed, see above). TinyGo and cgo are not used ( CGO_ENABLED=0 ). Recent toolchains (Go 1.26, 1.27) need no special flags: their wasm output stays under the engine's structural caps. The engine caps module structure before compiling it (its own gas.Limits check, not a wazero limit): block depth 512, 100k functions, 3M instructions. A Go compiler that inlines deep enough to exceed the block-depth cap makes the load fail with blocks nested deeper than 512 ; burrow script build / burrowscript build then retry automatically with -gcflags=all=-l (inlining disabled), and the error message names that flag. Build by hand with -gcflags=all=-l if you compile yourself (see below). The SDK is the package burrow-engine/sdk/burrowsdk . The module burrow-engine is not published; go.mod must point at it: require burrow-engine v0.0.0 replace burrow-engine => /path/to/burrow-checkout-or-sdk-folder Where the replace target comes from, in order: --burrow-root , $BURROW_SDK (a kit SDK folder), $BURROW_ROOT or the checkout burrow was built from, the sdk/ folder next to the executable (Windows creator kit). The kit's sdk/ holds only sdk/burrowsdk and declares go 1.24 . burrow script new writes the go line of the SDK module it points at (a checkout's current version, go 1.24 for the creator kit), so install that Go or let GOTOOLCHAIN fetch it. A go.mod written by an older burrow declared go 1.24 and made the first build fail with updates to go.mod needed : run go mod tidy once in the project. Inside the Burrow repository no go.mod is needed. Build by hand burrow script build is go build with fixed flags. If you build yourself, keep them: the module bytes (and so the pinned hash) then do not depend on where the engine or your project lives. GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm CGO_ENABLED= 0 go build -buildmode=c-shared -trimpath \ -ldflags= "-s -w -X=runtime.modinfo= -buildid=" -o assets/scripts/spin.wasm ./scripts/spin burrow script check assets/scripts/spin.wasm -buildmode=c-shared makes a reactor module (exports _initialize , no _start ); a plain go build produces a command module the engine rejects. Drop -s -w for a debug build with function names in fault traces. If the engine refuses the module with blocks nested deeper than 512 (deep inlining), add -gcflags=all=-l : GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm CGO_ENABLED= 0 go build -buildmode=c-shared -trimpath -gcflags=all=-l \ -ldflags= "-s -w -X=runtime.modinfo= -buildid=" -o assets/scripts/spin.wasm ./scripts/spin The module gets bigger and slightly slower; burrow script build and burrowscript build apply this flag automatically when needed. Commands burrow script <build|new|check> ; dir defaults to the current folder. Every subcommand accepts --json (machine-readable result on stdout; {"ok":false,"error":...} on failure). Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 failure, 2 usage error. command does burrow script new <name> [dir] [--template <t>] Writes dir/scripts/<name>/main.go (the skeleton above, or the template). burrow script templates lists them. name : lowercase letters, digits, - , _ . Refuses to overwrite. Writes dir/go.mod only when absent; with no SDK found it warns and prints the lines to add. burrow script build [dir] Compiles every dir/scripts/<name>/ to dir/assets/scripts/<name>.wasm (stripped), then loads each module through the engine's checker. Skips a module whose .wasm is newer than every file in its folder and than go.mod / go.sum . Fails with no scripts found when there is none. If the checker rejects a module for block depth ( blocks nested deeper than 512 ), it is rebuilt once with -gcflags=all=-l before failing. burrow script check [dir|file.wasm] Verifies ABI version, imports, exports, size and structure of one file, or of every .wasm found anywhere under dir (default . ). Prints OK path (bytes, entries) or FAIL path: reason ; exit 1 if any fails or none exists. flag subcommand default meaning --force build off Rebuild even when up to date. Needed after changing a shared package outside scripts/<name>/ . --burrow-root path new see above Burrow checkout for the replace line. --vox-root is an alias. --json all off JSON output. build: {"ok","scripts":[{name,source,wasm,bytes,hash,up_to_date}]} ; check: {"ok","modules":[{file,ok,error,size,hash,entries}]} . Related: burrow run [dir] and burrow test [dir] rebuild stale scripts first ( burrow run --no-scripts skips it); burrow build packs the modules into the game. The standalone tool burrowscript does the same per package: burrowscript flags build <pkg-dir> -o out.wasm (default <dir>.wasm ), -debug keeps symbols and DWARF (bigger module, function names in fault traces) new <dir> -burrow /path (alias -vox ) check <file.wasm> -max-bytes N (default 8 MiB), -strict-wasi rejects every WASI import beyond the startup set; prints imports, memory pages and gas-check counts See also Execution model : transactions, order, time, randomness, determinism rules.
