Sound, particles and shake on an event
Spawn every N ticks, with limits
x: Cookbook Complete, compilable scripts for common jobs. Each block is a whole main.go : put it in scripts/<name>/ , run burrow script build , attach the module to a node ( "script": {"module": "assets/scripts/<name>.wasm", "props": {...}} ). Input actions ( move , jump , pick , place ) are those of the scripted , platformer and builder templates and must exist in your input.json . move is an axis2d : x right, y forward. Forward is -Z; yaw is Rot[1] in degrees. Event kinds you pick yourself must stay below 0x40000000 (above are bus topics and timers). FindTag scans the scene and is charged per node: cache the result in State . Ignored errors are ones that cannot matter for the recipe; see errors and limits . Spin an entity What: rotate around Y at speed degrees per second. When: decoration, pickups, fans. package main import ( "math" "burrow-engine/sdk/burrowsdk" ) type props struct { Speed float32 `json:"speed"` } func init() { burrowsdk.Register(burrowsdk.Script{ OnTick: func (self burrowsdk.Entity, dt float64 ) { p, _ := burrowsdk.Props[props]() t, err := burrowsdk.GetTransform(self) if err != nil { return } t.Rot[ 1 ] = float32 (math.Mod( float64 (t.Rot[ 1 ]+p.Speed* float32 (dt)), 360 )) _ = burrowsdk.SetTransform(self, t) }, }) } func main() {} Move with input What: walk on the XZ plane from the move action. When: a top-down or test avatar without physics. package main import "burrow-engine/sdk/burrowsdk" func init() { burrowsdk.Register(burrowsdk.Script{ OnTick: func (self burrowsdk.Entity, dt float64 ) { x, y, ok := burrowsdk.Action( "move" ) t, err := burrowsdk.GetTransform(self) if !ok || err != nil { return } t.Pos[ 0 ] += x * 5 * float32 (dt) // 5 blocks per second t.Pos[ 2 ] -= y * 5 * float32 (dt) _ = burrowsdk.SetTransform(self, t) }, }) } func main() {} Jump pressed edge What: act once per press, not every tick the key is held. When: any button. Input is a level; derive the edge from your own State . package main import "burrow-engine/sdk/burrowsdk" type state struct { WasDown bool `json:"was_down"` Jumps int `json:"jumps"` } func init() { burrowsdk.Register(burrowsdk.Script{ OnTick: func (self burrowsdk.Entity, dt float64 ) { st, _ := burrowsdk.LoadState[state]() x, _, ok := burrowsdk.Action( "jump" ) down := ok && x > 0.5 if down && !st.WasDown { st.Jumps++ burrowsdk.Logf( "jump %d" , st.Jumps) } st.WasDown = down _ = burrowsdk.SaveState(st) }, }) } func main() {} Despawn after a lifetime What: remove yourself after ticks . When: bullets, effects, temporary blocks. package main import "burrow-engine/sdk/burrowsdk" const timerLife = 1 type props struct { Ticks int `json:"ticks"` } func init() { burrowsdk.OnTimer(timerLife, func (self burrowsdk.Entity) { _ = burrowsdk.Despawn(self) // the subtree goes too, at commit }) burrowsdk.Register(burrowsdk.Script{ OnStart: func (self burrowsdk.Entity) { p, _ := burrowsdk.Props[props]() _ = burrowsdk.After(timerLife, max(p.Ticks, 1 )) }, }) } func main() {} Coin pickup with tags and events What: a coin tells the player it was taken, then vanishes; the player counts. When: collectibles. Tag the player node "tags": {"tags": ["player"]} . Two scripts, one event kind. x: Embedding and the ABI The host side of scripting: running the runtime in your own program, and the plain-words contract for writing guests in a language other than Go. Everything the burrowplay game window does for you is described here so it can be done by hand. The pieces piece package role script.Runtime burrow-engine/script compiles, meters and runs modules; content-addressed module store; safe for concurrent use. One per App , shared with replays script.Plugin same installs the script / script.input / tags components, the journaled commands, the fixed system script.run and the frame systems that bind, reload and journal input script.Config same limits and budgets of a runtime (zero value is usable) host function registry burrow-engine/script/api every vox function once (name, params, doc, category, gas); read by tools Config script.NewRuntime(script.Config{}) . Every field, with its default. Zero means default. field default meaning Interpreter false wazero interpreter instead of the compiler (about 30 us per script call instead of 1.5-11; for platforms without a compiler backend). Same results MemoryPages 512 64 KiB pages per instance (32 MiB). A Go guest's post-init image is about 100-200 pages MaxModuleBytes 8 MiB largest .wasm accepted MaxModules 256 distinct module versions kept loaded; the oldest version that is neither pinned nor registered by name is evicted ( Stats.Evicted ) GasPerInvocation 50,000,000 deterministic instruction budget per guest entry call; exhaustion is a fault Watchdog 0 (off) wall-clock limit per call. Not deterministic: a trip journals script_disable , and the tick in which it fired may not replay identically. Costs about 10 us per call. Gas is the real bound MaxFaults 3 faults before a script is disabled until its module changes PerScript , PerTick below Budget per transaction and per tick across all scripts StrictWASI false reject modules importing any WASI function beyond the startup set NoWriteTracking false skip store instrumentation; resets compare all memory (slower resets, faster guest code). Same results Limits 512 nesting, 100k functions, 8M instructions, 2 MiB per function structural caps checked before compilation ( gas.Limits ) LoadTimeout 120 s validation plus compilation of one module; longer is rejected and remembered as bad PoolSize 8 idle instances kept per module Budget fields, per transaction / per tick: Calls 1,000 / 200,000; Bytes 1 MiB / 64 MiB; Spawns 32 / 1,024; VoxelEdits 4,096 / 262,144; Events 64 / 4,096 (events cover Emit , Publish and every effect request ). What each limit means for authors: errors and limits . Result-affecting fields. GasPerInvocation , MemoryPages , MaxFaults , both budgets, StrictWASI and MaxModuleBytes are folded into Runtime.Fingerprint() . Each script remembers it when bound; restoring or replaying under a different fingerprint fails instead of diverging. Keep these identical between a recording and its replay. Modules call does rt.Load(wasm) (*Module, error) validate, instrument and compile; idempotent per content hash; failed loads are cached by hash rt.Register(name, wasm) (hash, error) Load plus a name: a script component with "module": "name" binds to it rt.Hashes() hashes of all loaded versions: with the journal, the replay identity of the module set rt.Pin(hash) / rt.Unpin(hashes...) protect a version from eviction; the plugin pins every version it journals. Unpin versions older than your latest snapshot. When everything is pinned and MaxModules is reached, Load fails with an Unpin hint rt.Loader() the assets.Loader for .wasm files (register it in assets.Options.Loaders ): path and GUID modules, hot reload script.Inspect(wasm, cfg) load in a throw-away runtime and report entries, imports, gas sites, memory (what check prints) Resolution of script.module : first names registered on the runtime, then the asset database (GUID or project path). The engine writes the content hash into the component ( script_bind , journaled), so replays use the bytes the journal names. Replaying a state whose module the runtime lacks fails the tick with an error naming the hash; it never skips. A changed .wasm asset recompiles and is applied at the next tick boundary ( script_module_changed , journaled), clearing the fault count; a broken new file keeps the old module. Hot reload is off in multiplayer ( multiplayer ). Plugin &script.Plugin{Runtime: rt, Prefabs: prefabs, ReadAsset: read, PauseOnFault: true } field default meaning Runtime nil: a new runtime from Config , closed on cleanup share one runtime across an app and its replays Config zero used only when Runtime is nil Prefabs none prefabs Spawn(name, ...) can instantiate PrefabSource none func(name string) ([]byte, error) that serves .prefab bytes for a name Prefabs lacks (the game and the editor use the project's <name>.prefab and prefabs/<name>.prefab ); results are cached ReadAsset the *assets.DB resource, if present serves ReadAsset (project data files) PauseOnFault false pause the simulation ( SetPausedBy("script.fault") ) when a script faults, so you can inspect it. Frame domain, replays unaffected Order. The plugin fails to build ( script: needs the scene; add &engine.ScenePlugin{} before script.Plugin ) unless ScenePlugin came first. Add input , physics and physics3d plugins before it: when physics is present script.run is ordered before physics.character , and when input is present the input snapshot system runs after input.poll . netsim.Plugin (multiplayer registry), nav, levels, saves, assets, audio, particles, camera and gameui plugins may come in any order: the plugin looks up levels, saves and the asset database after every plugin has built. The standard game assembly adds scene, net, window, assets, voxel world, fluid, input, physics, physics3d, nav, weather, then scripts, then render, audio, particles, camera, gameui, levels, saves. Prefabs. Prefabs is a map[string]*scene.Prefab ; build entries with scene.LoadPrefab(voxscnBytes, schema) , or set PrefabSource to load them on demand. A prefab is the only way for a script to spawn a node that carries a script component: Spawn with a script component in SpawnOpts.Components is DENIED ( script , script.input and graph_script are protected). The burrowplay / burrow run game assembly and the editor set PrefabSource to the project's <name>.prefab and prefabs/<name>.prefab files. Example: run headless and read the hash Two runs of the same program give the same StateHash , and a journal replay gives it again. Seed and StrictCommands (a failed command is an error, not a log line) are what tests usually want. package main import ( "encoding/json" "fmt" "os" "burrow-engine/engine" "burrow-engine/mathx" "burrow-engine/scene" "burrow-engine/script" ) func check(err error ) { if err != nil { fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err) os.Exit( 1 ) } } func main() { rt, err := script.NewRuntime(script.Config{}) check(err) defer rt.Close() wasm, err := os.ReadFile( "assets/scripts/spin.wasm" ) check(err) hash, err := rt.Register( "spin" , wasm) // scenes may now say "module": "spin" check(err) app := engine.New(engine.Options{Seed: 1 , StrictCommands: true }) app.AddPlugin(&engine.ScenePlugin{}) app.AddPlugin(&script.Plugin{Runtime: rt}) check(app.Build()) tr := scene.IdentityTransform() tr.Pos = mathx.Vec3{X: 4 , Y: 3 , Z: 4 } check(app.Do(scene.SpawnNode{Name: "spinner" , Transform: &tr})) comp := fmt.Sprintf( `{"module":"spin","hash":%q,"props":{"speed":90}}` , hash) check(app.Do(scene.SetComponent{Path: "spinner" , Name: script.CompScript, Data: json.RawMessage(comp)})) check(app.RunHeadless( 100 )) fmt.Printf( "tick=%d StateHash=%016x faults=%d\n" , app.Tick(), app.StateHash(), rt.Stats().Faults) check(app.VerifyReplay()) } Putting the hash in the component pins the module for the journal. Without hash the plugin binds the module at the next frame with a journaled script_bind , which also works. Complete demo with seven scripts, built on the fly and run twice: go run ./examples/scripting_demo . Reading results: rt.Stats() (invocations, faults, gas, budget denials, evictions), rt.Profile() per script entity ( debugging ), the *script.Console resource (log lines and faults with guest stack), ScriptFault events. Writing a guest in another language The raw contract is script/ABI.md (version 1, normative; the host-function table in it is what Script API is generated from). In plain words: Module shape. A WebAssembly 2.0 core module (bulk memory, sign extension, multi-value and so on; no SIMD, threads or tail calls ). It must be valid on its own. Imports: only module vox (the host functions; the name predates the engine rename and is part of the ABI) and a few WASI stubs. Any other import module ( env , gojs , ...) is refused at load with a hint. Exports: memory (required); vox_abi_version: () -> i32 returning 1 (required); at least one of the entry points below; vox_alloc if you export on_event ; _initialize: () optional (run once at load). _start (a command build) is refused. No hidden state: a module that mutates tables or drops segments ( table.set/grow/fill/copy/init , data.drop , elem.drop ) is rejected. entry export signature called on_start (entity i64) first tick of the script on_tick (entity i64, dt_millis i32) every tick, dt_millis is always 50 on_event (entity i64, kind i32, payload_ptr i32, len i32) each pending event ( emit_event , bus messages, fired timers) before on_tick ; sender from event_from() on_destroy (entity i64) the entity is despawned by a script vox_alloc (size i32) -> i32 the host writes an event payload at the returned address Memory. Before every call the instance memory and mutable globals equal the image taken after _initialize . Nothing you store survives; persist through state_set (64 KiB, replaces Script.State at commit) and components. A module whose memory grew during a call is discarded afterwards, so reserve what you need before the image is taken (the Go SDK pre-grows 8 MiB). Calls. Pointers and lengths are i32 ; strings are UTF-8, not NUL-terminated; one argument is at most 64 KiB, component names at most 128 bytes. A function returns >= 0 on success and -code on failure, never a trap for bad input. i64 -returning functions return a negative error too. Output buffers are (out_ptr, cap) : the result is the length written, or -4 and last_required() tells the size needed. Entity handles are i64 ; 0 is none. code name meaning 1 INVALID bad value (NaN, out of range, unknown block id, empty name) 2 MEMORY pointer or length outside guest memory, or over the argument cap 3 NOT_FOUND entity, component, block or action does not exist 4 TOO_SMALL output buffer too small, see last_required 5 BUDGET call, byte, spawn, edit or event budget exhausted 6 DENIED not allowed for scripts (the script component, hidden asset paths) 7 UNAVAILABLE subsystem not installed, or called outside a tick (during _initialize ) 8 REJECTED JSON or schema validation failed 9 LIMIT a size cap hit (state, props, payload, inbox, timers) Determinism for non-Go guests. The WASI clock is tick*50ms ; random_get is a fixed stream seeded by the module hash; use rand_u64 for gameplay randomness. Floats are IEEE and deterministic except NaN payload bits: host floats are canonicalised (any NaN becomes 0x7fc00000 ) and non-finite values are refused by transform_set , raycast and others. Never store raw NaN bits in state. ABI versioning. vox_abi_version() must equal the host's script.ABIVersion (1), otherwise the load fails ( guest ABI version N, host speaks 1 ). Within a version the ABI is additive: functions are added, never changed. A module that imports a function this engine does not have fails to load ("built against a newer SDK") and a signature mismatch fails with both signatures shown. A module built against an older SDK keeps working. Checking a module burrow script check [dir|file.wasm] # one file, or every module under dir/assets burrowscript check [-max-bytes N] [-strict-wasi] file.wasm check loads the module in a throw-away runtime with the same validation as the game. Output on success (exit 0): OK , the ABI version, size and content hash, entry points present, the vox imports used, the WASI stub count, metering (gas checks and tracked stores), a warning for imports unknown to this engine, and memory pages (the reset image size). On failure it prints FAIL <file>: <reason and hint> and exits 1 (2 for a usage error). -max-bytes overrides the size cap and -strict-wasi also rejects the inert WASI imports. burrow script build runs the same check on every module it compiles; burrowscript build [-o out.wasm] [-debug] dir is the underlying compile ( GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm go build -buildmode=c-shared , Go 1.24+; -debug keeps function names for fault traces). Packing burrow build --pak game.voxpak (or a packed executable or app) stores vox.project , every file under asset_dirs (compiled .wasm included), the default scene, input map and world overlay. Files are stored or zlib-compressed with a SHA-256 each, paths are sorted and the whole archive is hashed, so building twice gives identical bytes. Stale script sources are rebuilt first ( --no-scripts on burrow run skips it). A Go module is about 4 MiB and about 1 MiB in the pak. The pak is untrusted data on load (size, ratio and path caps, no symlinks, a private 0700 extraction directory); the modules inside stay sandboxed. Modules are pinned by content hash, so a pak replays exactly what was recorded. Sandbox facts No files, sockets, threads, clocks or real randomness. The only imports are vox and inert WASI stubs: args_* and environ_* (empty), clock_time_get (tick based), random_get (fixed stream), fd_write on 1 and 2 (captured into fault text), poll_oneoff (returns at once), sched_yield , proc_exit (a fault). Go programs also link the rest of preview1 through os and fmt ; those functions exist but always fail ( EBADF / ENOSYS ; no preopened directories). StrictWASI rejects even those. Gas is injected into the module before compilation, so a runaway loop traps at the same instruction on every machine. Memory, module size, call, byte, spawn, edit and event budgets are all enforced by the host ( errors and limits ). A fault (trap, gas, panic, proc_exit , memory) drops the transaction's buffered effects, raises a ScriptFault event, and after MaxFaults disables the script until its module changes. The engine never crashes because of a script. Native build. The same SDK also runs in-process: outside GOOS=wasip1 , sdk/burrowsdk/abi forwards every call to the host installed with abi.SetHost ( script.Runtime does this for natively linked modules, see Native scripts ); without a host each call returns ErrUnavailable . abi_stub.go is generated from abi_wasip1.go ( go run gen_native.go in that directory); a test keeps them in sync. Scripts are trusted at build time (the Go toolchain runs on your project's source) and sandboxed at run time: see security . See also Execution model , errors and limits , debugging and testing . Multiplayer : what changes with runtime.plugins.net . ABI.md , Script API , CLI reference . Security , Determinism , Getting started : building a .voxpak .

The full field-by-field reference is the Types section of the script API : type role Entity a scene node handle; Exists checks it Script the four hooks ( OnStart , OnTick , OnEvent , OnDestroy ), installed with Register or RegisterNamed from init() Event one delivered message: From , Kind , Payload Error a failed host call: Op (the host function) and Code (an abi.Err* code); IsNotFound(err) matches ErrNotFound Transform Pos , Rot (Euler degrees), Scale ; read/write with GetTransform / SetTransform Writer / Reader binary codec for State (see below) Calling conventions Errors. Every host call returns an error that is an *Error ( Op + Code ), or nil . Check specific failures with IsNotFound . The error codes and their meanings are listed in errors and limits ; the raw codes are the Err* constants of sdk/burrowsdk/abi . Budgets. Every call is charged gas (50,000,000 per hook) and most calls have their own limits (payload 1 KiB, state 64 KiB, 4,096 block edits per call, ...). A call that exceeds a budget faults the whole transaction: its writes are discarded, see execution model . Results. Reads that return bytes or lists ( GetRaw , BlockDataIn , FindWith , ...) grow their buffer internally until the data fits; large answers report ErrTooSmall -style resizing transparently. Simulation domain vs frame domain domain files what it means for your script Simulation (journaled, hashed, replayed) voxsdk.go , fields.go , components_gen.go , scene.go , blocks.go , bus.go , level.go , nav.go , net.go , physics.go , fluid.go , model.go Changes commit with the call, are saved, hashed and replayed exactly. LightAt , Voxel and the scene queries read the committed state (plus this call's own writes where documented). Frame (queued requests) audio.go , particles.go , fx.go , anim.go , camera.go , gameui.go Requests take effect after the tick, in call order. They are deterministic (a replay shows the same effects) but never part of the StateHash , and they are ignored when the matching runtime.plugins.* is off. Pure Go (no host call) tween.go , codec.go , parts of items.go , bus.go 's BusKind , voxsdk.go 's Rand* / CanonF32 Free, safe to call anywhere — including from init() for everything except Rand* , which need a tick. Pure helpers worth knowing These need no host call and no component, so they are the building blocks of State logic: Binary state. Writer appends U8 / Bool / U32 / I32 / U64 / F32 / String little-endian; Reader (from NewReader ) reads them back, setting Reader.Err when it runs past the end. Encode with w.Bytes() , store with SetStateRaw , read with StateRaw . Faster and smaller than SaveState JSON, at the price of writing the layout yourself. CanonF32 canonicalises NaN so its payload bits never reach hashed state. Tweens and cooldowns in tick time. Tween is plain JSON-able data: NewTween(from, to, durTicks, ease) starts one now, t.At(tick) / t.Now() evaluate it, t.Done(tick) reports the end. EaseKind has 13 curves ( Linear , InQuad , OutCubic , OutBounce , SmoothStep , ...) and EaseKind.Apply maps [0,1] through one; Lerp(a, b, t) is the linear case. Cooldown is a one-field deadline: Start(n) , Ready() . Item stacks. ItemStack{Item, Count} with Empty , Encode (the 6-byte wire form, ItemStackSize ), DecodeItemStack , Split(n) and Merge(src, maxStack) . Ids and limits come from the project: ItemIDByName , ItemInfo ( ItemProps.MaxStack ). Block names with states. BlockBase("mymod:belt[facing=east]") gives "mymod:belt" , BlockProp(name, "facing") gives "east" . Deterministic randomness. Rand() , RandFloat() in [0,1), RandN(n) in [0,n): a private stream per script entity, derived from the seed, entity, tick and draw index; it never touches the shared simulation RNG. Event kinds. BusKind(topic) computes the kind a bus message arrives with; KindTimer , KindBlockBatch and KindBlockTick are reserved kinds handled by OnTimer / OnMessage and the block handlers. Generated component accessors components_gen.go holds one Comp<Name> constant per built-in component ( CompTransform = "transform" , CompRenderCamera = "render.camera" , ...) and, for every scalar field, a typed getter and setter ( TransformPos(e) , SetTransformPos(e, v) , built on GetFloats / SetFieldRaw ). It is generated from the same component schema as the inspector and the components reference : regenerate it with make sdk-gen after changing the schema ( make sdk-check fails when it is stale). For object fields and custom components use the generic Get / Set / Patch or the fields.go accessors. A complete example One module using registration, props, state, the codec, a tween, the bus and the transform — the same shapes the cookbook recipes use: package main import "burrow-engine/sdk/burrowsdk" type props struct { Speed float32 `json:"speed"` // degrees per second } type state struct { Turns int `json:"turns"` // ticks since start, kept as binary state } const kindDone int32 = 1 // below 0x40000000: our own event kind func init() { burrowsdk.OnMessage( "game.reset" , func (self, from burrowsdk.Entity, payload [] byte ) { _ = burrowsdk.SetStateRaw(new(burrowsdk.Writer).Bytes()) // clear the state }) burrowsdk.Register(burrowsdk.Script{ OnStart: func (self burrowsdk.Entity) { burrowsdk.Log(burrowsdk.LevelInfo, "spinner ready" ) }, OnTick: func (self burrowsdk.Entity, dt float64 ) { p, err := burrowsdk.Props[props]() if err != nil { return } var st state r := burrowsdk.NewReader(burrowsdk.StateRaw()) st.Turns = int (r.I32()) if r.Err { st.Turns = 0 // first tick: empty state decodes as zeros anyway } tw := burrowsdk.NewTween( 0 , 1 , 20 , burrowsdk.OutQuad) // ease in over one second t, err := burrowsdk.GetTransform(self) if err != nil { return } t.Rot[ 1 ] += p.Speed * float32 (dt) * float32 (tw.Now()) if err := burrowsdk.SetTransform(self, t); err != nil { return } st.Turns++ w := new(burrowsdk.Writer).I32( int32 (st.Turns)) _ = burrowsdk.SetStateRaw(w.Bytes()) if st.Turns == 20 { _ = burrowsdk.Emit( 0 , kindDone, [] byte ( "one second" )) } }, OnEvent: func (self burrowsdk.Entity, ev burrowsdk.Event) { if ev.Kind == kindDone { burrowsdk.Logf( "done, from=%d payload=%s" , uint64 (ev.From), ev.Payload) } }, }) } func main() {} Where the full reference lives Script API reference (generated by make docs-gen ): the host functions (the vox imports, from script/ABI.md ), then the Go SDK functions grouped by source file, then every type with its struct fields, then every constant and variable — all with their doc comments. From the command line or your IDE: go doc burrow-engine/sdk/burrowsdk and go doc burrow-engine/sdk/burrowsdk.<Name> show the same comments. sdk/burrowsdk/abi declares the raw imports one-to-one (one function per ABI row, same signatures as the host-function table); use it only for custom wrappers, and note that outside wasip1 every call returns ErrUnavailable so tests can run on the host. See also Getting started for building and attaching scripts, execution model for transactions and determinism. State and props , entities and scene , world , input, events and time , effects . OnFrame (frame domain) OnTick runs 20 times per second and drives the simulation. OnFrame runs once per rendered frame, at screen rate. It is for cosmetics only: it can write a visual overlay and nothing else. package main import ( "math" "burrow-engine/sdk/burrowsdk" ) func init() { burrowsdk.Register(burrowsdk.Script{ OnFrame: func (self burrowsdk.Entity, f burrowsdk.Frame) { // bob the node with the player's speed, smooth at any frame rate _ = burrowsdk.VisualAdd( "pos.y" , 0.05 *math.Sin(f.Time* 8 )*f.Speed) _ = burrowsdk.VisualSet( "ui.speed" , f.Speed) }, }) } func main() {} Frame info field meaning Dt seconds since the previous frame Time elapsed seconds Alpha position between the last tick and the next, 0..1 MouseDX , MouseDY mouse pixels per 60 fps frame, as in visual.bind Speed horizontal speed of this node in blocks per second, measured between ticks Yaw , Pitch the player's view angles Writes VisualSet(target, v) replaces the drawn value. VisualAdd(target, v) adds to it. VisualSetOn(e, ...) and VisualAddOn(e, ...) do the same on another node. Targets are those of visual.bind : pos.x|y|z , rot.x|y|z , scale , light.intensity|r|g|b , material.p0..p3 , camera.fov , ui.<key> . A write lasts one frame. Write it again next frame. Writes are never saved, journaled or hashed. At most 64 writes per call. A bad target or a NaN returns an error. What is blocked Inside OnFrame only these work: the writes above, Self , Props , LoadState , Log (the log is discarded) and imui_frame , the immediate-mode UI (see docs/game-ui.md , "Immediate-mode UI from scripts"). Every other host call returns ErrUnavailable : Set , Spawn , Emit , timers, voxels, Rand , Tick , physics, SaveState . The list is a whitelist, so a new host function is blocked by default. The reverse holds too: VisualSet in OnTick returns ErrUnavailable . Limits Budget: Config.FrameGas , default GasPerInvocation/20 . Memory is reset after every call, like in a tick. At most 256 scripts per frame, in ascending entity id. Skipped while the game is paused by the editor, a fault or loading. A pause by the game UI (a menu or an IMUI modal) keeps it running, with Frame.Paused set: see "Pause menu" in docs/game-ui.md . Also skipped with the editor free camera, and when no render plugin runs (headless, dedicated server). A module that exports only OnFrame is valid at the ABI level. The Go SDK exports every entry, so Go scripts always have all of them. Faults A fault in OnFrame (gas, trap) drops that call's writes. It never fails a tick, never rolls back, never journals script_disable and never changes the state hash. Faults are counted ( Runtime.FrameFaults ) and the first one is logged to the console. After 3 consecutive faults OnFrame stops for that node until its module changes. Determinism Replays and StateHash are identical with and without OnFrame scripts. A test runs the same project with and without the frame system and compares the hashes.

h: The rule: state lives in State and components
x: Native scripts The Unity model: scripts run as WebAssembly in the editor and for mods (hot reload, isolation, gas), and the shipped game compiles the project's Go scripts into its own executable , like IL2CPP. One game file, no .wasm in the archive, no wasm interpreter or JIT at run time. WebAssembly (editor, mods) Native ( burrow build --native ) Where sandboxed wazero instance linked into the game executable Hot reload yes no (rebuild) Gas (deterministic instruction budget) yes, a loop is a fault none ; debug watchdog only Memory linear memory, reset to the post- init() image before every call the Go heap; package-level variables persist Sandbox no files, network or clock none : the script is trusted code Host calls, budgets, transactions, journal, order, Script.Hash identical identical StateHash of a correct script identical identical Use burrow build my-game -o my-game --native # compile a player with the scripts linked in (needs the Burrow checkout, BURROW_ROOT, and Go) burrow test my-game --parity # same project, wasm run vs native run: the StateHash must be equal --wasm (the default) keeps shipping WebAssembly with the prebuilt player. BURROW_BUILD_NATIVE=1 makes --native the default of burrow build on your machine. Native is the recommended release build; it is not the default because it needs the source checkout and a C toolchain to recompile the player, which a plain burrow build does not. How it links: every scripts/<name>/ package ( package main ) is copied into the Burrow module as internal/nativemods/<name> with its package clause renamed, between two generated files whose init() functions bracket the package's own ( burrowsdk.NativeBegin / NativeEnd ). Everything the package registers ( Register , RegisterNamed , OnMessage , OnTimer , OnBlockChange , ...) belongs to that module, so any number of modules coexist in one binary. The copies exist only as a go build -overlay ; your project and the checkout are never written to. Each module keeps the identity of its wasm build ( sha256: of the .wasm , which burrow build --native builds first), so scenes, journals, saves and Script.Hash do not care which runtime ran them. Scenes must refer to modules by project path ( "module": "assets/scripts/game.wasm" ), as the templates do; the path is the name a native module is registered under. One module per project Prefer one script package with many named entry points ( RegisterNamed , selected per node by Script.Entry ) to one package per behaviour. Every wasm module is its own ~4.4 MB Go runtime image that the editor compiles, instantiates and pools, and every native module is another copy of the SDK registration. The platformer template already works this way ( game : player , coin , mover ). Split into several modules only for code that different people ship separately. The rule: state lives in State and components A wasm call starts from a fresh memory image, so a package-level variable always reads its initial value. A native call does not: the variable keeps what the last call wrote, and the two runtimes would diverge (and replays, rollback and snapshots break). Therefore: never write a package-level variable from a hook ( var count int; count++ ), including maps and slices you append to; read-only tables built at package initialisation are fine ( var table = [...]int{...} ); anything a script remembers goes in SaveState , a component, or the save store. Detection: with BURROW_NATIVE_DEBUG=1 (or script.Config.NativeGuard ) the runtime hashes every package-level variable of every native module right after init and after every call, and faults the script ("script changed package-level variable ...") when one differs. burrow test --parity runs the project once like that. The guard is structural (it follows pointers, maps and slices; functions and channels count only as nil/non-nil), costs a few microseconds per call and is off in release builds. It cannot see state hidden in closures or in other packages' variables. No gas: the debug watchdog A native loop cannot be metered. In debug runs ( BURROW_NATIVE_DEBUG=1 , or Config.Watchdog ) a per-call wall-clock watchdog is armed: the call is aborted (a watchdog fault, the script is disabled, like in wasm) at its next host call after the limit (default 5 s). A loop that makes no host call cannot be interrupted; after 10 x the limit the debug process prints every goroutine stack and exits, so the loop is found instead of freezing the game. Test the heavy paths of a script as wasm ( burrow test ): gas faults there are deterministic, the watchdog is not. Writing scripts that stay equal Register from init() (not from package-variable initialisers) so the generated brackets see it. Imports: the standard library, burrow-engine/... and your own project's packages ( scripts/shared , ... are copied along, once, and their variables are watched by the guard too). Third-party modules are rejected by the native build (vendor the code into the project). Register only from the script package, never from a helper package. float32 arithmetic : Go on arm64 may fuse a*b + c into one rounding (FMA); wasm never does. Write float32(a*b) + c where the last bit matters, or keep sim maths in integers/fixed point. The parity test catches a difference on the machine it runs on, not across CPU architectures: peers of a networked game must run the same build kind. Do not rely on fmt.Print* / os.Std* (wasm captures it as the script log; native writes to the real stdout; use burrowsdk.Log ). A panic is a fault, as a trap is in wasm. A fatal Go runtime error (stack overflow, out of memory) ends the process: there is no instance to throw away. Limits No hot reload, no per-module memory cap, no gas, no sandbox: use native only for scripts you trust (your own project), never for mods. Hashes match because the wasm module is built too; a --native build needs the wasm toolchain as well. Linux, macOS and Windows hosts only (the player is compiled for the host). on_frame cosmetic scripts run natively too, with the same frame-domain restrictions. See also Execution model | Errors and limits | Debugging and testing | Embedding and ABI

Security and trust model Burrow runs code and reads files that come from several places. This page says which of them are trusted, what is sandboxed and what is not. Trust boundaries Input Trusted? What runs, and how The Burrow source checkout ( --burrow-root , $BURROW_ROOT , the tree burrow was built from) yes burrow builds burrowplay , burrowedit and burrowasset from it with go build -trimpath and runs them. Only these three sources name a root; the working directory and its parents are never used . A project directory ( vox.project , scenes, assets) data only Parsed with strict validation (size caps, unknown and duplicate JSON keys rejected, finite numbers, bounded ranges, printable title). A symlinked vox.project is refused. Project scripts compiled by Burrow ( scripts/*/main.go to assets/scripts/*.wasm ) build time: trusted , run time: sandboxed burrow new , run , test , build and burrow script build call the Go toolchain ( go mod tidy , go build ) on the project's Go source. That executes whatever the project's go.mod and sources cause the toolchain to do (module downloads, replace directives, cgo is off for wasm). The resulting .wasm runs in the wazero sandbox with fuel, memory and call limits and no host access beyond the Burrow API. A project's own Go tests ( go test ./... ) trusted, unsandboxed Only run by burrow test --go-tests . Never run by default. They compile and execute natively with your user's permissions. A .voxpak or a packed game untrusted data Parsed defensively: caps on counts, sizes and decompression ratio (50:1 per file above 1 MiB, 256 MiB total by default, pak.MaxRatio / pak.MaxTotalSize ), strict path rules (no .. , drive letters, control, bidi or other Unicode format characters), per-file SHA-256, extraction without following symlinks into a private 0700 temp directory that is removed on exit and on SIGINT/SIGTERM. Packed games contain compiled wasm, which stays sandboxed. Texture packs and imported assets untrusted data Decoded with size limits; see texture-packs.md for licensing. AI agents ( burrow agent , burrowd , the editor MCP server) untrusted callers File operations are confined to the project directory and explicitly allowed directories ( --allow ) with fd-based, race-resistant checks. An agent can still change the project's files and scripts, so treat what it writes the way you treat any code you did not write before you build or test it. What to do Open projects you did not write the way you open any source repository: read go.mod (look for replace and toolchain lines) and scripts/ before running burrow run , burrow test or burrow build on them. Prefer a throwaway user account or VM for code you do not trust. Do not pass --go-tests to burrow test for projects you do not trust. burrow shell-env single-quotes its values, so eval "$(burrow shell-env)" is safe whatever the Homebrew prefix path contains. Treat BURROW_ROOT , BURROW_BIN_DIR and BURROW_BREW_PREFIX as trusted configuration: they decide which binaries burrow starts. Tool cache: ~/Library/Caches/burrow/bin/<key>/ (or $BURROW_CACHE_DIR ) is created 0700. Burrow refuses cache directories or binaries that are owned by someone else, are symlinks, or are group/world-writable, and rebuilds instead. Built games and tool binaries are compiled with -trimpath , so they do not contain your home directory or checkout path. Script (wasm) builds use -trimpath too. Signing The plain executable and the .app produced by burrow build are ad-hoc signed: they run on the Mac that built them. The .app ships the archive once ( Contents/Resources/game.voxpak ) and is signed as one bundle, so codesign --verify --deep --strict passes. For distribution (Gatekeeper, quarantine) you need your own Developer ID signature and notarisation; see "Signing and distribution" in getting-started.md . The plain executable keeps the archive appended after the Mach-O, which strict validation reports; use the .app when you need strict validation. Reporting Report suspected vulnerabilities privately to the maintainers rather than in a public issue.

h: Engine gaps found while building them
x: Genre templates Burrow is a voxel engine, not a sandbox. Four project templates prove it: each one is a burrow new -template <name> project (data, levels, UI documents and one WebAssembly game script) with no game logic in the engine, plus a runnable example and a scripted pilot that wins the game. template genre what it exercises platformer 2.5D side scroller side_scroller camera rig, hand-built .level files, checkpoints (zones), moving platforms (physics3d kinematic bodies carrying a physics.character ), coins, hazard blocks, kill plane, lives, HUD, pause menu, quick save/load, particles, sounds, level progression Multiplayer starters (not genre showcases): template what it exercises multiplayer the first-person controller plus a base script that moves one avatar per connected player from the server registry lobby_match runtime.lobby (2 to 8 players, 2 teams, map and length settings), the Lobby game UI screen, a script that loads the chosen map when the match starts, ends it with lobby_end_match ( {"placements": ...} ) and returns to the lobby; two arenas with a goal zone. See Lobby screen burrow new mygame -template platformer # also multiplayer, lobby_match cd mygame && burrow run # play; burrow test is the headless check go run ./examples/tpl_platformer # in a Burrow checkout: play (also -auto, -shot dir) make templates-test # all four, headless and on the GPU How a template is built templates/files/<name> holds vox.project (plugins on, rigs, UI screens), input.json , scenes/main.voxscn , levels/*.level , ui/*.ui.json and scripts/game/main.go.tmpl . The levels are binary assets written by go run ./templates/mkassets [name] (plain block boxes plus nodes, spawns and zones). All rules live in the script: named scripts ( burrowsdk.RegisterNamed ) selected by the entry of the script component. A script keeps nothing in guest memory: game data (score, ore, health) is in the save key/value store, which is simulation state, so it is hashed, replayed and restored by a quick load together with the world. Scripts avoid encoding/json on hot paths (one call costs about a millisecond in Go-in-wasm) and keep their private state as packed bytes. The -auto proof internal/tplkit scaffolds the template exactly like burrow new , builds the script, opens the project through the same internal/game.Build as burrowplay , and plays a pilot: a function of the world and the tick that returns the input of one frame (keys, mouse buttons and motion, the cursor). -auto is headless (one tick per frame): it asserts the goals of the example, then checks the journal replay ( VerifyReplay ), runs the whole game a second time and compares the StateHash , and runs a template-specific Extra (pause menu freezes the simulation, quick save then quick load restores the saved hash, mouse look turns by 0.1 degree per pixel). -shot dir plays the same pilot on a hidden GPU window with the validation layer on and writes PNGs; make templates-test fails on any VUID . Reached goal: platformer tick 875 (two levels, two deaths and respawns). Engine gaps found while building them Fixed (generic, with tests): Mouse look lost at 60 fps. Scripts run at 20 Hz but a mouse delta is a per-frame amount, so two of three deltas never reached the script. Relative actions (mouse delta, scroll) are now summed over the frames between two ticks ( script/relinput_test.go ). No pause. App.SetPaused / Context.SetPaused (frame domain: no fixed tick, no banked time) and the game UI document field pause_sim (the simulation is paused while the screen is visible). Also the built-in widget action game:quit , so a project without Go host code can have a Quit button. No physics3d overlap query for scripts ( physics_overlap only knows the old AABB physics ): added physics3d_overlap (ABI, host, SDK Physics3DOverlap , physics3d.OverlapBoxFixed ). No pointer for scripts. input.Frame gets CX, CY, HasCursor , a mouse_pos binding (axis2d, -1..1), runtime.cursor: "free" in vox.project ( WindowPlugin.FreeCursor ), Injector.SetCursor for scripted runs. Voxel bodies were not drawn by project games. physics3d/p3render is now installed for windowed projects with physics3d ( VoxelOnly : bodies that are scene nodes with render.mesh are not drawn twice). Sandbox HUD (crosshair, hotbar, frame statistics) in every project. runtime.hud ; default off when plugins.controller is false. Migration: a project that set controller: false and wants the old overlay adds "hud": true to runtime . Pause details. pause_sim also stops the first-person controller; several pausers coexist ( App.SetPausedBy ); relative input is dropped (not journaled) while paused; catch-up ticks do not repeat a mouse delta; TickAlpha is frozen while paused and follows the controller's accumulator. game:quit needs uiplug.Plugin.AllowQuit (set by the project runner for the project's own UI files only). No host handle on the scene tree. App.SceneReader() (read nodes and component JSON from tools and tests). No child enumeration or find by component. scene_parent , scene_children , scene_path , scene_find_with , scene_find_tag (bounded, gas per node scanned) and the tags component; coins and mobs no longer need to be found by name. Whole-component JSON only. field_get / field_set / field_get_num / field_set_num and component_patch access one value by schema path ( pos[0] , bodies[2].mass ) with schema-validated, replayed partial writes; typed accessors for the built-in components are generated ( make sdk-gen ). Scripts could not read data files, and block ids had no names. asset_read (project data files, 256 KiB, 16 reads per transaction) and block_count , block_name , block_info , registry_list . First-person look stepped at 20 Hz. A frame-domain look layer for rigs ( camera_rig.frame_look ): the view turns at frame rate and the sim receives the look once per tick, with no double rotation ( camera/camera_test.go ). Remaining (listed, not fixed): Time of day is fixed at 24000 ticks and not configurable; level settings (sky, weather, fog, gravity) are data that nothing applies in project games. The survival template defines its own 2400-tick night, the sky does not follow it. Enclosed rooms are black (no block light yet: a roofless design was used). LevelZoneAt returns only the first zone; the level kill_y respawns at the default spawn only (the platformer implements its own kill plane and checkpoints). Engine trigger and collision events are not bridged to scripts (frame-domain only). Scripts use physics_overlap diffing, gameui_poll and level_current polling. A UI button that goes through the simulation ( sim: actions) does nothing while the simulation is paused, so the pause menu only has Resume and Quit; save and load are keys. Not built: a minimap widget, a selection rectangle widget (the box select has no drawn rectangle; selected units are tinted), an item name in grid slots. Body positions authored in level nodes must be given in world coordinates (the body writes the node transform). Voxel body drawing showed nothing on the GPU in the shared tree while another change to the mesher was in flight ( examples/physics3d_playground -gpu too); a destructible voxel-body wall is correct in the simulation but the capture does not show it until that is back.

Texture packs The engine embeds one block texture pack, imported once as plain PNGs (there is no resource-pack loader): the full 1.16 block set of Pixel Perfection CE ( pixelperfection , albedo only) in assets/textures/pixelperfection , accessed through assets/blocktex . burrow assets textures lists it with licence and coverage. id licence files coverage pixelperfection (default) CC-BY-SA-4.0, attribution + ShareAlike; commercial use allowed 922 PNG + 67 .mcmeta , 322 KiB Minecraft Java 1.16.2 block set (454 block entries, 242 shapes reuse them) none - - flat colours default and new projects use pixelperfection ( burrow new writes "texture_pack": "pixelperfection" and "blocks": "shapes" ; burrowedit without -project does the same), for its complete coverage of the extended block set ( blocks.md ) and one coherent style. Without the textures ( -tags nopp ) every block draws its flat fallback colour. The extended blocks the pack lacks (1.17+: deepslate ores, copper, tuff, bamboo, cherry, mangrove, ...) are flat placeholders listed in blocks.md . Released builds embed no other pack; asking for any other pack id fails with "not included in this build". Pixel Perfection CE Source https://github.com/Athemis/PixelPerfectionCE , commit 28e38cab7c1f03f86364ef704f705bebcc13cb3d ; imported by scripts/import-pixelperfection.sh <checkout> <sha> <date> (byte for byte; manifest.json has the SHA-256, size, dimensions and frame count of every file; the tests verify it). Licence CC-BY-SA-4.0, authors in assets/textures/pixelperfection/NOTICE.md . ShareAlike : the textures and any adaptation stay CC-BY-SA-4.0 whatever the licence of your game; burrow build prints the reminder when the pack is bundled and records textures.licenses in the build manifest. Compile out with -tags nopp ( burrow build --no-default-textures builds burrowplay with novnr,nopp ). Only block/*.png and the *.png.mcmeta animation descriptors. 856 files are 16x16; 66 are vertical strips of 16 px frames (fire, lava, portal, kelp, command blocks, lanterns..., lava_flow / water_flow are 32 px wide); the loader crops frame 0 in memory, animation is not implemented. One orphan rail_golden_powered.png.mcmeta ships upstream. Leaves, grass top/side overlay, grass, fern, vine, lily pad and water are gray/neutral tintable textures (grass top averages ~(141,130,113)): they need the biome tints listed in mcnames.json tint_kinds . TintGain = 1.65 was calibrated for a gray level of 0.57; this pack is normalised to it: at load time ( blocktex.Faces.Images ) every tintable Pixel Perfection image (leaves, grass top, grass side overlay, ...) is converted to its gray luma and rescaled to a mean of TintReference = 0.58 , so the same TintGain yields the biome colour. Shaders and the soft renderer are unchanged. A test checks the mean. No 1.17+ blocks (deepslate, copper, amethyst, tuff, moss, mud, cherry, bamboo planks, ...): mcnames.json missing lists 146 of them with a suggested flat average colour; the 75 that are full cubes are registered as flagged placeholders. Animation is not implemented: only frame 0 of the vertical strips is used (command blocks, lanterns, magma, sea lantern, prismarine, ...). Style: consistent saturated hand-drawn pixel art; a pack-wide look (see docs/img/texture-pack-pixelperfection.png , one tile per block entry). Visible defects: about 220 files are optifine random variants ( stone1 .. stone10 , grass1 , ...), emissive overlays ( *_e ), legacy aliases ( fence_oak , brick5 ) or non-block assets ( debug , destroy_stage_* , empty_armor_slot_* ) listed under auxiliary ; cutout blocks (glass panes, iron bars, ladders) are mostly transparent; no texture is missing for a mapped block. mcnames.json assets/blocktex/mcnames.json (generated by scripts/gen-mcnames.py , loaded by blocktex.LoadMCNames ) maps canonical block names ( oak_planks , stone_bricks , white_wool ...) to files and faces: kind ( cube_all , top_side_bottom , cube_column , orientable , slab , pane , cross , tall_cross , crop , door , fluid , custom ...), tex roles, tint (grass, foliage, water, ...), emissive , translucent . derived shapes (slabs, stairs, walls, fences, buttons, carpets...) reuse a base block's texture; auxiliary classifies every other file; missing lists newer vanilla blocks without texture. Names are facts taken from the pack's file names; no game data is copied. A test checks that every imported PNG is covered exactly once. Replace or remove runtime.blocks in vox.project : "shapes" (default, the only supported value; "classic" and "extended" are deprecated and resolve to it, see blocks.md ). runtime.texture_pack in vox.project : "default" (the embedded Pixel Perfection CE), "pixelperfection" or "none" (flat colours); burrowplay -textures default|pixelperfection|none , burrowedit -textures override it. Your own textures: put assets/textures/block/<name>.png in your project (project overrides win over the embedded pack). Compile the pack out: go build -tags nopp ./... ( PackEmbedded is false, layers are flat colours). Channel layout Albedo sRGB RGB(A); normal R,G = xy, B = AO, A = height; specular R = smoothness, G = F0/metal index (230..255 metals), B = porosity/SSS, A = emission (255 = none). blocktex.BuildLayers mips albedo in linear light, renormalises normals and keeps the metal index (max) in specular. Rendering See rendering.md . Registry block names map to textures through engine.BlockTextureName (aliases: grass -> grass_block, wood/log -> oak_log, leaves -> oak_leaves, planks -> oak_planks); registered blocks without a texture stay flat. Tinted albedo (leaves) is multiplied by the plains tint; the grass side overlay is composited with the tint baked in at upload. Tint formula (T3) Vanilla-style tintable textures (grass top, leaves) are gray, about 0.57 on average once normalised (147/255 grass, 144/255 oak leaves). No colormap ships, so plains colours are used (grass #91BD59, foliage #77AB2F, water #3F76E4). Final colour, per channel in sRGB space (the same space as the sampled albedo): texel * tint * TintGain (scaled by 1/max instead of clipped per channel when a channel exceeds 1, so bright texels keep their hue) with TintGain = 1.65 ~ 1/gray , so the average on-screen albedo is about the tint colour (grass ~ (140,180,86)). Biome-varying colormaps are not implemented (fixed plains). AO on tinted faces is softened. Debug: BURROW_TEXDEBUG=albedo|tint|ao|normal|spec|light . Render options Strength of the maps is a render option, not part of the pack: normal relief x2.2 and specular x2.0 by default ( -normal-strength , -spec-boost ; they only act on packs that carry normal/specular maps); grass/foliage tint varies per world column ( -biome-tint ), see docs/rendering.md.

h: Library loading and the working directory (security hardening)
x: Troubleshooting Start with burrow doctor : it checks the requirements and prints the fix for each failure. SIP strips DYLD_* variables macOS System Integrity Protection removes DYLD_* variables when a command is started through /bin/sh or another protected binary (make recipes, sh -c , scripts with #!/bin/sh ). Symptoms: the variable is set in your shell but a program started by make or a shell script does not see it ("Library not loaded" or no Vulkan device). Fixes: Use burrow run / burrow edit : they start children with an explicit environment ( os/exec ). In a Makefile recipe pass it on the command line: env DYLD_FALLBACK_LIBRARY_PATH=/opt/homebrew/lib go run ./cmd/burrowedit . Run eval "$(burrow shell-env)" in an interactive shell for manual commands. Do not pipe a GPU run into another program and trust the exit code: cmd | tee log hides failures (use a temp file and capture $? ; make lint checks Makefiles for this). MoltenVK / "no Vulkan device" brew install molten-vk and check /opt/homebrew/etc/vulkan/icd.d/MoltenVK_icd.json exists. burrow shell-env prints VK_ICD_FILENAMES . The binaries do not link MoltenVK: they open the Vulkan loader at run time (inside the .app first, then next to the program, then Homebrew) and the loader finds MoltenVK through its driver manifest. BURROW_VULKAN_DIR , BURROW_VULKAN_LIB and VK_ICD_FILENAMES override the lookup; see Platforms . burrow build --app bundles the loader, MoltenVK and the manifest. Needs a Metal device: burrow doctor reports it. Virtual machines without Metal cannot run the windowed engine; use the headless tools. Run go run ./cmd/vkprobe to see what the Vulkan instance reports. Validation layers brew install vulkan-validationlayers vulkan-loader ; set VK_LAYER_PATH=/opt/homebrew/opt/vulkan-validationlayers/share/vulkan/explicit_layer.d (done by burrow shell-env , burrow run --validate , burrowplay -validate ). The layer needs the loader, which is not linked by default builds. make render-test , make ui-test and make edit-test fail when the log contains VUID or Validation Error . cgo The windowed engine needs cgo (GLFW, Cocoa, MoltenVK) and the Xcode command line tools ( xcode-select --install ). With CGO_ENABLED=0 the module still builds: WindowPlugin , RenderPlugin and burrowedit (windowed) report "needs cgo", while burrowplay -headless , burrow test , burrowd and burrowedit -headless work. Cross-compiling windowed builds is not supported. Scripts the Go toolchain cannot build GOOS=wasip1 : install Go 1.24 or newer from go.dev (Homebrew's go has the port). blocks nested deeper than 512 (the module is refused at load): the Go compiler inlined too deep for the engine's structural cap (its own gas.Limits check, run before wazero compiles — not a wazero limit). Rebuild with inlining disabled: GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -buildmode=c-shared -trimpath -gcflags=all=-l -ldflags="-s -w -X=runtime.modinfo= -buildid=" -o out.wasm ./scripts/<name> . burrow script build and burrowscript build retry with -gcflags=all=-l automatically and the error names the flag. no required module provides package burrow-engine/sdk/burrowsdk : the project's go.mod must contain require burrow-engine v0.0.0 and replace burrow-engine => /path/to/burrow (the Vulkan bindings are a package of that module, no second replace ; an old replace github.com/goki/vulkan line can be deleted). burrow new writes this when it can find the checkout ( --burrow-root or BURROW_ROOT ); then run go mod tidy . Faults: a script that traps, exceeds gas or panics is rolled back and disabled after 3 faults. burrow test fails on faults and prints the count. The game window's input map only sees the controller's keys (see scripting.md ). Library loading and the working directory (security hardening) dyld resolves a bare dlopen("libvulkan.1.dylib") against the current working directory first, so a hostile dylib of that name in a project directory would run inside the engine. Two defences: third_party_vulkan/vk_default_loader.c opens the Vulkan loader by absolute path only on macOS ( /opt/homebrew/lib , /usr/local/lib ), and window.Init and cmd/vkprobe chdir("/") while GLFW initialises, because GLFW itself dlopens the bare name (the old directory is restored afterwards). If the window fails with "Vulkan loader not found", install vulkan-loader (see burrow doctor ) instead of copying a dylib next to your game: a libvulkan*.dylib in the project directory is deliberately ignored. Any new program that calls glfw.Init itself must do the same chdir("/") dance; use window.Init . Builds and games ./game says the archive hash mismatches: the file was modified or truncated; rebuild. burrow build --target ... is refused except for the native target. A .app that does not start when double-clicked: run Contents/MacOS/<name> from a terminal to see the error. A missing Vulkan loader or driver is reported in a dialog with what to install. Gatekeeper blocks downloaded games: apps are ad-hoc signed, not notarised, so a copy with the quarantine flag is rejected. Run xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine <app> on it (see "Signing and distribution" in getting-started.md). Determinism surprises burrow test reports StateHash differs when a script or system reads something outside the simulation. Check for time , math/rand , map iteration and goroutines in FixedUpdate code; see concepts.md . burrowplay -replay names the first journal entry that fails.

Tutorial 1: your first project You will create a project from a template, open it in the editor, change one thing, save and press Play. It takes about ten minutes. Everything here works the same from the terminal ( burrow ) and from inside the editor. Before you start Install the tools once (see Getting started ): burrow doctor must report no missing requirement. You do not need to read any other page first. Press F1 in the editor at any time to open this documentation; the ? button of a panel opens the page that explains that panel. Steps Create the project from a terminal: burrow new mygame --template sandbox cd mygame The sandbox template gives you hills, trees, a first-person controller and a HUD. Use --template empty for a flat world and an empty scene. burrow new --list prints every template. Open it in the editor: burrow edit The window shows the menu bar, the tool bar on the left, the viewport in the middle, the Hierarchy and Inspector on the right and the Assets, Console, Profiler and Blocks tabs at the bottom. Already inside the editor? Use Project > New Project... , pick or create a folder, then press Open. Look around. Hold the right mouse button and use W A S D to fly, Q and E go down and up, the wheel changes the speed. Orbit with the middle button or Alt + left button , pan with Shift + middle button . F frames the selected node. Select a node in the Hierarchy and look at the Inspector. Every component has a section; hover a section title to read what it is for. Make a small edit: press 2 (Place), pick a block in the block chip of the context bar and click in the world. One click is one undo step: Ctrl+Z takes it back. Save with Ctrl+S . The scene is stored in scenes/main.voxscn and your voxel edits in the .voxworld overlay of the project. Press Ctrl+Shift+P (or the Play button). The editor snapshots the world and runs the simulation; the keyboard and mouse now go to the game. Esc stops and restores the snapshot exactly, so playing never costs you an edit. What you learned A project is a folder with vox.project , scenes, an input map, assets and scripts (see project file ). The editor and burrowplay share the same simulation: what you see in Play is what ships. F1 opens the documentation, Ctrl+P the command palette, Shift+F1 the shortcut list. Next: sculpt terrain .

Tutorial 2: sculpt terrain The terrain tools edit columns of voxels with a brush. Every stroke is one undo step and is recorded in the journal, so it is deterministic and replayable. Steps Open a project (tutorial 1) and look at an area you want to change. Press B to pick Raise . The context bar shows the brush options: size, shape (cube, sphere, cylinder, cone, disc), strength, hardness, mirror axes and the block. Move the pointer over the terrain. The preview shows what the next click changes: green voxels are added, red are removed, a read-out gives the counts and the size. Drag to raise a hill. The wheel changes the brush size, Alt + wheel the strength. Hold Shift to invert: the same stroke now lowers. Press N (Lower) to dig, G (Flatten) to level to the height of the first click (a blue plane shows the level) and U (Smooth) to soften edges. Press P (Ramp) and drag from a low point to a high point to build an even slope as wide as the brush. Press X (Extrude), grab the arrow of a face and drag it out or in. Press O (Scatter) to sow trees, bushes, rocks or plants. Density is a percentage; the result is deterministic for a given seed. Press Y (Surface paint) to recolour only the top layers, or K (Replace) to swap one block for another inside the brush. Undo with Ctrl+Z ; the whole stroke goes back at once. Tips The Options button of the context bar opens brush presets, radial symmetry (2 to 16 copies around the vertical axis) and the grid snap of the cursor. An edit larger than the limit is refused with the numbers in the message instead of freezing the editor. All terrain tools are available to AI agents through editor_tool_apply ( MCP tools ). The full list of tools and keys is in editor.md . Next: place blocks .

Tutorial 3: place and shape blocks Where sculpting moves terrain, the shape tools build things: walls, towers, houses. Steps Press 2 for Place . Click the block chip in the context bar to open the palette. Type in the search field: the palette matches names, display names and aliases (English and French), for example oak or pierre . Starred blocks and recent blocks stay on top between sessions. Click on a face of the world to put the block next to it. Press 3 to erase and 4 to paint. 5 is the eyedropper; Ctrl + click works as a temporary eyedropper from any tool. Build faster with the shape tools: 6 Box, 7 Sphere, 8 Line, 9 Fill. Drag the base of a box, then move the pointer to set its height (or use the wheel while dragging). Hollow makes a shell. Turn on a mirror axis ( X , Y , Z in the context bar) to build symmetric things, or radial symmetry in the tool options. Press 0 for Region select : drag a box, then copy, cut, paste, rotate (Shift+R), mirror (Shift+M), fill or delete it. A pasted region is one undo step. Some blocks have shapes (slabs, stairs, fences, doors, panes, torches) and some emit light. The block list shows names, hardness and light levels; block-shapes.md explains the non-cubic shapes. Tips The preview never changes the world: only a click does. Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Shift+Z (or Ctrl+Y ) walk through your edits. Hold the right mouse button to fly, so you can reach the face you want. Next: add a scripted entity .

Tutorial 4: add a scripted entity A script is a small WebAssembly module, written in Go, that runs inside the deterministic simulation. This tutorial makes a cube spin. Steps In your project folder, scaffold the script: burrow script new spin This creates scripts/spin/main.go . Replace the body of scripts/spin/main.go with a script that turns its entity: package main import "burrow-engine/sdk/burrowsdk" type props struct { Speed float32 `json:"speed"` } func init() { burrowsdk.Register(burrowsdk.Script{ OnTick: func (self burrowsdk.Entity, dt float64 ) { p, _ := burrowsdk.Props[props]() t, err := burrowsdk.GetTransform(self) if err != nil { return } t.Rot[ 1 ] += p.Speed * float32 (dt) burrowsdk.SetTransform(self, t) }, }) } func main() {} Build it: burrow script build The module lands in assets/scripts/spin.wasm . Every host function and SDK helper you can call is listed in the script API reference . In the editor, choose Edit > Create > Cube (or the + of the Hierarchy). Select the cube. In the Inspector press Add component , type script and pick it. Set module to assets/scripts/spin.wasm and props to {"speed": 90} . Hover the component title: the tooltip describes the component, and F1 opens its entry in the components reference . Press Ctrl+Shift+P . The cube spins at 90 degrees per second. Esc stops, and the cube returns to its angle from before Play. Save with Ctrl+S . Why it behaves this way Script memory is reset before every call. What a script remembers lives in components ( State , Props or any other) so snapshots, replays and rollbacks are exact. Time is the tick: dt is always 50 ms. Use burrowsdk.Rand() for randomness, never the wall clock. The editor hot-reloads a rebuilt .wasm while you edit. A script that does not behave: see debugging and testing . Go further with the Scripting category : execution model , state and props , cookbook and the ABI . Next: cameras and game UI .

h: Part A: a third-person and an isometric camera
x: Tutorial 5: cameras and game UI Cameras and the game UI are frame domain : they decide what the player sees, never what the simulation computes, so they cannot change a StateHash . Both plugins are off by default ( runtime.plugins.camera: true / gameui: true enable them). Part A: a third-person and an isometric camera Open vox.project (or Project > Project Settings ) and enable the camera plugin with two rigs: { "runtime" : { "plugins" : { "camera" : true }, "camera" : { "start" : "third" , "rigs" : [ { "name" : "third" , "kind" : "third_person" , "distance" : 6 , "collide" : true , "smooth" : 0.06 }, { "name" : "iso" , "kind" : "isometric" , "ortho_size" : 9 , "smooth" : 0.15 } ] } } } Rigs can also be nodes: add a camera_rig component to a node in the Inspector, which enables the plugin by itself. Open View > Cameras... . Choose a rig in the Rig list, check the live preview, then press Switch to rig (or Shake to test the trauma shake). Press Ctrl+Shift+P to play. The view follows the player through the first rig. Switch rigs from a script, with a blend: burrowsdk.CameraSwitch( "iso" , 0.6 ) The other camera commands (shake, cut) are in the script API reference . Rig kinds are first_person , third_person , top_down , isometric , side_scroller , free and fixed ; all fields are in cameras.md . Part B: a HUD Enable the game UI plugin in vox.project : "runtime": { "plugins": { "gameui": true } } . Create ui/hud.ui.json in your project: { "version" : 1 , "theme" : "hud" , "root" : { "type" : "stack" , "layout" : "none" , "children" : [ { "type" : "panel" , "anchor" : "top-left" , "offset" : [ 8 , 8 ], "layout" : "stack_v" , "children" : [ { "type" : "bar" , "bind" : "hp" , "bind_max" : "hp_max" , "size" : [ 150 , 16 ], "format" : "{v}/{max}" } ] } ] } } Every *.ui.json of the project is loaded and named after its file. Open Tools > Game UI Designer and open ui/hud.ui.json (or double-click it in the Assets panel). The screen is drawn the way the game draws it: click a widget to select it, drag it to move it, change its text, colours and bindings on the right. Preview values fakes the numbers the bars read, so you see them without running the game. Save with Ctrl+S: a running game reloads the file. Set the value the bar reads from a script, for example burrowsdk.UISetNum("hp", 14) (see the script API ). The bar eases toward its value. Press Play and check that the bar is drawn over the game. Widgets, themes, localisation and world labels are explained in game-ui.md . Next: levels and saves .

Tutorial 6: levels and saves A level is a hand-built voxel region with spawn points and trigger zones. A save is a slot holding a snapshot of the simulation, the current level and your own key-value data. Both are deterministic and off by default ( runtime.plugins.levels: true / saves: true enable them). Steps Enable both plugins in vox.project : { "runtime" : { "plugins" : { "levels" : true , "saves" : true }, "levels" : { "dir" : "levels" , "initial" : "hall" , "actors" : [ "/player" ] }, "saves" : { "game" : "my_game" , "version" : 1 , "autosave_seconds" : 60 , "autosave_slots" : 2 } } } Build the area you want to keep as a level, using the tools of tutorial 3 . Select the area with the Region tool ( 0 ), then open View > Levels... and press Save region as level : it writes a .level file into the levels folder. The popup also lists the existing levels; Open (place into the world) loads one. Still in the popup, use Mark spawn at focus to add a named spawn point where the camera looks, and Mark zone from the box to turn the current box into a zone; Clear draft starts over. A trigger zone whose target is another level switches level when an actor stands in it. The switch is a journaled command, so replays follow it. Press Play and walk into the trigger. Stop with Esc : the editor restores the world from before Play. Save games from a script with the save_* host functions, or let autosave do it. Loading a slot restores the exact StateHash it was saved with. Good to know Procedural worldgen stays the base layer. A level overlays it: mix: replace carves the whole box, mix: keep replaces only stored chunks, so a level can be a fixed building inside a generated world. Blocks are stored by name, so a level loads into any registry that has those blocks and fails naming a missing one. The format, zones and settings are in levels-saves.md . Next: particles .

Tutorial 7: particles Particles are frame domain: they never touch the simulation or its hash. The simulation only requests effects; the renderer shows them. Steps Enable the system in vox.project : "runtime": { "plugins": { "particles": true } } . This also registers the particle_emitter component. Open Tools > Particle Effects : the particle editor fills the window as a docked panel, with its Particles Settings panel (Ctrl+Space goes back to the editor). Click fire in the library on the left: the preview in the middle loops the effect, and every parameter on the right changes it live (drag a slider, the size curve or a colour). To keep your own copy, type an asset path in the File section of Particles Settings and press Save: it writes a .particles.json . The six built-ins are smoke , sparks , dust , splash , fire and debris . Make a continuous effect: create an Empty node ( Edit > Create > Empty ), name it campfire , then Add component > particle_emitter . Set asset to builtin:fire and enabled to true. Hover the fields to read what each one does; the component reference lists every field, range and default. Press Ctrl+Shift+P . The fire burns in the game view too. Fire a one-shot burst from a script, for example when something breaks: burrowsdk.ParticleBurstOn(self, "builtin:sparks" , burrowsdk.ParticleOpts{Count: 40 }) Write your own effect as a .particles.json asset and point asset at it. The Validate action of the editor_particles tool checks it. Limits and the format are in particles.md . Next: audio packs .

Tutorial 8: audio and sound packs Burrow ships no sound files . A sound pack is a folder of your own .ogg or .wav files on your machine that the game maps to engine events. You are responsible for the rights of the files you use. Steps Enable audio in vox.project : "runtime": { "plugins": { "audio": true } } (the sandbox template already has it). Open View > Audio... to see the mixer: master, music, sfx, ambient and ui buses with mute switches, and an audition list of the built-in sounds. Create the pack folder outside your project , for example ~/my-sounds , with this layout (a number at the end of a name is a variant): step/grass1.ogg stone1.ogg wood1.ogg dig/stone1.ogg grass1.ogg liquid/splash.ogg ambient/weather/rain1.ogg music/game/theme1.ogg Tell the game where it is, with the first that applies: -sounds <dir> on burrowplay , the BURROW_SOUNDS variable, runtime.audio.pack in vox.project , or ~/.burrow/sounds : { "runtime" : { "audio" : { "pack" : "~/my-sounds" , "fallback" : "none" , "music_volume" : 0.6 } } } Press Play and walk on different blocks: the step sounds follow the block material. In the Assets panel a .wav or .ogg has a play button; double-click auditions it. Play a sound from a script (a project sound file; the pack fills in the events the game raises itself): burrowsdk.PlayOn(self, "assets/thunder.wav" , burrowsdk.SoundOpts{Bus: "ambient" , Volume: 0.8 }) Rules worth remembering A pack is never bundled into an export : burrow build refuses a project folder that contains one. With sounds.json you map event names to files yourself; without it the folder layout above is detected. All the details (events, buses, sounds.json , limits) are in audio.md . Next: export for Windows .

Tutorial 9: export for Windows burrow build packs a project into a single-file game for the machine it runs on. Windows builds are cross-compiled from macOS or Linux with a mingw toolchain and are untested on real Windows hardware at the time of writing: read the checklist at the end. Steps Check that the project passes its own tests: burrow test Pack the game archive. This .voxpak holds vox.project , the asset directories, the scene, the input map, the world overlay and the scripts, with a SHA-256 for every file: burrow build --pak mygame.voxpak Keep sound packs out of the project folder: the build refuses to pack one ( tutorial 8 ). Install the cross toolchain once ( brew install mingw-w64 ) and build the Windows runner and editor from the Burrow checkout: make dist-windows This writes dist/Burrow-Sandbox-windows-x64.zip with Burrow.exe (the sandbox game), the licences and a short README. make dist-engine-windows writes dist/Burrow-Engine-windows-x64.zip , the creator kit ( BurrowEditor.exe , burrow.exe , burrowplay.exe , script SDK, docs, templates); make dist-all builds both. With the kit, burrow build produces a standalone game from any folder. Put your mygame.voxpak next to the executable and start the runner with it: Burrow.exe mygame.voxpak . A runner given no argument uses the archive appended to its own executable, else the current folder. Check the licence notes. A game that bundles the default block textures prints their licence warning at build time; use --no-default-textures to leave them out (blocks then render flat) or choose your own runtime.texture_pack . Checklist for players Windows 10 or 11, 64 bit, and a graphics driver with Vulkan 1.1. The executables are not signed: SmartScreen may warn; choose More info then Run anyway . Keep the whole folder together; do not run from inside the zip preview. What to know burrow build --target only accepts the native target today: cross-compiling the game runner needs the target's C toolchain, which is what make dist-windows sets up. Everything about a build is recorded in <out>.build.json . See the CLI reference for every flag, and security.md for the trust model of packed games.
