h: The same formula in the simulation
x: Frame visuals Effects that must follow the screen rate, not the 20 Hz simulation: a weapon that lags behind a turn, a light that pulses, a field of view that widens when running, a crosshair that opens while moving. Two layers layer runs in the StateHash replayed on a dedicated server Frame visuals (this page) every frame, at the screen rate no no no Simulation (scripts, physics, animation clips) 20 times a second yes yes yes A frame visual only changes what is drawn. Scripts, physics and the hash never see it. A value drawn on screen never flows back into the simulation. When gameplay needs the same behaviour (a recoil that moves the aim, a hit zone that follows a swinging arm), compute it in the simulation with the same formula and read that value. Moved nodes are already interpolated between ticks ( execution model ). The components below add what interpolation cannot: springs, mouse reaction and animated values. Turning them on Registering a component changes the StateHash , so the three components exist only when the project asks for them: set runtime.plugins.visual to true ( burrow config set runtime.plugins.visual true ), or use one in a scene or prefab (the project is scanned once, like the audio components). Projects that do not use them keep their hashes. The editor always offers them. Components All three are normal components: saved in the scene, shown by the inspector, editable by the editor agent ( editor_set_component ), undoable. They are ignored while editing with the free editor camera. visual.spring The drawn node follows its real position through a damped spring: it lags behind a move and settles with a little overshoot. Children and parts follow. field default meaning stiffness 120 spring constant k, higher is tighter damping 0.6 damping ratio, 1 is critical (no overshoot), below 1 bounces A jump of more than 8 blocks is a teleport: no glide. visual.sway A held node (one with render.viewattach ) reacts to the mouse and to walking: it lags behind a turn, tilts into it and bobs while the player moves. On a node that is not held it offsets the node in the world. field meaning look_pos blocks of lag per mouse pixel look_rot degrees of tilt per mouse pixel bob , bob_hz walking bob amplitude (blocks at 4 blocks/s) and frequency max largest offset in blocks (0 = 0.15) stiffness , damping the spring, as above Mouse values are in pixels per 60 fps frame, whatever the real frame rate. A held node is sized by render.viewattach.scale , not by its own transform scale: a unit cube with scale 0 is one block big, 0.6 blocks in front of the camera, and fills the screen. "render.viewattach" : { "offset" : [ 0.3 , - 0.25 , - 0.5 ]}, "visual.sway" : { "look_pos" : 0.004 , "look_rot" : 0.15 , "bob" : 0.015 } visual.bind Drives values from expressions evaluated every frame. "visual.bind" : { "binds" : [ { "target" : "light.intensity" , "expr" : "6 + 2*sin(time*5)" , "mode" : "set" }, { "target" : "camera.fov" , "expr" : "clamp(speed-4, 0, 4)*2" }, { "target" : "ui.crosshair" , "expr" : "0.2 + speed*0.05" , "mode" : "set" } ]} target drives pos.x pos.y pos.z position offset of the node, in blocks (camera space for a held node) rot.x rot.y rot.z rotation offset in degrees, around the node scale size factor (add: 1 + value) light.intensity , light.r light.g light.b the node's point light material.p0 .. material.p3 the first shader parameters of the node's mesh camera.fov field of view of the active camera, degrees ui.<key> a game UI number ( game.ui , key as in the UI file) mode : add (default) adds to the value, set replaces it. At most 16 bindings per node. Variables: time , dt , alpha , mouse_dx , mouse_dy , speed (horizontal blocks/s of the node, measured between ticks), vy , pos_x , pos_y , pos_z , yaw , pitch . Operators: + - * / % ^ , comparisons, a ? b : c . Functions: abs sin cos tan sqrt min max clamp lerp smooth floor ceil sign pow mix saturate pulse , constant pi . An expression cannot loop or allocate, is at most 512 bytes and 32 levels deep, and a non-finite result is 0. A wrong expression or target is refused when the component is set. The same formula in the simulation burrowsdk.Spring is the renderer's spring stepped once per tick. It is plain data, lives in the script State , is hashed and replayed: // recoil that moves the aim: the simulation owns the value var recoil burrowsdk.Spring // on fire: recoil.Kick(6) // every tick: recoil.Step(0, 90, 0.4) // k = 90, damping ratio 0.4 // aim: pitch := basePitch + recoil.X The frame layer draws a smoother version of the same motion (a visual.sway or visual.bind on the weapon). They agree in shape, not sample for sample: gameplay reads recoil.X , never the drawn value. A hit zone that follows an animated arm needs nothing new: animation clips run in the simulation, so a trigger node under the arm sits where the arm is at the tick, and the drawing interpolates it. Free code every frame For what the components cannot express, a script can export OnFrame ( frame scripts ). It runs every frame, can only write the same targets ( VisualSet , VisualAdd ), cannot read or write simulation state and never runs on a server. Limits Springs and bindings act on the node they sit on and its children, not on other nodes. visual.bind reads the node's own measured speed, not another node's. Frame visuals do not run on a dedicated server, in a replay check or with the editor's free camera.

Voice chat Proximity voice chat lets players talk through their microphone. The others hear them spatialised by the engine mixer: louder when close, panned left or right by direction, fading to silence at a radius, and not played at all beyond it. Voice is frame domain like chat: it is never simulation state , never journaled, never part of a snapshot or a StateHash . Packages: voice (the client and the engine plugin), voice/capture (microphones), voice/codec (frame format and codec), voice/route (the server's routing and limits), voice/voicecfg (the runtime.voice section). Setup Voice chat is off by default because it opens the microphone. Turn it on in vox.project (multiplayer, runtime.plugins.net , must stay on): { "runtime" : { "plugins" : { "voice" : true }, "voice" : { "radius" : 32 , "mode" : "push_to_talk" , "key" : "V" } } } Hold V to talk. When the project's input map defines a push_to_talk button action (or the action named by runtime.voice.action ), that action is used and can be rebound like any other. Otherwise the plugin reads runtime.voice.key directly, ignored while a modal UI context is open so typing in a text field never transmits. The plugin never adds the action to the map itself: the action list is journaled script input and gives the network button bits, so adding one would change the simulation. (Defining it in your own map does add it there, on purpose.) Playback needs the audio plugin ( runtime.plugins.audio: true ): each remote speaker is a spatial stream voice on the sfx bus at mixer priority 50. The listener is the audio listener (the active camera). Configuration reference ( runtime.voice ) key default meaning radius 32 blocks; farther speakers are not heard (1..512) ref_distance 2 full volume up to this distance, then inverse-distance falloff, fading to 0 over the last 10% of the radius mode push_to_talk or voice_activation (energy detector with an adaptive noise floor and 300 ms hangover) action push_to_talk input action held to talk, when the input map defines it key V key held to talk when the map has no such action max_speakers 8 remote speakers heard at once (1..32); further speakers are dropped until one stops channels ["proximity"] channels the player may speak on: proximity , team , global (the server allows global to admins only) vad_threshold_db -40 voice activation level in dBFS noise_gate_db -55 frames quieter than this are silenced while transmitting (-100 = off) mic_gain 1 microphone gain (0..8) volume 1 volume of every received voice (0..4) burrow check validates the section (an unknown key, mode, channel or key name is an error, and runtime.voice needs plugins.voice: true ). Configuration hash. Voice is presentation, so runtime.voice is not part of the session configuration hash. The radius matters for fairness (who can eavesdrop), but the server enforces it with its own route.Config and its own authoritative positions; a client that changes its radius only changes what it plays, never what it receives. In game code The plugin inserts a *voice.Voice resource: v := engine.Res[*voice.Voice](app) v.SetMuted(playerID, true ) // personal mute (also sent to the server when the transport supports it) v.SetMicMuted( true ) // close the microphone v.SetMode(voicecfg.ModeVoiceActivation) v.SetPushToTalk( true ) // push-to-talk from a UI button or a script v.SetChannel(codec.ChannelTeam) // one of runtime.voice.channels v.SetMicGain( 1.5 ); v.SetVolume( 0.8 ) for _, t := range v.Talking() { fmt.Println(t.Name, t.Distance) } // closest first state, err := v.Mic() // "none", "off", "starting", "on", "error" + why voice.SpeakerGain(cfg, listener, pos) returns the distance gain the mixer applies, for UI hints. HUD values Every change is published to the game UI ( gameui.Request events, frame domain), so a .ui.json screen can show speaker icons without code: value type content voice_talking items one row per remote speaker heard now: icon builtin:volume-2 , text = name voice_talking_count number rows of voice_talking voice_transmitting bool the local player is sending Names come from Plugin.NameOf (default Player <id> ). Network Voice rides the multiplayer session next to chat. Nothing to wire in a game: when the project has runtime.plugins.voice , netplay.StartHost ( burrow serve , burrow-server ) relays voice with the project's runtime.voice routing, and netplay.Join ( burrowplay -connect ) attaches the session to the voice plugin. netplay.StartHostApp (the editor's listen server) relays voice only when HostOptions.Voice is set. Messages (see Networking ): type name direction fields 0x80 VoiceUp C→S bytes voice frame (1..256): the sender's own voice; there is no speaker field to forge 0x81 VoiceDown S→C uv speaker (≥1), bytes voice frame (1..256), forwarded unchanged 0x82 VoiceBlock C→S uv player (≥1), bool blocked: a personal mute Server. replica.ServerConfig.Voice (a *VoiceConfig with the route.Config ) turns relaying on; nil refuses every voice message, counts it ( VoiceStatus , Disabled ) and records a violation. With voice on, each frame goes through voice/route with the server's positions, never the client's: the player's interest center (its authoritative avatar, else its leashed view), the position of replicated proximity chat; the listen host's own player uses the avatar / spawn point rule. Teams come from the lobby ( net/lobby , spectators have none) when installed; on a listen server only the host's own player is an admin (may speak on global ). A listener is Congested when its connection holds 64 KiB or more not yet consumed ( VoiceConfig.Congestion ): its copy is dropped, never queued, so voice never delays a batch or a frame, and a full window never kicks anyone because of voice. Voice is not part of the replicated bandwidth budget, the journal, a snapshot or a StateHash . A player who leaves is forgotten (limits, block lists); a server mute stays until lifted. Violations (each counts toward the kick for abuse like any refused message): a frame over the speaker's rate limit, a malformed frame header, more than 256 personal blocks, any voice message to a server without voice. An oversized message (over 256 bytes) or a VoiceDown sent by a client is a protocol error and ends the connection. Server API (both servers, and the netplay.Server interface): srv.MuteVoice(player, true ) // moderation: nobody hears the player (false when voice is off) on, m, muted := srv.VoiceStatus() // m: gate.VoiceMetrics{In, Out, Dropped, Refused, Disabled, Bad} srv.SubmitVoice(localPlayer, frame) // a listen server's own player (AddLocalPlayer) srv.BlockVoice(localPlayer, speaker, true ) A dedicated server has the admin commands voice mute <name> , voice unmute <name> and voice status ( Dedicated server ). Client. replica.Client implements voice.Transport and voice.Blocker : SendVoice never blocks and drops the frame ( ErrVoiceDropped ) when the client is not in a game or 32 KiB are already queued; OnVoice runs on the goroutine that polls the client. internal/netplay attaches them: Guest.Voice and Host.Voice (a listen server's own player) are the app's *voice.Voice with SetTransport done, PositionOf the world transform of each player's avatar as drawn (smoothed in the replicated model) and NameOf the registry name. A guest sends its personal mutes again after a reconnect. HostOptions.Voice (a *route.Config , default netplay.VoiceRoute(runtime) ) overrides the routing. For other transports the client side is one interface: type Transport interface { SendVoice(frame [] byte ) error // must not block: drop the frame when congested OnVoice( func (from uint32 , frame [] byte )) // frames from other players, any goroutine } Voice.SetTransport(t) attaches it after the session connects. A transport that also implements SetVoiceBlocked(player uint32, blocked bool) error ( voice.Blocker ) receives personal mutes so the server stops sending them. Plugin.PositionOf(player) (mathx.Vec3, bool) gives each speaker's frame-domain position (the interpolated avatar head); without it, or for team and global frames, voices play centred. The routing itself is voice/route , which has no session dependency: r := route.NewRouter(route.Config{Radius: 32 , Channels: []codec.Channel{codec.ChannelProximity, codec.ChannelTeam}}) to, err := r.Route(time.Now(), from, frame, players, nil ) // players: []route.Player{ID, Pos, HasPos, Team, Admin, Congested} for _, id := range to { sendVoiceTo(id, from, frame) // forward the frame unchanged } Route checks the header, the server mute ( SetServerMuted ), the speaker's rate limits (60 frames/s and 12000 bytes/s with a 1 s burst by default), the channel rules, the radius against the server's positions and each listener's block list ( SetBlocked ), then drops the copy for a listener whose connection is Congested , who is over its byte budget (50400 bytes/s by default) or who already hears MaxSpeakers others. Voice is always the first traffic to drop: losing a frame costs 20 ms of concealed audio, nothing else. route.Recipients is the stateless part (channel, radius, blocks) for callers that keep their own limits. Forget(id) cleans up after a player leaves. net/gate.VoiceHub wraps a router with the per-player bookkeeping both servers share (block list bound, persistent server mutes, counters). Format and bandwidth 16 kHz mono, 20 ms frames, IMA ADPCM (4 bits per sample). A frame is an 8-byte header (codec id, flags: start/end of a talk spurt and the channel, a 16-bit sequence number, the ADPCM predictor and step index) and 160 bytes of audio: 168 bytes, 50 per second, about 67 kbit/s per active speaker (plus the transport's own framing). Each frame carries the decoder state it starts from, so a lost frame is a 20 ms gap, never a corrupted stream. The codec id leaves room for a better codec later. Receivers keep a jitter buffer per speaker: 60 ms target, growing by 20 ms after an underrun (up to 200 ms) and shrinking back after 5 s without one, frames reordered by sequence number, late frames dropped, a missing frame replaced by the previous one attenuated (up to 80 ms), and a backlog skipped down to the target. Privacy Voice is never recorded or stored . Frames exist in memory between capture and send, and between receive and playback. Nothing is written to disk, to a replay or to a save. In push-to-talk mode the microphone is open only while the key is held . In voice activation mode it stays open while voice activation is enabled ( SetVoiceActivation(false) or SetMicMuted(true) close it); only frames above the threshold are sent. Muting a player drops their frames locally and, with a supporting transport, asks the server not to send them. Servers forward frames without decoding them and keep no copy. Microphone permissions OS backend permission macOS AudioToolbox AudioQueue through purego (no cgo) the system asks once per app. A packaged .app must declare NSMicrophoneUsageDescription in Info.plist , or macOS terminates it on first access: burrow build writes it for game apps, and the editor installer's plist has it. A binary started from a terminal is attributed to the terminal app. Denied: System Settings > Privacy & Security > Microphone. Linux PulseAudio record stream (PipeWire's pulse server works) through jfreymuth/pulse (pure Go) none beyond access to the user's sound server; sandboxed (Flatpak) builds need the --socket=pulseaudio permission Windows winmm waveIn through golang.org/x/sys/windows Settings > Privacy > Microphone > "Let desktop apps access your microphone" Opening the microphone never blocks a frame: it runs on a worker goroutine (the macOS prompt can take seconds). Failures are reported by Voice.Mic() ( capture.ErrNoDevice , capture.ErrPermissionDenied ) and retried every 5 s while push-to-talk is held. A microphone that delivers only digital silence for 2 s is reported too (a denied permission on some systems looks like that). BURROW_VOICE_MIC=off disables the microphone. Headless runs and servers never open one. Testing Tests need no microphone: capture.Fake feeds samples, a fake transport links two apps, and the null audio backend advances the mixer. go test ./voice/... covers the codec (SNR thresholds and a decoder fuzz target), voice activation, the jitter buffer (reorder, loss, late frames, wrap-around, adaptation), the spatial gain, the routing rules and limits, and a two-app loopback. BURROW_VOICE_REAL_MIC=1 go test ./voice/capture -run Real records one second from the real default microphone. Limits The capture backends build without cgo on all three systems, but automated tests use the fake device only: run the opt-in real-microphone test on each platform before relying on it. No echo cancellation: use headphones, or push-to-talk. No resampling on capture: the device must accept 16 kHz mono (PulseAudio and the Windows wave mapper convert; AudioQueue converts). IMA ADPCM is simple and robust but costs about 67 kbit/s per speaker; a narrowband codec would cut that by 4 to 8. Speakers beyond max_speakers are dropped first come, not by distance. Voice uses the sfx bus: the sound effects volume applies to it, and voice does not duck music.

h: Rules shared by coarse and fine cells (hysteresis)
x: Fine water (adaptive sub-cell bricks) The coarse automaton ( water-physics.md ) moves water in eighths of a block, four cells per second, with no volume: a source is infinite and a flowing cell drains when it is not fed. The fine water is the default replacement ( runtime.plugins.fine_water: false keeps the coarse automaton) that keeps a real, conserved volume of water at a resolution of 1/N block (N = 2, 4 or 8, default 4), only where water moves. Calm water folds back into ordinary blocks, which remain the truth for large still volumes. coarse (W1, projects not yet upgraded) fine ( Config.Fine ) state blocks water , water_1..7 blocks water (infinite source), water_1..7 and water_full (finite volumes) + bricks resolution 1/8 block in height, 1 block across 1/N block across, 1/(32 N) block in height rate one step every 5 ticks (4 Hz) one step every tick (20 Hz, FineInterval ) volume not conserved (sources spread, flows drain) conserved exactly, every exchange is ledgered pressure none communicating vessels through full cells Representation Units. A sub-cell holds 0..32 units ( voxel.FineCap ); a block of N^3 sub-cells holds 32 N^3 units (2048 at N=4). Coarse level l (1..8) is l V units with V = 32 N^3 / 8 (256 at N=4); per sub-column a level is q = 32 N / 8 units. Brick. The water of one block cell whose voxel is air : N^3 bytes, index x + N (z + N y) , plus a dirty bit. Bricks live in fluid.State (map + sorted order), never in the chunks. Coarse cells. water_1..water_7 hold l V units, water_full (registered only when Fine is on, after every other block, so a coarse registry keeps its ids) holds 8 V . They are finite. water stays an infinite source: it feeds neighbours up to level FineSourceLevel (default 2) and absorbs what is above that level, so a source behaves as a constant-head boundary and a sheet it feeds reaches a few blocks, not the whole world. A source with at least two source neighbours (a river, a lake, a reservoir) feeds at FineBodyLevel instead (default 6): the bank of a body holds water near the level of its surface, so a breach, a ditch or a basin fills up ( sourceHead in fine_step.go ). Setting it equal to FineSourceLevel turns this off. Streams. The water falling from a brick over free air (see Falling streams ): per lip brick, one integer queue per sub-column. Hashed, captured, snapshotted. Ledger (snapshotted, not hashed: it never feeds back into the rules, so an undo returns the exact StateHash): Created (sources, pours, edits that place flowing blocks), Drained (void, sources), Evaporated ( stagnant films ), Displaced (edits over water). Held is the water of the bricks plus Transit , the water in the streams. Exact law, checked by the tests: coarse finite units + Held - (Created - Drained - Evaporated - Displaced) never changes. One fine step Every FineInterval ticks (default 1). Everything is integer arithmetic on sorted slices; no map is iterated where order could matter (map loops only set flags or sum). A. Demands (refine a coarse cell, spawn a brick in air or a fragile block, turn lava into stone): coarse candidates (wake-ups, chunk scans, unserved demands) that satisfy the coarse predicate below; every dirty brick: a face whose neighbour is air and that would spill (bottom layer wet above it; or a lateral sub-cell that is supported and holds at least the film threshold), a coarse neighbour across a seam that disagrees, lava touched by water; the pressure pass: for each dirty brick touching a body of full cells (full bricks and water_full ) not yet reached this step, a breadth-first walk through that body (at most FinePressure cells per step, a cut walk does nothing) collects its surfaces: non-full bricks, partial coarse cells and empty cells beside or on top of it. They are compared by head Y 32 N^3 + units ; when the highest wet one and the lowest differ by more than 2 N^2 units ( V when a coarse cell is involved), up to one layer ( 32 N^2 units) moves at once from the top of the highest to the bottom of the lowest; a coarse or empty end is refined or spawned first (a demand). This is what fills a U-tube or a basin from below. Demands are sorted by target and served within FineSpawn per step and FineMaxBricks live bricks, starting at the hashed spawn cursor and wrapping (see Overload ). A brick whose demand is refused stays dirty (it retries); a refused coarse candidate stays in the work list. A brick created or a cell converted during this phase keeps its neighbours dirty one more step (their demands were computed before the change). B. Moves on the dirty bricks (sorted by (Y, Z, X) ), sequential on live values so a pair can never overshoot: Fall , FineFallPasses passes (default 2): each sub-cell drops into the sub-cell below up to its room; the bottom layer drops into the brick below, into the void (drained) or into a source (absorbed). A source above is a spring at constant head: once per step (first pass only) it tops each top sub-cell of the brick below up to FineSourceLevel eighths of a sub-cell (8 units at the default level 2, at most 128 units per step at N=4). It used to fill the whole top layer at every pass (1024 units, half a block of water per tick), more than any lateral spreading carries away: a source placed in the air built a tower of full bricks up to itself, drawn as a stack of glassy terraces ( TestFineFloatingSourceFallsAsStream ). Lateral , one pass: each sub-cell equalises with its four side neighbours (inside the brick or across a face): when the giver is supported (full sub-cell or a solid / full block below) and the difference is at least 2, half the difference moves. Into a dry sub-cell only when the giver holds at least the film threshold ( 32 N / 16 units, 1/16 block), so a puddle stops spreading. Across a face: a source gives or absorbs toward its virtual level, the void drains. The sweep direction and the order of the four sides alternate with the step parity so no direction is favoured. Legacy evaporation ( FineEvapEvery > 0 only, off by default): single-unit films with nothing above lose their unit every FineEvapEvery steps. The default sink is the evaporation of stagnant films . C. Settle and fold. A dirty brick that neither gave nor received anything and has no refused demand becomes clean; every brick that changed makes its six neighbours dirty. A clean empty brick disappears. Each connected set of clean bricks that contains a brick that just became clean is offered to the fold : each brick i of volume u_i gets level L_i = u_i / V ; the remainders u_i mod V are summed, k whole levels are given to the bricks with the largest remainders (ties by cell order), and the last remainder r < V stays in residue bricks (the next in that order, as few as possible while each keeps less than the film threshold per sub-cell, so a calm film does not spread again), flattened from the bottom; the result is checked against the same predicates the automaton uses (coarse predicate of every created or neighbouring coarse cell, seam and spill tests of the residue brick, support below every created cell). If any test would fire, nothing is folded (the bricks stay, clean and free, until something disturbs them). Folding moves less than one level ( V ) of water per brick inside a connected calm body. The total is exact. A calm component that the evaporation will take entirely (an isolated film in the sense below, every brick of it on a solid block) is not folded while the evaporation is on: folded, a thin puddle would become level-1 coarse cells, which nothing ever revisits. Any other component folds as before (a film larger than the budget, beside lava, the void or a stream, over air): kept in bricks without being evaporated, it would hold them forever ( TestFineEvapBigFilmFolds , TestFineEvapRefusedFilmFolds ). Evaporation of stagnant films Small leftovers (the film a spill leaves on a lawn, a puddle after the source was removed) clear by themselves after a while instead of lingering forever. It is an explicit sink: every unit removed is added to Ledger.Evaporated , so the conservation law stays exact. Pass. Every FineEvapPeriod ticks (default 20, one pass per second; -1 turns it off), also while the water is idle, a pass visits at most FineEvapBudget bricks (default 1024) from a cursor, in cell order, wrapping around. For each brick not classified yet in this pass it walks the brick's connected component (six faces, bricks only, at most the budget, all walks of a pass at most 4 budgets: the cursor then resumes at the first brick not visited). The component is an isolated film when it is no larger than the budget and every brick of it is: a film : no water column deeper than FineEvapDepth (in 1/256 metre, default 32: 1/8 m, 16 units at N=4), not the lip of a falling stream, free of coarse water (a source: sea, river, spring; finite water_1..7 or water_full : a lake), lava and the void on all six faces. A film touching anything deeper is part of that body: the shallow rim of a pool, the sheet of a spring and the shore of a sea never evaporate. Each brick of an isolated film that rests on a solid block with no water above it is tracked : since (the tick it became stagnant), at (the tick of its last evaporation), last (its units after the last visit) and rem (the remainder of the integer rate). A change of more than FineEvapEps units between two visits (default N^2, one unit per sub-column) other than its own evaporation restarts the dwell, and so does a since in the future (a malformed state; it never underflows into an immediate evaporation); a dirty brick waits. After FineEvapDwell ticks (default 500, 25 s) each visit removes floor((rate * climate * capRes * elapsed + rem) / (1000 * 1000 * 20)) units and keeps the rest in rem , so a slow rate (a cold shelter, a small FineEvapRate ) still evaporates at its rate instead of rounding to nothing. capRes is the volume of a film at the threshold depth, elapsed the ticks since the brick's last evaporation (or the end of its dwell), at most 10 periods (a long rain or dirty spell does not come back as one large step), rate the permille per second FineEvapRate (default 30: a film at the threshold depth clears in about 33 s, a thinner one sooner) and climate the permille factor: condition factor rain or snow on an open brick ( weather extra, local phase) 0 sheltered: a solid or opaque block within 64 cells above (a roof, a cave) x0.25 open: sun height (weather day clock) x0.5 at night .. x1.5 at noon temperature at the brick ( weather.Local.TempMilliC ) x0.1 at -5 C and below, x1 at 15 C, x1.5 at 25 C and above no weather extra installed, or the module installed but off (every game installs it, inert unless the project enables it) x1 (open), x0.25 (sheltered) The units are taken from the deepest columns first, one unit per column and round from its top wet sub-cell, so the film thins evenly; the brick and its neighbours are made dirty (the step settles them, an emptied brick disappears). The mesh draws the depth per corner (below), so the surface and its film look fade out with the volume, without a step. State and determinism. The since / at / last / rem of the tracked bricks and the cursor are hashed (appended to the brick digest only when something is tracked or the cursor has moved, so a state without films keeps its former hash), captured, snapshotted ( fine.evap , validated) and restored; a world file ( PrepareFineBytes ) drops them like the dirty bits. Every input of a pass is hashed state: the tick, the bricks, the voxels and the weather extra. A Config with an evaporation field set hashes them ( 'E' ). The rules changed without changing the default Config , so a fine Config also hashes the rules version fluid.FineRules (1 = with evaporation, 2 = overload , 3 = tall falls ): a journal recorded under the former rules fails its first hash check at replay instead of diverging later, a snapshot written by a newer rules version is refused with an explicit error, and an older snapshot (a save) restores and continues under the current rules. Stats.FineEvapVisited is the bricks examined by the last pass. An edit that removes a brick ( fluid_cell with an empty fill, a block placed over it) drops its tracking like its dirty bit; re-creating it (the editor's undo through fluid_cell ) starts a new dwell, so that undo, like the dirty bit it restores as dirty, does not return the exact StateHash of a state with a tracked film. Chunk-mode undo and rollbacks capture the whole extra and do return it. Cost. One pass per FineEvapPeriod : at most FineEvapBudget visits and 4 FineEvapBudget bricks walked (six map reads each), one column scan of at most 64 blocks per evaporating brick. 4096 droplets on a 128x128 map ( TestFineEvapBoundedCost , budget 256) clear without a pass examining more than the budget. Coarse water. The coarse automaton (W1) needs no equivalent: an unfed flowing cell, a level-1 puddle included, already drains (one cell per step from its edge). In fine mode, level-1 coarse cells that were folded before this rule existed (an older save) are left as they are. Tests ( fluid/fine_evap_test.go ): a puddle clears between its dwell and the expected time, the ledger exact at every tick; a lake of finite coarse cells, a pit of poured bricks and a river of sources keep every unit while a puddle beside them clears; rain stops the open puddle while a roofed one dries, and the open one clears after the rain; snapshot, restore, journal replay and same-hash-same-future while films are tracked (the dwell is in the hash); bounded passes on 4096 films; random edits with a fast evaporation keep the conservation law at every tick. Falling streams Before streams, a cascade was a column of bricks, one per block crossed: the fall rule moves a sub-cell down by at most FineFallPasses sub-cells per step, so the falling water sat as a thin packet (about 6 of 32 units) in one layer of each cell, and the renderer had to invent a curtain between the packets (notches where a cell had no brick at that tick). Water in free fall now has its own continuous representation. Lip. A dirty brick whose bottom layer is wet, whose cell below is air without a brick, and whose column has at least FineStreamMinFall (default 2) free cells under it. Its stream is created in phase A (demands, canonical order: dirty bricks sorted by cell; within FineMaxStreams , default 1024) instead of the spill demand that would spawn the brick below. A drop of one cell keeps the old rule (the brick below is spawned). State (per lip, sorted by lip cell): q , D slots of N^2 integers (units per sub-column), slot 0 arriving at the next step, slot D-1 the water that just left. Hashed (lip, D , every slot) after the bricks, only when a stream exists (a state without falling water keeps its former hash); captured (deep copy), snapshotted ( fine.streams , validated: sorted, in bounds, 1 <= D <= 181 , slots >= 0 , not empty, at most the cap), restored. The impact cell of the last step is carried for the renderer but neither hashed nor read by the rules. Step (phase B, after the fall and lateral passes of the dirty bricks): Leave the lip. In the fall passes, a bottom sub-cell of a lip that feeds its stream moves entirely into the stream's input of its sub-column (no room limit: free fall). The lip is "moved", so it stays dirty while it feeds. Walk. From the lip down through air cells without brick, at most 256 cells (64 before rules 3): the target is the first brick that is not full; a void or a source absorbs (drained, like the fall rule); a fragile block is the target itself (spawned, the block destroyed); anything else (wall, coarse water, lava, a full brick) puts the target in the free cell above it. With nothing free under the lip ( h = 0 ) that cell is the lip itself, which an edit may have turned into anything: a lip brick or air is the target as usual, a source or a void absorbs, any other block (stone, lava, coarse flowing water...) blocks the stream: what arrives is ledgered as Displaced (like an edit over water), so the stream empties and the automaton can go idle ( TestStreamBlockedLipDrains ). The fall height h is the number of free cells crossed. Everything is read from the hashed state of this step. Resize to the delay D ( delayOf ): free fall at 32 blocks/s^2 up to a terminal speed of 30 blocks/s (reached after 14 blocks and 0.94 s), 20 steps/s, rounded up, 1 for h = 0 : ceil(5 sqrt(h)) for h <= 14 , ceil(20 (64 h + 900) / 1920) above (150 blocks: 110 steps, 5.5 s; 256 blocks: 181). A shorter fall merges the slots beyond the new length into slot 0 (that water arrives now), a longer one appends empty slots (the water in the air keeps its schedule, the new water travels further). Deposit slot 0 into the target brick: each sub-column fills its own sub-column from the bottom, then the rest of the brick layer by layer; what does not fit, or what waits for a brick to be spawned, stays in slot 0. Shift : slot k takes slot k+1 , the input enters slot D-1 . A stream whose total is 0 is removed. A target that is free air with nothing below it in range asks for a brick in phase A of the next step (a demand served like the others, within FineSpawn and FineMaxBricks ; a refused one is simply asked again: the stream keeps the automaton busy). A stream that exists makes Idle false. Back-pressure. A lip feeds its stream only while slot 0 (the water waiting at the target) holds at most one brick of water ( N^3 FineCap units); past it the lip follows the normal rules (it asks for the brick below, starved when the cap refuses it), so a target that accepts nothing (brick cap, spawn budget, a full pool) never makes slot 0 grow without bound. One step moves at most FineFallPasses full sub-cells per sub-column into a stream, so every slot value of a reachable state is at most N^3 FineCap + 181 FineFallPasses FineCap ( streamSlotMax , 13632 at N=4), which is also the bound the snapshot parser enforces: every reachable state is restorable ( TestStreamBackPressureAtBrickCap , TestStreamBackPressureSourceAboveHoles , TestStreamSlotBoundRestorable ). A blob with any stream is rejected when streams are off ( FineMaxStreams: -1 ). Interruptions. A block placed in the fall, a lip that dries up or is removed, a basin that fills: the walk of the next step sees it (the water already in the air lands on the block, or arrives at the shorter delay, or keeps falling without new input until the queue is empty). Nothing in a stream can refer to a stale cell: the lip is only a key, the target is recomputed every step. Determinism. Streams are created and walked in sorted order, the deposit order is the stream order, and every input is a function of the hashed state, so two states with the same StateHash have the same future ( TestStreamSameHashSameFuture , the restored engine with every brick dirty included). Undo/redo in chunk mode and the rollback of a failed act capture the whole fluid extra, streams included ( agent : TestFineWaterStreamsChunkModeUndoAndReplay , TestFineWaterStreamsActRollback ). World files. A .voxworld holds voxels and bricks, not the water in the air: PrepareFineBytes ledgers the transit as displaced and clears the streams (a load replaces the water like the voxels; TestFineStreamsLoadWorldMidFallReplays loads a world saved mid-fall into editors holding other water and checks the journal replay and the hash, three loads). Bounds. At most FineMaxStreams streams (-1 turns them off: the fall goes through bricks as before), each at most 181 slots of N^2 integers (11.3 KiB at N=4); a step walks at most 256 cells per stream twice (demands and advance). A 500-block fall ( TestStreamVeryTallFallBounded ) is two chained streams and costs a few milliseconds per step at most. Tall falls (rules version 3). Before, a stream walked 64 cells: a 150-block fall was three streams, each landing in a brick hanging in mid-air and restarting from rest there (the water reached the foot after 108 ticks instead of the 61 of a free fall, with a splash ring and a thin filet in the sky every 64 blocks), and the renderer drew the whole curtain, lip to impact, at the first tick of a new stream (the water seemed to arrive at once). Now one stream covers 256 cells with a terminal speed, and the export carries FrontGap / TailGap (voxel.FineStream: the part of the fall below the oldest water in the air, above the newest one; both 0 for a steady stream): the curtain grows from the lip with its front (white tip, no splash at the foot before the water arrives) and a dried lip leaves a falling tail. The streamer re-meshes a chunk when the front or the tail moves by 1/64 of the fall, and meshes the chunk layers above the generated terrain that hold water but no edited block (the air beside a tower: the curtain had a gap in each). The curtain vertices carry the time since the lip (1/28 s, curtainTau ) instead of the fall in 1/4 block, which saturated 64 blocks down and froze the streaks into stretched lines; the shader advects the streaks with that time, so they accelerate, then run at the terminal speed. Tests ( fluid/fine_stream_test.go ): formation and exact conservation at every tick, a cascade without bricks in the air (and the same scene with streams off peaks higher in bricks), monotone delays, cut by a block / re-formed / dried up with conservation, snapshot mid-fall (other engine, same engine, transit in the hash), rollback of a failed tick, same hash same future, random edits in and around the fall (blocks, pours, the source toggled; two engines agree, law at every tick), the cap, the wire validation. Voxel size A world with smaller voxels ( sim.Engine.Subdiv() = 2, 4 or 8 voxels per metre) keeps the brick: N sub-cells per voxel axis, so the resolution per metre is N*Subdiv (finer, Subdiv^3 times more bricks per cubic metre; the user accepts the memory). The rules read the voxel size every tick ( Config.atScale , a working copy that is never hashed), so a scene switch to another size takes effect at once, with no registry change (the fine water keeps scale 1 blocks): Speed. The tick runs Subdiv fine steps (the whole step: spills, falls, sideways flow, streams, folds), so the front and the falls cover the same metres per second. The evaporation pass belongs to the tick. Subdiv 1 is one step. Spread. The heads of a spring and of a body ( FineSourceLevel , FineBodyLevel ) are depths in metres: eighths of a metre at scale 1, so Subdiv times more eighths of a voxel, no longer capped at one voxel (8). The part above the top voxel of a source column is served by the virtual head ( virtualHead , headRises ): the head is measured from the bottom source of the column, and an air cell beside a brick, reached from that column through air only, is a virtual source at the level the head still reaches in that layer ( head - 8 * layers above the bottom source ); a brick whose top layer is three quarters full against such a cell spawns the brick above it (water never spills upward). A spring is thus 25 cm deep at every voxel size (two voxels at Subdiv 8) and a deep lake adds nothing (its head is within its own voxels). A source belongs to a body of water when two of its side neighbours one metre away are sources (a one metre spring is no lake). The film threshold grows with Subdiv , capped at a half sub-cell up to Subdiv 2, 3/8 at 4 and 1/4 at 8 ( filmFor ): the finer sheet spreads by smaller steps and a thinner film keeps its reach in metres. Caps. FineMaxBricks , FinePressure , the evaporation budget and FineBurstBricks grow by Subdiv^2 (the sheet's area), the bricks (cap plus burst) up to 64 MiB of sub-cells; FineSpawn by Subdiv . The burst step stays an eighth of the scaled range. FineInterval and FineFallPasses are unchanged. The overload fold and the forced fold run every overFoldEvery / overForceEvery ticks (the step counter advances Subdiv times per tick). Metres. FineEvapDepth is a depth in 1/256 metre: the same metres at every size ( Subdiv times the voxel fraction, up to 3/4 of a voxel so a full brick is never a film). Plugin.FocusRadius is in metres ( radius * Subdiv voxels, within MaxFocusRadius ) and its snap is 8 metres; fluid_focus itself takes voxels. Mesh. mesh/finewater.go works in voxel units, like the coarse mesh: the 8/9 lowering of a free surface and the seams with coarse cells are fractions of the voxel, and the sheet's slope per sub-column does not depend on the size, so seams stay consistent ( TestFineSeamWithCoarseCell ). Tests: TestFineSubdivSpreadMetres (a one metre spring spreads within 0.75 m of the scale 1 front at 0.5 s, 1 s, 2 s and 0.5 m at 10 s, at Subdiv 2, 4 and 8), TestSpringHeadDeeperThanAVoxel , TestScaledCapsInMetres , TestEvapDepthInMetres , TestOverFoldPeriodInTicks , TestFocusSnapInMetres , TestFineSubdivSeamWithSource , TestFineSubdivBricksAndVolume , TestFineSubdivChangeAtRuntime , TestFineLakeSurfaceMetres (a 3 m x 3 m basin filled from a 1 m spring settles, at Subdiv 8 and at scale 1, to the same depth within 0.035 m, one sub-cell of a brick at 12.5 cm voxels; measured at the far corner and the far edge, not beside the spring where a scale 1 cell averages a metre of the head gradient; the depth is the evaporation film depth, 1/8 m, plus the spring's reach). Waking. An edit of a source wakes the bricks that read its head from up to ceil(head / 8) layers above it ( dirtyBody , State.headLayers ; one layer at scale 1), because the virtual head of a brick beside a column of air is measured from a source several voxels below: a removed spring drains the second layer too ( TestFineRemovedSpringDrains , TestFineSourceEditWakesTheVirtualHeadLayers ). voxel.Access (what sim.Chunks hands to systems such as the physics character) exposes the fine water like the map ( FineSource ), so a character's immersion sees the bricks. Opposing flows Sources whose water meets (a channel fed from both ends, springs facing each other, channels crossing, a loop, a spring against a finite coarse lake or lava) settle without oscillating: no state of the bricks comes back two steps later, and each scene of TestFineOpposingFlowsSettle goes idle (channel 235 ticks, head on 800, crossing 210, loop 323, lake 1899, lava 312) with the volume exact at every tick. A symmetric layout settles to the same water on both sides within one level (the fold gives its whole levels to the largest remainders, ties by cell order) or 2% (the lateral pass is sequential; its direction alternates every step, which leaves a bias of about 1%). Push. The current that pushes a body ( voxel.LiquidTable.Flow : the controller's water push, Immersion.Flow ) was a unit vector toward any lower neighbour: a film a few units higher than its neighbour pushed at full speed, and where two flows met the push flipped from full speed one way to full speed the other way every few ticks (25 flips in 300 ticks, amplitude 0.69 at the meeting line of TestFineOpposingPushNoJitter ). It now grows with the head difference up to full strength at one coarse level, so coarse water (whose differences are whole levels) pushes exactly as before and the meeting line of fine water pushes with an amplitude under 0.02. The water surface's current ( mesh flowOf ) was already proportional and clamped: no flipped or NaN direction where flows cancel. Rules shared by coarse and fine cells (hysteresis) A coarse cell only knows its level, so the coarse and seam tests use a tolerance of one level; this is what makes a fold stable instead of refining again: test fires when coarse predicate, cell of level L air, a fragile block or the void below; a partial coarse cell or a source below; liquid above a partial cell; a side neighbour that is air / void with L >= 2 , a coarse cell with abs(L - L') >= 2 , a source with abs(L - S) >= 2 , lava (when it can turn to stone) source predicate air or a fragile block below or beside it, lava beside it seam, brick face column a (units) vs coarse level L abs(a - L q) > q ; coarse partial below a wet bottom layer; coarse water above a top layer that has room spill into air bottom layer wet (down); a supported sub-cell with at least the film threshold (sides) Bricks are invisible to the coarse predicate (a coarse cell next to a brick is the brick's business). The thresholds are the same seen from both sides: a clean brick never has a coarse neighbour whose test would fire, so removing it or folding next to it cannot leave an unstable coarse cell that nobody woke. Waking and determinism Dirty bits are state : they are hashed, captured, snapshotted. Every voxel write ( voxel.Observer.BlockChanged ) marks the bricks of the 15 cells it can influence dirty synchronously ; ChunkReplaced (world loads, agent history, undo in chunk mode) marks every brick of the chunk and its one-cell border dirty, removes the bricks whose cell is no longer air (ledgered as displaced) and ledgers the change of coarse volume of the chunk; fluid_wake marks the bricks of its box. Writes commute (a flag, a sum), so the arrival order of a command's writes cannot matter. The chunk scans still to do (queue, sweep and its cursor) are hashed in fine mode, and a wake-up inside a chunk that is still to be scanned waits for that scan. The rest of the coarse work list (pending writes, unserved demands) works as in W1 (sorted multisets; past 8192 writes in one step the writes become the sorted set of their chunks; past 4096 queued chunks a sweep of the overlay chunks that also looks at the six neighbours of each chunk, base terrain included). It is not hashed: it is a superset of the coarse cells whose predicate fires outside the chunks still to scan, so two states with the same hash evaluate the same demands. Candidates are evaluated in cell order until 4 FineSpawn of them fired; a stale entry costs one predicate and neither budget nor a hit, and the rest is carried over untouched. Only the evaluated, refused candidates count against MaxActive and the hashed Dropped ; the carried ones are bounded separately ( MaxActive plus one step of wake-ups and scans) and an excess, which needs far more unstable cells than the spawn budget serves for a long time, is shed without being hashed ( Stats.CarryShed ). Every other choice (sweep direction, side order) depends on the tick, which is hashed. Hence: same StateHash , same future , including after Snapshot / Restore in the middle of a flow, a failed tick's rollback, a chunk-mode undo ( agent/hist.go captures the whole extra) and VerifyReplay after a world load. Assumption shared with W1: water of the base terrain that is unstable but never touched is not evaluated (the world generator only produces stable sea). Cost bounds cap default bounds FineMaxBricks 4096 (2048 before rules 2) live bricks: memory MaxBricks * (N^3 + ~150) bytes (0.9 MiB at N=4) and the work of a step FineSpawn 128 bricks created per step: a breach widens by at most that much per tick FineFallPasses 2 sub-cell moves per step: (passes + 1) * N^3 * dirty bricks FinePressure 8192 cells walked by the pressure pass per step FineMaxStreams 1024 falling streams: memory 40 N^2 * 4 bytes each at most, two walks of 64 cells each per step FineEvapBudget 1024 bricks examined per evaporation pass (every FineEvapPeriod ticks), 4x that walked MaxActive , wake queue, chunk queue as W1 coarse candidates An ocean breach therefore costs at most FineMaxBricks bricks and FineSpawn new bricks per step; past the cap a spill waits ( Stats.FineRefused ) and the overload rules make room. Measured numbers are in the measurements section . FineMaxBricks is part of the Config , which is replay state (hashed, identical on every engine of a world): it cannot follow the load radius of one viewer. Raise it for worlds that need more moving water at once (64 MiB of fills at most, FineMaxBricks * N^3 <= 2^24 ); the cost of a step grows with the dirty bricks, about 2 to 4 us each at N=4. Overload Many sources (or one large flood) can ask for more bricks than FineMaxBricks . Before rules version 2 this was a cliff: Deadlock. A brick whose spill the cap refused stayed dirty, and a connected set of bricks folds only when none of them is dirty. The waiting front of a sheet therefore kept the whole sheet in bricks, nothing ever folded, the pool never emptied: the water froze half spread, with straight cut edges drawn as skirts, dry ground between the sources, and a world that was never idle (100 sources on a plane: 2048 bricks and 1248 dirty bricks forever, 3.7 ms per tick for nothing; at 50 sources, 174 waiting bricks held 1874 calm ones). Starvation. The demands were served from the lowest target every step, so whatever room the budgets left went to the same cells again: the sources with the highest coordinates waited for every lower front. Rules version 2 ( fluid.FineRules = 2 ): Fair service. The demands of a step are served in target order from the hashed spawn cursor, wrapping; when a budget ( FineSpawn or the cap) refuses one, the cursor moves to it, so the next step starts where this one stopped. A pending demand is served within about pending / FineSpawn steps of room. The cursor is hashed (appended to the brick digest only while it is set: a state where every demand is served keeps its former hash), captured, snapshotted ( fine.spawn , validated) and dropped by a world file like the dirty bits. Overload fold. On a step whose cap refused a demand, every 4 steps, the clean bricks next to a brick that is held (dirty only because its demand was refused: it neither gave nor received) are offered to the fold without it: the calm water behind a waiting front becomes coarse cells with the same stability tests as any fold, plus no seam with the held brick (a residue brick may touch it). The freed bricks go to the waiting fronts. Forced fold. When that frees nothing (a pool made only of fronts and thin films that cannot fold alone), every 20 steps whole components whose dirty bricks are all held are folded with the lateral tests waived, in cell order from the spawn cursor, until 1/8 of the cap is free. Vertical tests stay (support, water above a partial cell), so no coarse water hangs in the air; a front cell becomes a coarse cell whose predicate fires, which asks for a brick again when there is room. A component with a brick that moved is never forced. Every fold moves less than one level per brick and is exact: the conservation law holds at every tick of every overload test. The water keeps spreading at the rate the pool allows and the scene settles to the same coarse water as with an unlimited pool, later. Signal. Stats.FineOverload (the last step's cap refused a demand), FineCapRefused , FineCapSources (of which raised by a source), FineCapSteps , FineOverFolds , FineOverFolded ; State.Overloaded() and State.OverloadNote() ("water overloaded: 2048/2048 bricks, 312 spills waiting (41 sources throttled)"). The fluid.Plugin writes one line to standard error when the water becomes overloaded and one when it recovers (held 100 ticks, at most one line per 200 ticks; Log redirects, Quiet silences) and, with OverloadHUD , adds the note to the HUD lines (the sandbox turns it on). Cost of a step. The move phases (fall passes, lateral pass) run on several goroutines ( fluid.Threads , default GOMAXPROCS up to 6; 1 is sequential) and give exactly the water of the sequential order: each brick gets a level one above the highest level of the earlier bricks it conflicts with (the brick and its four side bricks are written, the bricks under them are read), and the bricks of a level, which touch no common brick, run together. The StateHash does not depend on the number of threads ( TestFineThreadsDoNotChangeTheWater , also run under -race ). The bricks also keep pointers to their six neighbours (no map lookup to resolve them) and the pressure walk follows them. Together: 1.8x on the 1000-source plane and cave scenes (11.9 and 21.5 ms per tick at FineMaxBricks 16384, was 21.1 and 39.7), identical results. A brick costs about 1 to 1.5 us per step now, so FineMaxBricks 8192 to 16384 fits a 20 Hz budget on a desktop ( FineMaxBricks * N^3 <= 2^24 still holds); the default stays 4096 because the config is hashed. Adaptive cap. Config.FineBurstBricks (default 0: off) lets the cap on the live bricks follow the load: the effective cap ( State.FineCap , Stats.FineCap ) is FineMaxBricks + burst . On every step where the cap refused a demand the burst grows by an eighth of FineBurstBricks (up to it); after 100 calm steps (nothing refused, also at rest) it shrinks by the same amount once the bricks fit under the lower cap. FineMaxBricks + FineBurstBricks is the memory and cost ceiling (same limits as FineMaxBricks ). The burst and its calm counter are state: hashed while the burst is above 0 (a state at its base cap keeps its former hash), written in snapshots ( fine.burst , validated against the config) and captured for undo; the config field is hashed only when set. It is a function of the steps, not of the clock, so every engine agrees ( TestFineBurstIsState , TestFineBurstGrowsAndShrinks ). 1000-source plane, 4096 + 12288: every source served at tick 67 instead of 383, 12.4 ms per tick at the 16384 peak instead of 4.4 ms at the fixed 4096; the cave needs more than the ceiling and stays overloaded, at 16.5 ms per tick. Combine it with the focus: the focus bounds what needs bricks, the burst gives that part the room it needs for as long as it needs it. Focus. fluid_focus {points, radius} (or fluid.Plugin{FocusRadius: 48} , which follows the camera and FocusPoints ) limits the fine step to the bricks whose column is within radius voxels of a point (the plugin's FocusRadius is in metres). Outside the focus the water is frozen like an unloaded chunk: its bricks keep their dirty bits and are not evaluated, nothing spawns there (a demand outside waits; a brick inside forgets it and is woken when the focus reaches the target), calm bricks outside fold back to coarse cells (64 offered per step, in a window that rotates with the tick) and the engine goes idle when nothing inside the focus moves. A brick inside may still push water into a brick across the border. The focus (radius and sorted points) is hashed (only while set: no focus keeps the former hash), snapshotted, captured for undo and journaled; the points are sorted, so their order is not state. Widening or clearing the focus resumes the frozen water, which settles to the same coarse water as without a focus ( TestFineFocusFreezesOutsideAndResumes ). Compatibility Config.Fine is off by default: the coarse automaton, the registry (no water_full ), StateHash and every golden are unchanged ( TestFineOffIsTheCoarseAutomaton , the scenario goldens). In a project, runtime.plugins.fine_water is on by default and only read when runtime.plugins.fluid is true ; "fine_water": false selects the coarse automaton. The editor without a project ( burrowedit , -no-fine-water to turn it off) and burrowd sessions created with fine_water: true follow the same rule. Saves taken with the coarse water do not load with the fine water. burrowedit -project follows the project, so the editor and burrowplay simulate the same water. A .voxworld with bricks stores them after the chunks; a coarse engine refuses such a file with an explicit error. Commands and tools command effect fluid_pour {pos, units} add units to one cell (bucket, leak) fluid_cell {pos, fill} set the exact sub-cells of one cell (empty clears); the editor's undo uses it fluid_refine {min, max} turn calm coarse water of a box into bricks (to disturb it by hand) fluid_wake {min, max} rescan a box and mark its bricks dirty fluid_focus {points, radius} evaluate only the bricks within radius blocks of the points (empty clears), see Overload Editor tools: editor_water (read, with detail the sub-cells), editor_water_pour , editor_water_wake . For S3 (renderer) mesh.BuildFineWater(grid, reader, liquidTable, chunk, opts) (or mesh.Opts.FineWater on the mesher, which fills Result.Fine ) builds the surface of the bricks of one chunk from an immutable voxel.FineGrid ( State.ExportFine(lo, hi) , safe to hand to a mesher goroutine). The coarse faces are unchanged; the fine mesh is an extra indexed triangle list (quads of 4 vertices, 6 indices, counter-clockwise seen from outside) drawn in the water pass: mesh.FineVertex field type meaning Pos [3]float32 chunk-local position in blocks (fractional: the surface moves in 1/(32 N) block) Normal [3]int8 unit normal x127 (central differences of the corner heights for the top) Flow [2]int8 surface current (x, z) x127, from the column volumes, downhill Depth uint8 water depth of the column in 1/16 block (capped) Foam uint8 foam potential 0..255: speed, plus skirts (falling or spilling water) and undersides Face uint8 FineTop , FineSideXP/XN/ZP/ZN (skirts toward dry columns), FineBottom (water over air) Block voxel.BlockID (uint16) the water block, for its texture layer and tint 24 bytes in Go (packed: 22). The coarse vertex ( mesh.Vertex , integer positions) cannot hold fractional heights, so S3 needs a second vertex layout and pipeline sharing the water fragment shader. Seams: on a block corner that touches a coarse liquid cell the height equals LiquidCornerHeights of the coarse neighbours ( LiquidTable.BlockCornerHeight : the mean height of the liquid cells around the corner, bricks only when a brick touches it, see below), along a block edge shared with a coarse cell it is the straight line between the two corners, so the fine surface meets the coarse quads without cracks ( TestFineSeamWithCoarseCell , TestFineSurfaceHasNoCracks ). Elsewhere the surface is built from sheets (next section). Opts.FineMaxVertices (default 65536) truncates a pathological chunk and sets FineMesh.Truncated . Rendering (S3, done) The HDR shader levels draw it: the streamer exports the bricks and the streams once per simulation tick ( State.ExportFine , found by duck typing on the chunk map's fine source; FineGrid.Streams ), and re-meshes only the water of the chunks whose bricks (or one-cell border) or streams changed ( Mesher.BuildWater , on the mesh workers, at most every 2 ticks per chunk, never while a build of that chunk is queued). The renderer swaps the chunk's water buffer alone ( Renderer.UploadChunkWaterOnly ) and keeps drawing the old one until the new one is uploaded: no cube re-mesh, no gap. Water meshes are joined with the coarse liquid surface ( mesh.Opts.LiquidSurface , same FineVertex layout) and drawn by water2.vert + water_hdr.frag . Cascades ( mesh/cascade.go ; all frame domain, nothing written to the simulation): Curtain ( FineCurtain ): a ribbon from the lip surface (the height of the feeding neighbour, so the sheet continues the water above the edge, no lump) to the impact surface found by walking the voxels and bricks. It leaves the lip with a horizontal tangent along the flow over the edge and follows the free-fall parabola (horizontal speed from the debit: thick water shoots further), then drops. Its width covers the wet sub-columns; ribbons of neighbouring lips with the same direction join exactly (shared boundary vertices: thickness, lip and impact heights averaged at the boundary, the same row fractions for every ribbon), open ends taper (alpha to 0 over 0.22 block, wobbling in the vertex shader), and a thin filet narrows as it accelerates. Shader: thickness = debit ( Depth ), streaks advected along sqrt(fall) so they accelerate downward, wide "panels" across, aeration growing with debit and fall (thin = glassy, refracting the cliff behind through the scene copy with a sky reflection and a sun glint; thick = white, lit through), a white foot over the last block. Foot : spray droplets ( FineSpray , at most 20 per lip, ballistic loops animated on the GPU from a per-vertex seed), churning boils and a faint rising mist ( FineMist , 2..6 + 1..3 sprites per lip), expanding foam rings and boils on the water ( FineRing , a flat quad, radius from the energy). On the levels without HDR these are dropped in the vertex shader. The spray and mist sprites are soft: they fade over a short height above the impact level and a short depth in front of the opaque scene, and the curtain fades into the pool over its last half block, so the depth test does not cut a hard white line (a fake ledge) along the foot. Foam on the surface ( water_hdr.frag ): the current foam pattern is advected with a two-phase periodic drift (flow-map technique), not by flow * time , which sheared the pattern without bound where the flow varies (moire on the small basins under a rill). Shore foam uses the distance to the opaque scene ( max(vertical depth, path / 2) ), so a wall seen at a low angle gets a thin soft fringe instead of a wide band. The lip bricks are not drawn (their water is the head of the curtain) while they hold only falling water: at most half full and no wet bottom sub-column resting on a block, coarse water or a full sub-cell below (a lip whose fall was blocked keeps its puddle, TestCascadeSupportedLipIsDrawn ). A chunk resolves only the streams of its column and its one-cell border ( TestCascadeFarChunkSkipsStreams ); the streamer re-meshes the neighbouring column of a lip on a chunk border (joined curtains) and keeps exporting a grid that has streams but no brick left ( engine/TestSyncFineStreams ). The former stream heuristics of the brick mesh (packets joined into a sheet, gaps filled) remain for drops of one cell and for streams over the cap. Sheets ( mesh/finewater.go , clusterAt ): a sub-column draws a top quad only where its water is supported (every layer under its top wet, the bottom one on a solid block, coarse water or a full sub-cell) and uncovered . Each such surface, each coarse surface and each dry floor ("ground") of the four columns around a lattice point, in the rows floor(h)-2 .. floor(h)+2 , is a candidate; sorted by global height, candidates less than 0.55 block apart form one sheet, and the corner takes the mean of its sheet. A sheet spans at most three gaps, never the ends of the window, so every column of the sheet, whatever its row, gets the same corner (no crack, TestFineSurfaceHasNoCracks ): a mound or a slope over a step is one smooth surface across cell rows instead of terraces with vertical faces between them ( TestFineSheetAcrossRows ). A film next to dry ground averages with it and tapers to 0.015 above it: no skirt, no stair outline ( TestFineFilmTapersToGround ). A skirt is drawn only toward a neighbour that is not part of the sheet, from the corner heights down to the neighbour's lower sheet or the bottom of the water column (it can span several rows), and only when it is at least 0.07 block tall (a thinner one read as a blue line). Water that rests on nothing (a packet between two ticks) never enters a sheet: the stream heuristics below draw it, and a packet of less than one sub-cell in mid-air (a film spilling over a one-block step) is not drawn at all. Before, every corner averaged the columns of its own row: a falling packet or a covered column (height 1) next to a puddle pulled the corner up into spikes, and a partly filled brick pinned to its mean height at the block corners drew a sawtooth. Coarse/brick corners : LiquidTable.SurfaceCorners averages only the bricks at a block corner that a brick touches. A coarse source is drawn full but holds its fine neighbours at its low constant head ( FineSourceLevel ), so the old mean pinned the brick surface to a steep strip along the seam (a notched band seen from the side); the coarse cell now slopes down to the bricks over its own width. Shading of thin and standing water ( water_hdr.frag ): the foam of the current and of the shore needs a body of water (it fades out under ~0.2 block of column depth: a film is wet ground, not a field of white blotches); the current is the head difference across a column ( flowOf , a quarter block over two sub-columns is full speed), not the raw unit difference that made every film a torrent; a film reflects less and darkens the ground a little. A side face of standing water (vertex foam under 70) gets no falling streaks, and its refraction path is capped by the column depth (it crossed everything behind the face: blue slivers). The path under any surface is capped at three column depths. A steep slope seen from its back (water running over a ledge) is shaded as a surface from above with its normal turned toward the eye, not with the underwater colour (a dark blue band along every ledge). White water (curtain aeration, spray, mist, boils, rings): lit by the sky dome by day (the terrain's hemisphere term alone left it darker than the sky-reflecting pool: a grey, dirty band at the foot) and at half intensity under the moon (it glowed far above the moonlit ground); moonlight caustics are faint. The curtain's glassy part has more water body (absorption over 0.3 + 0.7 thickness block, stronger in-scatter) and brighter streaks. Each foam ring has its own phase from its centre and the boil is a world-space pattern on a soft white base, so the foot of a wide fall is one band of churning water instead of a chain of identical circles with dark holes. Depth per corner : the Depth of a top vertex is the sheet height at that lattice point over the bottom of its column (rounded to 1/16 block), not one value per column: over a flat floor the corner height is shared, so the depth (and every term driven by it: foam, the film look) varies continuously instead of in sub-column squares. Across a step in the floor the two columns still disagree at the shared corner. The attribute keeps its 1/16 block unit (shared with the coarse surface): a drying film loses its depth-driven look in 1/16 steps, while its surface height goes down continuously. Shallow water at noon ( water_hdr.frag ): the caustics gain is 1 + 1.2 c / (1 + 0.4 c) (at most x2.8; it was 1 + 1.4 c , up to x6 where two veins cross, which clipped a bright sand or grass bottom to white in shallow water and bloom smeared it); the shore foam needs about 0.3 block of water (in a pool a few tenths deep every pixel was within the shore distance of the bottom: white blotches over the whole pool), and so does the current foam (every shallow flowing film, and the calm finite water_1..7 sheets that the coarse surface marks with a flowing foam potential, was covered with white patches); the foam rings of a fall's foot fade out over less than half a block of water (a flat quad crossing a stepped film showed through as stepped white patches). Every pow with a base that can be negative or out of range is clamped or written as a product ( pow(x, 2.0) of a negative x in the rings returned NaN on NVIDIA, which bloom spread into a white smear) and the normals are normalised with a zero-length fallback. Merging : a brick whose N^2 top quads are coplanar (calm, flat, no skirt) is emitted as one quad keeping the attributes of its four corners; the per-corner current and foam of the sub-column quads are the mean of the columns around each corner (no flat square of foam per sub-column). LOD : beyond 96 blocks (horizontal distance to the chunk centre) the bricks are drawn by the coarse surface, one quad per cell at the brick's mean height ( Opts.FineLOD ); curtains are kept. Crossing the distance re-meshes the water.
